title: ‘Do we really need huge cruise ships here?’ Fears £150m Falmouth Docks plan threatens habitats – and town itself | Cornwall | The Guardian
description: Plans involve dredging and expanding docks to allow larger cruise ships to visit with up to 200,000 passengers annually
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Plans involve dredging and expanding docks to allow larger cruise ships to visit with up to 200,000 passengers annually
Content: The waterfront in Falmouth, Cornwall.Photograph: Abbie Trayler-Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe waterfront in Falmouth, Cornwall.Photograph: Abbie Trayler-Smith/The GuardianCornwall‘Do we really need huge cruise ships here?’ Fears £150m Falmouth Docks plan threatens habitats – and town itselfPlans involve dredging and expanding docks to allow larger cruise ships to visit with up to 200,000 passengers annuallySteven MorrisThu 6 Aug 2026 07.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJanavi Kramer had just enjoyed a swim with friends and was sitting on a bench taking in a wonderful Cornish view – headlands plunging into deep water, bobbing boats, a bustling harbour town.“We’re lucky to have this space,” said Kramer, who isan artist and scientific illustrator. “We use it for work, recreation and pleasure and it’s so scary to think that this could all be harmed. I worry about what we may be living with soon and what we’ll be leaving for future generations.”She is talking about a £150m plan to redevelop Falmouth Docks in south-westCornwall. It includes expanding the docks to allow larger cruise ships to berth, which many people worry will exacerbate environmental problems and put pressure on the fabric of the town.View image in fullscreenA CGI image of the proposed expansion to the docks, with space for much larger cruise ships.Photograph: BalaenaHannah Cocks, a marine social scientist, who had been taking a dip with Kramer, said she wasn’t opposed to redevelopment of the docks, which have been here for more than 150 years.“But I want it to be done in a way that is environmentally and socially just,” she said. “The community has not been adequately consulted about a decision that could have such adverse effects.“Even now Cornish infrastructure can’t cope with the number of people who come in the summer. Do we really need these huge cruise ships here?”The plans also involve dredging around the docks, which some fear could lead to harmful material being churned up from the seabed, such as heavy metals washed into the harbour when Cornwall was a mining superpower and toxic paints once used to protect boat hulls.View image in fullscreenHannah Cocks, a marine social scientist, says she is not against the redevelopment as a whole but wants it to be done in a way that is ‘environmentally and socially just’.Photograph: Abbie Trayler-Smith/The GuardianFishers and environmentalists are warning that precious habitats could be damaged, including oyster grounds andrare maerl beds– created when rare types of red seaweeds grow into hard, twig-like lumps.Gio Reale, a wildlife storyteller, said it had been a good summer for spotting marine wildlife. “I normally go out looking for sharks. We have seen small-spotted catsharks and nursehounds, quite a few octopuses and a lot of the usual lobsters and pipefish.“We have maerl beds, seagrass meadows, kelp here. It’s a beautiful but fragile ecosystem and I’m concerned it could be really badly harmed.”The UK government issupporting the redevelopment. Falmouth already hosts cruises, but ministers say the expansion will allow larger vessels – such as Excellence Class cruise ships, which are up to 345 metres (1,131ft) long, to berth.This could help to attract up to 200,000 cruise visitors annually by 2030, it says, injecting millions of pounds into the local economy and supporting hundreds of tourism-related jobs.View image in fullscreenShopping streets in Falmouth.Photograph: Abbie Trayler-Smith/The GuardianCornwall council will debate elements of the scheme in the coming weeks but much of it is going through the planning process under the government’s fast track system, designed to push complicated developments through and cut red tape.It means developers work with a single, lead environmental body – in this case the Marine Management Organisation (MMO) – rather than what the UK government calls a “merry-go-round of overlapping regulators”.But many in the town worry that fast-tracking may lead to a lack of scrutiny.View image in fullscreenJem Wallis, who runs a sauna on the seafront, said he had never had a cruise passenger visit.Photograph: Abbie Trayler-Smith/The GuardianJem Wallis, who runs a sauna on the waterfront, said he didn’t feel a clear case had been made for the project. And he had never had a cruise passenger visit his sauna. “It all seems a massive risk to me.”Zoe Young, a tour guide, added: “A terminal for stinky great ships to meet stinky coaches to Land’s End – is that the best we can hope for?”When the Guardian visited John Spargo’s souvenir shop Tall Ships Trading on Church Street, a passionate debate about the pros and cons broke out. Spargo said most cruise passengers who arrive in the town were taken by coach to other attractions such as the Eden Project. “They don’t bring as much money into the town itself as you think,” he said.View image in fullscreenJohn Spargo, who owns the Tall Ships Trading souvenir shop, said cruise ship passengers who arrive in the town do not bring much money to the area.Photograph: Abbie Trayler-Smith/The GuardianBernie, a visitor from Kent, said she thought cruise ships were dreadful. “Other places in Europe are trying to get rid of them. Why do you want bigger ones? It’s not worth losing the character of this place for cruise ships.”Susie, who lives in Falmouth, disagreed. “They do bring in money. They are good for many of the shops and the boat tours do well when they come.St Mawes Ferryis always packed when a cruise ship is here. The passengers say they don’t feel they are on a real boat when they’re on a cruise ship so love getting on a little one.”The government has said the fast-track system does not mean corners are being cut. It said the MMO was reviewing information submitted during the consultation period to support a “robust” marine licensing decision.View image in fullscreenJason Pascoe, an oyster fisher, is concerned about the impact of the redevelopment and dredging on his industry.Photograph: Abbie Trayler-Smith/The GuardianA spokesperson said: “The lead environmental regulator model is about ensuring better coordination between developers and environmental regulators to prevent delays in the planning process without lowering environmental standards.”Balaena, the maritime engineering and shipbuilding group that operates the docks, said the project would ensure the port remained fit for purpose, safeguard skilled jobs, create apprenticeship opportunities and support businesses across Cornwall and the wider south-west.View image in fullscreenThe waterfront in Falmouth.Photograph: Abbie Trayler-Smith/The GuardianIt said “targeted pocket dredging” was needed around the dock, which had been subject to a comprehensive environmental impact assessment. There would be no dredging in the main docks channel or wider estuary and material that is not suitable for disposal at sea would be taken to a facility inland.Jason Pascoe, who has worked the oyster fishery for 40 years, was unconvinced. “The river systems here are very complex. Can they be sure if they dump waste out to sea it won’t find its way back here? Ironically, we’ve just had our best ever season. This feels like a horrendous threat to me.”Explore more on these topicsCornwallInfrastructurenewsShareReuse this content

title: By day five of my labour, I didn’t want an ‘ideal birth’. I only wanted to survive | Natalie Morris | The Guardian
description: Yvette Cooper’s maternity reforms must change a system that too often fails women when they’re at their most vulnerable, says journalist and author Natalie Morris
Author: Natalie Morris
Headline: Yvette Cooper’s maternity reforms must change a system that too often fails women when they’re at their most vulnerable, says journalist and author Natalie Morris
Content: Illustration: PA/Alamy/Getty/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: PA/Alamy/Getty/Guardian DesignOpinionWomen's healthBy day five of my labour, I didn’t want an ‘ideal birth’. I only wanted to surviveNatalie MorrisYvette Cooper’s maternity reforms must change a system that too often fails women when they’re at their most vulnerableThu 6 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 13.13 EDTShareOn the third day of being in labour with my first child, I entered a new state of being. It was time to dig deep. This is what I had learned in all the childbirth classes. As long as I remained calm, breathed as instructed, moaned through the pain, things would happen as they were meant to. My body knew what it was doing. Only, it didn’t.On the fourth day, I started to beg. This wasn’t right. Despite contraction after relentless contraction, I wasn’t dilating. I hadn’t slept, I couldn’t even sit down. I needed help. And still, they waited. For what, I never understood.When Yvette Coopertold the Guardian this weekthat women must not “feel pressurised” to have “an ideal birth experience”, it was a relief to hear her name this all-too-common phenomenon in which maternity staff are reluctant – or refusing – to escalate. But Cooper’s characterisation of the problem is not the full picture. The harm here is not just in women being nudged towards a certain kind of birth experience, but in a culture that can completely override women’s physical and psychological safety in favour of a low-intervention ideal.Half of Britain’s maternal deaths areconsidered preventable, and low-intervention births are the ideal for a reason. Midwife-led care usually results inbetter outcomes for healthy womenwith straightforward pregnancies – lower risk of infection and severe bleeds, and quicker recovery. In 2024-25, 45% of all hospital deliveries in England (542,235 total births) wereperformed via caesarean section– it was the first time C-sections outnumbered unassisted natural vaginal births. (Another 11% needed extra support through instruments such as forceps.) There is a natural, and warranted, cautiousness about the over-medicalisation of birth, which can lead to avoidable complications, and leave women who would prefer a natural birth feeling pressured to take a different route. But we can’t ignore that there are also structural forces at play here: lower intervention also translates to lower cost for an overstretched, under-resourced system. One midwife told me explicitly that they would have admitted me to the labour ward earlier if there had been a bed.Of course most first-time mothers would choose the lowest possible intervention if they could. I had hoped to float blissfully in a birthing pool under the soft glow of fairy lights. But when it comes to the messy, unpredictable, dangerous act of bringing new life into the world, the concept of choice can quickly be revealed as a fallacy. By day five of my labour, I was not thinking about my birth plan. I was not thinking about very much at all. My only focus was survival.The demographic of people giving birth today looks nothing like it did 30 years ago. The average age of a mother in England and Walesis now 31, a figure that has been creeping up since records began. There is something deeply flawed about a system that pushes quite so strongly for low-intervention births despite the fact that mothers over 30 are more likely to require a higher level of medical involvement. Almost half of UK women aged 30-39 have caesareans, and for those over 40, it is nowthe most common wayto give birth. Yet the narrative of an “ideal birth” persists, leaving women who end up needing more help wondering where they went wrong. Maternity practices must reflect this reality, or risk perpetuating a cycle that leaves women at risk and then pushes the blame back on to them.After the best part of a week, I was eventually wheeled down for an emergency C-section. Even then, it wasn’t the desperate pleas from my husband and me that finally spurred action, it was the fact that my baby started showing signs of distress. The doctors who greeted us displayed clear consternation that I had been left in that state for so long, a factor that probably played a part in my child developing an irregular heartbeat. The ideal birth narrative – that low-intervention, midwife-led care is always best – has hardened into institutional bias, amid a system in which women’s choices about their medical care are too often sidelined.In one of her first acts as health secretary, Cooper said she intends to reintroduce binding national maternity standards. They will include ending the postcode lottery for levels of care, and tackling racial inequalities that have meant worse outcomes for poorer and for black and Asian women. Her promises sound reassuring, but we have heard similar things before. What’s needed is a fundamental cultural shift so that women’s voices are treated as clinical evidence, not background noise.There is a deep-rooted disconnect inNHSmaternity units. Between the needs of patients and the people treating them, and between different parts of the system itself. When midwife-led care and obstetric intervention are positioned in opposition, rather than as complementary approaches, escalation can be perceived as failure instead of necessary care. And in that gap, women at their most vulnerable have their pain minimised and their instincts questioned, sometimes to the point that risk becomes life-threatening.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrauma is a brutal introduction to motherhood, and one that is all too common. For me and thousands of other mothers, our births could have gone so differently if we had only been heard. My ideal birth is not defined by candlelight or calm breathing. It is one where I am listened to, believed and responded to in time. One that both my baby and I survive at any cost.Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern BritainDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsWomen's healthOpinionChildbirthHospitalsYvette CooperNHSPregnancyHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘James Dean has got nothing on that kid’: River Phoenix films – ranked! | Movies | The Guardian
description: As Stand By Me is re-released for its 40th anniversary, we look at the late actor’s most intense, enduring roles – from a goofball boffin to a narcoleptic hustler
Author: Ryan Gilbey
Headline: As Stand By Me is re-released for its 40th anniversary, we look at the late actor’s most intense, enduring roles – from a goofball boffin to a narcoleptic hustler
Content: River Phoenix as young Indiana Jones in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989) .Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreenRiver Phoenix as young Indiana Jones in Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989) .Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyRankedMovies‘James Dean has got nothing on that kid’: River Phoenix films – ranked!As Stand By Me is re-released for its 40th anniversary, we look at the late actor’s most intense, enduring roles – from a goofball boffin to a narcoleptic hustlerRyan GilbeyThu 6 Aug 2026 10.35 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google16. Circle of Violence: A Family Drama (1986)Issue-of-the-week TV movie about elder abuse, with Tuesday Weld as a harried mum taking out her frustrations on her own ageing mother. Phoenix slaps on the hair gel as the essentially decent son who blasts his music too loud, lets his rowdy if unusually spiffy pals put their feet on the furniture and resents the new house guest: “Grandma is really getting on my nerves!”15. Silent Tongue (1993)View image in fullscreen‘Mad with grief’ … Phoenix in Silent Tongue.Photograph: United Archives GmbH/AlamySam Shepard’s turgid western premiered at Sundance in early 1993, then sat on the shelf for a year. As with his unfinished final film, Dark Blood, Phoenix plays a desert-dwelling widower gone mad with grief. In this case, his father (Richard Harris) steals a second wife for him from the travelling showman (Alan Bates) who sold him his first. Nuance is not required from Phoenix here, just doleful, brooding twitchiness. A family connection: his brother Joaquin later played Harris’s son, too, in Gladiator.14. The Thing Called Love (1993)Directed by Peter Bogdanovich, this was the last film Phoenix completed. Samantha Mathis (his then girlfriend), Dermot Mulroney and a pre-fame Sandra Bullock are aspiring country-and-western musicians convening in Nashville, but their warm, lively work only underlines how ill at ease Phoenix seems on screen. As the most gifted performer of the bunch, he is remote in ways that can’t easily be explained away as acting choices. “He looks ill,” observed the critic Roger Ebert, who thought the performance “should have been seen by someone as a cry for help”.13. Little Nikita (1988)View image in fullscreenSon of a sleeper agent … Phoenix in Little Nikita.Photograph: Cine Text/Sportsphoto/AllstarEspionage for dummies. Phoenix is the all-American high-schooler Jeff, who has no inkling that he is really Nikita, son of Russian sleeper agents. That’s until undercover FBI man Sidney Poitier cosies up to him and spills the beans. Both deserve better than this minefield of spy-movie cliches, but you’ll never catch Phoenix coasting. He delivers the line “Truth has no meaning in this house!” with all the conviction of James Dean in Rebel Without a Cause screaming, “You’re tearing me apart!”12. Surviving: A Family in Crisis (1985)Despite a strong cast (Ellen Burstyn, Molly Ringwald, Paul Sorvino) and direction by British television veteran Waris Hussein (Doctor Who, Henry VIII and His Six Wives), this TV movie about a teen suicide pact is mostly soapy and simplistic. Phoenix is affectingly uninhibited, though, as the grieving sibling: “Boy, he must have hated us,” he weeps after the death of his beloved older brother. He won a Young Artist award for his troubles, beating his co-star, Poltergeist poppet Heather O’Rourke, who died three years later at the age of 12.11. Dark Blood (1993/2012)View image in fullscreenOn-set tensions … Phoenix with Judy Davis and Jonathan Pryce in Dark Blood.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyA little more than half of Phoenix’s final movie was in the can when he died of a drug overdose on 31 October 1993. Director George Sluizer stole the footage to prevent it being destroyed, then used stills and narration to plug the gaps in a patchwork cut which premiered in 2012, two years before his own death. Phoenix plays a widowed recluse who rescues a married couple (Jonathan Pryce and Judy Davis) after their Bentley breaks down near his desert shack; Knife in the Water-style thriller dynamics ensue. Phoenix is a haunted, enigmatic presence but only Davis’s performance truly coheres. On-set tensions were rife between her and Sluizer; he accused her of giving Phoenix hell, though producer Stephen Woolley recalls the young actor kissing Davis’s feet.10. I Love You to Death (1990)Broad, wacky comedy about a wronged wife (Tracey Ullman) plotting to murder her philandering husband (Kevin Kline, whose performance in A Fish Called Wanda beat Phoenix to the best supporting actor Oscar in 1989). She is encouraged and assisted by, variously, her own mother (Joan Plowright), who sets the plan in motion; an earnest hippy (Phoenix), whom the couple employ at their pizza joint, and who has his own reasons for wanting the husband out of the way; and a pair of stoned amateur hit-men (William Hurt and Keanu Reeves). Phoenix denied that his character, with his crystals, beads and mysticism, bore any resemblance to himself (“Nope, no similarities whatsoever”) but he feels at the very least like a riff on the actor’s persona.9. Sneakers (1992)View image in fullscreenCode-breaking caper … Phoenix in Sneakers.Photograph: Universal/AllstarAccording to Esquire magazine, Phoenix was embarrassed by the commercialism of this engaging code-breaking caper, and even advised his friends not to watch it. Admittedly, there isn’t a whole lot for him to do on screen, but at least he and Poitier, previously paired in Little Nikita, get to participate in a superior espionage adventure this time around. They’re part of the eccentric tech-security team headed by Robert Redford (who had just picked Brad Pitt for the lead role coveted by Phoenix in the fly-fishing drama A River Runs Through It). The rest of Redford’s crew includes David Strathairn and Dan Aykroyd, who in one scene is wearing a T-shirt advertising Aleka’s Attic, the jangly folk-pop outfit fronted by Phoenix.8. A Night in the Life of Jimmy Reardon (1988)View image in fullscreenWith Matthew Perry in A Night in the Life of Jimmy Reardon.Photograph: 20 Century Fox/AllstarPhoenix was a reluctant heartthrob, so it follows that his one bona fide teen movie would be unorthodox and melancholy. As Jimmy, a slick, priapic but troubled young poet whose sexual partners include one of his mother’s friends, Phoenix flirts with the dislikable and unsympathetic. In one scene, he loses interest during his girlfriend’s elaborate masked-intruder sex fantasy: “I don’t feel like Jack the Ripper today.” In another, he is scolded by his best pal (a pre-Friends Matthew Perry), who tells him: “Your goddam pecker leads you around like a mule chasing a carrot.” Twentieth Century Fox re-edited the movie as a splashy comedy; director William Richert’s cut, retitled Aren’t You Even Gonna Kiss Me Goodbye? after his original novel, is the classier version. He and Phoenix were reunited when Richert played the Falstaffian vagabond Bob in My Own Private Idaho. Richert died in 2022; his website still advertises a crowd-funding campaign to pay for “deepface [sic] technology” that would insert Phoenix into the director’s version of The Man with the Iron Mask.7. Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989)The most delirious part of this threequel is its breakneck, origin-story prologue, with Phoenix (who was recommended for the role by his Mosquito Coast co-star Harrison Ford) showing how the young Indiana Jones acquired his bullwhip, battered fedora, chin scar and ophidiophobia. It’s such a hoot that only a spoilsport would ask why a strictly-parented Boy Scout in 1912 Utah sports the unruly surfer-dude fringe of a 1980s teen idol.6. Explorers (1985)Joe Dante used his Gremlins clout to make this charming goofball fantasy starring Phoenix and Ethan Hawke, both 14, as friends who build and pilot a rinky-dink spaceship. Making his movie debut after several years of TV work, Phoenix was already on course to be a teen pin-up but was cast against type as the boffin Wolfgang. Hawke recalls seeing his co-star for the first time walking back and forth outside their motel: “[I] asked him what he was doing, and he said he was trying to figure out how Wolfgang walked … from that moment forward he was always ahead of me.” Next to him, said Hawke, “I never felt more ordinary in my life.”5. The Mosquito Coast (1986)View image in fullscreenWith Harrison Ford, Helen Mirren and Hilary Gordon in Mosquito Coast.Photograph: Cinetext Collection/Sportsphoto/AllstarPeter Weir’s dogged, Paul Schrader-scripted adaptation of Paul Theroux’s novel about a ranting, idealistic inventor who drags his family off to live in the Central American rainforests is dominated by Harrison Ford’s oppressive performance. The rest of the cast, including Helen Mirren as his wife, scarcely get a look-in, though Phoenix makes a strong impression as the adoring eldest son whose idolatry gives way to mounting horror at his father’s murderous insanity. Phoenix’s then-girlfriend, Martha Plimpton, has a memorable scene in which she speaks for his thousands of teenage fans by admitting: “I think of you when I go to the bathroom.”4. Dogfight (1991)Hot from his Oscar nomination for Running on Empty, Phoenix was granted director approval for this drama about a group of callous young Marines competing in a “dogfight” to find the ugliest date during their last night before being shipped off to Okinawa, and then to Vietnam. He wisely chose the film-maker Nancy Savoca, who brings a complex tenderness to the emotional tussles between Eddie (Phoenix) and his prey, the shy waitress and amateur balladeer Rose (Lili Taylor), who turns out to be nobody’s fool. Phoenix doesn’t soft-pedal Eddie’s cruelty, which makes his pangs of conscience even more resonant. “How did we get to be so full of shit?” he asks his fellow Marines the morning after the dogfight before. “How did we become these fucking idiots?”3. Stand By Me (1986)View image in fullscreenBad reputation … Phoenix in Stand by Me.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyIf modern audiences want to know why Phoenix was so loved, said Ethan Hawke in 2014, “Go watch Stand By Me … James Dean has got nothing on that kid.” As the toughest but most complicated of the 12-year-old friends who trek into the woods to find a corpse in the late Rob Reiner’s film of Stephen King’s novella The Body, Phoenix evokes vividly the boy’s inner tensions, his hurt at the unfairness of his bad reputation; “I’d like to go some place where nobody knows me,” he sobs. Then there’s his exit. Each of the actor’s three greatest films gives him a killer final shot which has only gained in poignancy since his death. But it is his silent farewell in Stand by Me – waving at the camera, then plodding away and literally dissolving into thin air as the voiceover reveals that his character died prematurely – that hits the hardest.2. Running on Empty (1988)Phoenix received his only Oscar nomination for this fine drama about a pair of former radicals (Christine Lahti and Judd Hirsch) wanted by the FBI for their involvement in a bombing years earlier. He plays their eldest son, a sensitive piano prodigy who has learned never to let down his guard, which causes complications when he falls for his music teacher’s daughter (Plimpton). Under the direction of veteran auteur Sidney Lumet, who declared that Phoenix “couldn’t be ordinary if he tried”, the actor is achingly sad and true as the boy unfairly shouldering his parents’ burdens. It’s striking, too, that even in his short career, Phoenix starred in so many portraits of mysterious, idealistic and/ or itinerant families not unlike his own. This one, though, is the best.1. My Own Private Idaho (1991)View image in fullscreenBold … with Keanu Reeves in My Own Private Idaho.Photograph: Warner Bros Inc.Three decades ago, queer parts for straight-identifying actors were still thought of largely as awards bids (see William Hurt’s transparently covetous performance in Kiss of the Spider Woman) or career-killers (even at the end of the 1990s, Matt Damon, Brad Pitt and Leonardo DiCaprioall turned down Brokeback Mountain). In that context, the boldness of Phoenix and Keanu Reeves in unselfconsciously playing sex workers in My Own Private Idaho, a kind of Midnight Cowboy cross-pollinated with Shakespeare’s Henry plays, should not be underestimated.But the narcoleptic hustler Mike, who turns tricks while searching for his mother, was no ordinary job for Phoenix. “He was already this amazing actor,” said writer-director Gus Van Sant, “but with this film, he was able to have an effect on what the film was becoming … He was very excited he could control the destiny of his character.” The most obvious example is the campfire confession in which Mike admits his true feelings for Scott, the Prince Hal figure played by Reeves. The dialogue was scripted by Phoenix himself and scribbled on napkins, the scene moved to the end of the shoot so that he could build up to it emotionally. “The character I wrote was blasé and noncommittal,” said Van Sant. “River made him gay and committal; he redeemed him with emotions.”He did the same for the film, too. Van Sant’s innovative touches – shirtless studs coming to life on the covers of porn magazines, or the eerie pseudo-freeze-framed sex scenes – are cunning and cool, but it is Phoenix’s performance, from his opening orgasm to his final collapse on a deserted country road, that gives the movie its heart and its kick.Explore more on these topicsFilmRankedRiver PhoenixfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I knew Rod Liddle and hated what he became. He would have wanted me to say so | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: A man who prized blunt speaking has been selectively eulogised. There’s a balance between decency and honesty: I’m sad he caused such harm, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: A man who prized blunt speaking has been selectively eulogised. There’s a balance between decency and honesty: I’m sad he caused such harm, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: Rod Liddle at the Edinburgh international book festival in 2014.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRod Liddle at the Edinburgh international book festival in 2014.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianOpinionRod LiddleI knew Rod Liddle and hated what he became. He would have wanted me to say soZoe WilliamsA man who prized blunt speaking has been selectively eulogised. There’s a balance between decency and honesty: I’m sad he caused such harmThu 6 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 16.27 EDTShareAs tributes poured in forRod Liddle, the Sunday Times and Sun columnist who has died at the age of 66, they were markedly coy and sanitised. Paradoxically, those were the exact deficiencies obituaries praised Liddle for avoiding – they said he shot from the hip and ruffled feathers, remorselessly attacked the liberal establishment and was ebullient. Michael Gove called him “special and brave”. But brave in the face of what? Attacked the liberal establishment how?This delicacy was particularly noticeable in a segment on Radio 4’s Today programme, of which Liddle was editor in the 90s,between Justin Webb and Amol Rajan. “If there was a golden thread that connected the person you saw back then with the person of a few weeks ago,” Webb said, “it was a distrust of authority.” But Liddle’s targets as a columnist were not the authorities. Often they were Muslims and immigrants, transgender people and chronic illness sufferers, African-Caribbean men from Harlesden. He did not attack the establishment, he attacked the marginalised, constantly.There is sometimes a dilemma in how we process death. Decently, we seek not to speak ill of the dead, and certainly one hopes to never increase the grief of those who loved them. But does that mean we are also duty-bound not to discuss more uncomfortable issues? Here I feel the dilemma.I was friends with Rod Liddle in the 90s. He was a different Rod then. The principal target of his satire was himself. He would lampoon guys having affairs, guys who were a shambles, guys who had run out of road. If there was any ethno-caricaturing, it read as a footnote to a worldview in which nobody was more ridiculous than he, Rod Liddle. This carried on into his collection of short stories, Too Beautiful for You (2003), in which the most memorable escapade was a man getting into a train crash, after seeing his mistress, rushing across a field carrying his severed arm so that he could get to a hospital without blowing his alibi, and realising as he bleeds out that he must actually really love his wife.In 1983, he was a member of the Socialist Workers party and by 1990, a researcher for the Labour party, but what made him seem left-left, rather than centre left, didn’t have a membership card. It was the self-parody coupled with an overall dishevelment that conveyed a deep-seated humanity and pluralism: “I’m a mess, you’re a mess, let’s get out of this mess together.” I know that is maddeningly unspecific, but I also know that anyone on the left will get what I mean.So his transformation into an attack dog for the race-baiting right was painful to watch, if not exactly unprecedented. On Tuesday, sociologist Will Daviescharacterised this post-68 type, “drawn to norm-breaching, moving via adolescent rebellion, punk, revolutionary socialism and eventually ending up at racism, because by the 21st century that was the most efficient transgression still on offer”. The rightwing media will pay absolutely top dollar for a big-name left-to-right defector.Peter York, in his bookA Dead Cat on Your Table, examines the nexus of rightwing thinktanks, the mainstream right and “alt-right” media to argue that what we call “culture wars” aren’t ideological, they’re about hegemonic capture in the service of capital. Depressingly, it does work: GB News, which hedge-funder Paul Marshall hosed money at, to widespread ridicule, now secures higher average audiencesthan Sky News or BBCNews. Arguably, the greater victory is that all we ever talk about is what GB News wants to talk about.View image in fullscreenRod Liddle, when he edited Radio 4’s Today programme.Photograph: Graham Turner/The GuardianOne thing the obituaries did mention was Liddle’s feudwith Yasmin Alibhai-Brown– “they loathed each other,” Justin Webb said, then, later he asked: “Deep down, did he really? There was no loathing in Rod that I could ever divine.” But “feud” is doing some heavy lifting there: Liddle attacked Alibhai-Brown constantly in his columns, for opinions which many of us hold but seemed unaccountably more obnoxious to him coming from her. This culminated in a clashon Channel 4 in 2014, after which the then Conservative MP Michael Fabricant, tweeted that he might have ended up punchingAlibhai-Brown in the throat.Liddle the Today editor, listening to much of the discussion, would have said, “what the fuck are you playing at, trying to describe this outrageous character without naming any of his outrages?” Not least as they are so easy to Google – the time he said he couldn’t have been a teacherbecause he would have ended up shagging the children, “right in there, on day one”; the endless attacks on Muslims, arguing that it was the faith itself, not unhinged individuals, that drove terrorism, that the 2019 election should be held on a day when “Muslims are forbiddento do anything on pain of hell” to suppress their vote. The editor Liddle of the 90s would have also said: “You can’t have two blokes on the radio, explaining why whipping up racist misogyny is fine so long as, underneath, you have a heart of gold.” Not because of diversity and whatnot, but because it’sjust not cricket.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenTelegraph, 3 August 2026One of the last times I saw Liddle was a couple of months ago when we were both on Sky News. He looked really different, because he hadCOPD(chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). I asked him how he was and he said “depressed”, and I asked why, but I was just being tactful, because it was obvious why. My mum died with COPD last year, and by the time your face goes grey, life is pretty horrible, like drowning in air. “I’m no longer priapic,” he replied.I felt ineffably sad; that privately, his persona was still the same, standing there with his arm hanging off, insisting that the first thing he would do, once he got it sewed back on, was get a hard-on; sad at the pantomime of it, cartoon prejudices with real-life consequences, trotted out on command, funded by people with mountains of money who wish society ill; sad about the empathy and solidarity that had once built a collective firewall against hate-for-fun, which had been slowly extinguished.In fact, I wanted to start crying but I’d just had my makeup done, so we went on air and argued about Andy Burnham in Makerfield, and he said he would only win it if he “sorted out” immigration. I won’t miss Rod Liddle, but I miss the person he was when the world was different, and I miss that different world.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘We crafted it from our hearts’: the Womack Sisters on continuing a great soul music dynasty | Soul | The Guardian
description: Their parents were Womack & Womack, Uncle Bobby was a superstar and so was their grandfather, Sam Cooke. The trio explain how, after driving Ubers and being told soul was dead, they joined the family business
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Their parents were Womack & Womack, Uncle Bobby was a superstar and so was their grandfather, Sam Cooke. The trio explain how, after driving Ubers and being told soul was dead, they joined the family business
Content: ‘We’re committed’ … the Womack Sisters.Photograph: Rosie CoheView image in fullscreen‘We’re committed’ … the Womack Sisters.Photograph: Rosie CoheSoulInterview‘We crafted it from our hearts’: the Womack Sisters on continuing a great soul music dynastyAlexis PetridisTheir parents were Womack & Womack, Uncle Bobby was a superstar and so was their grandfather, Sam Cooke. The trio explain how, after driving Ubers and being told soul was dead, they joined the family businessThu 6 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 16.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBackstage at a London festival, on a Sunday afternoon, the Womack Sisters are assembling themselves on a sofa, still clad in the clothes they were wearing on stage a few minutes ago. They look very stylish in their black dresses, tights and high heels, but they are not, it has to be said, dressed appropriately for the weather, which is sweltering. “You don’t feel anything on stage,” says Zeimani with a shrug. “You just feel amazing, like you’re floating.”“And we’re committed,” nods her sister BG. “You know, we were taught byprofessionals.”View image in fullscreenLinda and Cecil Womack on stage in 1988.Photograph: Frans Schellekens/RedfernsIndeed they were. BG, Zeimani and Kucha Womack’s father was Cecil Womack: he wrote Teddy Pendergrass’s oft-sampled classic Love TKO, as well as hits for the O’Jays, the Four Tops andPatti LaBelle, and was one half of Womack and Womack, of Love Wars and Teardrops fame. The other half was their mother, Linda Womack, the daughter of “king of soul” Sam Cooke. Their uncle was Bobby Womack, who initially performed with Cecil in early-60s band the Valentinos – their most famous song was It’s All Over Now, later covered by the Rolling Stones – before going on to record a string of classics that earned him the unofficial soubriquet The Greatest Soul Singer in the World: from Across 110th Street to If You Think You’re Lonely Now to the triumphant final album he made before his death in 2014, The Bravest Man in the Universe. Their half-brother’s mum, meanwhile, was Mary “My Guy” Wells.Given their heritage, Zeimani says her father thought a career in anything other than music was a waste of time: when she approached him with the idea that she might go to medical school, he reacted with something approaching horror. “He said, ‘Just go in the studio and make music.’ I told him I needed to have a Plan B. He was like, ‘Plan B? Do Plan A, go hard, get on it.’”In fairness, the Womack Sisters had long been apprenticed in the family business. They had spent their childhood travelling the world with their parents: Compass Point Studios in the Bahamas or Bob Marley’s studio in Jamaica; homes in Bangkok, Phuket, Johannesburg, London and, slightly less glamorously, Southend-on-Sea. “We were raised between London, Thailand, Paris and Amsterdam, but mostly here in London,” recalls Kucha. Their mum and dad didn’t just take the kids along with them, they got them involved “in everything they did, in the studio, on stage, in meetings. They wanted to make sure that we knew what they were doing with their time, so they communicated with us a lot.”View image in fullscreenThe Womack Sisters … ‘I could do this for the rest of my life!’Photograph: Rosie CoheBG says that if I had interviewed her parents back then, “We would have been in the interview. If they went on a television show, we were on the couch with them.”View image in fullscreenConscience, featuring Zeimani.Photograph: Island RecordsZeimani made her first public appearance as a baby, in her mother’s arms on the cover of Womack and Womack’s Conscience, the 1988 album featuring Teardrops. The sisters made their recording debut, alongside their four other siblings, on the 1993 album Transformation to the House of Zekkariyas. “We opened their shows,” remembers Zeimani. “And it was the start of us realising that we could be a group, because before, we were just sisters. ‘Yo, actually this is a good feeling, I could do this for the rest of my life.’”But still, she says, “we didn’t take our dad’s advice”. They decided they did need a Plan B. “We were a little hard-headed. We wanted to go out and explore.”The three sisters moved to Los Angeles and attempted to balance regular jobs with getting a musical career off the ground. There was a cleaning company, and a brief stint, as Zeimani puts it, of “selling drugs”, which turns out to mean they ran a marijuana dispensary. But it wasn’t as easy as they had hoped. “We kept getting fired,” says BG. “I got fired from Zara for trying to take a couple of trips out of town for shows.” The sisters also drove Uber taxis. “Uber was a lifesaver! I swear, without it I would have been turning tricks,” BG laughs.View image in fullscreen‘We crafted the album from our hearts.’Photograph: Rosie CoheTo compound their problems, there was the music industry’s attitude towards them. The group “always had soul in mind,” says Zeimani – they were huge fans of Amy Winehouse – but the labels they met with kept pushing them towards pop. “We would go to them with our demos and tell them what we would like to accomplish, with a live band, an orchestra, everything. They were just like, ‘Soul’s not what’s happening right now, here in the States, particularly for brown artists.’ So for years we were trying other things. We dabbled in R&B. They even had us rapping a couple of times.”Hang on – are you saying you were told that Black artists shouldn’t make soul music?“Yeah, I know,” nods BG, rolling her eyes. “They told our manager that, and he didn’t want to tell us, he was so embarrassed. Eventually, we just put our foot down and said, ‘We’re not doing anything else.’ Couldn’t get anyone to invest in what we were doing, so we funded our own thing.”Happily, their own thing caught the attention of Daptone Records, home toJalen Ngonda,Thee Sacred Soulsand the lateSharon Jones, whose house band the Dap-Kings are best known for backing Winehouse on her Back to Black album. “An instant connection!” enthuses BG of their meeting with the label’s co-founder, Bosco Mann, who now plays bass in their backing band. “We just hung out and listened to music for a year before we actually recorded anything. So when we finally came down to it, it just rolled, it flowed, the music was just pouring out.”The result was a string of acclaimed singles, among them Chauffeur – which details the downsides of the sisters’ period as Uber drivers, including realising that you’re invisible to the “fine-looking” man you just picked up – and If I Let You, which last month enjoyed a burst of social media virality after support from a startling array of luminaries: SZA, Timbaland, Ghostface Killah, Pharrell Williams, Erykah Badu and Questlove. One suspects the stars were drawn by the Womack Sisters’ fusion of traditional and modern: the music on their upcoming debut album is as deeply rooted in soul’s past as you’d expect (“We are,” as Kucha puts it, “so familiar with these streets”), but it never feels self-consciously retro.But it does feel strikingly raw, racked with very real emotion. “We crafted it from our hearts,” says Zeimani. “I wouldn’t say that we had a lot of sorrow to get off our chests, but there is a lot of relationship drama in our family, you know? Our father passed away, our Uncle Bob passed away shortly afterwards. Our aunt, our Uncle Jude’s wife, there was a car accident and she didn’t make it. I lost my husband in Atlanta in 2020 – he was robbed, he got shot, he didn’t survive. You find love, there’s nothing that impacts you more, and to lose it before you can fully experience it – like, we were married but we were about to start a family … I had a really hard time moving through that.“You know how when we were in the pandemic, we couldn’t do anything? That’s really what you need to do to reset from loss – stop doing everything, just love on yourself, go to the beach, find a reason to smile again.”View image in fullscreenThe Womack clan … top (L-R), Bobby, Curtis and Harry; bottom (L-R), Friendly Sr, Friendly Jr and Cecil.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesTheir live shows, meanwhile, are proving triumphant. At the London festival, their set featured a roaring take on Teardrops, their parents’ most enduring hit. No, they say, they aren’t intimidated by their family’s legacy. “We’re proud of them, but they exist in their own right. The time they came up in and the things they faced – segregation, things we can’t even imagine – they saw that,” says Zeimani.“If you can imagine, our mother came up behind Sam Cooke – and we saw her win Grammys,” nods Kucha. “So I’m just like, well, she did it.”“She focused on herself – that was her advice to us,” says Zeimani. “And Uncle Bob’s career was piping hot at the same time as my dad’s career was piping hot, so we saw that we could coexist without competing, because they were very different from one another. They always told us: you’re not us and you don’t have to be. You’re you, and there’ll never be anyone like you. We tookthatseriously.”The Womack Sisters is released 14 August via DaptoneExplore more on these topicsSoulBobby WomackinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Bombs, heists and big cats: TV’s 25 best true-crime shows ever | Television | The Guardian
description: From mind-boggling murder investigations to decade-long scams, there’s no shortage of documentaries about real-life awfulness. We list the most incredible
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: From mind-boggling murder investigations to decade-long scams, there’s no shortage of documentaries about real-life awfulness. We list the most incredible
Content: Investigative film-making with the pull of reality trash … Tiger King: Murder, Mayhem and Madness.Photograph: NETFLIX/Courtesy of NETFLIXView image in fullscreenInvestigative film-making with the pull of reality trash … Tiger King: Murder, Mayhem and Madness.Photograph: NETFLIX/Courtesy of NETFLIXTelevisionBombs, heists and big cats: TV’s 25 best true-crime shows everFrom mind-boggling murder investigations to decade-long scams, there’s no shortage of documentaries about real-life awfulness. We list the most incredibleMichael HoganThu 6 Aug 2026 09.10 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 09.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince the true-crime explosion a decade ago – kickstarted by Netflix’sMaking a Murderer– audiences have been fed a steady small-screen diet of cold-case killings, catfishing scams and creepy cults. And, after years of varying results, Netflix’s latest show,A Toxic Love Story– which recounts how a California couple framed an innocent woman for stalking, intimidation and recruiting men from Craigslist to rape her ex’s new wife – is being billed as a return to true-crime form. But when it comes to similar shows worth your viewing time, what else is up there?Here’s a selection of the genre’s 25 standout shows and where to watch them – which, let’s face it, is mainlyNetflix. Let the boggle-eyed bingeing begin.OJ: Made in America (2016)Disney+This ESPN-produced five-parter, which won an Oscar and an Emmy, is the definitive account of the fairytale rise and steep fall of the former NFL running back OJ Simpson. It chronicles the buildup to and fallout from the 1995 trial at which Simpson was accused (and acquitted) of the brutal murders of his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ron Goldman. A stunning state-of-the-nation study of race, gender and celebrity.The Jinx: The Life and Deaths of Robert Durst (2015-24)Sky/Now (UK), HBO Max (UK/US/Australia), Foxtel Now (Australia)An oldie but a goodie. The HBO series remains groundbreaking for reasons we won’t spoil. The film-maker Andrew Jarecki follows Durst, a billionaire New York real estate heir, who is suspected of three murders across 19 years. When Durst agrees to a sit-down interview, it proves to be the biggest miscalculation of his life.Girl in the Picture(2022)NetflixThe director Skye Borgman, whose 2017 film Abducted in Plain Sight also merits a watch, keeps the victim front and centre inthis jaw-dropper. In 1990, a young woman was found in critical condition at the side of an Oklahoma highway. What begins as an investigation into an apparent hit-and-run soon escalates into a harrowing tale of abduction, abuse and identity fraud.The Alabama Solution (2025)Sky/Now (UK), HBO Max (US/Australia), YouTube TV (US)People behind bars in Alabama used contraband phones to film the footage and make the calls from whichthis startling documentarywas largely assembled. The result of a six-year investigation by the directors Charlotte Kaufman and Andrew Jarecki (of The Jinx pedigree), it viscerally lays bare the cruelty inflicted on prisoners as they are beaten, abused and even killed by prison guards. It’s a righteous howl of protest about systemic failures.Evil Genius: The True Story of America’s Most Diabolical Bank Heist (2018)NetflixIn 2003, Brian Wells, a pizza delivery man, walked into a Pennsylvania bank with a bomb locked around his neck and demanded $250,000 in cash.He was killed when the device detonatedbefore cops could disarm it. The film-makers Barbara Schroeder and Trey Borzillieri unravel the conspiracy across four episodes, until a climactic revelation flips everything on its head.Capturing the Friedmans(2003)Prime Video (UK), HBO Max/YouTube TV (US)It starts as a HBO film about clowns hired for children’s parties. It soon morphs into a haunting deep dive into the retired New York schoolteacher Arnold Friedman andhis 18-year-old son, Jesse. In 1987, the pair were convicted of owning an extensive cache of child sexual abuse images and abusing local boys who took computing classes in their basement.American Murder: The Family Next Door (2020)NetflixIn 2018, a pregnant woman, Shanann Watts, and her two toddler daughters were murdered in their Colorado home by Shanann’s husband, Chris. Only days before, he had posted smiley family snaps on social media. Via text messages, home videos, Facebook reels and police bodycam footage, the director Jenny Popplewell constructs a digital portrait of domestic tragedy.Mommy Dead and Dearest(2017)HBO Max (UK, US, Australia), Foxtel Now (Australia)The stranger-than-fiction story of Gypsy Rose Blanchard. From birth, the Missouri girl was in and out of hospital, diagnosed with all manner of debilitating diseases. She used a wheelchair and was tube-fed and shaven-headed due to cancer. Or so everyone thought. When Gypsy Rose learned the truth, she murdered her mother, Clauddine. This compelling film interviews her in prison. She has since beenreleased on parole.Unknown Number: The High School Catfish (2025)NetflixA true-crime phenomenon that doesn’t involve murder. Just don’t Google it first or you may ruin the head-spinning twist. This cleverly crafted film from Skye Borgman (Girl in the Picture) follows a teen couple in small-town Michigan who are relentlessly cyberbullied by an anonymous caller. A community is torn apart by finger-pointing before the culprit is unmasked. Cue your jaw hitting the floor.The Keepers (2017)NetflixThe unsolved murder in 1969 of a nun called Catherine Cesnik is the gateway intoa panoramic exposé of endemic abuseat the all-girls school in Baltimore where she taught. Was Sister Cathy killed by a priest when she tried to blow the whistle? This searing seven-parter gives voice to victims, while the lead investigators aren’t journalists but two retired former pupils, working from their kitchen tables.One Night in Idaho: The College Murders (2025)Prime VideoThose who had followed the tragic case were agog last summer when Bryan Kohberger, accused offatally stabbing four university housematesin 2022, took a plea deal to avoid the death penalty. Directors Liz Garbus and Matthew Galkin rushed to update their forensic four-parter, which follows not just the investigation but the impact of social media sleuths. A second season is in the works.Making a Murderer(2015-18)NetflixAlong with The Jinx, which was released months earlier, this is the one that began the true-crime boom. The directors Laura Ricciardi and Moira Demos spent a decade immersed in the case of Steven Avery and Brendan Dassey, Avery’s teenage nephew and alleged accomplice, to build a genre-defining masterpiece. Hard-hitting and heartbreaking, it sparked national outrage anda presidential petition demanding justice.I’ll Be Gone in the Dark (2020)HBO Max (UK, US, Australia), YouTube TV (US), Foxtel Now (Australia)The crime author Michelle McNamara spent years obsessively hunting the Golden State Killer – a nocturnal home invader responsible for at least 50 rapes and 13 murders in California in the 1970s and 1980s.This HBO series from Liz Garbus(One Night in Idaho) weaves together the manhunt with a profile of McNamara, who died before the bogeyman wascaught at last.‘Without my daughter, drinking would have been a problem’: Patton Oswalt on bereavementRead moreGone Girls: The Long Island Serial Killer(2025)NetflixAnother Garbus-directed banger – less a whodunnit, more a look at how the legal system values certain lives above others. She spent nearly a decade researching the Gilgo Beach killings, in which more than a dozen women, many of them sex workers, were murdered between 1993 and 2011. Garbus shows empathy for the victims and ​illustrates how those left behind built a supportive community from their shared pain. In June, Rex Heuermann pleaded guilty to seven murders and admitted to an eighth; he was sentenced tolife in prison without parole.The Staircase (2004-18)NetflixWhen the eccentric novelist Michael Peterson called 911 in 2001 and said his wife, Kathleen, had died after drunkenly falling down the stairs of their North Carolina mansion, he was soon arrested for murder. For this Canal+ (and latterly Netflix) series, the director Jean-Xavier de Lestrade was embedded with Peterson’s defence team, capturing the courtroom drama up close as he defended the charges. In 2017, Peterson entered an Alford plea to voluntary manslaughter, maintaining his innocence but agreeing there was enough evidence to result in a guilty verdict. Not to be confused withthe 2022 HBO dramatisationstarring Colin Firth and Toni Collette.The Mother of All Cons (2026)BBC iPlayer (UK), Britbox (US)This BBCthree-parter tells the devastating story of Jean O’Brien and her daughter Megan Bhari, who set up a charity for terminally ill children in 2012 after Bhari was diagnosed with a brain tumour at 13. Other parents started to question O’Brien’s claims about her daughter’s condition, while funds raised for Believe in Magic – including millions from the boyband One Direction –went unaccounted for.Wild Wild Country (2018)NetflixIn 1981, the utopian Rajneesh cult – led by the Indian spiritual teacher Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh, AKA Osho – established itself on a ranch in rural Oregon. Three years later, its followers committed the first and biggest bioterrorist attack in US history. This mesmerising, Emmy-winning series interviews perplexed locals and Ma Anand Sheela, formerly a PA to Osho, who died unrepentant in 1990.Last Call: When a Serial Killer Stalked Queer New York (2023)Sky/Now (UK), HBO Max (UK, US), YouTube TV (US), Binge (Australia)In the early 90s, the serial killer Richard Rogers – AKA the Last Call Killer – murdered and dismembered four gay men on the east coast of the US. The case was covered by the media in a sensationalist, homophobic style, while the justice system failed the victims;Anthony Caronna’s infuriating but ultimately redemptive serieshumanises them at last. Each of the four episodes is dedicated to one of the men killed.Jeffrey Epstein: Filthy Rich (2020)NetflixWe all know the enraging story by now, butthis gut-punch seriesabout the notorious sex trafficker – based on James Patterson’s book – lays bare the human tragedy behind the headlines. The director, Lisa Bryant, hears the candid testimony of survivors, includingVirginia GiuffreandMaria Farmer, along with former members of Epstein’s staff and the police who investigated his exploitative empire.The Perfect Neighbor(2025)NetflixGeeta Gandbhir’s unflinching documentary investigates the fatal shooting of a Black Florida woman,Ajike Owens, by her white neighbour,Susan Louise Lorincz. Comprised mostly of police bodycam and interrogation footage, it builds into a searing indictment of community tensions, the state’s controversial“stand your ground” lawand systemic racial bias.Paradise Lost Trilogy (1996-2011)HBO MaxIn 1993, the murders and mutilation of three eight-year-old boys in Arkansas sparked a moral panic about heavy metal and satanic rituals, resulting in the wrongful arrests of three teenagers. Paradise Lost: The Child Murders at Robin Hood Hills remains the only docuseries for which Metallica have allowed their music to be used. Two sequels followed the case’s progress over the next 15 years.The Vow (2020)HBO Max (UK, US, Australia), YouTube TV (US), Spectrum (US), Foxtel Now (Australia)Nxivm styled itself as a global self-improvement organisation. Of course, it was a cult – one that abused, blackmailed and branded its female members. Its svengali-like leader, Keith Raniere, was ultimately convicted ofcharges including sex trafficking and racketeering. This unsettling HBO docuseries began filming inside Nxivm years before the FBI investigated, capturing the mechanism of manipulation in action.Night Stalker: The Hunt for a Serial Killer (2021)NetflixReminiscent of the Zodiac Killer in 1960s San Francisco, Richard Ramirezterrorised Los Angeles in the summer of 1985with a string of brutal, seemingly random murders and sexual assaults. This four-parter documents his deadly rampage through the lens of the two detectives, Gil Carrillo and Frank Salerno, who became consumed by the case and doggedly tracked him down.Tiger King: Murder, Mayhem and Madness (2020)Netflix“Hey, all you cool cats and kittens.” It’s now inextricably linked with the early months of the Covid pandemic, but if this talking-point series managed to escape you, it’s worth seeing what all the fuss was about. Investigative film-making with the pull of reality trash, it follows an eccentric Oklahoma zookeeper, Joe Exotic, who allegedly hired a hitman to kill a big-cat activist,Carole Baskin.Don’t F**k with Cats: Hunting an Internet Killer(2019)NetflixA twisting, turning thrillerwith the kicker that it’s all too real. This three-parter beggars belief as it follows Facebook sleuths who launch an amateur investigation into online videos of kitten cruelty. The armchair detectives repeatedly express their fears that the culprit will escalate to murdering more than just pets – and are proved correct.Share your favourite true crime TVYou can tell us your own favourite true crime TV show using this form.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions.
