title: Dons call for Cambridge leaders to take blame for Jason Arday appointment | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Academics call for inquiry, saying university must be held accountable for ‘grotesque racism unleashed’
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Exclusive: Academics call for inquiry, saying university must be held accountable for ‘grotesque racism unleashed’
Content: Jason Arday at the time of his appointment to a professorship at Cambridge University in 2023.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJason Arday at the time of his appointment to a professorship at Cambridge University in 2023.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianJason ArdayDons call for Cambridge leaders to take blame for Jason Arday appointmentExclusive: Academics call for inquiry, saying university must be held accountable for ‘grotesque racism unleashed’Richard AdamsEducation editorThu 6 Aug 2026 15.54 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 14.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe University of Cambridge’s leaders deserve blame for the “grotesque racism unleashed” by Jason Arday’s appointment as professor, according to academics calling for the university to hold an independent inquiry.The Guardian understands that senior dons at Cambridge are circulating a joint letter calling for an inquiry into the processes and circumstances around Arday being given the position, with many suggesting the university wanted a “quick fix” to improve the diversity of its staff.Arday was appointed as professor of sociology of education in 2023 at the relatively young age of 37 and despite a slim track record of research and publications compared with those appointed to similar chairs at Cambridge.Arday resignedon Wednesday after more than a week of public questions involving plagiarism in his PhD thesis and other publications, allegations of exaggerating his academic appointments, mounting controversy over his claims to have raised millions of pounds for charity, and lurid statements involving masked attackers and even a pig’s head delivered to his parents’ home in London.Arday is preparing to publish his memoir in the US and UK in the coming days and told the Guardian that its publisher,Simon & Schuster, is to pay him “1.4 million”for his extraordinary backstory, which includes being unable to speak until he was 11 years old.The group of Cambridge academics want any inquiry to include external members and be given independent status. They point to concerns over the appointment committee for Arday’s post, and to previous disputes within the university’s faculty of education where Arday was based.Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge’s English faculty and one of the group organising the letter, said: “An independent investigation must scrutinise how such an early-career appointment to a very senior and prestigious professorial chair was made and what both the faculty of education and university management may have got very badly wrong.”She added: “Whatever the results of any investigation, the university bears no little responsibility for the grotesque racism which this whole business has unleashed, and for the harm done both to the individual in the line of fire, to Black academics as a group, and the broader field of critical race studies.“This requires accountability now from those responsible, not a cover-up.”Other academics who spoke to the Guardian said they had been surprised by Arday’s appointment in 2023, with one sociologist admitting to never having heard of Arday before: “When it was announced I looked for his body of work, and it was disappointing to say the least.”Gopal said Cambridge had been too tempted to “cut corners on the hard work of fostering equality and inclusion” by opting for a media-friendly appointment.“The extent to which this appointment wasparaded in the mediaby the university … raises questions about whether the university sought public kudos for itself rather than teaching and research from this appointment.“It is highly unusual, to say the least, to appoint such an early-career academic to a very senior post,” Gopal said.“Academic misconduct also needs more robust and transparent procedures in place, as more than one case at Cambridge indicates.“The university must also pay attention to the consequences of putting young people of colour in highly visible places to carry the burden of representation before they are ready to withstand scrutiny.”Playbooks, plagiarism and a pig’s head: new claims surrounding a star Cambridge professorRead moreWhen the controversy first erupted, the university briefed journalists that it stood by its appointment process, and publicly defended Arday as “the victim of a vile campaign” to discredit him.But on Wednesday night the university abruptly announced that it wouldopen a fresh investigationafter receiving “new information” about his qualifications and appointments.Shortly afterwards Arday said he would resign, adding: “I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgment.”The university and other organisations have since distanced themselves from Arday by deleting webpages and excising references, which one academic described as “wiping away the traces”.Jesus College, Cambridge, and the university’s faculty of education have taken down Arday’s staff profiles.Arday had signed up to speakers’ bureaus and, since his Cambridge appointment, has addressed a number of commercial organisations, including the annual conference of the Association of British Insurers in 2025.Simon & Schuster’s speakers bureau lists Arday as “an internationally sought-after speaker for industry conferences, corporate events, university lectures, and more, and has travelled across the United States for speaking engagements”.In 2024 Arday was a keynote speaker at US National Association of Funeral Directors international convention in New Orleans. His subsequent appearances, however, may dry up: an appearance in Arizona promised for October this year has also been removed.Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayUniversity of CambridgeHigher educationRaceAcademicsPlagiarismUniversitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Safety fears as scientists make first viruses designed by AI | Science | The Guardian
description: Researchers say breakthrough offers hope for new medicines but also raises urgent biosecurity questions
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Researchers say breakthrough offers hope for new medicines but also raises urgent biosecurity questions
Content: A scientist holds an agar plate containing a bacteriophage, which can be used to treat patients with persistent infections.Photograph: Samyukta Lakshmi/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA scientist holds an agar plate containing a bacteriophage, which can be used to treat patients with persistent infections.Photograph: Samyukta Lakshmi/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesScienceSafety fears as scientists make first viruses designed by AIResearchers say breakthrough offers hope for new medicines but also raises urgent biosecurity questionsIan SampleScience editorThu 6 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScientists have made the first viruses designed by artificial intelligence in a milestone that raises hopes for new medicines but also concerns over how to ensure the technology remains safe.The viruses are specific kinds known as bacteriophages, which only infect bacteria and are used around the world to treat patients with persistent infections. In lab tests, a cocktail of the AI-designed viruses killedEcolibugs that were resistant to natural bacteriophages.Dr Brian Hie, a chemical engineer at Stanford University in California, used genome language models, the genetic equivalent of the large language models behind AI chatbots, to design functioning genomes for bacteriophages. The viruses were then made in the laboratory and pitted againstEcoliin a dish.The ability to “rapidly design” genomes and tune them for specific bugs while overcoming resistance could “transform phage therapy” and “expand biotechnological toolkits”, the researchers wrote in the journalScience.But beyond the potential benefits, the scientists said the work raised “important biosafety, biocontainment and biosecurity considerations” and urged others who were designing whole genomes to “consult both safety and security professionals throughout the project”.In anaccompanying article, Prof Tom Inglesby and Dr Moritz Hanke at the Center for Health Security at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, reinforced the warning, writing: “Although this is promising for life sciences applications, it also raises urgent biosafety and biosecurity questions. The ability to compose viral genomes using generative AI now exists; the governance to safely steer it does not.”Hie and his colleagues used AI models called Evo1 and Evo2 to design the new viral genomes. The models were trained on genetic data from 2 million bacteriophages. The genetic code for viruses that can infect plants, humans or other animals was intentionally excluded from the AI’s training to reduce the risk of it designing dangerous viruses.The AI generated thousands of potential genomes from which the researchers selected nearly 300 to make in the lab. These were dropped into bacteria, which read the genetic code and churned out the new bacteriophages. The process was not efficient: only 16 bacteriophages proved to be viable, but a cocktail of them swiftly overcame resistance in two different strains ofEcoli.Bacteriophage genomes are tiny, but Inglesby and Hanke said the work nevertheless proved that generative AI could create functioning viral genomes. Whether the same approach could be applied to other viruses was unknown, but they said work on pathogens that could infect humans, animals or plants should not be pursued.“Such genomes might encode new pathogens that … cannot be contained by existing countermeasures,” they wrote.Tom Ellis, a professor of synthetic genome engineering at Imperial College London, said the work was impressive, but revealed how hard it would be to make more complex genomes. “This is literally the smallest and easiest genome to make,” he said.An AI trained on the genetic code of dangerous bugs could be used to design more harmful viruses, Ellis said, but controlling access to genetic data and having restrictions on making genomes that look dangerous would help. “Governments are working hard to do this already,” he added.“But honestly,” he said, “the threat from full AI design and writing of a genome of a virus or bacteria is very overblown when we consider that just taking existing pathogens and making gain-of-function changes to their genomes is so much easier and much more likely to be a real pathogenic threat.”Dr Filippa Lentzos, a reader in science and international security at King’s College London, said the most important point to intervene at the moment was when DNA was being manufactured. “It’s important to see the bigger governance picture and not focus regulation solely on the AI model,” she said. “A layered approach makes more sense: safeguards around model development and access, responsible research review, synthesis screening, and established laboratory biosafety and biosecurity.”Explore more on these topicsScienceSynthetic biologyInfectious diseasesGeneticsMedical researchAI (artificial intelligence)HealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: E-scooters far more dangerous than motorbikes or cycles, analysis suggests   | Science | The Guardian
description: Study of accidents in England and Wales shows e-scooter riders three times more likely to suffer traumatic brain injury than bikers
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Study of accidents in England and Wales shows e-scooter riders three times more likely to suffer traumatic brain injury than bikers
Content: The study also showed e-scooter riders sustained more internal organ and blood vessel damage than motorcyclists or pedal cyclists.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe study also showed e-scooter riders sustained more internal organ and blood vessel damage than motorcyclists or pedal cyclists.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesScienceE-scooters far more dangerous than motorbikes or cycles, analysis suggestsStudy of accidents in England and Wales shows e-scooter riders three times more likely to suffer traumatic brain injury than bikersIan SampleScience editorThu 6 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElectric scooter riders are three times more likely to suffer traumatic brain injuries than motorcyclists, according to an analysis of accidents inEnglandand Wales – which found women were particularly at risk of serious harm.Brain injuries accounted for more than a third of adult injuries on e-scooters, but riders also sustained more internal organ and blood vessel damage than did motorcyclists or pedal cyclists, the study found.The government has backed trials of rental e-scooters in England since 2020, but an additional 1m or so e-scooters are privately owned in the UK. These cannot legally be used on public roads, paths or cycle lanes, but police forces across the country have confiscated thousands because their owners were breaking the law.The accident analysis reveals that women were involved in about a third more collisions than men – and were more than twice as likely to report severe injuries. Children were also at risk with, 16% of e-scooter injuries in under 18s.The findings have led to calls to make e-scooters more stable and safer, especially for women who suffer more chest injuries because the handlebars are typically set at a height for men. Mandatory safety training and making helmets compulsory would also help, experts said.David Bodansky, a consultant hand, trauma and orthopaedic surgeon at Chelsea and Westminster hospital NHS foundation trust, turned to the national major trauma registry to analyse injuries from e-scooter, motorbike and bicycle collisions in 18 cities in England andWalesbetween 2020 and 2022.He found e-scooter riders were more than three times as likely to suffer traumatic brain injury or blood vessel damage and 1.5 times more likely to injure internal organs than motorbike riders, and they fared worse than cyclists for these injuries. Their risk of bone fractures was lower, however, than cyclists or motorcyclists.The data shed no light on why e-scooters are involved in so many accidents, but Bodansky believes that design is a factor. “They’ve got very small wheels and it’s very easy to jam one of those into a pothole. You’ll then go head over heels over the front and land on your head,” he said. Less than 6% of e-scooter riders reported wearing a helmet, according to the study, inScientific Reports.While someprevious workfound women were more likely to ride e-scooters on the pavement, other research saw no sex differences. In a2024 study, Dr Petya Ventsislavova, senior lecturer in transport psychology at Nottingham Trent University, found more than half of e-scooter riders rode on pavements, and with another person at the same time, while men reported using their phones and shooting red lights more than did women.“These figures highlight the urgent need for comprehensive legislation governing private e-scooters,” said Ventsislavova. The legislation should clarify not only where and how e-scooters can be used but also include mandatory safety training, she said.“Unlike cars and motorcycles, e-scooters were introduced without any requirement for formal training, despite being motorised vehicles,” she said. “E-scooters handle very differently from bicycles. Riders stand upright, have a higher centre of gravity, use more sensitive steering, and are more vulnerable to sudden stops caused by small wheels striking kerbs, potholes or road debris. These characteristics make them inherently less stable and contribute to the severity of injuries when crashes occur.”A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “These are concerning findings, and our thoughts are with anyone who has been injured on our roads.Road safetyis our top priority, which is why our e-scooter trials are testing their use in a controlled environment now, before updating the law to ensure they can be used safely more widely.”Explore more on these topicsScienceRoad safetyRoad transportEnglandWalesHospitalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It is British life’: No 10 vows to stop councils trying to limit standing in pubs | London | The Guardian
description: Westminster council has recommended banning ‘vertical drinking’ or ordering at the bar in new draft licensing policy
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Westminster council has recommended banning ‘vertical drinking’ or ordering at the bar in new draft licensing policy
Content: The prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the chancellor, John Healey, at a London pub in July.Photograph: Richard Pohle/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the chancellor, John Healey, at a London pub in July.Photograph: Richard Pohle/AFP/Getty ImagesLondon‘It is British life’: No 10 vows to stop councils trying to limit standing in pubsWestminster council has recommended banning ‘vertical drinking’ or ordering at the bar in new draft licensing policyHelena HortonThu 6 Aug 2026 17.07 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo 10 has vowed to confiscate powers from local councils which try to restrict customers from standing up while drinking in pubs or ordering at the bar.It comes after the Guardianrevealed on Thursdaythat Westminster council in central London recommended not allowing “vertical drinking” or ordering at the bar in itsnew draft licensing policy.The draft document, now out for consultation, recommends that pubs applying for new licences allow only table service rather than bar ordering. It also suggests new pubs in popular nightlife areas including Soho call last orders at 10pm, to reduce noise and disturbance.A Downing Street spokesperson said: “Busy pubs full of people talking to each other is not a public nuisance, it is British life, and it is thousands of jobs.“The government is devolving new licensing powers to the mayor [of London] to help support pubs and nightlife. Soho did not become world famous by taking last orders early, switching the lights off at 10 o’clock.“The prime minister encourages local leaders to work with the industry so that pubs can continue to thrive.”Diageo to nearly double Guinness production and cut jobs in turnaround planRead moreThe government is due to grant new powers to the London mayor,Sadiq Khan, allowing him to “call in” local council decisions he opposes.Khan said of the proposals on X: “You can’t run a world-famous nightlife district with a village-hall mindset.”A spokesperson for the mayor previously said he was against “restrictive and anti-growth policies” and said he hoped to use new powers to be granted to him by the government to stop councils from overreaching.The draft policy says pubs should “discourage excessive drunkenness and encourage the provision of more seating in premises that serve alcohol for people to sit and enjoy a drink and order food by table service in place of open bar space that caters for high-volume vertical drinking”.It goes on to recommend that sales of alcohol and food should be “by waiter or waitress service only”.Operators of pubs and bars in Soho have criticised what they see as overly restrictive licensing policies and said the proposals could kill off West End nightlife.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPaul Swaddle, the Conservative leader of Westminster council, denied the plans amounted to a ban on “vertical drinking”.He told the Press Association that newspapers had carried “confusing stories” about the document and added: “I want to be straight with people. There is no plan, and never has been, to ban drinking while standing up in a Westminster pub.”Responding to Khan’s criticism, he said: “We don’t need lectures from city hall on backing hospitality when they have directed the police to object to every new licence application as their solution to curbing crime in the West End.”The council also plans to ban the opening of new pubs and bars in what it terms the “cumulative impact zone”, encompassing Soho and large parts of the West End.Areas such as Victoria and Mayfair will also face restrictions on new openings if the draft policy is made official.Explore more on these topicsLondonLocal governmentFood & drink industryHospitality industryPubsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: US federal judge halts order for Trump to turn over financial records to BBC | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Judge issues temporary pause while he considers Trump’s request to revise his libel lawsuit against BBC
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Judge issues temporary pause while he considers Trump’s request to revise his libel lawsuit against BBC
Content: Donald Trump speaks at an event at the Red Rock casino resort and spa in Las Vegas on Wednesday.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump speaks at an event at the Red Rock casino resort and spa in Las Vegas on Wednesday.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APDonald TrumpUS federal judge halts order for Trump to turn over financial records to BBCJudge issues temporary pause while he considers Trump’s request to revise his libel lawsuit against BBCMarina DunbarThu 6 Aug 2026 13.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA federal judge has temporarily halted an order requiringDonald Trumpto turn over detailed financial information about his business empire to the BBC as part of an ongoing libel lawsuit.US district judge Roy Altman issued the temporary pause while he considers Trump’s request to revise and narrow parts of his lawsuit against theBBCover a 2024 documentary that aired in the UK.Trump’s legal teamsought to stopthe discovery order that would have given the BBC access to the president’s financial records in the multibillion-dollar case.Trump team pushes to block court order giving BBC access to financial recordsRead moreTrump has argued the BBC’s 2024 documentary about the January 6 attack harmed his business interests. Last month, a Miami-based judge ruled that Trump would have to begin producing extensive financial records by 6 August, including information covering the hundreds of businesses held by the Trump family trust.On Wednesday, Trump’s attorneys asked the court to temporarily suspend that order, arguing the BBC had demanded a “shockingly broad amount of information based on clearly political motivations”.In afour-page ordersigned on Wednesday and released on Thursday, Altman said Trump’s effort to remove his claims that the documentary damaged his brand and businesses could reduce the BBC’s need to obtain his financial records. Trump’s lawyers are seeking to narrow the claim to alleged reputational harm.The BBC has argued that Trump’s business value remains relevant because his public reputation was closely linked to his success as a businessman.The broadcaster’s lawyers also pointed out that Trump’s proposed amended complaint, which has not yet been made public, still seeks $10bn in damages. They contend that amount would be difficult to support if the case was based only on reputational harm.At the center of the lawsuit is a scene from the BBC documentary Trump: A Second Chance, which edited together portions of Trump’s 6 January 2021 speech in a way that made it appear he directly encouraged supporters to attack the US Capitol. The BBC has apologized for the edit but maintains the defamation allegations lack merit.The lawsuit is part of a series of legal actions Trump has launched against media organizations over coverage he says is defamatory or unfair.In a separate case, Trump’s attorneys argued that his $10bndefamation lawsuitagainst the Wall Street Journal should proceed to trial after the newspaper reported on a “bawdy” letter the president was said to have contributed to a birthday book for Jeffrey Epstein in 2003.Trump’s justice department also issued subpoenas to New York Times journalists following the newspaper’s reporting on security concerns involving the Air Force One presidential aircraft before laterwithdrawingthose subpoenas.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpBBCTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Farmer who killed lodger and hid body in concrete in South Yorkshire jailed for life | South Yorkshire | The Guardian
description: Christopher Wright, 73, who shot Richard Dyson and dismembered his remains, given 35-year minimum term
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Christopher Wright, 73, who shot Richard Dyson and dismembered his remains, given 35-year minimum term
Content: DCI Andy Knowles reads a statement outside Sheffield crown court alongside family members of Richard Dyson.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAView image in fullscreenDCI Andy Knowles reads a statement outside Sheffield crown court alongside family members of Richard Dyson.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PASouth YorkshireFarmer who killed lodger and hid body in concrete in South Yorkshire jailed for lifeChristopher Wright, 73, who shot Richard Dyson and dismembered his remains, given 35-year minimum termRaphael BoydThu 6 Aug 2026 10.33 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man who killed his lodger and concealed his dismembered body in a barrel filled with concrete for more than five years has been jailed for a minimum of 35 years.Christopher Wright, a 73-year-old farmer from South Yorkshire, was convicted in July in Sheffield crown court of murdering Richard Dyson, 55, in 2019.Dyson had been living in his car on Wright’s farm in Hoyland and had been doing jobs for the then 67-year-old when the pair had a falling out.Wright, an antique firearms collector who was described as a “weapons fanatic” during his trial, suspected Dyson of stealing some of his prized possessions and selling them.The court heard that when Wright confronted Dyson with his suspicions in November 2019 an argument broke out that ended with Dyson being shot in the chest and arm with a shotgun, killing him.View image in fullscreenChristopher Wright has been jailed for a minimum of 35 years.Photograph: South Yorkshire Police/PAWright, a former butcher, dismembered Dyson’s body over the course of several days, then placed the remains in a barrel which he filled with concrete. He then placed the barrel in a trailer and asked an unsuspecting neighbour to keep the vehicle on their property.Wright was aided in covering up his crime by Karl Schwalbe, a lifelong friend who received a three-year sentence for conspiracy to pervert the course of justice.Dyson’s disappearance was initially treated as a missing person inquiry and his remains went undiscovered for more than five and a half years.While South Yorkshire police were aware that he had been on Wright’s land in the days leading up to his disappearance, they could not find evidence implicating the farmer, who denied any knowledge of Dyson’s whereabouts.Dyson remained missing until July 2025 when police, driven by new evidence that showed Wright had contacted a local farmer about storing a vehicle on his property in the days after Dyson disappeared, searched the farm and found a barrel containing concrete and human remains, which were later identified as Dyson’s.Speaking after sentencing him on Thursday, Mr Justice Cotter told Wright he would probably die in prison and said the killer’s experience as a butcher made him “skilled enough to do such a terrible thing, something few ordinary people would have the stomach for”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExtreme rightwing referrals to Prevent rise 20% amid record anti-terror reportingRead moreDyson’s daughter Bethany Dainty, who filed a missing person report in the days after her father was murdered, read a victim impact statement in court detailing how hard it had been not knowing her father’s fate: “I couldn’t grieve because I did not know the truth.”She added: “While I cried myself to sleep, while I begged for answers, while I prayed my dad would walk through the door again, someone already knew where he was. Someone watched me suffer for years and said nothing. That level of cruelty is impossible for me to understand.”After the sentencing, DCI Andy Knowles praised Dyson’s family for the strength they showed during a “long, complex and emotionally draining” investigation.Knowles said: “Wright and Schwalbe knew what happened to Richard and even with the evidence against them, they continued to deny accountability, making Richard’s family endure a trial, listen to harrowing evidence and distressing testimonies.“The strength and dignity in confronting each moment of this process has been nothing short of extraordinary.”Explore more on these topicsSouth YorkshireCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC hires 26-year-old entrepreneur to help reach younger audiences | BBC | The Guardian
description: Brandon Relph, who founded first company at 13, joins strategy team in ‘much-needed step’ for the broadcaster
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Brandon Relph, who founded first company at 13, joins strategy team in ‘much-needed step’ for the broadcaster
Content: Brandon Relph has jokingly described himself as ‘the go-to guy who knows the youth’.Photograph: FacebookView image in fullscreenBrandon Relph has jokingly described himself as ‘the go-to guy who knows the youth’.Photograph: FacebookBBCBBC hires 26-year-old entrepreneur to help reach younger audiencesBrandon Relph, who founded first company at 13, joins strategy team in ‘much-needed step’ for the broadcasterMichael SavageMedia editorThu 6 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 26-year-old business prodigy and self-styled gen Z whisperer has been drafted in by the BBC as it battles to reach young audiences increasingly choosing content creators onYouTubeand TikTok over traditional broadcasters.Brandon Relph, who founded his first company aged 13, and has been praised by Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak, has joined the BBC’s strategy team to help counter the existential threat of falling audiences among young people.Relph has jokingly described himself as “the go-to guy who knows the youth” and has already had a dizzying career. He made his first £10,000 before the age of 16 with a company based around the Minecraft video game and founded several other tech and marketing companies as a teenager.The BBC, along with all broadcasters, is facing a huge generational shift in the way young audiences consume media. While 78% of the over-75s still watch live TV on a television in the course of a month,less than half of 16 to 24-year-olds do so, turning instead to content creators on digital platforms such as YouTube.Matt Brittin, thenew director generalbrought in for his experience in the tech world, has pledged to reshape the BBC as part of the renewal of its royal charter, which is being negotiated with ministers.View image in fullscreenMatt Brittin took over as the new BBC director general in May.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersPrioritising digital content will be reflected in the major cuts being made across the BBC’s services. The corporation is already trying to adapt, recently announcing a deal to producebespoke YouTube content.Relph, who previously claimed the title of the UK’s youngest ever chief executive, has specialised in talking to executives about marketing to young audiences, stating his businesses have been “built on people’s lack of understanding of our generation”.His exploits have included building a large online audience for live video gameshows, while his company also built a Minecraft version of a Tesla after he and his business partner met Elon Musk at a convention.Those familiar with his past entrepreneurial efforts said he had encountered resistance within the media industry to embrace online content creators, which he sees as necessary to reach young audiences. That resistance is now melting away.Another of his projects, touted as a “Netflix for the creator generation”, could not find the venture capital needed. Relph was subsequently hired by the consulting firm Accenture, from where he joined the BBC.Relph has already started in the BBC’s strategy team, with insiders praising his gen Z focus. Previous colleagues described him as a “special case”, stating he was popular with his teams and willing to politely question senior executives over their strategy despite his young age.His appointment has been praised by figures pushing the BBC to take a radically different approach to reaching young audiences, but they also said it needed to reflect a wider effort.“Brandon looks great – he’s somebody who’s had a very successful career, done brilliant work and is obviously very talented,” said Jordan Schwarzenberger, the manager ofthe SidemenYouTube collective. “He’s clearly an entrepreneur at heart.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The BBC’s challenge is a bigger issue than one hire. They need to address that institutional media, distributed traditionally, can’t reach an audience who have simply gone to other places. Young audiences are not watching linear. And the BBC is pretty much built upon its linear broadcasting foundation.”Relph has previously criticised the iPlayer over its user experience and said that the “BBC won’t have a long term future” without a greater focus on younger people.AI labels to be compulsory on authentic-looking content under EU rulesRead moreSome in the BBC argue its efforts to adapt to young audiences are already well under way. It is the only UK brand in the top five most used media for the 16-34 age group, alongside YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and Netflix. It still reaches 63% of the age group on average, each week. However, BBC figures are acutely aware of the scale of the challenge.“Brandon’s appointment is a much-needed step,” said Jo Redfern, a former BBC insider and digital media expert. “Anyone tasked with making the BBC indispensable to the under-24s requires a momentum internally and externally because there’s an urgency.“The BBC has been foundational in British life and envied around the world, but it risks losing that position with younger [groups] and it would be a shame if that were to happen.“The BBC’s instinct is that of a broadcaster, the very definition of which is one way, at a time when young people demand a participatory relationship with media. Every barrier to that is a reason to go elsewhere and there’s no shortage of places to find media that fulfils their needs.”Explore more on these topicsBBCDigital mediaYouTubenewsShareReuse this content

title: Possession review – a nightmarish plantation drama with a divisive paranormal twist | Television | The Guardian
description: Gugu Mbatha-Raw is a lawyer sent to Jamaica to get to the bottom of a mystery about an inheritance. What unfolds is an evocative story packed with horrors, past injustices – and a supernatural element that you will rate or hate
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Gugu Mbatha-Raw is a lawyer sent to Jamaica to get to the bottom of a mystery about an inheritance. What unfolds is an evocative story packed with horrors, past injustices – and a supernatural element that you will rate or hate
Content: A dual-timeline mystery … Gugu Mbatha-Raw in Possession.Photograph: Des WillieView image in fullscreenA dual-timeline mystery … Gugu Mbatha-Raw in Possession.Photograph: Des WillieTV reviewTelevisionReviewPossession review – a nightmarish plantation drama with a divisive paranormal twistGugu Mbatha-Raw is a lawyer sent to Jamaica to get to the bottom of a mystery about an inheritance. What unfolds is an evocative story packed with horrors, past injustices – and a supernatural element that you will rate or hateLucy ManganThu 6 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat do you do when a client worth £50m – thanks to family ownership of a Jamaican sugar plantation upon which a modern fortune was built – pops his clogs and is unexpectedly revealed to have cut his only child out of his will, leaving the lot to a hitherto unknown “African national” called Cudjoe East? Why, you call in your firm’s (likely only) biracial lawyer, Claudia (Gugu Mbatha-Raw), to go over to Kingston, find him and discredit him as soon as possible. “Sounds like a job for a partner, really,” replies Claudia and, promotion thus secured, duly heads out for her mother’s homeland. She may wish, before we are very far in, that she had gone for senior partnership instead.The planter’s house is one that has been appearing to her in recent nightmares that have been full of fires, terrified figures and strange symbols. But! She is a woman of the law, not superstition, so she sets the screaming Afro-gothic warnings aside and gets on with searching the house for anything that could suggest the pro-Cudjoe will is invalid and questioning the locals for any clue as to where Cudjoe himself might be. Her late client’s driver Angelo (Jeff Crossley) tells her that he introduced the pair about six months ago when his boss wanted to learn more about local history. Angelo assures her that she will not be able to talk Cudjoe into giving up his legacy.Soon Oliver (Jonny Lee Miller, in posh, nervy mode), the disinherited son, has joined her so that they can investigate and – he is divorced as well as disinherited – build sexual tension together.What follows is a dual-timeline mystery. One story unfolds in the present, another 300 years ago when the estate was staffed by enslaved people, overseen by increasingly cruel members of Oliver’s ancestral line and facing the series of rebellions known as Tacky’s War – with a supernatural inflection that allows the two increasingly to mesh. Claudia’s nightmares increase, populated perhaps by spectral members of other ancestral lines. Images and objects that appear in the dream world turn up in the house, along with documents that make the abstract horrors of colonialism concrete. The spirits with which the local people think the house, their land, their culture is infused become increasingly restless. If you believe in that kind of thing, of course – but it does become much harder to deny once Oliver has been levitated and bounced off the ceiling by an unseen force.View image in fullscreenA potent conjuring … Possession.Photograph: Des WillieWhen Claudia meets Cudjoe (Sheldon Shepherd), he is as unmoving as Angelo promised, but also claims to be nearly 300 years old – the surviving, or surviving incarnation of, Matthew, the illegitimate son (which is to say, a child conceived by the rape of an enslaved woman) of the then landowner. Matthew was promised his freedom and the estate by his father, but was denied it by Charlotte (Bel Powley), their father’s legitimate daughter. Who may or may not have hastened her father’s death from tongue cancer – strangely contracted after he cut out Matthew’s grandmother’s tongue as a punishment for possible involvement in an abortive uprising.So the past’s injustices, sufferings and legacies work themselves into and through the present. Possession is the first full-length work from Karla Crome, so far best known for her acting roles in Misfits, You, Me and the Apocalypse and most recently in Something Very Bad Is Going to Happen. It is a potent conjuring of the pervasive, enduring evils and toxicities of colonialism. It’s a powerful look at how unadmitted sins and guilt manifest themselves and whether justice for some crimes – such sprawling, normalised, heinous crimes that you begin almost to warm to those who act out of simple depravity and malevolence – can ever be done. Are reparations possible? Where does responsibility begin and end? What is better: ancestral spirit vengeance being visited upon the guilty’s descendants, or the parlaying of a boss’s modern exploitation of your skin colour for “optics” into money and promotion?For some the accumulating paranormal-mystical element will add to the dread and horror. For others, there is a danger that it obscures the truth of the story and the suffering. Where you land, I suppose, largely depends on whether you feel that ghosts and spirits are capable of thinking up and delivering any worse experiences than man seems able to conjure and visit on his fellow man. Part of me always feels that recourse to the diabolic or ineffable is a cop-out, but that is undoubtedly a vast failure of imagination on my part.But either way, Possession is a well-textured, evocative tale touching on many important questions, if never quite digging down far enough into any of them to be truly satisfying.Possession aired on Sky Atlantic and is available on Now.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewJonny Lee MillerThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Which type of thinker are you? + US explosive diarrhoea outbreak |  | The Guardian
description: Madeleine Finlay is joined by Ian Sample, Guardian science editor, to discuss three eye-catching science stories including an investigation that has identified four distinct types of thinker. Also on the agenda is the unprecedented cyclosporiasis outbreak in the US which has now been linked to two fatalities, and the funding cuts that threaten the iconic Jodrell Bank world heritage site, home to the Lovell telescope
Author: Ellie Bury

title: Throwing Muses frontwoman Kristin Hersh: ‘I was compelled to make music after cracking my skull open’ | Kristin Hersh | The Guardian
description: The alt-rock veteran answers your questions on Buddhist time travel techniques, duetting with Michael Stipe, and her autobiographical new album
Author: Priya Elan
Headline: The alt-rock veteran answers your questions on Buddhist time travel techniques, duetting with Michael Stipe, and her autobiographical new album
Content: ‘No one’s ever left the Throwing Muses’ … Kristin Hersh.Photograph: Peter MellekasView image in fullscreen‘No one’s ever left the Throwing Muses’ … Kristin Hersh.Photograph: Peter MellekasFilm & Music reader interviewKristin HershInterviewThrowing Muses frontwoman Kristin Hersh: ‘I was compelled to make music after cracking my skull open’As told toPriya ElanThe alt-rock veteran answers your questions on Buddhist time travel techniques, duetting with Michael Stipe, and her autobiographical new albumThu 6 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 16.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo you think Throwing Muses would have sounded differentwere it not for your bicycle accident?[Hersh was struck by a car when she was 16, resulting in a concussionthat changed the way she heard sound.]Bhafc99Yes. I think people might have liked us more, but we would have been more forgettable. Our songs were not very marketable. They came from a place of such utter honesty that it was difficult for us to become a band with an image, ambition or direction, which plays well on a human level, but not on a corporate one. Some people hate our music; they can’t deal with it because it’s triggering [emotionally], which I get.I was compelled to make music after cracking my skull open and then my life was very upsetting. But at the same time, I had real listeners. If you happen to come across a song that resonates with you, then it’s yours – you can ignore the musician who played it, because they were just the messenger.Your guitar sound and playing is so distinctive, creative and superb – do you have an influence orherowho has inspired or guided you?GoonergeofNobody. We started the Muses when I was 11, so I didn’t have time to invent a sonic vocabulary. I wish my music could be that palatable. I think there’s a place where music can touch people and not be off-putting, but I couldn’t engage in that way.View image in fullscreenOn stage at Krankenhaus festival, Cumbria, 2025.Photograph: Paul HudsonBut I babysat for this music critic and, every time I put his kids to bed, I was allowed to sit in his office and listen to records that hadn’t been released. One was the Violent Femmes’ first album [in 1983]. I remember the music critic told me that the boy in the band was “the male me” and I admit when I heard it I was like: “He’s right!” They had this simple, percussive and raw sound that was very effective. [Singer] Gordon Gano sat in his adolescent-boy self and was just being very honest. That first record is a reminder that we’re all attracted to that sweet spot where we seem to be in enthusiastic agony. And it turns out to be a party!What was the inspiration behind the song Counting Backwards?_Tiana_Time-tripping! I was raised Buddhist by hippy parents and I never thought I was made for letting go of the past, which any therapist will tell you is really unhealthy! But I felt very strongly that I could alter the present by altering the past in a dream state. And that it has to be done with kindness.I am curiouswhyLeslie Langstonleft Throwing Muses betweenHunkpapa[1989] andThe Real Ramona[1991]. What happened?Androo1984She has a health issue with her skin where she couldn’t play bass for decades. She didn’t play on The Real Ramona, but then she came back for our next record, Red Heaven. Leslie ended up moving to the west coast and didn’t want to tour, so Bernard [Georges] came in. Leslie’s just now starting to play bass again and she almost played on the last record. She’s a social worker and my hero; we spend a lot of time thanking each other for being on Earth. I lean on her – she’s one of my favourite people.View image in fullscreenThrowing Muses –(from left)David Narcizo, Hersh, Tanya Donnelly and Leslie Langston – in Chicago, 1989.Photograph: Paul Natkin/WireImageAny chance of you working with [her step-sister and Throwing Muses co-founder] Tanya Donelly again?ChrisOwensYes – she was on tour with us a couple of years ago. She sang on the second self-titled Muses record [2003]. And my son Ryder just stayed at her house when he flew into Boston. All doors are open: anybody who is in the musical moment with me is allowed in, but it’s a big ask. No one’s ever left the Throwing Muses, it’s more like: “You feel like playing? OK, let’s do it!”I supported you in Dublin in 2001 and you said I reminded you of Frank Black. Have you seen Frank lately?PaulOReillyThe first time I heard the Pixies was when we were in soundcheck. A painter friend was at the bar and he said: “You should listen to this band,” which I would never normally do. I thought Charles [Thompson, AKA Frank Black] was a woman at first. I thought she was so cool – she had a shaved head and was singing about her dick. I was like: “She rocks!”But I forgave him for not being a girl and then I said: “I’m never letting go of you. You’re playing all of our shows with us, and here’s my manager, and here’s my label, and you’re coming on tour, and we’re gonna make all of this happen.” I did it for selfish reasons, because I wanted to hear them the whole time and I didn’t want to be alone any more. That relationship lasted for years. Charles once drew a pie chart on the wall of a dressing room and said: “This is a Throwing Muses song.” It was a moment where I forgave myself for carrying my musical treasure into the hurricane of the music biz.Watch the video for Dark Eyed Junco.Your Ghost [from herdebut solo album, featuringREM’s Michael Stipe] is one of the most gorgeous songs I have ever heard – twounique voices coming together on such a haunting duet. Was it written with Michael Stipe in mind and are you still in contact?Frou1967I wasn’t ever going to have a solo career; I wasn’t interested. But I had to get off Warner Brothers and breaking up the band wasn’t going to work. [In order to fulfil the recording contract, she was required to make another album.] I had this tape of leftover acoustic songs and Michael Stipe picked it up. He called me up and said: “I love this tape.” He knew I was going to fuck up the recording of it because I didn’t care. He called the studio as I was having trouble recording Your Ghost and I realised I needed his voice on it.Not too long ago, I was in New York playing a solo show and he was in the audience and I didn’t know. When I was playing Your Ghost, apparently he was in the back singing his parts and freaking out all the people around him. But I didn’t know!You’vebeen prolific over the past decade. Is it safe to assume your EMDRnightmare is over? [Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing is a psychotherapy techniquethat Hersh used to treatpost-traumatic stress disorder and a dissociative disorder.]JosephKyleMy life has been so very difficult; my whole system was just confused. I reacted to the real [PTSD] triggers by passing out, vomiting and screaming. My band members knew to protect me from my triggers, but that’s hard in life. Thanks to EMDR, I can still play music, which I didn’t think I would be able to. I wouldn’t recommend it for everyone. EMDR is like psychological chemo. I would collapse every time I did it. And then you can’t stop it – it’s like a snowballing process, where all the pain you dissociated from comes back to you at once.Phoebe Bridgers: Lost Weekend review – long-awaited return is a thrilling, daring study in dislocationRead moreYour upcoming album, Sugar on Blackstone, has such an evocative title. Where did it come from?VerulamiumParkRangerMaking this album, I was back in my home town of Providence, Rhode Island, living in a street called Hope. It’s off a street called Blackstone, which has this intense path on it that’s like this ship of lost souls. So I had “Hope” on the one side and the ship of lost souls on the other. These songs are autobiographical. They are very old stories from childhood, some of them dating back to the 1970s. There is one [Dark Eyed Junco] about me and my little brother, how we were scared to go home because our stepfather was there. So we just played basketball until we couldn’t any more. The song is about how the feel of the basketball is more important than getting it in the hoop. I don’t even want to aim for the hoop.Sugar on Blackstone is released on 18 September via FireExplore more on these topicsKristin HershFilm & Music reader interviewIndiePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like a jet taking off’: the cicada that can top 120 decibels and nearly break the pain threshold | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: The palm-sized greengrocer comes in many colours and has long been a collectible item for Australian children
Author: Petra Stock
Headline: The palm-sized greengrocer comes in many colours and has long been a collectible item for Australian children
Content: Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianInvertebrate of the year 2026Wildlife‘Like a jet taking off’: the cicada that can top 120 decibels and nearly break the pain thresholdThe palm-sized greengrocer is bright, loud and abundant, and has long been a collectible item for Australian childrenRevealed: the top 10 invertebrates of the yearSupported byAbout this contentPetra StockThu 6 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore marbles, stamps and trading cards, there were cicadas.There are thousands of cicada species globally, but for Australian children the craze centres on one particularly collectible item: the greengrocer.“In both Sydney and Melbourne, greengrocers come out every now and again in fairly decent numbers, and they’re coming out in leafy gardens and parks, quite close to where people are,” says the environmental consultant Dr Lindsay Popple. Searching for and collecting cicadas has become an activity firmly entrenched in children’s folklore, he says.Most of their lives are spent as nymphs underground, but when they emerge in late spring, greengrocers are bright and abundant.About the size of an eraser, this perfectly palm-sized minibeast comes in a variety of vividly coloured morphs, each with a nickname to match. There’s the yellow Monday, the masked devil, red warrior and chocolate soldier, and the appropriately rare, blue moon. Who wouldn’t want to collect them all?View image in fullscreenThe greengrocer’s peer, the yellow Monday cicada.Photograph: Ken Griffiths/AlamyDom Yates, a Guardian reader from New Zealand, is a fan. “They sing joyously after living years underground so we should appreciate their happy efforts all the more,” he says.Unlike the North American cicada, which emerges in a 17-year cycle, greengrocers materialise en masse in alternating batches, roughly at seven yearly intervals, with 2027 the next big event.When cicada nymphs become adults, they shed their skins and grow wings, leaving behind their exoskeletons on trees and fences These are extra treasures for children to discover and stash inside lunchboxes.Every cicada species has its own acoustic identity, Popple says, and the Australian greengrocer, found along the east coast in some of the most populated parts of the country, is one of the loudest.View image in fullscreenMale greengrocers broadcast their tune throughout the day and at dusk to attract a mate.Photograph: FLPA/AlamyGreengrocers produce two main tunes, one a continuous drone, and the other a kind of croaking pulse, using drum-like organs on either side of their bodies called tymbals, and amplifying the sound with their hollow abdomens.Popple says the males broadcast at intervals throughout the day and often at dusk, trying to attract a mate. Its Queensland cousin, the northern greengrocer, is known as the “seven o’clock cicada” for its propensity to pipe up at dinnertime.It’s a spectacular racket. “Close to them, it’s like being near a jet taking off, it’s really loud,” Popple says. “On a really, really, warm morning, if you get a really hot day, they can start up calling pretty early in the day, which can be a bit of a wake-up for some people.”As the 16-year-old Guardian reader Matteo says: “They’re loud and gorgeous and they climb trees and shout. What’s not to love?” Indeed.Greengrocer cicadas are among the loudest invertebrates on land, reportedly reaching volumesas high as 120 decibelsat close range – that’s nearing the pain threshold for human hearing, according to the Australian museum.In general, the closer you are the louder they sound.But, perhaps luckily, if you get too close they’ll stop singing.It’sinvertebrate of the year again! From August 3-12, every day we’ll becelebrating one of the thousands of amazing invertebrates that our readers have nominated, and then, when you’ve got to hear about all of them, we’ll open the voting so you can choose your favourites. Don’t hesitate to get in touch with thoughts and ideas: email us atenvironment.desk@theguardian.comwith Invertebrate in the subject line.Explore more on these topicsWildlifeInvertebrate of the year 2026featuresShareReuse this content

title: American witchhunt: how the McCarthy blacklist annihilated the Hollywood left | Movies | The Guardian
description: A retrospective at the Locarno film festival looks back at the era of Huac’s domination of US culture, uncovering some sobering lessons for now
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: A retrospective at the Locarno film festival looks back at the era of Huac’s domination of US culture, uncovering some sobering lessons for now
Content: Eleanor Parker in Caged (1950).Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenEleanor Parker in Caged (1950).Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyMoviesAmerican witchhunt: how the McCarthy blacklist annihilated the Hollywood leftA retrospective at the Locarno film festival looks back at the era of Huac’s domination of US culture, uncovering some sobering lessons for nowPhuong LeThu 6 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 01.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn September 2025, Disney and ABC announced that Jimmy Kimmel and his late-night talkshowwould be taken off the air indefinitely, after a conservative backlash against the host’s comments about the murder of far-right influencer Charlie Kirk. President Donald Trump personally championed the decision,calling it “great news for America”. He further called for other programmes critical of his administration to be removed. Though Kimmel’s suspension was reversed within a week, many commentators viewed this concerning development not as a sudden escalation of crisis, but a continuation of Hollywood’s habitual acquiescence to authoritarian pressure.View image in fullscreenEdward Dmytryk answers questions before the House Committee on Un-American Activities in 1951, in Washington.Photograph: Associated PressIn aguest essay for the New York Times, journalist and Trump biopic]The Apprenticescreenwriter Gabriel Sherman explicitly linked Kimmel’s cancellation to the Hollywood blacklist of the 1940s and 1950s, during which hundreds of film workers were accused of communist sympathies and unpatriotic subversion, barred from practising their craft, some forced into exile. “Each time, studios claimed they had no choice,” writes Sherman. “Each time, they did – and they made it.”This sordid chapter in Hollywood history – and the long shadow it continues to cast – comes under renewed scrutiny at this year’s Locarno film festival. Curated by Iranian film-maker/critic Ehsan Khosbakht,director of Celluloid Underground, an expansive retrospective programme showcases features, shorts, archival newsreels and recent documentaries. The bulk of the screenings are devoted to blacklisted stars, writers and directors and the works they made at the height of the “red scare” – much of which was produced under pseudonyms. But Khosbakht has also made space for controversial figures such as Elia Kazan and Edward Dmytryk, infamous for informing on their peers in front of Congress. It’s a fascinating juxtaposition that finesses the popular Us-v-Them narrative, and illustrates one of the most tragic outcomes of the blacklist, namely the annihilation of a once-thriving Hollywood left. Under McCarthyism, people previously united by shared political ideology found themselves enemies.View image in fullscreenMarked man … John Garfield with Shelley Winters in He Ran All the Way (1951).Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyPerhaps the most prominent victim was John Garfield, a consummate actor of rare intensity and one of the pioneers of method acting on screen in films such as The Postman Always Rings Twice, Body and Soul and Gentleman’s Agreement. His studio assignments soon dwindled and his career was cut short when he declined to name names to the House Un-American Activities Committee (Huac). Garfield’s precarious final years are eerily mirrored inHe Ran All the Way, from 1951, the actor’s final film before his death at 39 from a heart attack. In this taut noir, one of the highlights of the retrospective, he plays a thief and a murderer on the run. Much of the film takes place inside a claustrophobic flat where the marked man has taken a family hostage while the police close in. Such a setup is not uncommon in the noir genre, yet the socially conscious script, co-written by fellow blacklisteeDalton Trumbo, transforms this criminal tale into a potent allegory. For the politically hunted in Hollywood, there seemed to be no escape.Themes of persecution, entrapment and warring allegiances recur again and again in this period. Prime examples include John Cromwell’s 1950 women’s prison film Caged; Fred Zinnemann’s classic western High Noon, from 1952; and Irving Lerner’s 1959 fugitive drama City of Fear. These films allude to the culture of fear endured by the blacklisted; other titles exemplify the radical, socialist beliefs that first landed them in trouble. There are pro-labour tales of working-class struggle such as Dmytryk’s 1943 Tender Comrade, about the women left behind while men were away during the war, and Salt of the Earth, about a miners’ strike in New Mexico, which was made outside the studio system by blacklistees in 1954. At the same time there were searing indictments of racism and sexism: Smash-Up: The Story of a Woman, from 1947, starring Susan Hayward as a singer who gives up her career for her husband, and Intruder in the Dust, a noir adapted from William Faulkner about a black man accused of murder.View image in fullscreenSearin indictment … poster for Smash-Up (1947).Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyThrough this season, we can see the Hollywood left as an artistic movement as well as a political one, with its own recurring visual and storytelling motifs. It also captures the ideological catch-22 of working within the studio system where films commissioned for the war effort – sometimes containing sympathetic but politically naive depictions of the USSR, then an ally of the US against Axis powers – would later be used as examples of treasonous subversiveness.Exile was the fate of many of the blacklisted workers, and this retrospective tellingly gathers productions from Argentina, Spain, Italy and elsewhere. Britain emerged as a vital creative haven, with the largest number of American blacklistees residing in London. But all was not all smooth sailing, as many struggled to find work. Though he would become an essential contributor to British cinema with classics such as The Servant (1963) and The Go-Between (1971), American director Joseph Losey felt pure panic when he first arrived in the capital: “I was petrified. And I had physical attacks. I thought that I was going to die.” Losey poured his turmoil into the strikingly self-reflexive 1956 film The Intimate Stranger, co-scripted by blacklisted screenwriter Howard E Koch. Centring on a US film-maker banished to London, the film swaps political persecution for an adulterous scandal, but the atmosphere of paranoia remains the same. “I feel as if I’m out in the open with somebody ready to take a potshot at me,” exclaims the tortured protagonist, “and I don’t know who or where or how.”View image in fullscreenHappy ending? … Charlie Chaplin, left, in A King in New York (1957).Photograph: Chaplin/AllstarA footnote to the Hollywood blacklist story was the brief return to the UK of England’s prodigal son, Charlie Chaplin. Though targeted by Huac, Chaplin was never called to testify, and his re-entry permit to the USwas revoked in 1952as he travelled to London to promote his new film Limelight. After settling in Switzerland, Chaplin made A King in New York on a soundstage at Shepperton studios. Like Losey’s dramas, it carries shades of autobiography. Chaplin plays a deposed European king who is suspected of communism after taking an American boy with a socialist upbringing under his wing. Despite Chaplin’s previous ordeal in America, the film ends on a markedly hopeful note: wrapping the weeping boy in his arms, Chaplin’s fallen king reassures the despondent child of a not-so-far future when “all this hysteria is over”.Considering how the political compass has once again veered towards extremism in the US, Chaplin’s gentle optimism seems sadly misplaced. Most of these films sound an urgent warning from the past. Whether produced independently or abroad, masked by pseudonyms or fully credited, these acts of artistic resistance attest to the resilience of creative integrity against the odds.Red & Black – Hollywood Left and the Blacklist is at the Locarno film festival until 15 AugustExplore more on these topicsFilmCommunismCensorshipfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘They were told bikes were for men’: how Latin America’s city of cycling is breaking gender barriers | Cycling | The Guardian
description: With less than a third of cycling journeys taken by women, Colombia’s capital, Bogotá, is installing bike lanes, teaching cycling and making sure ‘stereotypes are left behind’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With less than a third of cycling journeys taken by women, Colombia’s capital, Bogotá, is installing bike lanes, teaching cycling and making sure ‘stereotypes are left behind’
Content: Eliana González rides around her neighbourhood on a cargo bike with her baby, son and dog.Photograph: Al Colegio en BiciView image in fullscreenEliana González rides around her neighbourhood on a cargo bike with her baby, son and dog.Photograph: Al Colegio en BiciSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanCycling‘They were told bikes were for men’: how Latin America’s city of cycling is breaking gender barriersWith less than a third of cycling journeys taken by women, Colombia’s capital, Bogotá, is installing bike lanes, teaching cycling and making sure ‘stereotypes are left behind’Supported byAbout this contentChristina Noriega in BogotáThu 6 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEliana González has a busy morning ahead of her, dropping off her son at school and picking up groceries. Her trusted vehicle to get around in Bogotá is a colourful cargo bike, adapted to carry her two children and occasionally her dog.“For me, my cargo bike is a way to carry my children safely and comfortably without polluting the environment,” she says.Widely regarded as a global cycling success story, the Colombian city of 10 million people records nearly 900,000 bicycle trips each day – more than any other city in Latin America.Now, city officials are working towards another milestone: achieving gender parity in cycling by 2039. Women accounted for only 28% of Bogotá’s daily bicycle trips in 2023,according to the city’s latest mobility survey. “Our goal is to move from a [nearly] 30–70 split to 50–50 parity,” says Claudia Díaz, Bogotá’s secretary of mobility.Closing the gender gap makes for a more inclusive city, but also brings environmental benefits. Transportation isBogotá’s largest source of greenhouse emissions, and officials say that boosting the number of female cyclists could support the capital’s goal of becomingcarbon neutral by 2050.View image in fullscreenEvery Sunday, Bogotá closes off major roads and opens them to cyclists and pedestrians as it works towards becoming carbon neutral by 2050.Photograph: Al Colegio en Bici“The challenge we face is how to increase the number of cycling trips,” says Díaz. “The more we increase the number of cycling trips, the more environmental benefits we see for our city.”Experts say gender equality is essential for cities to fully realise the benefits of investing in sustainable transportation, which can lead to lower greenhouse gas emissions, cleaner air and reduced traffic congestion.“Those impacts aren’t really going to happen if only half the population is ever going to use that [transport] system,” says Dana Yanocha, a senior manager at the Institute for Transportation and Development Policy, a nonprofit organisation promoting sustainable transport.Increasing women’s participation in cycling remains a challenge, especially across the global south, Yanocha says. In many of the cities where her organisation works, women make up only a small share of cyclists, often accounting for less than 10% of daily bicycle trips.In 2021, Bogotá adopted a new cycling public policy, the first of its kind in Colombia, that incorporated a gender perspective. As part of the initiative, researchers withC40 Cities Finance Facility, a programme that helps cities develop climate infrastructure projects, looked at why women cycle less than men in Bogotá.They identified several barriers.About 60% of women surveyedsaid they avoided cycling because they feared theft or assault, 40% expressed concerns about being hit by a vehicle and nearly one-third said they had never learned to ride a bicycle.View image in fullscreenA woman learning to ride a bicycle in Bogotá.Photograph: Al Colegio en BiciOne way officials have since been addressing safety concerns is by building more cycle lanes, whichresearch showshelps female cyclists feel safer. Bogotá’s network of protected bike lanes –the largest in Latin America– nowspans 425 miles (683.9km), according to the city council.The city is also repairing deteriorated lanes, installing lighting, improving connectivity andincreasing police patrolsalong busy cycling corridors. “By improving infrastructure, we can help women feel that riding a bike is a viable option for them,” says Diaz.For many women, however, the biggest barrier is simply never having learned to ride. Sergio Prieto helps to overseeBogotá’s Bike School, a city programme that teaches about 40,000 residents to cycle each year. He says that about 80% of participants are women.“Many older women come here because they were never allowed to ride a bicycle as girls,” Prieto says. “They were told bikes were for men, that women shouldn’t be riding them. Here, those barriers and stereotypes are left behind.”In 2018, González foundedMamacitas en Bician initiative that encourages mothers to cycle. Her work addresses an often overlooked reality: the leading reason why women move across Bogotá is for caregiving trips, such as taking children to school,according to one study.But caregivers face discrimination for choosing to cycle, González says. When she first started riding with her baby, strangers shouted at her, calling her irresponsible, she says. But rather than quit, she created a community, helping mothers customise their bikes to safely carry children, organising group rides for families and teaching women and children to cycle.“I realised how important it is to have safe spaces where we can move through the world as women, in a body that is treated differently by society and subjected to violence,” she says.View image in fullscreenSergio Prieto (centre) helps run Bogotá’s Bike School programme. He poses with two teachers after a class in May.Photograph: Al Colegio en BiciGonzález says she encourages women to take up cycling because of its social benefits, including greater independence and improved health. But for her, riding a bicycle is also a way to help shape the kind of city she wants for herself and her children.“We still have so many green spaces in our city, and I want to do my part to help protect them,” she says. “If I get around by bicycle, I’m contributing to that environmental effort.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanColombiaWomen's rights and gender equalityAmericasSexual violenceTravel and transportfeaturesShareReuse this content
