title: The takedown of Jason Arday has overjoyed the right, and must be a wake-up call for the left | Jason Okundaye | The Guardian
description: The Cambridge academic has rightly now resigned. But that won’t end the targeting of senior black figures or the lazy way institutions promote faux equality, says Guardian columnist Jason Okundaye
Author: Jason Okundaye
Headline: The Cambridge academic has rightly now resigned. But that won’t end the targeting of senior black figures or the lazy way institutions promote faux equality, says Guardian columnist Jason Okundaye
Content: Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianOpinionUniversity of CambridgeThe takedown of Jason Arday has overjoyed the right, and must be a wake-up call for the leftJason OkundayeThe Cambridge academic has rightly now resigned. But that won’t end the targeting of senior black figures or the lazy way institutions promote faux equalityThu 6 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 14.01 EDTShare‘To be honest with you, I thought you’d just believe me.” That was the breathtaking response of Prof Jason Arday whenthe Guardianinterrogated the details he provided of an alleged racist campaign of intimidation against him, which involved a severed pig’s head, a masked man wielding a knife and bullets in the post. Arday had been unable to provide evidence, and when the Guardian contacted the relevant parties, including a south London butcher and the police, his claims were either refuted or could not be verified.Arday, whose appointment as professor of sociology of education at Cambridge became a widely lauded moment in the aftermath of Black Lives Matter, has found himself in the eye of the storm. Allegations of extensive plagiarism in his doctoral thesis, completed at Liverpool John Moores University, recently made their way from the Substack of self-described “race realist” academic Nathan Cofnas into the national press. The defence of Arday had rested on the fact that an investigation had already been conducted, and cleared him of plagiarism. And yet the case has taken on a life of its own.In recent weeks, more of Arday’s story has come under scrutiny: from claims of having installed water points in South America and west Africa with the charity WaterAid (WaterAid said it does not send volunteers abroad), to having run 30 marathons in 35 days, the last dozen or so after suffering a hairline fracture in his leg. After mounting pressure, Cambridge announced that it hadlaunched a formal investigationinto his academic qualifications and honorary appointments. Following this announcement, Arday resigned from his positions at the university. Though he has chosen to step aside topreserve his “wellbeing”, this has become a national story that will not go away.Allegations of plagiarism in a doctoral thesis do not usually make for riveting, front-page news. Indeed, in 2023, when the Cambridge history professor William O’Reilly faced allegations of plagiarising student essays, thepress coverageconsisted of barely half a dozen articles (a tribunal ruled the plagiarism was “the product of negligent acts but was not deliberate”). Few people could care less about what academics get up to.But Arday could not expect to be similarly insulated by academia’s remoteness. This story has endured, stubbornly, because it is so perfectly calibrated for some of the most combustible charges of Britain’s culture wars: namely, that academic standards have been surrendered to a woke orthodoxy, and that minorities are unfairly advanced in the name of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives.View image in fullscreen‘Prof Jason Arday has found himself in the eye of the storm.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianThe instinct of progressives had been to defend Arday; indeed, many went on to sign an open letter in support of him, seeing him as simply another black man under a sustained press attack. This was not least because the charges against him originated with Cofnas, who had beendismissed from his postat Emmanuel College, Cambridge, in 2024 after making pseudo-scientific claims that under a true meritocracy black people would “disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment”. And for many in the rightwing press, this is their victory lap, their vindication. The spectacle of it is just too grim to behold. The headlines of “DEI darling” and “diversity poster boy” barely conceal their excitement. Gotcha!I do not care to examine the quality of Arday’s scholarship, research or life story beyond what has already been written elsewhere. What concerns me is how little space remains for a genuinelyprogressive critique of institutional diversity practices– one capable of scrutinising how for many organisations and corporations symbolic representation has been a substitute for deeper reform, leaving it vulnerable to just this kind of backlash. It has also meant that the right has enjoyed a near monopoly on criticism of DEI, leaving it to frame it entirely on its own terms.Let’s take a look back at the coverage of Arday’s appointment at Cambridge in 2023. The headline was that Arday, then 37, was to become the “youngest black professor” ever appointed at Cambridge and that his feat was particularly remarkable considering that he supposedly only learned to speak at 11, and to read and write at 18, having been diagnosed with global development delay and autism spectrum disorder as a child. The media circus around this appointment rivalled Hollywood press junkets, with newspaper, television and radio slots covering him on both sides of the Atlantic, including an NBC News item on his “inspiring story”.I am not privy to the hiring process for a professorial chair at Cambridge. I do not know exactly why and how Arday got the job or who else was in the running. But what happens when an academic’s story is sold through him being the “youngest black ever” (sitting alongside familiar monikers such as “the first black” or “black excellence”) and asterisked by a tale of hardship? You are not encouraged or invited to engage with the substance of their scholarship; instead, you are invited to clap. Instead of his appointment conjuring the question “what new opportunities for research will this lead to?”, it was “doesn’t this make you feel good?”What this means is that Arday was treated not as a scholar but as a mascot, one who was particularly expedient for an institution that had been regularly embarrassed by its historic record on race:too few black students(in my cohort at Cambridge matriculating in 2015there were only 15 black males out of 3,449 students); single-figure black academics (which is still the case);allegations of institutional racism. Independent of the merits or pitfalls of his own scholarship, what success looked like for Arday in this role was limited; what accountability could look like if misconduct occurred was constrained by him being a vehicle for Cambridge to signal its institutional progress.These are not arguments that progressives should shy away from. Instead, they should own them. There is a real risk of this case being used to undermine black academics and others in positions of seniority. For all the talk of preferential treatment for black people in academia, it remains true that there are documented,systemic barriersfor black students, including in theiraccess to funding to advance their studies.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPlaybooks, plagiarism and a pig’s head: new claims surrounding a star Cambridge professorRead moreThe mass investigation into Arday’s PhD may be presented as the pursuit of public and intellectual integrity, and yet the origin of this is grievance politics from those who feel diversity has blocked their own advancement. It comes with that malign charge of being a “DEI hire” or being in your position to “fill a quota”, the accusation that so often stalks black people elevated to senior positions. And so with Arday as an avatar for the black colleague who was promoted over you, the black child who was made head boy over your son, that process turbocharges.In Arday, those on the right feel that they have found what they are looking for; that is why every drop is being wrung out of this story. His resignation will not end that.The next step will be to make this single case bear the weight of the ideological arguments they pile on it.How do you resist that? By embracing and learning from the mistakes that were made here, not avoiding them out of discomfort. That means advocating for diversity without tokenism, the celebration of excellent black scholarship without the need for exceptionalism or academic celebrity. If we let only our opponents tell the story, then it becomes a parable about the hazards of striving for progress and equality, rather than about the institutions that reduced equality to a mere PR exercise.Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the GuardianDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Tech companies know everything about me – so why do they try to sell me so much rubbish? | Joel Snape | The Guardian
description: No, Amazon, I do not want to buy another version of the thing I just bought, or any other random object I don’t recognise or understand, writes Joel Snape
Author: Joel Snape
Headline: No, Amazon, I do not want to buy another version of the thing I just bought, or any other random object I don’t recognise or understand, writes Joel Snape
Content: Don’t know they know red is not my colour?Photograph: Alistair Berg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDon’t know they know red is not my colour?Photograph: Alistair Berg/Getty ImagesOpinionAdvertisingTech companies know everything about me – so why do they try to sell me so much rubbish?Joel SnapeNo, Amazon, I do not want to buy another version of the thing I just bought, or any other random object I don’t recognise or understandThu 6 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.08 EDTShareWe live, as I’m sure someone’s chief growth officer has recently boasted on an earnings call, in a golden age for data capture. Jeff Bezos knows what I buy, read and watch; Mark Zuckerberg will be aware that I recently sold a car transport box for a medium-sized dog. I’ve been ruthlessly conditioned into clicking Accept All Cookies every time I want to check how much cumin my favourite chilli needs, and I simply accept that my washing machine is probably spying on me.All of which raises the obvious question: with all of these terabytes of personal information available, why can’t advertisers try to sell me something I might actually like? Every time I swipe open my Kindle, for instance, I dismiss an advert for a bestselling trilogy called something like Ruthless Faerie Werewolves or Evil Mafia Hunk, even though I have never once – in my life – read a book where the main character could be described as a “morally grey shadow daddy”. I stopped watching Stranger Things after one season, and yet Netflix, which should know this better than anyone, has suggested the stage-play version to me so many times that I can recite its ad from memory. Amazon seems to have given up on predicting my needs and advertises the same one-off purchases that I’ve just bought, while Reddit and X want me to buy software products that I genuinely don’t understand.‘Genuinely changed my life’: why Groundhog Day is my feelgood movieRead morePart of me is heartened by this: maybe I’m too dazzlingly individual to be defined by the things I click on. Another part is saddened: what would be better, after all, than being bombarded with recommendations for the sort of books I can never find enough of (micro-histories of things like cod, say, or AK-47s, or 19th-century navigation).But a tiny part of me is desperately worried that the algorithm really does know me better than I know myself, and that I’m denying myself by refusing to heed its call. I’ll let you know, just as soon as I’m done with Mean Pixie Mob Daddy.Joel Snape is a freelance writerExplore more on these topicsAdvertisingOpinionSocial mediaMarketing & PRcommentShareReuse this content

title: The social media algorithm has left me behind. I’m unc and I’m chopped – and that’s OK | Rebecca Shaw | The Guardian
description: If you have to Google an internet or gen Z/alpha slang term, you absolutely shouldn’t be using it. I’m accepting this milestone with quiet dignity
Author: Rebecca Shaw
Headline: If you have to Google an internet or gen Z/alpha slang term, you absolutely shouldn’t be using it. I’m accepting this milestone with quiet dignity
Content: ‘Instead of one internet, there are endless overlapping internet microcultures, each with their own language evolving independently.’Photograph: NBCView image in fullscreen‘Instead of one internet, there are endless overlapping internet microcultures, each with their own language evolving independently.’Photograph: NBCOpinionYoung peopleThe social media algorithm has left me behind. I’m unc and I’m chopped – and that’s OKRebecca ShawIf you have to Google an internet or gen Z/alpha slang term, you absolutely shouldn’t be using it. I’m accepting this milestone with quiet dignityThu 6 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 21.23 EDTShareI’ve just reached an important adult milestone. Getting married? No. Having a baby? No. Buying a house? Don’t be ridiculous, I’m a writer in Australia. This milestone was small but important: I finally had to Google a gen Z slang term.I know this may be something many of you have passed already, along with your houses and babies, but I am someone who has been online for a long time. It’s been necessary for my career but it’s also my favourite hobby: going on the internet.I never needed to research slang, not because I use the terms or have a specific interest in the youth of today, but because spending a lot of time on the internet meant I absorbed them through osmosis. It’s science! I would see a post start popping off in a far-flung corner of the world and watch as it migrated platforms. I knew the context. I knew who was using it. I knew when it should be used. I knew when it was already embarrassing to use it. I wasn’t speaking the language but I was fluent. Now, I’m joining the ranks of the bamboozled elderly andGoogling “quiet on the creek”.My parents might have been able to keep up with slang back when people my age were doing it but the craziest we got was “roflcopter” and “pwned”. The internet was less fragmented. There was a time when someone terminally online could feel as though they had a rough map of the place and knew where all the cultural hubs were.Today’s internet has no centre.The rise of ‘unc’: is this gen Alpha’s way of saying ‘OK boomer’?Read moreInstead of one internet, there are endless overlapping internet microcultures, each with their own language evolving independently. Reddit, Discord,Twitch, TikTok, streaming culture, gaming culture – they all experience an endless flow of changing language. It’s no longer possible to understand everything, even if you wanted to. Technology and culture are moving so fast, all the time, it makes sense that young people are constantly coming up with new terms.There are pedants and young people haters out there who get het up about the slang and the memes and the 6-7 of it all but, generally, I love it. Some slang terms, the ones that trickle down from streaming or “incel” culture, can be ugly or negative. Many of the more creative or sticky terms originate in POC or queer culture. A lot of what makes it to the mainstream is clever or funny or right. For example, it’s already probably outdated now, but “rizz” for “charisma” is delightful.I appreciate the rapid evolution of language, the inventive wordplay, even if it does get annoying at times. Some of it will stick, some will get left behind. But now I no longer have a front-row seat. The algorithm has left me behind.That’s OK, it has to be that way. As you can see, I am accepting this with quiet dignity. Others should follow my example – if you have to Google a slang term, you absolutely shouldn’t be using it. If you are a politician or police PR person, please avoid using slang to try to appeal to young people. It will never work, it will only ever embarrass you and in some cases it will kill the poor term dead in its tracks.I’m still going to keep finding out what slang means for my own interest, and to ensure I can make some sense of what the kids in my life are trying to communicate. But I know my limits. I’m no longer absorbing the language just by being online; I am studying it. I’m unc and chopped – and that’s OK.Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in SydneyExplore more on these topicsYoung peopleOpinionInternetSocial mediaRedditTikTokTwitchcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘The first time I felt art in my nose’: why a  critic missed the point when he called my exhibition meaningless | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Projects like London’s Backyard Biennial East are collective endeavours aiming to reach people who feel excluded by art galleries
Author: Laisul Hoque
Headline: Projects like London’s Backyard Biennial East are collective endeavours aiming to reach people who feel excluded by art galleries
Content: Creating the conditions for people to encounter one another … Elo Melo by Laisul Hoque.Photograph: Courtesy the artistView image in fullscreenCreating the conditions for people to encounter one another … Elo Melo by Laisul Hoque.Photograph: Courtesy the artistArt and design‘The first time I felt art in my nose’: why a  critic missed the point when he called my exhibition meaninglessLaisul HoqueProjects like London’s Backyard Biennial East are collective endeavours aiming to reach people who feel excluded by art galleriesThu 6 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTShareIn 2018, on the outside wall surrounding the entrance of the National Theatre of Bangladesh, I first encountered a work by the artistReetu Sattar. A group of musicians were perched on construction scaffolding, all dressed in white and playing a single note on the harmonium – an instrument used in Bengali classical music. Together, they produced a low hum that seemed to vibrate through everything around me. The work was called Lost Tune.I came across the work at a time when I desperately wanted to learn a musical instrument, but music was not allowed in my house. A growing sentiment in many Bangladeshi Muslim households held that music was prohibited in Islam, despite our long histories of musical traditions. It felt as though everything we knew of the past had been locked away inside theJadu Ghor, the “magic house” (the Bangla words for museum), quietly collecting dust.East of the Aldgate Pump review – this morose and meaningless exhibition gave me a migraineRead moreIt amazed me that an artist could gather so many people to commit themselves to an artwork when nobody around me seemed to believe art had any value at all. Until then, I had only felt art in my eyes and my mind. In Lost Tune, I felt art in my chest.I continued following Reetu’s practice, though much of it took place abroad. Eventually, I too left Bangladesh to study art in the UK.It was here that I discovered the work ofAdam Farah Saad. At his exhibition at Camden Art Centre in London, I smelled KA soda the moment I entered the room. A fountain bubbled it endlessly. It was the first time I felt art in my nose.View image in fullscreenOpening minds … Shabnam by Reetu Sattar.Photograph: © Reetu Sattar Courtesy the artistIt was also in London that I discovered Brick Lane’s Bengali sweet shops. There I found my father’s favourite childhood snack: one sweet and one savoury item that he always mixed together. I remembered the first time he had taken me to a sweet shop in Bangladesh. That memory has always been yellow, a display cabinet glowing beneath warm tungsten light. It is my earliest emotional memory of him.That memory became the foundation for the work I conceived two years ago and am re-presenting inEast of the Aldgate Pump, a group exhibition at London’s Whitechapel Gallery as part of a new collaborative East End arts festival, Backyard Biennial. Every day, members of the Bengali social enterpriseOitij-jo Kitchenhelp maintain the work, preparing and bringing the specific mixture of snacks into the gallery. Their contribution isn’t separate from the artwork. It is part of it. In many ways, that collaboration feels like a direct descendant of Lost Tune: people choosing to sustain something collectively.A recent reviewin the Guardian of East of the Aldgate Pump provoked questions around where meaning in art actually resides. During conversations with the curators, I found myself thinking about the Aldgate Pump itself. For centuries it has marked the symbolic gateway to east London while witnessing continuous movement, migration and change. I thought about the geographer Doreen Massey’s idea that places are not fixed locations but meeting points of multiple journeys. Every artwork in the exhibition seemed to have travelled a different route to arrive there.View image in fullscreenPlaces are not fixed locations … All About Survival (The A406 Orbital Class Mix) by Adam Farah-Saad.Photograph: Damian GriffithsWhen my mother visited London in 2023, she went to Brick Lane with a friend. They came out of Aldgate East station, and her friend pointed out Whitechapel Gallery.“Did you go in?” I asked later.“No,” she replied. “We were scared.”I want art spaces to become less scary to enter, for me, for my mum, for everyone. I hope, more and more, they become places where people feel that they belong.If projects like Backyard Biennial have a purpose, it is not to provide tidy answers or singular narratives. It is to create the conditions for people to encounter one another, their histories and themselves. It is to give people an opportunity to recognise something of themselves in a space the previously may have felt closed to them. That meaning may be messy, partial and collective. But it is not meaningless.Backyard Biennial: East is at various venues in London until 6 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designArtcommentShareReuse this content

title: The American left is making strides. But can they win in November? | Ben Davis | The Guardian
description: The left is increasingly winning within the Democratic party. But it still needs to prove that it can build general-election coalitions capable of beating Republicans
Author: Ben Davis
Headline: The left is increasingly winning within the Democratic party. But it still needs to prove that it can build general-election coalitions capable of beating Republicans
Content: ‘The left has been battle-tested in primaries against moderate candidates ... But a general election in a swing state is a different and less hospitable terrain.Photograph: Rebecca Cook/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The left has been battle-tested in primaries against moderate candidates ... But a general election in a swing state is a different and less hospitable terrain.Photograph: Rebecca Cook/ReutersOpinionUS midterm elections 2026The American left is making strides. But can they win in November?Ben DavisThe left is increasingly winning within the Democratic party. But it still needs to prove that it can build general-election coalitions capable of beating RepublicansThu 6 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.43 EDTShareThe ideological struggle within the Democratic party continued on Tuesday night with primaries in Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, Virginia and Washington. The results showed an increasingly intense conflict within the party, with high Democratic primary turnout and bruising ideological battles up and down the ballot.The Democratic electorate is shifting, becoming more progressive and more willing to challenge party leadership, but not as quickly or uniformly as many assumed.Progressives and socialists scored another round of victories, most notablyAbdul El-Sayedfor Senate, but also downballot with Donavan McKinney and Will Lawrence in congressional races, and in state legislative seats such as Chris Gilmer-Hill in Detroit. But the scale and breadth of those victories fell short of the expectations created by polling and media coverage.Abdul El-Sayed offers a template for Democrats to defeat Trumpism | Peter BeinartRead moreA few key lessons have emerged. First, building a mass left in the United States is a slow and bruising process, and there is no single tipping point at which the party and its voters suddenly become committed leftwing partisans.Second, the left is nonetheless growing rapidly, able to win beyond young, deep-blue urban areas where concerns about general-election viability againstRepublicansare relatively limited, and across an entire statewide Democratic primary electorate in a swing state.This is a major step in the left’s development as an electoral force. Third, the left’s next and most important challenge is winning swing states and competitive seats against Republicans.The left has enjoyed a string of notable electoral victories during the second Trump administration, beginning withZohran Mamdani’s primary win in New York City, and continuing up through the 2026 primaries. The Democratic electorate’s attitudes are changing: party leadership has grown less popular, while democratic socialism has gained support. The left has quickly gone from an extremely marginal force, with just a handful of members of Congress, largely confined to deep-blue urban districts and a small number of favorable constituencies, to a driving force in the party. Much of the media coverage has portrayed the party as being overtaken by an ascendant left. That broader narrative, reinforced by favorable polling, created an expectation that El-Sayed would win resoundingly.In practice, the recent wave means that a meaningful additional share of Democratic primary voters, perhaps 10-15%, is now willing to consistently support left candidates, on top of the existing leftwing base.double quotation markBuilding a mass left in the United States is a slow and bruising process, and there is no single tipping point at which the party and its voters suddenly become committed leftwing partisansIt does not mean that every candidate backed by the DSA or the broader progressive movement will automatically win, or every Democrat backed by Aipac will lose. The actual campaign still matters tremendously; a large share of Democratic voters remain moderate, cross-pressured or primarily candidate-driven.Politics just doesn’t move that fast. The project of building a leftwing base and turning it into a durable majority, even within the Democratic party, is still a long-term one.El-Sayed’s narrow victory has been described as disappointing, because of favorable polling and the expectations created by the recent wave of leftwing victories. It is anything but. The polling miss has distorted how the result is being interpreted.Viewed against Michigan’s demographics, the left’s previous statewide performance, spending disparities, endorsements and comparable results elsewhere in the country, the victory was historically significant.The left has not previously won a genuinely competitive statewide Democratic primary of this kind, nor has a left candidate previously assembled a winning primary coalition extending this far beyond the movement’s urban base, especially in a swing state where voters are likely to weigh general-election viability.The left’s strategy over the past decade has been one of patience, winning seats in friendly areas, knocking doors and slowly building a base. It began by winning city council and state legislative victories and expanded more recently into successful mayoral and congressional races, all in deep blue areas.The Democrats have one last chance to halt the erosion of US democracy – and it’s less than 100 days away | Timothy Garton AshRead moreThis is the first time the left has real proof of concept that beyond urban cores with friendly demographics, it can win over a majority of Democratic voters. It also offers early evidence that a left candidate could compete seriously in a Democratic presidential primary in 2028.The next test is November. The left has been battle-tested in primaries against moderate candidates, party institutions and well-funded outside groups such as Aipac and the crypto lobby. But a general election in a swing state is a different and less hospitable terrain.El-Sayed, along with Francesca Hong if she advances in Wisconsin, needs to demonstrate the left can win not only a winning Democratic primary coalition, but a broad enough general-election coalition to prevail outside deep-blue territory. This matters in the near term, for Democrats to win the Senate and retain governorships; in the medium term, because presidential primary voters in 2028 will want evidence that left candidates can win competitive general elections; and in the long term, because the leftwing political project rests on being able to twin and govern with durable electoral majorities.On Tuesday, the left continued its string of victories, activating young voters and bringing Arab and Muslim voters back into the Democratic fold. But these victories do not resolve the movement’s central challenges.Every primary remains a brutal fight, highly contingent on candidates, organization, spending and local conditions. And the movement must now prepare for the more difficult terrain of November. The left is increasingly winning within the Democratic party, but it still needs to prove that it can build general-election coalitions capable of defeating Republicans.Ben Davis works in political data in Washington DC. He worked on the data team for the Bernie Sanders 2020 campaign and is an active member of the Democratic Socialists of AmericaExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionRepublicansUS politicsTrump administrationUS SenateSocialismcommentShareReuse this content

title: Should I try the ‘18 summers’ parenting trend? Only if I want to ruin the school holidays | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: Long days with nothing to do is the whole point of summer. Turning it into a ‘making memories’ exercise is creepy and controlling, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Long days with nothing to do is the whole point of summer. Turning it into a ‘making memories’ exercise is creepy and controlling, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: ‘The bigger drag behind this concept is the need to turn every last human impulse into an item on a to-do list.’Photograph: Mariya Borisova/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The bigger drag behind this concept is the need to turn every last human impulse into an item on a to-do list.’Photograph: Mariya Borisova/Getty ImagesOpinionParents and parentingShould I try the ‘18 summers’ parenting trend? Only if I want to ruin the school holidaysEmma BrockesLong days with nothing to do is the whole point of summer. Turning it into a ‘making memories’ exercise is creepy and controllingThu 6 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 12.39 EDTShareThere are a great many things to dislike about modern parenting trends – take your pick fromhelicoptertosnowplowtoFafo– but the least appealing, perhaps, is the temptation present in all of them to treat raising a child like an extended school project.The latest addition is something called18 summers, in which clingy parents count down the school holidays they have left with their children before they leave home, pre-grieving the end as they go. There is no quicker way to ruin something than by filtering it through an internet trend, but this one is particularly insidious: an invitation to inject weird notes of anxiety into what might otherwise be an unstudied thing.Let’s put to one side for a moment the fact that, in these economic times, kids don’t stop going on holiday with their parents until they’re roughly 35. The idea behind the “viral concept” of 18 summers – tagline “you only get 18 summers with your kid” – is to remind us that life is short and we should cherish each moment, a banality that, if it is ever true, is particularly untrue during the summer holidays, which are very, very long indeed. I would rather sign up to a movement called 18 minutes, in which we recognise the time-warping effect of the slow-crawl towards September, or even 18 seconds, in which we study the fascinating variables in time perception as it relates to unstructured periods with children, which might also be marketed as 18 millennia.The rise of Fafo parenting: is this the end of gentle child rearing?Read moreEighteen summers on the other hand is designed, like most social media trends, to make us feel as if we’re misusing our time by showing us how other, better motivated people are using theirs. This is achieved via a set of social media posts carrying the18 summers hashtagand which, no matter where in the world the images are generated, looks like a set of adverts for Center Parcs Longleat.There has always been something creepy about the formalisation of quotidian parts of life, and I would put the phrase “making memories” into that category. It’s the animating ethos behind 18 summers, whichcomes with a retail shelffull of diaries, binders and other products to ensure we document every precious moment with our children – without enjoying any of them. I’m currently in New York, ground zero of acute parenting trends, where “experiencing joy” may be tackled with the same, furrow-browed intensity as “learning Mandarin” andwhere parents can become so feverishly intent on “making memories” for their children that they badger them into a state of complete mania. (In this world, going for a bike ride becomes so fraught with meaning it becomes Going For A Bike Ride and you’d better hope it hits that platonic ideal).The bigger drag behind this concept is the need to turn every last human impulse into an item on a to-do list. Do you enjoy summer while also finding it enraging and boring? Well, try holding it up against an idealised version that relies for its power on a sense of loss, fear and competition with others. The word “magical” hangs heavily over this scene, too, and, who among us needs reminding that anyone who uses the word magical more than once or twice a year is a joyless weirdo. Other phrases encountered when you browse the endlessInstagramreels around 18 summers: “ultimate family formula” (sounds fun!), “three steps to deepen your relationship with your child”, and “holding sand”, which refers to how fast the time goes (although in the case of this particular scene, not fast enough).All of this is, of course, just another form of parental overreach, a way of normalising and celebrating controlling personalities. The flipside to 18 summers is the romanticisation of our own childhoods, in which, to listen to us go on, we spent six weeks out on bikes like the kids in ET rather than, say, inside watching telly. Still, no one interfered with us much. I took my kids to a climbing wall this week – making memories! – and it was like a comedy sketch, watching parents stand at the foot of the wall directing their perfectly able kids to the top. (“Honey, put your left foot on that one diagonally – no, not that one, the one next to it; up and to the right, yep, yep. YES! Good job! You’re so good at this!” As one dad standing next to me muttered bleakly, “back-seat climbing”).I love the summers. Even when things get frazzled towards the end, I love the sense of having nothing to do, which makes a walk to the shops with my kids something to draw out for as long as we can, rather than race through to get to the next thing. The whole point of summer is that you’re not held to account, or a schedule, or in this case, a hashtag. For a short time, we can inhabit that state hovering right on the edge of boredom that – if we don’t ruin things by overthinking – seems to go on for ever.Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsParents and parentingOpinionFamilyInstagramTikTokSocial mediaSchool holidayscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on mental health: the new secretary of state should make it a priority | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Parity for people with physical and psychological ailments has been promised for years. New neighbourhood clinics are a step in the right direction
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Parity for people with physical and psychological ailments has been promised for years. New neighbourhood clinics are a step in the right direction
Content: Yvette Cooper pictured during a visit to a community-based mental health centre in Sheffield.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAView image in fullscreenYvette Cooper pictured during a visit to a community-based mental health centre in Sheffield.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAOpinionMental healthThe Guardian view on mental health: the new secretary of state should make it a priorityEditorialParity for people with physical and psychological ailments has been promised for years. New neighbourhood clinics are a step in the right directionThu 6 Aug 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 13.49 EDTShareThe rise in children and young people with mental health problems makes this week’s announcement of anew network of community clinicsin England particularly welcome. A&E departments have recorded an increase indifficult-to-manage symptomsincluding aggression and hallucinations. New specialist walk-in mental health services should take some of the pressure off. The bringing forward of a deadline for ending out-of-area acute placements, and a pledge to reduce waiting times for children, are also positive.Declining mental health was among the key themes of Alan Milburn’sinterim reporton young people and work. It is a big factor behind the rise in claims for illness and disability benefits. Children’s anxiety and other psychological difficulties are also among the many challenges facing schools. Recent years have seen steep rises inemotionally based school avoidance, as well as in autism and neurodiversity.But while concerns about mental health are shared across government, they have not been prominent in policies put forward by the department where you might expect them to feature most: health. Partly, that is due to other pressing issues including social care and enormous hospital waiting-lists. Partly, it is because ministers have been waiting for areview led by Prof Peter Fonagyinto mental health conditions, ADHD and autism. Its recommendations are expected soon, and will feed into an upcoming strategy. In her first interview with the Guardian as health secretary, Yvette Cooper focused onmaternity servicesand the need toprepare for future heatwaves. But the commitment to expand community mental health points to a welcome recognition that this should be an area of focus too.Parity between mental and physical healthcare became a policy goal in 2011, with the launch of aNo Health Without Mental Healthinitiative. Efforts to stress the importance of psychological wellbeing, and its interconnectedness with physical health, long predate that. The commitment made in last year’s 10-year health strategy to shift resources gradually away from acute hospitals and towards community services would seem to dovetail with this balanced, holistic outlook. But one year on from its launch, experts including Siva Anandaciva, of the King’s Fund, haveraised doubtsabout “whether the NHS really will be committed to the fundamental shift away from hospital care that the health plan proposed”. This week it was revealed that one mental health trust, in east London, is planning to make£230m of cuts. Mental health is not ringfenced within NHS budgets, and as a proportion of overall health spendingfell from 9.0% of the total in 2023/24 to 8.78% in 2024/25.The reasons for the lower priority placed on mental health, compared with physical diseases and injuries, are complex, and reflect cultural as well as structural factors to do with the way that the NHS is organised. Socioeconomic determinants of poor mental health including incomes, work andhousing, are outside Ms Cooper’s remit. But the disparities in access to treatment are irrational and unjust. Severe depression and anxiety are highly debilitating conditions. Expectations about waiting times and treatment options need to be clarified.There are no easy fixes in a system as complicated as theNHS. It is not clear where the new neighbourhood centres fit in existing plans – or who will staff them. But providing that further details are produced in due course, the shift in focus that they signal should be supported.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Italy’s new far-right party: the rise of a rogue general | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The early success of Roberto Vannacci’s National Future sends an ominous signal as extreme politics become normalised
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The early success of Roberto Vannacci’s National Future sends an ominous signal as extreme politics become normalised
Content: Roberto Vannacci at a National Future news conference in Rome on 5 August. ‘The rest of Europe should sit up and take notice of Mr Vannacci’s rise.’Photograph: Roberto Monaldo/LaPresse/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRoberto Vannacci at a National Future news conference in Rome on 5 August. ‘The rest of Europe should sit up and take notice of Mr Vannacci’s rise.’Photograph: Roberto Monaldo/LaPresse/ShutterstockOpinionEuropeThe Guardian view on Italy’s new far-right party: the rise of a rogue generalEditorialThe early success of Roberto Vannacci’s National Future sends an ominous signal as extreme politics become normalisedThu 6 Aug 2026 13.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 13.49 EDTShareWhen a serving Italian general published a far-right tract in 2023 entitled The World Turned Upside Down, a disciplinary inquiry swiftly followed. Roberto Vannacci’s text was a sustainedexercisein bile and bigotry, attacking among other things the “normalisation” of homosexuality, and questioning whether a high-profile black volleyball star could really be considered Italian. The controversy sent the book into the bestseller charts, and its author was suspended for bringing the army into disrepute.A year out from Italy’s next general election, Mr Vannacci is a problem not for the military but for the country’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni. Now a member of the European parliament, in February he exploited his notoriety tofoundNational Future, a political party which argues that Ms Meloni’s coalition government has sold out its far-right supporters through not being extreme enough. The “true right”, according to the former paratrooper – who once served as a military attache in Moscow – should be pro-Putin and anti-Ukraine, anti-EU, and committed to restoring the “cultural homogeneity” of Italy through the expulsion of immigrants and their descendants.Shockingly, polls are nowplacingNational Future just behind Forza Italia, the second-biggest party in Ms Meloni’s hard-right coalition, and ahead of its third main component, Matteo Salvini’s League. For Ms Meloni, Mr Vannacci’s rapid rise now threatens to become a major dilemma. To beat the combined forces of the left next year she may require the support of a party that does not disguise its sympathy with Italy’s fascist past. But to seek it would give the lie to efforts to present her own Brothers of Italy party (whichretainsa neo-fascist political symbol in its logo) as part of the mainstream conservative tradition.The rest of Europe should sit up and take notice of Mr Vannacci’s rise. At a time when Russian influence on the far right isalreadya cause for concern, he has declared himself open to the idea of funding from Moscow and also Beijing. More broadly, the emergence of National Future confirms that as well as dragging mainstream politics towards more extreme positions on immigration, the continent’s far right is itself radicalising.Here, the equivalent can be found in Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain party, which has beenexertinga rightwards gravitational pull on Reform UK. Poland’s nationalist and Eurosceptic Law and Justice party hasembarkedon a similar trajectory, in order to compete with two newish and growing far-right parties. In Germany, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) stands on the brink of a historic breakthrough in state elections in eastern Germany, andleadsin national polls.The ominous political consequences were on display last week in the panicked overreaction of leaders to the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. With one eye over her right shoulder, Ms Meloni was at the forefront of divisive earlycallsfor action to be taken against Spain following an incursion by irregular migrants. For his part, Mr Vannacci used the incident toamplifyhis calls for a Europe-wide “remigration” strategy.Mr Vannacci’s repugnant politics are beyond the pale. In Germany, the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, continues to rule out any form of national alliance with the AfD. Were Ms Meloni to countenance any form of accommodation with Italy’s rogue general, it would demolish her fragile claims to mainstream respectability.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Early release is a sign of a broken prison system | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Andy Burnham’s review of controversial measures for the early release of thousands of prisoners to free up space in jails
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Andy Burnham’s review of controversial measures for the early release of thousands of prisoners to free up space in jails
Content: Wandsworth prison in London. ‘We  should be asking … what imprisonment is actually intended to achieve.’Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWandsworth prison in London. ‘We  should be asking … what imprisonment is actually intended to achieve.’Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesPrisons and probationLettersEarly release is a sign of a broken prison systemReaders respond to Andy Burnham’s review of controversial measures for the early release of thousands of prisoners to free up space in jailsThu 6 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 13.13 EDTShareThere is something deeply incongruous about a penal system centred on incarceration having to release prisoners early because it has run out of room to incarcerate them (PM to tighten early release rules but men jailed over PC Harper’s death can be freed, 4 August).The government’s latest early-release measures may be necessary to prevent our prisons from becoming completely overwhelmed, but they are surely a symptom of a much deeper failure. We appear to be operating a revolving-door policy: tougher sentencing fills the prisons, overcrowding forces early release, public concern produces calls for tougher sentencing, and the cycle begins again. It is rather like baling water out of a sinking boat without ever fixing the hole.The question we should be asking is not simply how many prisoners we can accommodate, but what imprisonment is actually intended to achieve. If the purpose is punishment, routinely cutting sentences undermines the principle. If it is public protection, we should concentrate prison places on those who pose the greatest risk. And if rehabilitation is the objective, we should question the wisdom of short custodial sentences when properly supervised community sentences can sometimes produce better outcomes.Early release may therefore be an unavoidable short-term expedient. But it cannot sensibly become a permanent method of managing a prison system whose fundamental assumptions have never been properly examined.Name and address suppliedIf the current early-release policy puts women at risk from violent men, and most women in prison have no history of violence, doesn’t it follow that early release should be focused primarily on women prisoners? With a little reorganisation, and resources redirected towards mental health services, whole prisons could presumably be freed up.Marcia SaundersLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Catholic or not, many of us share Andy Burnham’s beliefs | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Julian Coman on Andy Burnham’s faith and the influence of Catholic social teaching on his work
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Julian Coman on Andy Burnham’s faith and the influence of Catholic social teaching on his work
Content: ‘Burnham may well have been strengthened by his Catholic upbringing, but compassion, solidarity and social responsibility are not the preserve of any one faith.’Photograph: Design Pics/Con Tanasiuk/Getty Images/Design Pics RFView image in fullscreen‘Burnham may well have been strengthened by his Catholic upbringing, but compassion, solidarity and social responsibility are not the preserve of any one faith.’Photograph: Design Pics/Con Tanasiuk/Getty Images/Design Pics RFAndy BurnhamLettersCatholic or not, many of us share Andy Burnham’s beliefsReaders respond to an article by Julian Coman on Andy Burnham’s faith and the influence of Catholic social teaching on his workThu 6 Aug 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 13.13 EDTShareJulian Coman’s article about Andy Burnham resonated with me, as I share his belief in compassion, social responsibility and concern for those who are struggling (Like Burnham, I was an altar boy. His Catholic upbringing is shaping the way he governs, 1 August). Where I differ is in the suggestion that these values are rooted primarily in Catholicism.I grew up in inner-cityManchesterduring the Thatcher years, in a low socioeconomic working-class community facing unemployment, poverty and drug misuse. My parents were not religious, but they instilled in me a humanist outlook based on empathy, fairness and our shared responsibilities to one another.The same values were reinforced at my primary school. In a diverse inner-city neighbourhood, children from different backgrounds learned side by side. Looking back, religion barely featured in our day-to-day lives at school. Faith was generally considered a private matter. What united us was a simple understanding that everyone deserved respect, fairness and kindness. We learned to see one another not as representatives of different beliefs, but as fellow human beings with a shared stake in our community and society.It was an inclusive environment that left me comfortable and confident in Britain as a diverse society. Through our families, teachers and local community, we came to appreciate the secular institutions that bound us together: the NHS, social housing and the welfare state. Children whose families had lived here for generations learned alongside those whose families had arrived more recently, but there was a shared understanding that these institutions represented something valuable, something to be respected, strengthened and improved. Civic responsibility, inclusivity and social justice were not religious lessons; they were human lessons.Those values shaped me, too, but they came from a secular humanist upbringing, my community, and Britain’s civic institutions. The compassion that Coman admires in Burnham may well have been strengthened by his Catholic upbringing, but compassion, solidarity and social responsibility are not the preserve of any one faith or worldview. If there is a moral tradition worth celebrating, it’s the broader human one: the belief that we flourish not alone, but through our obligations to one another, regardless of faith.Lorna PetersManchesterJulian Coman’s article was encouraging. The faith communities I know are all deeply involved in politics, justice, homelessness work and much more. At a recent local Labour party meeting, there were two Methodists (I was one), several Catholics and a couple of Quakers.Coman mentions the Methodist worldview that Margaret Thatcher inherited from her father. But Mrs Thatcher didn’t know her Methodist roots. Our founder, John Wesley, said: “The gospel of Christ knows of no religion, but social; no holiness but social holiness.” So when she said “there is no such thing as society”, she was denying her Methodist roots. Much worse, though, was that she was wrong and set in train the rise of individualism.Rev Richard ParkesNewcastle-under-Lyme, StaffordshireJulian Coman has it pretty much spot-on. “The problem with Christianity is that no one has ever really tried it,” as my wise mother, Peggy Brown, always said.While I continue to disappoint myself in that regard, perhaps Andy Burnham will succeed in being the first to preserve integrity and hope in the fire of political separatism and selfishness.John BrownHartford, CheshireAndy Burnhamis Britain’s first lifelong Roman Catholic prime minister. Tony Blair converted to Catholicism while in office and Boris Johnson, though baptised a Catholic as a baby, converted to Anglicanism at a later stage in his life.For hundreds of years – after the Protestant Reformation in the 16th century, until the Repeal of the Penal Laws in the early 19th century – Roman Catholics in Britain were stripped of economic, political and religious power. They could not hold civil or military office. They could not get educated, vote or practice a profession. Until 2013, a British royal could not marry a Catholic and, in fact, the monarch today still cannot be a Catholic.But now, in 2026, we have a Catholic prime minister, who has said his Catholic upbringing means a lot to him. If this upbringing is shaping the way he is governing, we might see a focus on the common good and the influence of the social teachings of the Catholic church, including the need to put the poor and vulnerable first, the dignity of the human person, the dignity of work, the worker and the rights of workers, the call to the family and community, the work towards peace and solidarity in the world, and the care for the stewardship of God’s creation.Let us wish Andy Burnham luck in his endeavour to create a just and equitable society.Julia O’SheaKilcummin, County Kerry, IrelandHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: How private schools could help Afghan girls – and justify their charitable status | Taliban | The Guardian
description: Letters: Margaret Owen suggests that Britain’s well endowed independent schools have a part to play in offering Afghan girls living under the Taliban the chance to get an education
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Margaret Owen suggests that Britain’s well endowed independent schools have a part to play in offering Afghan girls living under the Taliban the chance to get an education
Content: Afghan girls at a madrasa in Kandahar in August 2025.Photograph: Sanaullah Seiam/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenAfghan girls at a madrasa in Kandahar in August 2025.Photograph: Sanaullah Seiam/AFP/GettyTalibanLettersHow private schools could help Afghan girls – and justify their charitable statusMargaret Owensuggests that Britain’s well endowed independent schools have a part to play in offering Afghan girls living under the Taliban the chance to get an educationThu 6 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 13.13 EDTShareHere is another plan for Gordon Brown (After five brutal years of Taliban rule, Afghan women and girls need our help – and I have a plan, 4 August). In a very few years Afghanistan will have no female doctors, nurses or midwives. For the Taliban have not only stopped girls’ education and codified child marriage, but have banned contraception and forbidden women and girls to access male health providers. Inevitably, there will be a huge increase in maternal and neonatal mortality.One way the UK could help is by its well endowed independent girls schools offering A-level science bursaries to those Afghan girls who wish to study medicine, have learned English online and can show that they have the ability to follow such a course.I have been corresponding with such a girl, now 15, who longs to become a doctor so she can care for her sisters. Even if passports, visas, travel, etc may be problematic, just offering such bursaries would be a way of keeping this gender apartheid inAfghanistanin the spotlight. Independent schools enjoy questionable charitable status. Here is a way of justifying it.Margaret OwenPresident, Widows for Peace Through DemocracyHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Lloyds Bank should publish the human cost of its AI savings | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Letter: Banks should factor in the time spent by humans checking invented facts, writes Dr Gleb Tsipursky
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Banks should factor in the time spent by humans checking invented facts, writes Dr Gleb Tsipursky
Content: ‘Lloyds should publish a simple scorecard for each consequential AI workflow.’Photograph: Lloyds Banking GroupView image in fullscreen‘Lloyds should publish a simple scorecard for each consequential AI workflow.’Photograph: Lloyds Banking GroupAI (artificial intelligence)LettersLloyds Bank should publish the human cost of its AI savingsBanks should factor in the time spent by humans checking invented facts, writesDr Gleb TsipurskyThu 6 Aug 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 13.13 EDTShareYour report (Lloyds Bank to cut £2bn in costs as part of AI-powered strategy, 30 July) raises a question that financial targets alone cannot answer: who absorbs the work when automation fails?Banks often count the minutes saved by the employee who uses an AI tool. They should also count the time colleagues spend checking invented facts, repairing customer messages, explaining rejected applications and escalating errors. A system can make one team look more productive while moving risk and effort elsewhere.Lloyds should publish a simple scorecard for each consequential AI workflow: total time saved across the process, error and rework rates, customer complaints, successful human interventions and changes to entry-level roles. It should also name the executive with authority to pause a system when the evidence turns negative.The bank’s relationship managers and customers need a clear route to challenge automated recommendations. Staff must be able to report weak outputs without being branded resistant to innovation.AI may shorten mortgage decisions and improve advice. Those gains will deserve trust only when Lloyds measures the whole workflow and shows that £2bn in savings did not become hidden costs for workers and customers.Dr Gleb TsipurskyBehavioural scientist, Columbus, Ohio, USHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Uefa maintains World Cup boycott still stands despite Fifa’s backing for Infantino | Uefa | The Guardian
description: Uefa is not standing down in its fight with Fifa, saying ‘conditions have not been met’ for it to call off its current boycott of competitions
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Uefa is not standing down in its fight with Fifa, saying ‘conditions have not been met’ for it to call off its current boycott of competitions
Content: The Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, with his Fifa counterpart, Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenThe Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, with his Fifa counterpart, Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAUefaUefa maintains World Cup boycott still stands despite Fifa’s backing for InfantinoEuropean body says Fifa statement ‘changes nothing’Fifpro condemns ‘profound abuse of presidential power’Nick AmesandMatt HughesThu 6 Aug 2026 10.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUefa has doubled down on itsthreat to boycott Fifa-run competitionsand reiterated its loss of confidence in Gianni Infantino’s presidency.The latest damning intervention from European football’s governing body came as criticism of Infantino continued to rain in from several angles. The global players’ union, Fifpro, condemned “a profound abuse of presidential power” while the South American confederation, Conmebol, usually a strong Infantino ally, was moved to chastise “repeated unilateral actions taken without resorting to dialogue”.It is Uefa’s continued stance, though, that may damage Infantino most severely. In a statement it saidFifa’s public backing of Infantinoon Wednesday night “changes nothing” and explained it was not convinced repeats of the past nine days’ crisis will not occur.Uefa planning to check if Infantino tried to sell stakes in World Cup on cheapRead moreLast week Uefa’s 55 member associations agreed to boycottFifatournaments if Infantino did not withdraw his privately funded Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme and, although the plan was scrapped last Friday, it said the terms necessary to avert the boycott have not been met.“Uefa’s associations were very clear about the conditions attached to their non-participation inFifacompetitions,” it said. “First, the proposals to sell off the major competitions had to be withdrawn and, secondly, assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again.“These conditions have not been met. In addition, Uefa made it abundantly clear in its statement on Saturday that it has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino’s presidency. That position holds. Yesterday’s announcement that some people employed by the Fifa president (and whose careers depend on his favour) agree with him changes nothing.”It heightens the turmoil enveloping football’s governance. If no accord is reached before the Under-20 Women’sWorld Cup, which begins in Poland on 5 September, that would be the first tournament subjected to a Uefa-led boycott.Uefa remains hopeful it can exploit divisions within Fifa’s leadership despite the Infantino-led show of unity following Wednesday’s meeting of some of its management board in Rabat.There were several notable absentees, however, and it is understood that Arsène Wenger declined an invitation to travel to Morocco in his capacity as Fifa’s chief of global development because of a desire to distance himself from Infantino. The former Arsenal manager hadlaunched a scathing attackon the World Cup sell-off plans, saying it was “absolutely necessary and beyond question” that they were scrapped.In contrast to Wenger, Fifa’s chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, who had described the proposals as “the project of one person”, was not invited to the summit in a development that will raise further questions over his future. Additionally Jill Ellis, the chief football officer, and Sarai Bareman, the chief women’s football officer, were not present in Rabat.While Fifa has sent apologies to the Fifa council and member associations for their exclusion from the FFE process, it is believed that those sentiments failed to sway a large percentage of council members.Infantino is getting his karmic kicking, but why did football take so long to rebel against Fifa? | Jonathan LiewRead moreA handful of Uefa federations have withdrawn letters of support for Infantino’s re-election for a fourth term, although the early rush to make such declarations has slowed. The Football Association has now written to Fifa formally retracting its backing.Uefa’s repeat of its boycott threat was followed by a scathing release from Fifpro. Before theWorld CupFifpro signalled its intention to work with Fifa by signing a memorandum of understanding but that has proved the briefest of truces.Alongside the criticism, Fifpro wrote to Fifa making a series of demands, including giving players voting rights on the Fifa council, which is supposed to be the main decision-making body but has often been bypassed by Infantino.“Fifa Forward Enterprise is gone, but the abuse of power that produced it is not,” Fifpro said. “Governance reforms, not a cover-up, are urgently needed. The withdrawal of FFE was inevitable. But withdrawing the proposal does not erase what it revealed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“A plan capable of permanently altering the ownership and governance of the Fifa World Cup … was conceived in secrecy, negotiated behind closed doors and brought to the brink of agreement before the Fifa council, the member associations, players and football’s recognised stakeholders even knew it existed. That is not merely a governance failure. It is a profound abuse of presidential power.”Conmebol, three of whose members are in line to host matches at the 2030 World Cup, had waited more than a week to comment publicly. While its disapproval was clear it stopped short of pushing for immediate change.In a statement it said the Conmebol council “unanimously expresses its concern regarding the repeated unilateral actions taken without resorting to dialogue or to the institutional mechanisms established to address situations of this nature”.While Uefa is leading efforts to unseat Infantino before Fifa’s election in March, Conmebol pointed out the timeline for the process has already been set. “Accordingly, Conmebol will not support any action or procedure that disregards or departs from those institutional mechanisms,” it said.Earlier on Thursday the Jordan Football Association president, Prince Ali bin al-Hussein, said Fifa had paid bonuses owed from last December’s Arab Cup but clarified he would still oppose Infantino.The money appears to have materialised after Prince Aliaccused Fifa of “blackmail”, saying the governing body had threatened to withhold funds if Jordan refused to back Infantino’s re-election.“Thank you to the Fifa administration for suddenly this morning delivering what was owed to our players and coaching staff, for the Jordan national team’s accession to the final of the Fifa Arab Cup in Qatar last December,” he wrote.“This was funding that should have been received eight months ago … It is symptomatic of those exact difficulties that we all face, and that are usually linked to the Fifa presidential elections. And it does not change my clear position concerning the leadership of Fifa: my FA and I will not endorse president Infantino, nor will we vote for him.”Meanwhile on Thursday, the executive committee of the African confederation (Caf) unanimously confirmed its support for Infantino. In a statement it said: “The CAF executive committee unanimously endorses the joint update by the Fifa president and secretary general on the FFE and will continue to focus on making African Football amongst the best in the world and adhering to governance and transparency global best practices.”Explore more on these topicsUefaGianni InfantinoFifaWorld CupWorld Cup 2026Football politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal hopes dashed after Vinícius Júnior extends Real Madrid contract to 2032 | Vinícius Júnior | The Guardian

Content: Vinícius Júnior has been at Real Madrid since joining the club as an 18-year-old in July 2018.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenVinícius Júnior has been at Real Madrid since joining the club as an 18-year-old in July 2018.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAVinícius JúniorArsenal hopes dashed after Vinícius Júnior extends Real Madrid contract to 2032Brazil international has agreed a new six-year deal‘Eight years at the Bernabéu are too few,’ says ViníciusAgenciesThu 6 Aug 2026 18.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVinícius Júnior has ended summer speculation over his future by agreeing a new six-year contract with Real Madrid.
