title: Top Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stones | Soccer | The Guardian
description: David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone
Content: David Owori was described as ‘an inspiration to a generation’ by the Federation of Uganda Football Associations.Photograph: SC VillaView image in fullscreenDavid Owori was described as ‘an inspiration to a generation’ by the Federation of Uganda Football Associations.Photograph: SC VillaSoccerTop Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stonesDavid Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phoneCarlos MureithiThu 6 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatally injured during a robbery in the capital, Kampala, on Tuesday night.David Owori, who captained Sports Club Villa, a Uganda Premier League club, and represented the national team, was attacked after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings near his home in Makindye division.Racheal Kawala, a spokesperson for the Kampala Metropolitan police, said he was found unconscious by ​passersby, who took him to a nearby hospital. He was ​transferred to another hospital, where he was pronounced dead on Wednesday.Witnesses said attackers hit the footballer with paving stones before robbing him and fleeing, leaving him unconscious,the BBC reported.Owori, 27, was a right-back and midfielder for SC Villa. He helped the team win a record 17th Uganda Premier League title in 2024.He started his senior career in 2016 at the Uganda Premier League side Vipers Sports Club and had stints in Europe with Vélez CF in Spain and Utsiktens BK in Sweden.He played for the national team in the qualifiers for the 2021AfricaCup of Nations.SC Villasaid: “It is with profound sorrow that we announce the untimely passing of our captain, Owori, who had been receiving treatment at Case Clinic following an attack by suspected thugs. Our deepest condolences and prayers are with his family.”The Federation ​of Uganda Football Associationssaid: “David was not just a footballer. He was ​both a leader and an inspiration to a generation. As ​Captain of SC Villa, he led with courage, humility and passion. In the Uganda Cranes jersey, he carried the hopes of a nation.”It added: “We have lost a son, a leader and a star. His light on and off the pitch will never be forgotten.”The Ugandan parliament observed a minute of silence in Owori’s honour on Wednesday.In June Sydney Gongodyo, a Ugandan rugby international, ​died after a mob attacked him in Kampala, mistaking him for a thief, police said.Uganda’s National Council of Sports said: “Sadly, ​Ugandan sport has been hit with many such ​tragedies lately, and we hope for justice and a lasting solution.”Explore more on these topicsFootballUgandaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Kerolin failed to report for pre-season at Manchester City before Barcelona switch | Manchester City Women | The Guardian
description: The Brazil forward Kerolin failed to report for pre-season training at Manchester City before transfer to Barcelona had been agreed
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: The Brazil forward Kerolin failed to report for pre-season training at Manchester City before transfer to Barcelona had been agreed
Content: Kerolin has joined Barcelona from Manchester City on a deal worth an initial £1m.Photograph: Marta Perez/EPAView image in fullscreenKerolin has joined Barcelona from Manchester City on a deal worth an initial £1m.Photograph: Marta Perez/EPAManchester City WomenKerolin failed to report for pre-season at Manchester City before Barcelona switchCity taken aback by forward’s absence from trainingWSL champions wait two days before mentioning dealExclusive byTom GarryThu 6 Aug 2026 15.35 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Brazil forward Kerolin failed to report back for pre-season training at Manchester City in July beforeher transfer to Barcelonahad been agreed.Barcelona announced their signing of the 26-year-old on Tuesday but it was not until Thursday evening when Manchester City first made any reference to the transfer, eventually confirming they had received a WSL record fee for a sale more than 48 hours later.Alessia Russo: ‘When you join the club, you take on a part of Arsenal and the love’Read moreSeveral staff and players at Manchester City were disappointed at what were perceived to be efforts by Kerolin to force a transfer to Barcelona and that her time at the club ended on a surprisingly sour note. She did not join pre-season withthe Women’s Super League champions, which began in late July, despite previously having been felt to have been on good terms with the squad.The deal, worth an initial €1.2m (£1m), represents the largest transfer fee received by a WSL club, and it could rise with add-ons to approximately £1.25m, although this has not been officially confirmed. It is one of the largest transfer fees in women’s football.City said of Kerolin: “She grabbed 14 goals and six assists during that time, helping City to a WSL and FA Cup double in her solitary full season in England. And upon her transfer to Barça, City have received a WSL-club record transfer fee of €1.2m.“Everyone at Manchester City would like to thank Kerolin for all her efforts at the club and wish her the very best in her future career.”Kerolin was part of the City side that lifted their first WSL title in a decade last season and also helped them winthe Women’s FA Cup. But within weeks of those celebrations many of her City colleagues have been stunned after she did not say goodbye in-person. Kerolin’s representatives have been contacted for a response.High-profile examples of such transfer standoffs have been seen in men’s football, but incidents in the women’s game have been comparatively rare.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCity have no objections to the transfer in principle but sources have said the team were taken aback by the former North Carolina Courage star’s absence from pre-season fitness testing. For Kerolin, it is a dream move to the European champions,who beat OL Lyonnesin last season’s Women’s Champions League final.City and Barcelona will meet in a friendly at the Joie Stadium on 15 August as the reigning champions of England and Spain step up their pre-season preparations.Explore more on these topicsManchester City WomenBarcelona WomenTransfer windowWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Barcelona step up Rodri interest after Real Madrid talks with Manchester City star stall | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Barça are ready to hijack their rivals’ attempts to sign the Spain captain as Real Madrid failed to reach an agreement with the Manchester City midfielder
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Barça are ready to hijack their rivals’ attempts to sign the Spain captain as Real Madrid failed to reach an agreement with the Manchester City midfielder
Content: Rodri is in the final year of his contract at Manchester City.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenRodri is in the final year of his contract at Manchester City.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersTransfer windowBarcelona step up Rodri interest after Real Madrid talks with Manchester City star stallBarça ready to hijack rivals’ plans to sign Spain captainManchester City will allow midfielder to go for £60mEd AaronsThu 6 Aug 2026 12.39 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarcelona have stepped up their attempts to hijack Real Madrid’s move to sign Rodri fromManchester City.While City have not given up hope that Spain’s World Cup-winning captain will sign a new contract after he entered the final year of his deal, they are thought to be willing to allow him to leave for about £60m. Despite weeks of talks with Rodri and his representatives, Real have yet to reach an agreement andBarcelonaare hoping to take advantage.It is understood that Rodri spoke to their manager, Hansi Flick, and sporting director, Deco, about a potential move on Wednesday and indicated he is keen to return to Spain. Barça, who will be without midfielder Frenkie de Jong for several months after the Netherlands midfielder sustained a knee injury, are now expected to make contact with City to negotiate the structure of the fee for the 30-year-old,who won the Golden Ballfor the World Cup’s best player.Men’s transfer window summer 2026: all deals from Europe’s top five leaguesRead moreReal, who have signed RB Leipzig’s Yan Diomande for aclub record fee of £115m, have also agreed a lucrative six-year contract extension with Vinícius Júnior to ward offinterest from Arsenal. They may have to offload players first if they are to sign Rodri as well. Aurélien Tchouaméni and Eduardo Camavinga are possible departures, with Manchester United having been linked with the France midfielders.Rodri has hadminor surgery on his backand will miss most of City’s pre-season programme. Theyhave signed Elliot Andersonfrom Nottingham Forest for £116m and remain in negotiations with Lille over a deal for the 18-year-old Morocco midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi.Meanwhile, Barcelona have been frustrated in their efforts to persuadeAtlético Madridto sell Julián Alvarez. After Robert Lewandowski’s departure, Barcelona have targeted Alvarez all summer, but Atlético continue to insist the Argentina striker is not for sale at any price.Deco was in the Spanish capital to meet Alvarez’s representatives on Wednesday. All eyes will be on whether the 26-year-old former City forward will return to pre-season training on Monday or attempt to force through a transfer. Arsenal also retain an interest in him.Ferran Torres – who scored the winning goal forSpain in the World Cup finalagainst Argentina – has entered the final year of his contract at Barcelona and said he is waiting for them to begin talks over extending his deal. “All I know is that I have to be in training for Barcelona on 12 August. Let’s see what happens.” Asked what Barcelona needed to do to keep him, he said: “Show me they want me, come to negotiate.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, James Trafford sealed a club-record move to Leeds after completing a medical at Elland Road. Leeds have agreed a £40m fee plus add-ons with City for the 23-year-old, who will become the world’s fourth most expensive goalkeeper.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowManchester CityBarcelonaReal MadridAtlético MadridnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tour de France Femmes: Reusser stays ahead as Le Court savours stage win | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Kim Le Court won the sixth stage of the Tour de France Femmes in Tournon-sur-Rhône while Marlen Reusser retained the overall lead
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Kim Le Court won the sixth stage of the Tour de France Femmes in Tournon-sur-Rhône while Marlen Reusser retained the overall lead
Content: Kim Le Court shows her delight as she crosses the finish line to win the stage.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKim Le Court shows her delight as she crosses the finish line to win the stage.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesTour de France FemmesTour de France Femmes: Reusser stays ahead as Le Court savours stage winMauritian rider outsprints Kerbaol and Pieterse‘Winning a stage in a Tour de France is very special’Jeremy Whittlein Tournon-sur-RhôneThu 6 Aug 2026 13.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 20.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarlen Reusser retained the overall lead in theTour de France Femmesfrom rival Demi Vollering after another broiling stage through central France saw Kim Le Court take the second Tour stage win of her career in Tournon-sur-Rhone.The Mauritian rider Le Court recovered from a mechanical problem earlier in the stage on the climb of the Col de Lalouvesc to join the day’s breakaway group and outsprint Cédrine Kerbaol of France, and Queen of the Mountains classification leader, Puck Pieterse.“I was on the limit,” Le Court said of her winning sprint. “I can’t believe I still had the legs to sprint. It was really hard, this close, before I could give up. I will never give up after the big effort my team did.”Tour de France Femmes 2026: Kim Le Court wins stage six sprint after breakaway – liveRead moreLe Court had originally been considered a contender for final victory but lost ground after Tuesday’s individual time trial. “I’ve been really struggling since the time trial day but I think this really makes our Tour,” she said.“We’ve still got ambitions for the general classification, but winning a stage in a Tour de France is very special. People don’t really remember top 10 or top five riders in Tour, but they do remember stage winners.”Le Court’s success is a popular one, after a difficult season in which she has dealt with serial injuries. But she has also shown considerable sportsmanship, stopping to help Kasia Niewiadoma after the 2024 Tour Femmes winner crashed heavily in Milan-San Remo.Despite missing out on the stage victory, it was a successful day for Pieterse as she now has 47 points in the mountain classification, the highest total ever recorded in the history of the Tour de France Femmes.“I wanted to win the stage of course,” Pieterse said, “but I think I did everything else today. I decided to gamble, but Kim was still the strongest in the sprint, so I don’t think I can be too sad.”As the heatwave continued, the peloton raced over six classified climbs into the Ardeche, with Friday’s ascent of Mont Ventoux now very much in their thoughts.After three days she will want to forget, defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prevot arrested the decline in her form and finished the stage in the group of favourites alongside Reusser, Vollering and Niewiadoma. She is still languishing in 15th place overall, five minutes behind race leader Reusser, and on Wednesday had conceded that: “It’s over.”However, while her deficit seems almost insurmountable, her rivals will have taken note of her improved performance and of her experience of the Ventoux, which she first rode in 2021.“I think it’s the most iconic climb in France,” Ferrand-Prevot said of the Provençal mountain. “Everyone knows about it, even if you’re not a cyclist.”The inclusion of the Ventoux in the Tour de France Femmes is the latest indicator of a race growing in stature, year by year.“We try to align with the most mythical summits,” Tour de France Femmes director Marion Rousse said. “They’re part of the history of the Tour and the history of the sport.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBoth Vollering and Niewiadoma have prior experience of the mountain, but not at this level of racing, and only from the less demanding north side, rather than the more daunting southern ascent. However, there is no doubt that the ascent of the Ventoux, by a women’s peloton that only a few years ago was derided by some for its abilities, will be a Rubicon moment.One rider who never shared those doubts is current race leader Reusser. “It’s proof that human beings aren’t always such a smart species,” she said of those who had disparaged the women’s peloton.View image in fullscreenMarlen Reusser shows her delight at retaining the lead.Photograph: Alex Broadway/Getty ImagesIn terms of past exploits by women on the “Giant of Provence” Nicole Cooke’s solo attack over the Ventoux, which took her to overall victory in the 2006 Grande Boucle Feminine, is perhaps the most memorable.“I don’t suppose anybody wanted to chase me all the way up the Ventoux,” Cooke recalled. “The heat was a big factor. People don’t want to chase on a day when the heat is so debilitating.”Cooke won the stage by four minutes and the race overall by more than six. “After the finish, we went to a cafe and had ice-creams,” she said. “It was one of the special days.”At that time, women’s cycling had little profile and media coverage was almost nonexistent. Cooke’s achievement never really got the recognition it deserved, due to what she considered to be media’s preoccupation with the prevalence of doping in men’s cycling. The rebirth of the Tour de France Femmes however has dramatically reversed that trend. The heat will also be big factor in toFriday’s stage to the Ventoux, 20 years after Cooke’s own moment in the sun. But the inclusion of a climb that the French still call the “killer mountain”, is a total vindication of the quantum leap achieved by the women’s peloton.Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Springboks and All Blacks flex financial muscles with ‘Greatest Rivalry’ tour | Rugby union | The Guardian
description: The Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry tour rekindles memories of the game’s past, but the focus is very much on financial realities of the modern game
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: The Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry tour rekindles memories of the game’s past, but the focus is very much on financial realities of the modern game
Content: The Springboks face the All Blacks’ haka before the 2023 World Cup final in Paris. The All Blacks tour of South Africa begins on Friday.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Springboks face the All Blacks’ haka before the 2023 World Cup final in Paris. The All Blacks tour of South Africa begins on Friday.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianRugby unionSpringboks and All Blacks flex financial muscles with ‘Greatest Rivalry’ tourThrowback series rekindles memories of the past, but the focus is very much on realities of the modern gameGerard MeagherThu 6 Aug 2026 10.48 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust in case you were unaware that the series between South Africa and New Zealand, styled as Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry (RGR), is a “tour like no other”, the Springboks have just unveiled a jersey to prove it. “A jersey like no other” to be worn four times and then consigned to history.The RGR, though, kicks off with a looming legal battle in South Africa in the background over the series’ commercial identity and the unauthorised use of its branding. And you thought sporting romance was dead.Inexperienced halves pair get nod for first Wallabies Test under new coach Les KissRead moreEnough of the cynicism. The series promises to be a blockbuster. It is a throwback, with New Zealand’s men facing four matches against provincial sides, starting with the Stormers in Cape Town on Friday, as well as four Tests against the Springboks with the first on 22 August. The countries’ women’s sides also face each other in a one-off Test.The series has further allure in just how rare tours such as this are these days. Add in the fact that the rugby calendar is pretty much barren at the moment and a series between the two best sides in the world is enough to quicken the pulse.It is the first of its kind by New Zealand since 1996 – an unforgettable tour and the first won by the All Blacks on South African soil – a year after their World Cup final defeat at Ellis Park. The marketing departments have wasted no opportunity, to impressive effect, in evoking the history of this particular series, which dates back to 1921. Even the name is designed to do just that.What it means for the future Test landscape is just as fascinating. RGR comes a few weeks after the launch of the inaugural Nations Championship – a competition that has effectively brought an end to traditional tours, certainly those made by northern hemisphere sides heading south.The key exception remains the British & Irish Lions and it was instructive to hear Mark Alexander, president of the South African union, say he believes RGR can eclipse even those quadrennial tours. All the more so because the Lions are having their heads turnedby advances from, among others, Franceand the lucrative potential of moving away from their traditional destinations. Should they do so, it would be financially catastrophic for South Africa, New Zealand and Australia, so it stands to reason they would seek to diversify revenue streams.With the Lions heading to New Zealand in 2029 and the Springboks arriving a year later for the second instalment of RGR, whichever proves more commercially successful will be significant in determining what the future global calendar looks like. Three-Test tours for England, Ireland et al are off the table for now but if RGR becomes the most successful enterprise on the Test scene beyond the World Cup then the northern hemisphere unions will surely react accordingly and plot their own Rivalry series.View image in fullscreenAll Blacks fans cheer their side during an event to mark the team’s arrival in Cape Town.Photograph: Rodger Bosch/AFP/Getty ImagesIf RGR puts the launch of the Nations Championship in the shade somewhat – the Springboks’ head coach, Rassie Erasmus, has barely tried to conceal which he has prioritised and opinion among the players would be pretty unanimous – South Africa and New Zealand have left Australia and Argentina hanging, too. There is no Rugby Championship this year, which feels like a mistake afterthe thrilling 2025 editionand, viewed through the lens of the Wallabies and Pumas, RGR seems a selfish move.That said, who can really blame South Africa and New Zealand? They have won the past five World Cups between them and, unlike Australia, they have no realistic chance of hosting the tournament again any time soon. For all that the evocative history between the two sides is invoked, the imperatives for RGR are undoubtedly commercial, hammered home for those at the back by the fact the fourth and final Test takes place in the United States. The series revenue is a clean 50:50 split and askip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA lucrative add-on in Baltimore will swell the coffers further, strengthen both teams’ brand awareness in the US and is welcome news for World Rugby, who are putting a brave face on it, but are desperate to ensure the 2031 World Cup does not pass unnoticed by the locals.The Breakdown | Nations Championship fails to solve rugby’s ability to get in the way of itselfRead moreThe benefits of RGR, beyond the bottom line, are obvious. South Africa would be quick to point out it was New Zealand’s decision to break up the traditional Super Rugby format, but there is no doubt the All Blacks have been hurt by the absence of regular fixtures for their provinces against their South African counterparts. More exposure to South African beef is a welcome addition to the menu. That the provincial sides will be shorn of their Springboks in the coming weeks detracts from the spectacle – it is a problem the Lions have run into on their past two tours – and ticket sales for Friday’s opener have been slow, but it does allow thenew All Blacks coach, Dave Rennie, to strengthen his player pool.South Africa tick along with their provinces in the URC and their best players in Japan, but a conveyor belt of raw talent at home will benefit from playing the travelling All Blacks. Having a foot in both hemispheres does not seem sustainable with reports that the South African clubs are pulling out of the Champions and Challenge Cups, but it is a unique position for the double world champions. They continue to find new ways to thrive and new ways to set the benchmark despite the continued concentration of financial power in the north. RGR is just the latest.Explore more on these topicsRugby unionSouth Africa rugby teamNew Zealand rugby union teamfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Burnham ‘personally intervened’ over possible early prison release of grooming gang perpetrators | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Government ‘urgently’ identifying men convicted in historical cases who could be freed in scheme loophole
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Government ‘urgently’ identifying men convicted in historical cases who could be freed in scheme loophole
Content: About 5,000 people are expected to be released early under sentencing changes designed to tackle overcrowding in jails.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAbout 5,000 people are expected to be released early under sentencing changes designed to tackle overcrowding in jails.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesPrisons and probationBurnham ‘personally intervened’ over possible early prison release of grooming gang perpetratorsGovernment ‘urgently’ identifying men convicted in historical cases who could be freed in scheme loopholeRajeev SyalHome affairs editorThu 6 Aug 2026 11.32 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham’s government is “urgently” identifying any grooming gang perpetrators who may still be eligible for early prison release after concerns were raised about a potential loophole in the system.The prime minister has “personally intervened” after men convicted of assaulting children inBradfordwere expected to be freed from prison early despite a promise earlier this week that they would remain behind bars.In a statement, No 10 said it would ensure that “everything possible is being done so that vile groomers are dealt with in the way their victims deserve”.About 5,000 people are expected to be released early under sentencing changes in England and Wales, down from 6,000 afterministers excludedgrooming gang members, rapists and “serious” child sex offenders from the scheme designed to reduce overcrowding in jails.Critics have questioned the scope of the exemptions after reports that some men convicted in relation to historical grooming gang cases could be among those freed.Some of the offending took place before sexual abuse laws were changed in 2003 and the perpetrators were charged with crimes such as indecent assault, which do not fall within the exclusions to the scheme starting in October.A spokesperson for Burnham said: “As part of the review of sentences, the prime minister asked the Ministry of Justice to conduct an in-depth review of cases to ensure that grooming cases were identified.“This work is happening urgently. This is extremely important to the PM and he has personally intervened to ensure everything possible is being done so that vile groomers are dealt with in the way their victims deserve.”Burnham suspended the schemein his second week as prime minister after coming under intense pressure from MPs, victims, campaigners and frontline prison officers to halt the early release of serious sexual and violent offenders.Prisons have become a major point of political contention, with Labour blaming the Conservatives for creating the overcrowding crisis between 2010 and 2024 by increasing sentences while failing to build enough jails.The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, wrote to Burnham on Thursday demanding to know which offences would be eligible for early release and accusing the government of “yet another betrayal of the victims”.As first disclosed bythe Times, there are a number of instances where men convicted of assaulting children in Bradford as part of historical investigations into Asian grooming gangs were not excluded from the early release scheme.As many of the assaults took place before anti-grooming laws were introduced in 2003, the men were charged with indecent assault, which does not fall within the exemptions announced by the prime minister this week.The government has also resisted pressure to exempt two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers from early release as the boss of his former force considersjoining a potential legal challengeover the plans.View image in fullscreenTwo of the killers of PC Andrew Harper, Jessie Cole (centre) and Albert Bowers (right), could be freed early under the scheme, but not Henry Long (left).Photograph: Thames Valley police/PAJessie Cole and Albert Bowers could be freed halfway through their 13-year sentences for manslaughter after the officer’s death in 2019.Harper sustained fatal injuries after getting caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and being dragged down a country road as the killers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire. The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence for manslaughter and will not be eligible for release under the scheme.The Thames Valley police chief constable, Jason Hogg, said he was receiving legal advice on whether the force could join a legal challenge mooted by the local Police Federation chief, Aileen O’Connor, to prevent Cole and Bowers being freed.The prime minister has said he wanted to “go further” with the exemptions, but this was “not possible without the prison system reaching capacity and collapsing”.Those released will face tougher probation conditions, including electronic monitoring, random drug testing and possible bans from driving, pubs and events such as football matches.The changes were part of theSentencingAct passed earlier this year, which cut the minimum amount of time many offenders would have to spend in prison.Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationRape and sexual assaultUK criminal justiceSentencingViolence against women and girlsBradfordAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Baby safely delivered 30 minutes after mother died in nine-storey fall | Leeds | The Guardian
description: Emma Atkinson, 38, was seven months pregnant when she fell from window of flat in Leeds tower block, inquest told
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Emma Atkinson, 38, was seven months pregnant when she fell from window of flat in Leeds tower block, inquest told
Content: The inquest into Emma Atkinson’s death could not conclusively say whether she intended to die when she jumped from flat in Shakespeare Towers, Leeds.Photograph: Leeds City CouncilView image in fullscreenThe inquest into Emma Atkinson’s death could not conclusively say whether she intended to die when she jumped from flat in Shakespeare Towers, Leeds.Photograph: Leeds City CouncilLeedsBaby safely delivered 30 minutes after mother died in nine-storey fallEmma Atkinson, 38, was seven months pregnant when she fell from window of flat in Leeds tower block, inquest toldRaphael BoydThu 6 Aug 2026 12.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA pregnant woman who died from a nine-storey fall had her baby safely delivered 30 minutes after her death, an inquest has heard.Emma Atkinson, 38, was seven months pregnant when she fell from the window of her father’s flat in Shakespeare Towers in the Burmantofts area of Leeds, on 22 October 2024.Wakefield coroner’s court heard on Thursday that Atkinson was pronounced dead by paramedics who arrived at the scene shortly after she fell at 10.20am. Atkinson’s body was taken to Leeds general infirmary, where an emergency caesarean section was performed.The baby girl was born soon after arriving at the hospital. She sustained some injuries from the fall, including a punctured lung and fractured tibia, requiring her to remain in intensive care for the first weeks of her life, but has since recovered. The girl, who is now 21 months old, is reportedly “being raised happily” by family members.In a narrative verdict, the inquest ruled that Atkinson had “deliberately propelled herself” from the window of the tower block, but was unable to decide if she had done so with the intention of ending her own life.The coroner Naomi McLoughlin said that while “the deliberate act of removing the safety catches from the window” and “the manner of her falling, captured by the CCTV” was significant, other evidence such as the lack of concerning signs in the weeks prior, and the fact she had made plans beyond that day with her family, meant she could not conclusively say Atkinson meant to die when she fell.The court heard that at the time of her death, Atkinson was suffering from poor mental health and was worried about the possibility of being incarcerated after failing to attend a court date for a shoplifting offence.Her father, David Atkinson, told the inquest via a summarised statement that his daughter had come to visit him at his flat that morning. While there, she began to smoke a cigarette in front of a window in his living room, which she then opened fully after removing the safety catches.Atkinson said that he asked his daughter what she was doing, to which she told him “not to worry (as) she was just getting some fresh air”, before she said “I’m off” and fell through the window head first. He also said he believed his daughter had intended to end her own life that morning.Other members of her family who attended the inquest said Atkinson would not have intentionally taken her own life, stating that she “would never have left her kids” and that her “life revolved around her children”.Explore more on these topicsLeedsEnglandYorkshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump administration to pay German firm $1.22bn to cut offshore wind leases | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Agreement with RWE is fifth deal Trump team has made with energy companies, offering payouts to give up projects
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Agreement with RWE is fifth deal Trump team has made with energy companies, offering payouts to give up projects
Content: Wind turbines, including some from RWE's new Kaskasi offshore windfarm, are pictured north of Helgoland, Germany, in 2023.Photograph: Christian Charisius/ReutersView image in fullscreenWind turbines, including some from RWE's new Kaskasi offshore windfarm, are pictured north of Helgoland, Germany, in 2023.Photograph: Christian Charisius/ReutersTrump administrationTrump administration to pay German firm $1.22bn to cut offshore wind leasesAgreement with RWE is fifth deal Trump team has made with energy companies, offering payouts to give up projectsMaya YangThu 6 Aug 2026 14.20 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe German energy company RWE has reached a $1.22bn deal with the US government to relinquish its offshore wind leases and instead redirect funds towards fossil fuel investments.The agreement marks the fifth deal the Donald Trump administrationhas struck with energy companies, offering payouts in exchange for abandoning renewable energy projects and redirecting investment towards fossil fuels.This latest deal takes it to almost $4bn of taxpayer money spent on killing offshore wind projects.Announcing the dealwith the US interior department on Thursday, RWE said it had agreed to give up its offshore wind leases off the coasts of New York, California and Louisiana.“After careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the US for the foreseeable future,” the company said, referring to the leases it initially secured with a “long-term commitment to develop offshore wind capacity”.RWE paid $1.1bn for its New York lease in a 2022 auction held by the Joe Biden administration, while its leases in Louisiana and California cost a combined $163m, Reutersreports.“The settlement resolves RWE US Offshore’s legal claims and provides $1.22 billion in settlement funds,” RWE continued, adding that the deal would allow it to “direct resources toward energy projects that can be advanced with certainty.”As part of the agreement, RWE will spend $900m to acquire a 16% stake in an unnamed Louisiana liquified natural gas (LNG) project. The company said the settlement proceeds would be used to fund construction of the terminal.RWE has also signed a $300m turbine reservation agreement under which it will develop a pipeline of 15 natural gas peaker plants across the country.The interior secretary, Doug Burgum, hailed the deal, saying on Thursday: “We welcome RWE’s agreement and voluntary investment in projects that strengthen our nation’s energy security, provide dependable baseload power, and help keep electricity affordable for hardworking Americans today while supporting our country’s long-term energy future.”The RWE agreement appears to be the largest deal theTrump administrationhas struck with an energy company to kill clean energy projects. Earlier agreements with other companies, including TotalEnergies and Duke Energy, amounted to $2.7bn in taxpayer money.Following the Trump administration’s$928m dealwith French energy company TotalEnergies to cancel its offshore wind lease off the coast of New York, seven states, including New York, sued the administration over what the New York attorney general, Letitia James,describedas a “sham deal” and “illegal agreement”.The administration has also spent up to $1.1bn to boost coal, a movecritics argueis “fattening the wallets of his cronies” while raising working Americans’ energy bills, particularly as the US’s war on Irandrives upfuel prices.At the same time, the federal government is seeking toslash public input periodsfor fossil fuel drilling on federal lands while shifting more of the financial risks of cleanup to taxpayers.Meanwhile, a report released last fall by the Environmental Integrity Project found that every fully operational LNG facility in the US hadviolated federal pollution limitsin recent years.According to the non-profit research organization, violations included the discharge of illegal amounts of bacteria, zinc, oil and other pollutants into waterways, as well as failures of terminal managers to submit monitoring reports for waterway discharge.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationRenewable energyEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: All bodies of water in England polluted with toxic chemicals, official data shows | Water | The Guardian
description: Environment Agency assessments find just 14.3% of country’s surface waters in good ecological status
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Environment Agency assessments find just 14.3% of country’s surface waters in good ecological status
Content: Rubbish and debris in a partially dry section of the Rochdale canal in central Manchester last September.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRubbish and debris in a partially dry section of the Rochdale canal in central Manchester last September.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesWaterAll bodies of water in England polluted with toxic chemicals, official data showsEnvironment Agency assessments find just 14.3% of country’s surface waters in good ecological statusPippa NeillEnvironment reporterThu 6 Aug 2026 06.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery single English water body is polluted with toxic chemicals, new government data shows, while just 14.3% of surface waters achieved good ecological status.Each of the country’s rivers, lakes and estuaries was assessed by theEnvironment Agencyas part of a six-yearly evaluation of England’s water quality. The EA checked for a range of toxic chemicals, from Pfas – or “forever chemicals” – to microplastics. Waters were also checked against a range of standards covering wildlife, water quality and physical habitat.If concentrations of the chemicals exceed the set standards, the water body fails to meet good chemical status. In the latest assessment, every surface water body inEnglandfailed on this measure.Under water framework directive regulations, the official target date for all water bodies to reach good chemical and ecological status is December 2027, although some chemicals have deadlines in the 2030s.The Environment Agency said this failure was driven almost entirely by the presence of mercury, Pfos – a type of Pfas withlinks to cancer- and PBDEs, which were formerly used as flame retardants. These chemicals are persistent, meaning they do not break down and can accumulate in the environment.England’s water bodies are not predicted to reach good chemical status until 2063, when the EA says the persistent chemical pollutants should have degraded sufficiently for waters to again be considered unpolluted.MapAmi McCarthy, Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, said the scale of the crisis was “sobering”. The government needed to take “urgent action to turn off the chemicals that are destroying our land at the source”, they said.The UK government has been accused of failing to take action on toxic chemicals after itsplan to tackle Pfas chemicalsfailed to match the tougher stance being taken in Europe. It has also been accused of failing to tackle mercury pollution, with Britain being one of the few countriesyet to ban mercury in dental fillings. The metal is a potent neurotoxin that can harm the nervous, digestive and immune systems, as well as the lungs, kidneys, skin and eyes, even at low levels of exposure.Craig Bennett, chief executive of The Wildlife Trusts said if it was a “foreign power maliciously poisoning every single water body in England with cancer causing chemicals, politicians right across the political spectrum would be utterly horrified and demand the government of the day do absolutely everything in their power to fight back, stop it immediately, and seek some sort of retribution”.Instead he said “politicians across the political spectrum have come together with a conspiracy of silence and inaction”.Richard Benwell, the chief executive of Wildlife and Countryside Link, said: “With thousands more forever chemicals on the market from cosmetics to clothing, government must act now to stop another wave of contamination by matching EU safeguards and making the polluting companies pay for clean up.”Water campaigner Feargal Sharkey said the EA has “failed every waterbody in the country” and “overseen the collapse of an issue they were supposed to be policing”.He called on the environment secretary to rewrite the guidance and enforce the law as it stands.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Environment Agency said it was undertaking a range of activities to improve understanding of chemicals in the environment and identify potential sources affecting rivers, groundwater and drinking water catchments.“Water companies must be made to take responsibility for their part, but pollution from agriculture is now one of the biggest drivers of environmental damage in UK rivers. It’s time for the government to work with farmers, providing proper support to rein in runaway use of fertilisers and pesticides, and boost nature-friendly practices,” McCarthy said.Assessment against a range of standards covering wildlife, water quality and physical habitat also showed that just 14.3% of England’s surface waters achieved good ecological status, a decline from 16.3% in 2019. However, the EA said the two datasets were not directly comparable because it had updated its analytical methods.The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, said the results “underline the need for wholesale change across the water sector”.The chief executive of the campaign group River Action said despite successive government’s promises, England’s rivers remained among the “filthiest in Europe, poisoned by sewage from polluting, profit-driven water companies and by industrial-scale agriculture, including chicken manure runoff from intensive poultry units that rear tens of millions of birds for fast-food chains and supermarkets”.Prof Alex Ford, professor of biology at University of Portsmouth, said he is “not surprised” by the analysis and said if regulators added more chemicals to the list that should be monitored, he is “confident we would be failing on a larger list of contaminants.”Explore more on these topicsWaterEnglandWater industryRiversPollutionPfasEnvironment policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Human-driven climate crisis fuels Canada’s deadly wildfires, study finds | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: Current blazes roaring across country more than twice as likely to occur because of fossil fuel-driven global heating
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Current blazes roaring across country more than twice as likely to occur because of fossil fuel-driven global heating
Content: People in Lake Country, British Columbia, watch as the Quilpituk Creek wildfire burns across Okanagan Lake, near Fintry, on 3 August 2026.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPeople in Lake Country, British Columbia, watch as the Quilpituk Creek wildfire burns across Okanagan Lake, near Fintry, on 3 August 2026.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockWildfiresHuman-driven climate crisis fuels Canada’s deadly wildfires, study findsCurrent blazes roaring across country more than twice as likely to occur because of fossil fuel-driven global heatingOliver MilmanThu 6 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe human-driven climate crisis made the conditions that led to blazes roaring acrossCanada, which have caused toxic smoke to spew throughout the country and into the US, twice as likely to occur, a new analysis has found.Heightened global temperatures, caused by the burning of fossil fuels, amplified the risk of fire-prone weather in Ontario and the Northwest Territories, scientists found. These provinces have been racked by fires this summer, causing towns to be evacuated andunhealthy smoketo unfurl across multiple cities in North America.There are currently nearly 700 firesablazeacross Canada, with a huge 3.8m hectares of the country, mainly in its sprawling boreal forests. But the study byWorld Weather Attribution, a consortium of scientists that analyses climate change’s influence upon extreme events, found that fire weather seen in Canada this year is no longer a rare event.The climate-influenced conditions that dry out vegetation and soils, making them more prone to combustion, are now expected every two to six years in the Northwest Territories and every six to 15 years in Ontario. If humanity hadn’t overheated the planet by burning coal, oil and gas, the scientists determined, such extreme fire conditions would occur less than once every 40 years.Canada, which has a quarter of the world’s boreal forests, has always experienced fire. But the climate crisis has made fire conditions more extreme and since 2023, when huge fires also spread across Canada, the country has suffered a “fundamentally different” scale and intensity of blazes, according to Theodore Keeping, an expert in extreme weather at Imperial College London and part of the WWA research team.View image in fullscreenThe Brunswick Creek wildfire from Boston Bar, British Columbia, Canada, on 7 July 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images“The geographic spread of these fires is scary and shows that despite preparedness from wildfire governance, adaptation alone is not enough,” Keeping said. “We need to rapidly move away from fossil fuels to avoid events like this becoming even more of a reality.”The WWA group finalized the study of Canada’s fire conditions shortly afterunveiling findings showing the climate crisis had an even larger rolein record fires raging in Spain and France, which has staged its largest ever peacetime evacuation due to the flames.“What is going to be next?” said Friederike Otto, a climate scientist at Imperial College London and WWA study co-author.View image in fullscreenSmoke from huge wildfires in Canada engulfs the New York City skyline, reducing visibility and casting an orange haze on 16 July 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images“Time and again we see the same results: climate change is a key driver behind uncontrollably large and unprecedented fires. This shouldn’t come as a surprise. The science has been clear for decades: burning fossil fuels is making these wildfires more frequent, more intense and more difficult to contain.”Despite the clear science linking the climate crisis to wildfire conditions, Donald Trumphas sought to pin the blame upon Canada for not better controlling firesthat are burning, often in wild, inaccessible areas.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Climate change kills’: Pedro Sánchez speaks plain truth to Spain’s deniersRead moreTrump, who has dismissed established climate science as “crap” and “a con”, said last month that the US was “being unnecessarily invaded by filthy, polluted and unhealthy air” and threatened reprisals such as new tariffs against his country’s northern neighbor.Asked what “punishment” Canada will receive, the US president said on Sunday: “You’ll find out about it.”Experts have condemned Trump’s remarks, with WWA scientists pointing out that most of Canada’s boreal forest is unmanaged and is being warped by planet-heating emissions coming from around the world, with the US the historic largest emitter.“I don’t think we should blame Canadians for that,” Jonathan Boucher, a researcher at the Canadian Forest Service, said.The fires continues to cause havoc across Canada, beyond the provinces studied by the new research. In British Columbia, 8,000 people are under an evacuation orderamid“explosive and extremely dangerous” fire conditions.Explore more on these topicsWildfiresClimate crisisCanadanewsShareReuse this content

title: Accused arsonist studied how to maximize Washington wildfire’s harm, police say | Washington state | The Guardian
description: Court documents allege Aaron Farinacci, who faces slew of arson charges, set 25 fires in Spokane area over past year
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Court documents allege Aaron Farinacci, who faces slew of arson charges, set 25 fires in Spokane area over past year
Content: A firefighter hoses down the remains of a home destroyed in the Old Trails fire in Spokane on Friday.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA firefighter hoses down the remains of a home destroyed in the Old Trails fire in Spokane on Friday.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesWashington stateAccused arsonist studied how to maximize Washington wildfire’s harm, police sayCourt documents allege Aaron Farinacci, who faces slew of arson charges, set 25 fires in Spokane area over past yearUwa Ede-Osifoand agenciesThu 6 Aug 2026 17.24 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe 37-year-old man accused of sparking a devastating fire in Washington allegedly studied how to maximize the blaze’s destruction and was responsible for setting 25 other fires in the Spokane area over the past year, according to a court affidavit.Aaron Farinacci, who faces a slew of arson charges, is accused of starting the Old Trails fire, which began on 1 August and is still burning – one of three “Spokane complex” fires that have scorched hundreds of homes and displaced thousands of residents.The other two fires were also started by people, though not necessarily deliberately, investigators have said. They remain under investigation.Farinacci allegedly knew Spokane county was under a “red flag warning”, an advisory the National Weather Service issues when low humidity and powerful winds raise the risk of hazardous fire conditions.According to court documents, Farinacci lit a homemade ignition device and placed it in grass on 1 August, reasoning that, with the strong gusts of wind he observed, if he started a fire it “was gonna get bad”.Three individuals observed Farinacci in the vicinity of the fire. When questioned by police about the witnesses’s statements, Farinacci initially denied being responsible for the blaze.If confronted by police, Farinacci said he planned to draw a knife so they would shoot him, but instead settled instead on feigning innocence, the affidavit stated.Farinacci told investigators he viewed fire as “powerful” and “beautiful” and said it spurred “a kind of rebirth”. He researched the arsonist John Leonard Orr, a former fire captain who sparkedroughlyover 2,000 fires in southern California, court records show.He also told investigators he allegedly set five fires in the span of 24 hours in 2025 to overwhelm the capacity of fire suppression efforts.Farinacci wasarraignedin court on Thursday, where a Spokane county superior court judge increased his bond to $2m. He was initially being held on a $1m bond.Farinacci has run into trouble with law enforcement before. In 2012, he pleaded guilty to manslaughter and aggravated assault after fatally shooting his father, Maricopa county court records show.He told investigators that he had recently been struggling with “life issues” after the birth of his son in 2025.As of Wednesday, the Old Trails fire was 5% contained, according todatafrom the National Interagency Fire Center.The wildfires raging in the US Pacific north-west are blanketing the region with thick smoke and delivering some of theworld’s worst air quality.In portions of central and eastern Washington and Oregon, sensors detected air quality indexes reaching above 200, which is categorized as “very unhealthy”.Suspect in Washington state wildfire was questioned about blazes last yearRead moreIn the Seattle area, the smoke is expected to clear up by Friday, according to the Washingtondepartmentof ecology, but poor air quality may persist to the east in Spokane. An air quality advisory issued by Oregon officials for the Portland area is expected tobe liftedon Thursday evening.In Washington, there are 16 uncontained wildfires burning more than 672 sq miles (1,740 sq km) and being fought by more than 7,000 fire personnel, said Thomas Kyle-Milward, a spokesperson for the Washington department of natural resources.“We’re looking down the barrel at one of the worst fire seasons in state history,” he said.Firefighters have taken advantage of cooler weather to begin getting a handle on wildfires that have displaced tens of thousands of people. But hotter, drier and breezier days lie ahead.Officials said firefighters had established containment lines around the perimeters of all three fires affecting Spokane and that they were focused on reinforcing those lines. Temperatures were expected to climb from the 80s into the upper 90s, with less humidity, late this week.Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsWashington stateUS weatherWildfiresWest CoastPollutionAir pollutionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Covent Garden victims stabbed in the back with pair of scissors, court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Stella Gollovena, 47, has been charged with four counts of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Stella Gollovena, 47, has been charged with four counts of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm
Content: Police cordoned off the area in London’s West End on Wednesday after the attack.Photograph: Tayfun Salcı/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolice cordoned off the area in London’s West End on Wednesday after the attack.Photograph: Tayfun Salcı/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockUK newsCovent Garden victims stabbed in the back with pair of scissors, court hearsStella Gollovena, 47, has been charged with four counts of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harmPress AssociationThu 6 Aug 2026 14.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman has appeared in court accused of stabbing four men in the back with a pair of scissors in one of London’s busiest tourist districts.Stella Gollovena, 47, is accused of attacking Patrick De Barr, Thomas Harding, Adrian Lovett and Mantas Jankus during the attack in Covent Garden on Wednesday lunchtime.She has been charged with four counts of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm and one count of possession of an offensive weapon, a pair of scissors, in a public place.Gollovena, of no fixed address, faced the five criminal charges for the first time in a hearing at Highbury Corner magistrates court on Thursday afternoon.The hearing was told police were flagged down in Endell Street, a popular tourist area filled with bars, theatres and restaurants, at about 12.25pm by one of the injured victims. He and a second man reported being stabbed, before the suspect was chased and Tasered.The court heard police took statements from four men who were treated in hospital for stab wounds to their backs, while a fifth person said at the scene that they had also been stabbed but did not want to give a statement to police. It is alleged Gollovena had a pair of scissors – also described as a “pair of shears” – on her when she was arrested.The deputy chief magistrate, Tan Ikram, remanded Gollovena in custody until the next hearing at Snaresbrook crown court on 3 September. Gollovena spoke to confirm her identity but did not enter any pleas to the charges.An air ambulance helicopter landed in a packed Trafalgar Square on Wednesday afternoon after the stabbings and London ambulance service said it had “treated four patients at the scene and took them all to a major trauma centre as a priority by road”.The Met said the four men – aged 34, 39, 42 and 56 – had stab wounds but had since been discharged from hospital as their injuries were not deemed life-threatening or life-changing.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Norfolk police arrest two men after officers injured during unrest over asylum plans | UK news | The Guardian
description: Homes of people believed to be asylum seekers attacked during two nights of violence in Thetford
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Homes of people believed to be asylum seekers attacked during two nights of violence in Thetford
Content: Protests have been held over plans to house asylum seekers on the RAF Barnham site near Thetford.Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtests have been held over plans to house asylum seekers on the RAF Barnham site near Thetford.Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty ImagesUK newsNorfolk police arrest two men after officers injured during unrest over asylum plansHomes of people believed to be asylum seekers attacked during two nights of violence in ThetfordMatthew WeaverThu 6 Aug 2026 14.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo men have been arrested after police were injured as they intervened to protect men believed to be asylum seekers from angry mobs trying to break into their homes.The arrests followed two nights of unrest in Thetford, Norfolk, involving more than 100 people protesting against plans to house asylum seekers in former military barracks near the market town.The unrest followed the circulation online of a list of properties whose landlords have contracts with a government contractor to provide homes for asylum seekers.Policing powers in Norfolk were boosted in Thetford on Thursday evening and public safety measures have been imposed.Norfolk police said on Wednesday one of its officers was struck by a rock, another officer was bitten and a third was spat at while responding to reports of protesters trying to break into a home in the north of the town. The injured officers were taken to hospital.One man in his 40s, who was arrested on suspected public order offences, remains in custody. A second man, Brian Thompson, 68, has been charged with possession of an offensive weapon, a wooden bat. He is due to appear at Norwich magistrates court on 25 August.View image in fullscreenDamage caused to a house in Thetford where protesters allegedly tried to break into the homes of people believed to be asylum seekers.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAOn Tuesday night, officers intervened to protect five men who were being threatened by dozens of protesters, some of whom tried to break into a property, smashed a window, and damaged a fence and letterbox. Police were responding to a report that between 30 and 50 people were trying to enter a house in the west of Thetford.Video footage of the incident showed the men being escorted to safety by officers as dozens of protesters jeered and shouted abuse at police and the men. Shouts of “refugees not welcome”, “get out” and “bye” could be heard. In another video of the unrest, a man could be heard shouting: “They don’t want the white man any more, they want to swap us.”Later on Tuesday, officers responded to reports of residents being threatened at two homes in the south of the town. Police believed some of those involved had been present at the earlier attempted break-in.At one of the homes, windows were smashed. At another, a resident was forced out and had their mobile phone stolen when a small group forced entry.A man in his 30s who was arrested over Tuesday’s night’s unrest on suspicion of a public order offence had since been released and issued with a conditional caution, police said.The local Labour MP, Terry Jermy, who has previously criticised plans to use the former barracks at nearby RAF Barnham to house up to 1,000 asylum seekers, condemned the violence and what he called “mob rule”.View image in fullscreenThe arrests followed two nights of unrest in Thetford involving more than 100 people protesting against plans to house asylum seekers at the RAF Barnham site (pictured).Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty ImagesJermy said protesters were targeting a list of houses of multiple occupation used by Serco to house asylum seekers. “There doesn’t seem to be protests at all of the properties known about thus far, so the potential for increase and escalation is clearly there,” he said.“I’ve had constituents contact me of mixed ethnicity who are terrified that they will be misidentified as asylum seekers and what that might mean for their families.”Jermy said he recognised many of the protesters as local people in the videos of the unrest, but that he believed tensions were being “whipped up by outside forces”.In a statement, Jermy said: “The ugly scenes in Thetford over the past few days have been difficult to watch and are deeply concerning.“People have been pulled from their homes – a place of safety – and forcibly removed, with reports of members of the public breaking into homes, taking property and smashing windows.“I do not know the immigration status of the people placed in these properties or their legal status, but I know they are human beings that must be afforded the same rights that we all expect in this country.“Whatever our own individual views on immigration – mob rule and vigilantism is not acceptable.”View image in fullscreenUnder the proposals, the RAF Barnham site could house 1,000 asylum seekers.Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty ImagesNorfolk police also condemned the violence. The assistant chief constable Julie Dean, who is overseeing the response to the unrest, said: “We will always facilitate and support the right to peaceful protest. However, no matter how strongly those views are held, there is no place for violence, intimidation or criminal behaviour.“We will not stand by and allow violence to take place, whether that is directed towards members of the public, local residents or police officers carrying out their duties.”Policing powers in Norfolk were increased in Thetford on Thursday evening.Public safety measures have been imposed, including people being required to remove a face covering if asked to do so by officers. Police will also be permitted to direct anyone committing, or whom they suspect may commit, antisocial behaviour to leave the area.The measures are in place from 6pm on Thursday until 7am on Friday. Anyone who refuses to remove a face covering when asked to do so may be arrested, the force said.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nearly 50 asylum seekers deported under ‘one in one out’ scheme have returned to the UK | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Figure raises questions about deal with France despite UK ministers insisting repeat arrivals will be removed
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Figure raises questions about deal with France despite UK ministers insisting repeat arrivals will be removed
Content: Migrants clamber on to a UK Border Force vessel.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/GettyView image in fullscreenMigrants clamber on to a UK Border Force vessel.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/GettyImmigration and asylumNearly 50 asylum seekers deported under ‘one in one out’ scheme have returned to the UKFigure raises questions about deal with France despite UK ministers insisting repeat arrivals will be removedDiane TaylorThu 6 Aug 2026 09.32 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost 50 asylum seekers deported using the “one in one out” scheme have been recorded as returning to the UK a second time, the Guardian has learned.In addition to the returnees detained by theHome Office, an unknown number are believed to have arrived in the UK undetected.The scheme, which began last September, allows the UK government to return people arriving on small boats toFrance, in exchange for a similar number of asylum seekers being brought to the UK legally. The aim is to deter asylum seekers from crossing the Channel in small boats.The Guardianpreviously revealedthat the first asylum seeker who returned to the UK a second time did so last October, a few weeks after being forcibly returned to France. But until now the number of people returning to the UK after forced return was not known.So far this year small boat crossings havereducedby about 43%. This fall is likely to be due to a variety of factors, including bad weather and a reduction in migrants arriving in Europe overall by about a third, as well as efforts by UK and French authorities to disrupt people smugglers.The rationale for sending a proportion of small boat arrivals back to France is that France is a safe country. Asylum seekers who have subsequently returned to the UK have argued that they faced threats from people smugglers in France, or feared being returned by French authorities to their home countries or to countries they passed through.Has the UK government’s strategy on small boat crossings been effective?Read moreAbout4% of small boat arrivalshave been returned to France so far under the “one in one out” deal.According to the Home Office, as of 30 June 2026, there were 1,117 individuals transferred to the UK and 1,087 individuals returned to France under “one in one out”. Officials say the treaty between UK and France has been amended so that second-time returnees to the UK will be once again returned to France.One asylum seeker who returned to the UK a second time in a lorry was eventually returned to France after spending five months in detention. He said he was accommodated for only a few days by French authorities. “There is nowhere for asylum seekers to go and be safe and have peace inEurope,” he said. “I’m sleeping on the streets of Paris because France wants to send me back to Bulgaria where I was fingerprinted. I was better off in a UK detention centre.”Griff Ferris, of Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants, said: “People fleeing war, persecution and climate destruction are forced to take incredibly dangerous routes to cross the Channel and get to the UK because there is no other way. We must let everyone access the same safe routes to travel that are open to so many, like the daily ferries between Calais and Dover.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Home Office spokesperson said: “Anyone looking to return to the UK after being removed under the UK-France agreement is wasting their time and money – and will be removed again. Under our payment by results returns agreement with France, we have removed more than 1,000 illegal migrants from British soil.“Hundreds of enforcement actions, including arrests, investigations, and sanctions have been pursued against migrant smuggling networks since the election, and we’ve returned or removed almost 70,000 illegal migrants.”France’s interior ministry has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeMigrationFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Is King Charles a ‘white Briton’? Restore Britain leader Rupert Lowe won’t say | Restore Britain | The Guardian
description: Lowe questioned on BBC about definition in report for hard-right party that both parents need to be born in UK
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Lowe questioned on BBC about definition in report for hard-right party that both parents need to be born in UK
Content: The then Prince Charles with his father, Prince Philip, in 2016. Philip was born in Greece.Photograph: Mark Cuthbert/UK Press/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe then Prince Charles with his father, Prince Philip, in 2016. Philip was born in Greece.Photograph: Mark Cuthbert/UK Press/Getty ImagesRestore BritainIs King Charles a ‘white Briton’? Restore Britain leader Rupert Lowe won’t sayLowe questioned on BBC about definition in report for hard-right party that both parents need to be born in UKCaroline DaviesThu 6 Aug 2026 06.21 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 16.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRupert Lowe, the leader ofRestore Britain, refused to say he believes King Charles can be classified as a “white Briton” in an extraordinary interview on the BBC’s Today programme.Questioning Lowe, the MP for Great Yarmouth, over his claims that “white Britons will become a minority by 2063”, the presenter, Nick Robinson, noted that the forecast Lowe referred to defined a “white Briton” as someone whose parents were both born in the UK.With the king’s late father,Prince Philip, having been born on the Greek island of Corfu, Robinson asked Lowe: “Are you aware that, by the definitions used in that particular report, King Charles is not a white Briton? Do you think he is a white Briton?”Declining to address the question, Lowe responded: “Well, many people have different interpretations of that, Nick. I mean, we can split hairs.”View image in fullscreenRupert Lowe: ‘By 2063, white British people will be a minority on current trends.’Photograph: Jason Bye/The GuardianRobinson interjected: “We’re not splitting hairs – do you think the monarch of this country is a white Briton?”Lowe said: “The experience of what we’re talking about is quite clear and I think most British people, if you speak to them, would agree.”Accused of ignoring the question, he continued: “It is a fact that, by 2063, white British people will be a minority on current trends. I don’t think anyone disputes that.”As Lowe continued to decline to give a direct answer, Robinson said: “So, because Prince Philip was born in Greece, King Charles is not, under your definition, treated as a white Briton. Now let me go on and ask you a different question.”View image in fullscreenMon Repos, the villa on the Greek island of Corfu where Prince Philip was born in 1921.Photograph: Alkis Konstantinidis/ReutersLowe said: “I did come on to speak about ostensibly the economic paper we’ve just put out, and about the issue with Nigel Farage, and you’ve managed to turn it into a discussion about British people becoming minority, white British people, by 2063.”Nigel Farage has said Restore could inflict “great harm” on his party, Reform UK. Lowe, who was expelled from Reform,said in a video messageearlier this week he and Farage should set aside differences and cooperate “to destroy the looming leftwing alliance”.He said he had made a “genuine” effort to reach out to Farage “in good faith”, adding: “Now, so far, I had one message from Nigel on a Sunday morning at 10.30 saying, will call later. Now, in his press conference, he said he was waiting for a call from me.”Lowe was also asked several times to provide evidence “that Britain, in your words, is hurtling towards becoming an Islamic country”.He pointed towards Restore’s “219-page rape gang inquiry report”. TheBBChad not covered it at all, Lowe said, adding: “And if you had the intellectual appetite to actually read the report, I don’t think you’d even need to ask me this question.”Explore more on these topicsRestore BritainThe far rightRupert LoweKing Charles IIIPrince PhilipRaceRadio 4newsShareReuse this content

title: Perez Hilton ‘able to communicate’ after hospitalization following live stream | Perez Hilton | The Guardian
description: Family says celebrity blogger remains under medical care after viewers raised alarm over disturbing TikTok broadcast
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Family says celebrity blogger remains under medical care after viewers raised alarm over disturbing TikTok broadcast
Content: Perez Hilton speaks during Liberace's birthday celebration and charity benefit on 17 May 2023 in Las Vegas, Nevada.Photograph: Gabe Ginsberg/Getty Images for Admit VIPView image in fullscreenPerez Hilton speaks during Liberace's birthday celebration and charity benefit on 17 May 2023 in Las Vegas, Nevada.Photograph: Gabe Ginsberg/Getty Images for Admit VIPPerez HiltonPerez Hilton ‘able to communicate’ after hospitalization following live streamFamily says celebrity blogger remains under medical care after viewers raised alarm over disturbing TikTok broadcastMarina DunbarThu 6 Aug 2026 11.44 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 12.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePerez Hilton is “able to communicate”, according to a new statement released by his family, one day after the celebrity blogger appeared to self-harm during a disturbingTikToklivestream that prompted his hospitalization.In amessageposted to Hilton’s blog on Wednesday evening, his family thanked supporters for the outpouring of concern.“Our family wants to once again thank everyone who has reached out with prayers, kind messages, and support for Perez,” the statement reads. “Your compassionate humanity during this profoundly heartbreaking time has meant more than words can express.”The family said the ordeal has been “incredibly difficult and emotional”, but added that they “remain hopeful” about Hilton’s condition.Hours before that update, Hilton’s team and family confirmed in a separatestatementthat he is “receiving medical care” and his “family’s focus right now is on his well-being”, while also thanking fans for their support.Hilton wastaken to a hospitallate Tuesday after a TikTok live stream led many viewers to contact authorities, the Miami-Dade county sheriff’s office confirmed to multiple media outlets.During the live stream, Hilton appeared to be covered in blood and was shown to be self-harming as viewers flooded the comments urging him to stop.Emergency responders were seen outside Hilton’s Miami, Florida, home on Tuesday night after members of the public reported witnessing the incident on the live stream. Minutes later, Hilton’sTikTokaccount was suspended.In a statement issued on Tuesday, the Miami-Dade sheriff’s office did not identify Hilton by name but confirmed deputies responded after receiving reports of a man “livestreaming acts of self-harm on social media”.The sheriff’s office toldCNNthat authorities “spoke with family members on scene, and confirmed he was alone inside” before de-escalating the situation.Although TikTok removed the livestream, screen recordings quickly spread across platforms including X and Instagram. The circulation of the footage prompted users to encourage others to disable video autoplay and mute mentions of Hilton, while also drawingcriticism of TikTokfor allowing the graphic live stream.Born Mario Armando Lavandeira Jr, the blogger adopted the namePerez Hiltonas a play on the hotel heiress Paris Hilton. He has long described himself as the “original influencer”, launching his celebrity gossip blog in 2004 and becoming one of the most recognizable figures during the rise of blogs and online tabloids in the early internet era.In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsPerez HiltonCelebrityTikToknewsShareReuse this content

title: Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials say | Ebola | The Guardian
description: Cases have passed 4,000 and health watchdog plans to go door to door to find patients in major response escalation
Author: Kat Lay
Headline: Cases have passed 4,000 and health watchdog plans to go door to door to find patients in major response escalation
Content: Members of a Congolese Red Cross team with the coffin of a woman suspected of having died from Ebola virus in Bunia last June.Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMembers of a Congolese Red Cross team with the coffin of a woman suspected of having died from Ebola virus in Bunia last June.Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty ImagesEbolaEbola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials sayCases have passed 4,000 and health watchdog plans to go door to door to find patients in major response escalationKat LayGlobal health correspondentThu 6 Aug 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe virus causing a massive outbreak of Ebola in theDemocratic Republic of the Congocould be mutating, health officials fear, as confirmed cases pass 4,000.Africa’s public health watchdog said the time for incremental action was over as they announced plans to scale up every aspect of the response and go “door to door” looking for patients.TheEbolaoutbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, was first reported on 15 May, although there are suspicions the disease could have been spreading since January.There have been3,973 cases and 1,801 deathsrecorded as of 4 August, according to the DRC’s national public health institute. Speaking on Thursday, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), told a press briefing cases had topped 4,000.The outbreak is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record.
