There are eight times more cases, and six times more deaths than were recorded 11 weeks into the West Africa Ebola outbreak in 2014-18, which infected more than 28,000 people and killed at least 11,000.Kaseya said he had spoken to the director general of the World Health Organization, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, and they planned studies “to check if there is no additional issue, or maybe if the virus is not mutating. Because thelevel of severityof this Bundibugyo outbreak is unprecedented.”More than two-thirds of Ebola deaths are happening in the community rather than in treatment centres. In a treatment centre run by MSF in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province, 90% of admitted patients do not appear on authorities’ lists of contacts of known cases. Both factors indicate high levels of untracked transmission.Kaseya said contact tracing in the DRC was insufficient, with only 10 contacts identified for every Ebola patient, when about 40 would be the expected number.Ebola is a viral haemorrhagic fever that can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, organ damage and internal bleeding. The outbreak is centred on the conflict-affected mining province of Ituri, but has spread to Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo. There were 20 cases recorded in neighbouring Uganda before itbrought its outbreak under control.Dr Wessam Mankoula, acting head of emergency preparedness and response at Africa CDC, said response teams planned a shift “from contact tracing to active case search”, which would mean community health workers “moving from door to door” asking households if they had anyone sick with Ebola symptoms.He added: “I think the time for incremental action is over and we’re starting now the phase for scaling up.”Kaseya promised a “village-centered response” that would involve communities, more use of digital tools and greater action in the camps for people who have been internally displaced by conflict in affected provinces.Officials also said they planned to begin using antiviral remdesivir on a compassionate use basis to treat patients. They will also start testing whether Ervebo, a vaccine licensed for use against a different strain of Ebola, should be offered in the affected province, after receiving data suggesting that Bundibugyo caused less serious disease and “zero death” among people who had received that jab.“Seeing the expansion of this outbreak, only the public health measure will not be enough to quickly control or stop this outbreak,” said Dr Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC director of research, clinical trials and innovation.DRC authorities said they were investigating a suspected Ebola death on a boat heading to the capital, Kinshasa, from the north-east of the country, and that the other passengers on board would be quarantined and tested.Unicef warned that essential healthcare was being disrupted by the outbreak as fear of infection and service disruptions kept families away from clinics. In the outbreak’s centre, the mining town of Mongbwalu, the proportion of children receiving their first measles dose has fallen 69%.Explore more on these topicsEbolaDemocratic Republic of the CongoAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: TikTok creator Sydney Towle, who shared cancer journey, dies aged 26 | US news | The Guardian
description: The creator documented her battle with rare bile duct cancer, inspiring more than a million followers online
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: The creator documented her battle with rare bile duct cancer, inspiring more than a million followers online
Content: Sydney Towle speaks onstage at Connection in the Age of Disruption during the Business of Beauty Global Forum 2025 on 10 June 2025 in Napa, California.Photograph: Monica Schipper/Getty Images for The Business of FashionView image in fullscreenSydney Towle speaks onstage at Connection in the Age of Disruption during the Business of Beauty Global Forum 2025 on 10 June 2025 in Napa, California.Photograph: Monica Schipper/Getty Images for The Business of FashionUS newsTikTok creator Sydney Towle, who shared cancer journey, dies aged 26The creator documented her battle with rare bile duct cancer, inspiring more than a million followers onlineEdward HelmoreThu 6 Aug 2026 14.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 14.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSydney Towle, aTikTokcreator who shared her battle with stage 4 cholangiocarcinoma, or bile duct cancer, with over a million online followers, has died at age 26, her family announced on Thursday.Towle gained fame for her posts about her life as a spirited young woman who encouraged her TikTokfollowersto rethink how a cancer patient might look and live.Towle’s family announced her death, nearly three years after she was first diagnosed,via Instagram: “We will always love you so much Sydney,” the caption read. “I am so proud of how hard you fought. I love you.” Earlier this week, her family said that she had entered hospice care.In 2023, Towle was living in Los Angeles after graduating from Dartmouth College, and working at a remote-office marketing job, surfing and posting bikini selfies and dance trend videos online.A bulge and burning sensation in her abdomen landed her in urgent care and she later was diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, a rare cancer most often diagnosed in adults over age 50.“The doctor thought I had a hernia, but he was like, ‘I’ll send you in for an ultrasound, just in case,’” Towle toldTodayin 2024. “I got an ultrasound, and it showed a solid mass.”Towle turned her medical ordeal as a young woman with cancer into content, creating videos of ahike in Spainduring a solo adventure in Europe, her mom wrapping her head inice packsto help combat hair loss from cancer treatments, and the day-to-day of her struggle balanced with gratitude and hope.She blended her life as a cancer patient with lifestyle posts and faced online trolls who doubted the reality of her condition and online persona. “I’m not a television show that you’re watching, which I think people have a really hard time understanding,” she told the New York Times in a 2025 front-pageprofile. “I’m not a fake character. I’m a person.”In a TikTok postedlast year Towle danced in her apartment advising her fans: “Go get a pint of Ben and Jerry’s, watch your favorite movie, remember that life is good and bad things happen sometimes but that doesn’t make it a bad life.”Melinda Bachini, of the Cholangiocarcinoma Foundation,told the Timesthat Towle’s role as an influencer had persuaded her audience to reconsider living with a serious illness.“Syd had a keen sense of how sharing her life could help others, and she used that to promote understanding of young adults facing cancer, the importance of research funding and the beauty of living life in the moment,” she said.After her death was announced on Thursday, her mother and brother Austin Towle’sTikTok video updatewas flooded with messages of condolence.Explore more on these topicsUS newsTikTokCancernewsShareReuse this content

title: Diageo to nearly double Guinness production and cut jobs in turnaround plan | Diageo | The Guardian
description: New CEO Dave Lewis lifts investors’ spirits by promising strategic overhaul worthy of his nickname ‘Drastic Dave’
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: New CEO Dave Lewis lifts investors’ spirits by promising strategic overhaul worthy of his nickname ‘Drastic Dave’
Content: In the months after Lewis’s appointment, some City pundits speculated that he might take the radical step of selling Guinness to raise up to £8bn.Photograph: NurPhoto SRL/AlamyView image in fullscreenIn the months after Lewis’s appointment, some City pundits speculated that he might take the radical step of selling Guinness to raise up to £8bn.Photograph: NurPhoto SRL/AlamyDiageoDiageo to nearly double Guinness production and cut jobs in turnaround planNew CEO Dave Lewis lifts investors’ spirits by promising strategic overhaul worthy of his nickname ‘Drastic Dave’Rob DaviesThu 6 Aug 2026 12.12 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDiageo’s new chief executive has unveiled plans to nearly double Guinness production while hacking back a “significant” proportion of its 30,000-strong workforce, in a strategic overhaul worthy of his nickname, “Drastic”Dave Lewis.Shares inDiageobounced on Thursday, as the former Tesco boss faced down the first big test of his initial half-year in the job, after being parachuted in last November to revive the flagging fortunes of the UK-based drinks company.Speaking after the company announced a decline in sales but slightly better-than-expected operating profit, Lewis said his turnaround plan would involve job cuts, adding that the “consequences of that are not great for anybody”.But he added: “Nobody [inside the company] is saying to me that this is the wrong thing to do.”Lewis declined to give a figure for the expected reduction in the worldwide headcount.However, Diageo has told investors that it expects to incur $514m (£382m) in charges relating to employee severance and Lewis said he had discovered “massive” duplication in roles since becoming CEO.Lewis, who earned the “Drastic Dave” moniker in the City for his cost-cutting zeal, promised to deliver $1bn of annual savings over two years through a restructuring that would cost $1.2bn and was aimed at making the company more agile.While this will involve slashing jobs, Lewis vowed to harness the seemingly unstoppable popularity of Guinness around the world.A $1bn investment in the brand is aimed at increasing global sales, particularly in North America, and helping the company avoid a repeat of shortages reported in the UK in recent years, including during the important festive period.“We’re going to double the capacity of Guinness during the course of this plan [by 2031],” said Lewis, adding that the future of the brand was “very bright”.Production capacity is slated to increase from 8.2m hectolitres (mHL) today to 15.7m by 2031, an increase equivalent to 300 Olympic-sized swimming pools of the black stuff a year.In the months after his appointment, some City pundits speculated that he might take the radical step of selling Guinness to raise up to £8bn. The companymoved quickly to quash any suggestionof selling its best-performing big brand.Diageo was not actively seeking to sell less well-performing brands, Lewis said.In the past decade, the company has focused on “premiumisation”, banking on discerning drinkers choosing upmarket brands. That strategy has left Diageo with an overloaded stable of more expensive labels, just as cash-strapped consumers stopped drinking from the top shelf.Lewis said Diageo would not be “hawking our brands” and was not looking to buy assets either, but would focus more on a broader portfolio, including mid-market brands and smaller-pack sizes that were likely to suit cost-conscious drinkers.He also promised to amend Diageo’s failure to cash in on the so-called ready-to-drink category, such as premade cocktails or “gin in a tin”. “We’re just going to roll our sleeves up and get on with our own business,” Lewis added.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCan ex-Tesco boss Drastic Dave refresh the fortunes of drinks giant Diageo?Read moreShares in Diageo rose by more than 6% in afternoon trading after the release, indicating early contentment among investors with the early fruit of the turnaround plan.Lewis’s appointment was announced last November after alacklustre period under his immediate predecessor, Debra Crew, a former captain in US military intelligence who took over after the sudden death of the longtime chief executive Sir Ivan Menezes.The global purveyor of brands such as Johnnie Walker and Smirnoff had thrived in the period immediately after the Covid-19 pandemic, but fell out of favour with investors as Crew’s tenure was tainted by strategic errors and a surprise profits warning, leading to her exit.Diageo’s share price jumpedlast year after the arrival of Lewis, who came with a reputation built during five years in charge of Tesco and nearly three decades at the global household brands company Unilever.But investors punished Diageoin February after he slashed the dividendand reported weak demand in the US and China, eroding some of the market gains.On Thursday, the company said annual pre-tax profit fell by 26%, from $3.5bn to $2.6bn, including $900m one-off charges related to Lewis’s restructuring of the business and a $1.5bn hit from its Turkish business.Without the one-off impact and other charges such as debt interest, operating profit was slightly ahead of analysts’ forecasts at $5.7bn.Sales were down by 2% to $19.6bn amid continued weakness in China and the US. Lewis said he expects the North American business, Diageo’s largest region by revenue, to take two years to return to growth.The annual dividend remains at $0.50 a share, slightly less than half the level before Lewis slashed the payout to fund his turnaround strategy.Explore more on these topicsDiageoFood & drink industryDave LewisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Paramount concessions lead UK to approve takeover of Warner Bros  | Mergers and acquisitions | The Guardian
description: Culture secretary Lisa Nandy says she will not intervene in £85bn deal after securing guarantees on Channel 5
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Culture secretary Lisa Nandy says she will not intervene in £85bn deal after securing guarantees on Channel 5
Content: Lisa Nandy in Downing Street. The acquisition still faces a big final hurdle in the US.Photograph: Anadolu/GettyView image in fullscreenLisa Nandy in Downing Street. The acquisition still faces a big final hurdle in the US.Photograph: Anadolu/GettyMergers and acquisitionsParamount concessions lead UK to approve takeover of Warner BrosCulture secretary Lisa Nandy says she will not intervene in £85bn deal after securing guarantees on Channel 5Michael SavageMedia editorThu 6 Aug 2026 10.57 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, has said she will not intervene in Paramount’s proposed acquisition ofWarner BrosDiscovery, removing one of the remaining obstacles to the blockbuster deal.However, Paramount has made significant concessions to secure the UK government’s backing for the$110bn (£85bn)takeover, which will create a global media powerhouse and effectively bolster the influence of Paramount’s chief executive, David Ellison.Nandy’s decision to order Britain’s media and competition watchdogs toexamine the dealin June came as a shock. However, she has now approved the deal, with conditions attached around protecting UK-based content.The UK’sCompetition and Markets Authorityhas also cleared the deal, which has already been approved by the EU.Under the UK guarantees, Paramount’sChannel 5will continue to ‌operate as a public service broadcaster until the end of 2034. Channel 5 News will retain its editorial independence and will remain separate from other news operations covered by the merger, CBS News and CNN International.Paramount has agreed that its linear and on-demand services in Britain would retain distinct editorial identities for five years, including its children’s TV content.Nandy’s department also secured a guarantee that the deal would not reduce the number of people commissioning content in Britain, while Channel 5 would continue to back UK-originated content covering drama, factual and entertainment shows.Nandy will meet with Paramount “in the coming weeks” to seek assurances about the deals’ impact on Britain’s wider creative industries.The news means Ellison is a step closer to closing the deal, which would create a group encompassing the Hollywood studios behind film franchises including Superman, Batman and Top Gun, the UK’s Channel 5, the news channel CNN and TNT Sports.The acquisition still faces a big final hurdle before being completed, following a legal challenge by a coalition of US states and writers’ guilds to block it.There are also concerns in the media about the potential impact on the news coverage of Warner’s global news network, CNN. Paramount’s own network, CBS News, has facedjob cuts, tensions and claims ofpolitical interferenceto push coverage more in line with Donald Trump’s agenda.Ellison, the son of the tech mogul and Trump ally Larry Ellison, has faced other accusations of attempting to curry favour with the White House as he pursued acquisitions. In a recent essay, however,he denied having a pro-Trump bias.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I have regularly voted for candidates of both parties,” he wrote. “I hold some views that would be called conservative and others that would be called liberal, just like most Americans.”Responding to the UK government’s decision to clear the deal, Paramount said in a statement: “These clearances recognise that the combination of Paramount and WBD will enhance consumer choice and enable a creative-first company to invest in more projects and bring stories to audiences worldwide.”Ellison and his legal team can now focus on the US lawsuit, which is aimed at blocking the deal on antitrust grounds.A California federal judge has scheduled the trial for March 2027, which represents a costly delay. Paramount soon has to make shareholder payouts, which will continue until the deal is completed.Explore more on these topicsMergers and acquisitionsParamount PicturesWarner BrosLisa NandyCompetition and Markets AuthorityTelevision industryChannel 5newsShareReuse this content

title: Octopus Energy denies it is anti-union as GMB pushes for recognition for workers | Octopus Energy | The Guardian
description: Union says that as a top-rated ethical company, UK’s largest energy firm should welcome its involvement
Author: Matthew Taylor
Headline: Union says that as a top-rated ethical company, UK’s largest energy firm should welcome its involvement
Content: A spokesperson for Octopus Energy said it was up to staff whether to push for union recognition.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA spokesperson for Octopus Energy said it was up to staff whether to push for union recognition.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOctopus EnergyOctopus Energy denies it is anti-union as GMB pushes for recognition for workersUnion says that as a top-rated ethical company, UK’s largest energy firm should welcome its involvementMatthew TaylorThu 6 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGMB is pushing for union recognition at the UK’s largest energy company,Octopus Energy, known as a progressive organisation with a focus on renewable energy.The union is planning to submit a formal proposal for voluntary recognition at the London-based company and says Octopus, as a top rated ethical business, should welcome the involvement of trade unions.But the company, which has risen to prominence in the UK energy sector with its tech-driven approach, has said there is currently no need – or demand from staff – for union recognition.A spokesperson for OctopusEnergydenied the company was anti-union, adding it was up to staff whether to push for union recognition. “We’ve engaged constructively with unions and will continue to do so whenever our team asks us,” they added.They said Octopus was “an outstanding employer” and “consistently named one of the UK’s best places to work and every employee is a shareholder”.But Tony Tanushi, a regional energy officer at the GMB, said the company’s management had shown “no appetite” for unionisation and that if its application for voluntary recognition did not work, he would be willing to take it to arbitration.“Simply put, their staff want to unionise, they see that their competitors provide a genuine platform for their employees to provide feedback and they want the same opportunity. As a union we identify those with leadership qualities to help organisations unlock their full potential.”He said the fact staff at Octopus had a share in the company did not change the need for union recognition.“Many companies provide a share scheme for their employees and this doesn’t translate to having a genuine voice on terms and conditions that would be achieved through a formal recognition and bargaining rights.”GMB has been criticised by climate groups for its calls for more drilling of fossil fuels in the North Sea andits oppositionto thegovernment rollout of heat pumps.The Octopus spokesperson said: “Opposing heat pumps and EVs means turning our backs on the very industries that will create the next generation of skilled jobs and directly jeopardises thousands of jobs across our business.”Mel Evans, the head of climate at Greenpeace UK, said it worked closely with Octopus Energy on the just transition and supported its efforts to move the UK to a successful low carbon economy. But she said unions must be involved in that transition.“Jobs are needed across the renewables sector to provide alternatives to the fossil fuel industry as it is replaced – and those jobs must be secure, well-paid, unionised jobs …We need unions and workers onboard to power this transition – we simply can’t do it without them.”The Octopus spokesperson suggested Greenpeace should focus on persuading unions to reverse their stance on fossil fuels, heat pumps and electric cars.Explore more on these topicsOctopus EnergyTrade unionsEnergy industryRenewable energyEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: EasyJet agrees to £5.7bn takeover by US private equity firm | easyJet | The Guardian
description: Airline says it has accepted offer from Apollo Global Management after rival bidder Castlelake walks away
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Airline says it has accepted offer from Apollo Global Management after rival bidder Castlelake walks away
Content: The decision means the deal will go through at £7.15 a share.Photograph: Imago/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenThe decision means the deal will go through at £7.15 a share.Photograph: Imago/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.easyJetEasyJet agrees to £5.7bn takeover by US private equity firmAirline says it has accepted offer from Apollo Global Management after rival bidder Castlelake walks awayGwyn TophamTransport correspondentThu 6 Aug 2026 10.56 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEasyJet has formally agreed to a£5.7bn takeoverfrom US private equity firm Apollo Global Management.The airline announced it had accepted a firm offer on Thursday after a rival bidder, Castlelake, said it would no longer pursue its attempted acquisition.The decision means the deal will go through at £7.15 a share, which Apollo tabled last month after the easyJet had initiallyrecommended a sale to Castlelake. The formal agreement came 24 hours before a deadline set for both parties to submit a final offer, but Castlelake declined to enter a bidding war.Under the agreement, the airline’s founder, Stelios Haji-Ioannou, and his family will retain their shareholding in the new ownership structure. Shareholders have been offered the opportunity to either sell or transfer, up to a maximum of 49.9%.View image in fullscreenStelios Haji-Ioannou, pictured in 2015, and his family will retain their shareholding under the new ownership structure.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAn “EU Trust” shareholding group will retain up to 5%, a structure that appears designed to comply with the European Union’s foreign ownership rules for airlines, with Apollo limited to 49.9%.The takeover is expected to complete by the end of March 2027.Apollo, which has committed to retaining easyJet’s UK and EU head offices, has indicated it would back the airline’s current strategy and support it in generating long-term, sustainable growth.Alex van Hoek, the US firm’s European private equity lead, said: “EasyJet is a leader in European aviation, having built a differentiated market position through its compelling customer proposition, expansive network and strong brand. Apollo strongly supports easyJet’s commitment to enhancing the connectivity of travellers throughout Europe and the UK and the important role that its employees play in serving customers.”Stephen Hester, the airline’s chair, said: “The easyJet board has carefully evaluated the proposal from Apollo alongside easyJet’s standalone prospects. While we remain confident in the strength of our business and the opportunities ahead, we believe this offer appropriately recognises the quality of the business we have built and delivers immediate, certain and attractive value for shareholders.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKenton Jarvis, easyJet’s chief executive, said: “We welcome Apollo’s commitment to our business and our people, and believe that its experience in the aviation sector makes it a strong partner for easyJet as we accelerate our growth plans and continue to deliver great value and service for our customers.”EasyJet’s share price, which dropped 10% on news of Castlelake’s exit, rebounded to 3% up from the start of the day.Explore more on these topicseasyJetAirline industryMergers and acquisitionsPrivate equitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Ravyn Lenae: Blue Island review – from Suicide to Squarepusher, grunge to Janet, a pop one-off plots her unique path | Music | The Guardian
description: Evoking everyone from Janet Jackson to Squarepusher, the US singer follows up her huge hit Love Me Not with stylistic diversity – and lyrics that defy her doubters
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Evoking everyone from Janet Jackson to Squarepusher, the US singer follows up her huge hit Love Me Not with stylistic diversity – and lyrics that defy her doubters
Content: Buffed to a state of pop perfection … Ravyn Lenae.View image in fullscreenBuffed to a state of pop perfection … Ravyn Lenae.Alexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewRavyn Lenae: Blue Island review – from Suicide to Squarepusher, grunge to Janet, a pop one-off plots her unique path(Atlantic)Evoking an astonishing range of artists, the US singer follows up her huge hit Love Me Not with stylistic diversity – and lyrics that defy her doubtersAlexis PetridisThu 6 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt sometimes seems like no musical success in the 2020s is allowed to pass without some degree of online controversy. There are accusations that the artist in question is an “industry plant” – a phrase which, as far as can be discerned, can basically be applied to anyone with a manager or a label deal – or that there’s something deceptive about the way in which they’ve been promoted, or that they’re possessed of some other form of moral bankruptcy that reflects not merely on the performer but the people who like them. Which brings us to Love Me Not, an ostensibly harmless 2024 track by Chicago singer-songwriter Ravyn Lenae.View image in fullscreenRavyn Lenae: Blue Island.Photograph: EMI/Atlantic/APAfter enjoying a burst of online virality, it became a huge hit single, making the Top 5 on both sides of the Atlantic. Taken from Bird’s Eye, an album that also featured collaborations with Childish Gambino and Ty Dolla $ign, its blend of retro-soul styling, distorted guitar arpeggios and infernally catchy chorus was noticeably poppier than Lenae’s previous work: it came with a remix that featured British bedroom-pop star Rex Orange County. You could understand why fans of the glitchy, abstract R&B found on 2015’s EP Moon Shoes, or of her more neo soul-flavoured debut album, 2022’s Hypnos, might consider it a straightforward bid for mainstream acceptance. But you’d argue against it necessitating an online interrogation that, Lenae has suggested, involved not just “picking apart what kind of music I make” but “questioning my identity and Blackness”.Said interrogation seems to have prompted a degree of doubling-down. The first thing you hear on Blue Island, as opener Handle gets under way, is another earworm pop chorus, followed by a squeal of feedback and a distorted electric guitar arpeggio that feels faintly grungy or, more specifically, that recalls the early 90s moment where grunge began having an effect on the sound of mainstream artists. It’s followed by Familiar Dreams, retro pop-soul that sounds almost exactly like what you’d expect of a well-turned follow-up to Love Me Not. Meanwhile, Lenae’s list of inspirations for the album features not just Santigold and Janet Jackson but Blondie, the Cranberries, the Sundays and, most surprisingly, Martin Rev. If Wish You Well definitely sounds like a charming gene-splice between the Cranberries and the soft-hued Janet Jackson of Runaway or That’s The Way Love Goes, it’s a little harder to discern the musical influence of Rev’s confrontational electronic punk duo Suicide on Blue Island. But perhaps it’s present in more of a spiritual capacity, Suicide having relentlessly pursued their own artistic path in the face of some fairly concerted efforts by the public to get them to stop.Ravyn Lenae: Handle – videoThere are certainly a lot of lyrics here that present as love songs but seem suspiciously like they’re about something else: “I’m leaving without you”; “breaking those walls … can never be wrong if you don’t go where everybody goes”; “all those limits to your pleasure keep me climbing”. And there’s palpable glee in the album’s sudden stylistic shifts. The 90s R&B-infused Never Let Me Go and Babygirl rub up against In & Out’s sparkly alt-rock; Potential proceeds along prettily enough in pop-ballad form before it unexpectedly erupts into a squall of guitar noise and a ferocious, juddering rhythm that sounds remarkably like Squarepusher or Aphex Twin. You could suggest its shifts carry a hint of the streaming playlist so eclectic it only really makes sense to the person who made it, but better that than an artist audibly chasing currently popular trends. And Blue Island isn’t as jarring as that suggests, partly because of the unifying power of Lenae’s voice – a lovely, breathy soprano – but largely because the writing is buffed to a state of pop perfection.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I was so self-assured in my early 20s. Then my frontal lobe hit’: Rachel Chinouriri, every pop star’s favourite UK pop starRead moreIts hit rate isn’t perfect. There are a couple of moments among the 14 tracks that feel a bit boilerplate: an acoustic duet with Dominic Fike, Reputation, is pleasant enough but could be the work of pretty much anyone; the electro-influenced beat of Saturday Night is great, the song itself not so much. And it could maybe have done with a couple more moments like Potential, when Lenae metaphorically lets her freak flag fly – not least because when she does, it’s hugely exciting, as on the chaotic, distorted closer Let Us In. It’s another song that seems to obliquely address the controversy caused by Love Me Not – you could read its lyrics as a plea for acceptance for artists that decline to fit a standard mould – but, in truth, Blue Island has already answered Ravyn Lenae’s critics long before it appears: its collage of styles makes for an original, idiosyncratic pop album, something worth celebrating rather than picking apart for ulterior motives.This week Alexis listened toThe Durutti Column – Your Shadow at MorningBeneath its TS Eliot-inspired title lurks a sun-dappled but melancholy drift of electric and acoustic guitar: Vini Reilly doing what Vini Reilly does exceptionally beautifully.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekR&BPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Basically, you give yourself to the man’: Trewley Precious Temple on her life as a Gypsy wife – and beyond | Reality TV | The Guardian
description: The TikTok influencer is now a TV star. But this independent, opinionated woman still lives with her mother, on the Clacton council estate where she grew up. Will she ever leave? And how does she feel about Mum’s curfew?
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: The TikTok influencer is now a TV star. But this independent, opinionated woman still lives with her mother, on the Clacton council estate where she grew up. Will she ever leave? And how does she feel about Mum’s curfew?
Content: ‘I’m a council-estate kid. I’m a businesswoman. There’s a lot of layers to me’ … Trewley Precious Temple.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’m a council-estate kid. I’m a businesswoman. There’s a lot of layers to me’ … Trewley Precious Temple.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianReality TV‘Basically, you give yourself to the man’: Trewley Precious Temple on her life as a Gypsy wife – and beyondThe TikTok influencer is now a TV star. But this independent, opinionated woman still lives with her mother, on the Clacton council estate where she grew up. Will she ever leave? And how does she feel about Mum’s curfew?Emine SanerThu 6 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSince eyes are turned to Clacton-on-Sea and a certain candidate facing questions about a£5m “gift”and a byelection battle witha man dressed as a bin, let’s take a look across the town at a young woman in a pink house and be reminded of some values – generosity, decency – that appear absent from much of public life.Trewley Precious Temple, who became well known on TikTok, where she has 1m followers, is the star of the Channel 4 showSecret Lives of Gypsy Wivesand is fast becoming a phenomenon. The show features her mum, Tina, her sisters Honey, Pearl and Ruby-Anne and her brother Jamie; they’re like the Kardashians, says Temple in every episode’s intro, if the humourless US reality TV family were “fat and broke and on benefits”. What comes across most strongly is the family’s love and big-heartedness, not just for each other, but for their wider community, too.In Temple’s area of Clacton-on-Sea,56% of children live in low-income families, compared with 38% in England. Her council estate is particularly deprived: it has been the focus of visible police patrols after being identified as an antisocial-behaviour hotspot and has a high level of unemployment.We don’t spend long talking about Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader fighting for re-election as an MP; Temple says she doesn’t have an opinion of him. But what does she wish politicians understood about the people she grew up with, her neighbours? “Don’t underestimate the struggle. Don’t underestimate these people,” she says. “Talk to them, know what they want. Think of their ideas, too. I’ve got lots of ideas how we could build this up. I’d love to talk to someone who wants the power to fix this place. All I’m saying is see it as teamwork.”She says she wants everyone to have chances and help, if they need it: events that would bring the community together; vouchers for food and school uniforms. “Just give people opportunities that haven’t had them before.” She is stunned by the opportunities she has had. “To get a brand deal [she has promoted makeup, among other products] – amazing. Even to get this opportunity to be interviewed – amazing. Because I don’t come from a place where people get interviewed.” She laughs. “Unless you get nicked.”View image in fullscreen(From left) Ruby-Anne, Honey, Trewley, Tina and Pearl.Photograph: Optomen/Channel 4We are sitting in Tina’s pristine living room; before I took my place, Temple tried to give me a bag of crisps and a chocolate bar, for the journey home. She lives here with Tina and Ruby-Anne; the others live nearby. Her late father, Sidney, “gave us permission” to paint the house pink when he was nearing the end of his life. She adds, sadly: “I realised he did that because he knew it was gonna be a girls’ house.”The idea of permission is a big one for Temple. Sidney died in 2022. He was the central presence in the family – a physically imposing man, but also very much in charge. He was a Gypsy and, although Tina is not (she’s a “gorja”, or non-Gypsy), the family was raised with his traditional values. Temple’s show is about figuring out who she wants to be and how many of those expectations she wants to keep. “I didn’t really question it until my dad passed,” she says, legs tucked up under her on the sofa. “Up until 22 [she is 26 now], I had that thing of: whatever my dad says goes. I did the marriage, I did all that, I tried to do everything he wanted.”In the show, Temple says “women are seen, not heard”. How did her dad feel about her blossoming social media career? “He thought it was a load of shit,” says Temple with a laugh. “My dad was old school. He didn’t like that girls worked. He didn’t like that girls would get tattoos. He didn’t like girls going to school. So me doing something [such as becoming big on social media] was so, like: what are you doing?” She misses him every day, she says. “And I love him dearly; he makes me think about every aspect of my life.” But there is also a kind of liberation without him. “It’s just nice not to feel that thing of: oh, have I done that right? Am I going to get told off for that?”Temple has star quality. She’s quick and hilarious and it helps that she’s gorgeous – tall, curvy, lips bursting at the seams. Later, Tina says that her daughter has always lit up a room; she’s obviously biased, but it’s true. Some people are just born like that.View image in fullscreen‘I did the marriage, I did all that’ … Temple.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianTemple always said she would become famous (she made an early TV appearance at 13, on a BBC children’s show about kids struggling in school). “But I never had that thing of, like: I’m going to be famous and better than everyone. It was more: I’m going to be known and I can help everyone. I come from an estate where people were trying to hustle. There was always that thing of people being hungry and I didn’t want to starve any more.” She smiles. “Not physically, because I’m chubby as shit. I didn’t starve, trust me. But I’m saying that money-hungry feeling is what I had.”She was inspired by the influencers she was seeing on YouTube and started making her own videos, but she didn’t start posting them until she was 17, gradually growing a following. She appeared on the Channel 4 reality competition show Tempting Fortune in 2023; by 2024, her videos were doing so well that she was thinking about trying to make her own reality show.Her manager put her in touch with the TV production company Optomen, which pitched it to Channel 4. The channel had been home to the programmes Benefits Street and My Big Fat Gypsy Wedding, which had been accused of being exploitative of people from her background. Was she nervous about how she would be portrayed? No, she says. “When I pitched it, it was like: show my estate, show the funny parts, but I want it to be known that I love this estate. I’m not here to mock it.”That love is clear. “You couldn’t buy loyalty, you couldn’t buy this community, and that’s what I’m grateful for.” Before she made the show, she was walking around with some of the production crew. “All of a sudden, my mate come out of nowhere. ‘Trew, you all right? Are they undercover old bill? They about to nick you?’” She laughs. Now, neighbours put off fans who come to the estate searching for her. When her dad was dying, she says, “we couldn’t leave this house; us girls were nursing him. I didn’t have one influencer drop us food. I didn’t have one Gypsy drop us food. I had the people on the estate, who would wait for the benefits to hit their account because they’ve got nothing, drop milk and cereal at the door.”It makes it all worth it, says Temple, when she gets people telling her she has inspired them. “I’ve got girls coming over to me in, like, the nail bar, going: ‘My daughter keeps saying: “I know I can be something now.’” When you’ve got people that actually live these lives, live these struggles, telling me thank you ‘because I’m gonna do this next’, it’s an amazing feeling. I’m not just a Gypsy. I’m half Gypsy, half gorja. I’m a council-estate kid. I’m a businesswoman. There’s a lot of layers to me and I’m glad if at least one person from each of those things I’m representing can go: ‘Wow, I can do that.’” Some have responded to her mixed heritage. “I even had one Gypsy [influencer make] a video; I didn’t know she was half. She was, like: ‘I just want to let everyone know I’m half and I’ve always been ashamed about it my whole life. But now Trewley’s saying it, so am I.’ And my jaw was on the floor out of love.”Temple is the youngest of Tina’s five children and has seven other siblings from her father’s previous relationships. Her father, she says, “hated that we were settled [lived in a house]”. She says she doesn’t know if he worked: “That’s something I wasn’t allowed to ask, what he did.” But their financial situation was “unstable”, she says. Sometimes they had money, but “the majority of the time we were very poor”.View image in fullscreenTemple at the National Reality TV Awards in London in 2023.Photograph: Jack Dredd/ShutterstockShe has experienced anti-Gypsy prejudice all her life. One of the reasons she is so attached to her estate is that it felt safe – playing football with the other kids or hanging out at the community centre was also a refuge from her often chaotic and strict home life – and she didn’t really question her difference. It was when she went outside the area, to secondary school, that she was marked out. “People were like: ‘Why do you talk like that? Why do you wear makeup? Why do you have a trailer?’” Internally, she questioned it: “I’m like: ‘I don’t know. Why do I have that?’” Externally, to deal with it, she became tough and funny.Now, a lot of the negative comments online are from Gypsies who say she’s not “real”. It was always hard to know where she fitted in, she says, “because you’re not accepted from your mum’s side and then you’re not accepted from your dad’s side and we’re the product of both. I’d be too Gypsy for the gorja kids and too gorja for the Gypsy kids. I could never win.” That’s partly what she wants to explore in her show. “I’m making my own lane. OK, I’m not accepted by you. Well, I’m accepted by me and I’m here. And anyone else that ain’t accepted, you’re accepted by me as well.” She smiles. “That’s what it’s for.”Her two older sisters had children fairly young, as is expected of Gypsy women, and for a while Temple looked to be going the same way. She had a boyfriend at 18, someone she was considered to be married to within Gypsy culture (although not legally). “Basically, you give yourself to the man,” says Temple. “That’s how they see it: I gave myself to him.” In the show, she implies the relationship was unhappy. Temple left him when she was 22. “I should have left him two years prior. But I’m not raised to leave him.” By then, her father was seriously ill and Temple moved in to help look after him. She felt intense guilt, she says. “I feel like I’m failing my family. I’m nursing him and now I’ve got to tell him I’m leaving [my partner]. You can only imagine the shame, every bit of responsibility I felt.”View image in fullscreen‘I never had that thing of: I’m going to be famous and better than everyone.’Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe rules for the girls growing up, especially about where they were allowed to go, and with whom, were “quite suffocating”, she says. “My brothers didn’t have the same rules as us.” It felt unfair. “But I wasn’t allowed to say that.” Even now, at 26, her family needs to know where she is and Tina has set a curfew. Does she mind? Tina, who is doing the ironing in the conservatory, looks in. Temple laughs. “I wouldn’t question her because she’s the captain of the ship. I can’t disrespect my mum. I have always respected my mum and dad.”In one of the episodes, Temple’s sister Honey says that while she always wanted to be a mother – she had her first child at 19 – she would like more options for her daughter: “I’d want my daughter to be like Trewley, go around the world, be out there and do it all.” At 20, Romany (Gypsy) or Irish Traveller women areeight times more likelyto have no educational qualifications than other women in the wider population.Things are gradually changing for women in these communities, Temple believes. “I do think more women are reaching out on jobs and I see some Traveller girls graduate, which is amazing. I want girls to know there’s other options. I’m not saying being a young mum and being a housewife ain’t fine. My mum was a young mum. My sisters are young mums. I rate that. But I also want girls to know it’s OK if you don’t want that yet. Sometimes I feel like I get seen as less as a woman because I haven’t had a child yet.”View image in fullscreenIn a scene from Secret Lives of Gypsy Wives.Photograph: Optomen/Channel 4Her older sister Ruby-Anne is a trailblazer in the family – she isn’t married, doesn’t have children and has the frowned-upon tattoos – and Temple is still working out what she wants. “That’s the thing about the show. I’m still trying to figure out what I’m doing. Is this the right career path? Am I supposed to be married again by now? Am I supposed to have a child? It’s trying to explore these questions I have without my dad’s answers.”She says she doesn’t think she’ll move away from her estate, no matter how successful she gets. Who knows? Temple is still early in her career and money and fame do strange things to people. But, for now, she seems solid in herself and her values. She says she turned down £100,000 to promote weight-loss injections, which was hard. “I felt like I’ve worked for years to get to a point where I could earn that and I still had to say no because it went against me morally. I feel like I represent a lot of girls and I sit there all the time saying: love who you are. But then, what, I’ve been bought out?”Her life is “on here [the estate]. My mum and dad’s work is in us children on here.” In the school holidays especially, she says, her parents would watch out for local children who had been left while their mums went to work, or who didn’t have the security of a school dinner. “They showed me how to be a caring adult and I want to carry that,” she says. Instead of fame for fame’s sake, “I actually get more excited knowing that I can help.”She wants to share whatever she gets with her family and her community. People are proud and don’t ask her for money. “But I’ve got eyes. If I know a woman’s struggling, that’s fine, I’m from the struggle, so there’s no judgment.” She has dropped off food for people or bought school uniforms. Mainly, she wants to take care of Tina. “All I’ve ever seen is a strong, hustling mum and now I want to be the strong, hustling daughter. I’ll take it over. That’s what my goal would be.” She seems to have taken on her father’s role, but she’s doing it her way.Secret Lives of Gypsy Wives is on Channel 4Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Shards review – murder, 80s mayhem and the Ryan Murphy comeback we’ve been waiting for | Television | The Guardian
description: Murphy is back on form with this gorgeously curated, shot and scored adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’s novel – about a serial killer stalking privileged LA teenagers
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Murphy is back on form with this gorgeously curated, shot and scored adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’s novel – about a serial killer stalking privileged LA teenagers
Content: Beautifully curated … (from left) Igby Rigney, Hayes Warner and Kaia Gerber in The Shards.Photograph: FXView image in fullscreenBeautifully curated … (from left) Igby Rigney, Hayes Warner and Kaia Gerber in The Shards.Photograph: FXTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Shards review – murder, 80s mayhem and the Ryan Murphy comeback we’ve been waiting forMurphy is back on form with this gorgeously curated, shot and scored adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’s novel – about a serial killer stalking privileged LA teenagersLucy ManganThu 6 Aug 2026 05.34 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world can finally begin to hope again. It looks as though Ryan Murphy has pulled out of his dive and is beginning to find his glorious groove again. The uber-showrunner reached a nadir last year with All’s Fair, a legal drama that was so bad it was existentially awful, garnering a number of rare, zero-star reviews (including mine) and which has duly been commissioned for a second series.But after All’s Fair cameThe Beauty. Which was chaotic and underdeveloped but fun. And then there wasLove Story, about the short lives and love of JFK Jr and Carolyn Bessette, which was pitch-perfect, properly good trash. And now there is The Shards, Murphy’s adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’s 80s-set metafictional/autobiographical novel of the same name. I have not read the book. An enfant terrible’s reminiscences are too often simply terrible and I was exhausted by the very idea. But a TV version? Run through the Murphytron? That sounds like a very good idea – and so it has proved. Theirs is a marriage made in pop-culture heaven.We open in the 1980s with a laconic voiceover from our main man, Bret (Igby Rigney, still a little rough in places, but he nevertheless does great work here, allowing just enough glimpses of the roiling emotion beneath the shiny, protective carapace to keep Ellis’s avatar recognisably human). He is sketching out the immediate future for him and his select, gilded group of high school friends. “A season of horror and murder that would destroy us all.” Think Gatsby with quaaludes, settle back and enjoy.Metafiction demands meta-commentary, so Murphy has stuffed the cast with the offspring of 80s icons – most notably Kaia Gerber (the absolute image of her supermodel mother, Cindy Crawford) and Homer Gere (son of Richard and Carey Lowell), both of whom acquit themselves very well. Gerber is straight-A student and class president Susan, the childhood friend with whom Bret is in love, despite his girlfriend Debbie (Hayes Warner) and his assorted secret boyfriends and Susan’s own long-term boyfriend, Thom (Graham Campbell). Gere is Robert, the beautiful, troubled new boy who looks set to shatter their charmed circle. “He was a virus,” Bret’s voiceover tells us, as Robert starts gaslighting him and befriending all the young men Bret has recently had sex with, “who was going to invade and destroy the school and me.”View image in fullscreenCharmed circle … (from left): Kaia Gerber, Igby Rigney, Hayes Warner, Homer Gere and Graham Campbell in The Shards.Photograph: FXIt is the 80s, it is Los Angeles and so, as well as metaphors for the coming Aids epidemic, there is a literal killer at work. Young women get heavy-breather phone calls, go missing and then turn up horribly mutilated and deeply dead. By the time the third victim is found, the serial killer has been nicknamed the Trawler and bloody pentagrams are appearing on doors and in homes, leading to the city living in fear. Bret keeps a knife by his typewriter as he works on his first novel late into the night.The Trawler moves on to young male victims. When one of Bret’s former secrets, Matt Kellner, accuses Bret of repeatedly calling him and messing with his home while he is out, even darker suspicions of Robert begin to form in our otherwise disaffected hero’s mind. Then he gets a phone call himself, and hears the sounds of Matt being tortured to death.The Shards is beautifully curated, shot and scored. The sea of Gucci loafers, Ralph Lauren shirts and Calvin Klein everything elses ebbs and flows under a permanently azure sky. And the soundtrack is either contemporary bangers or specially written for the occasion byTroye Sivan, who is by some sorcery able to evoke a time nearly two decades before he was born with precision and then add some heartfelt melancholy for it, too.Perhaps it’s this that marks out The Shards as a true return to form for Murphy. Nostalgia is not just memory of times past – it’s a yearning for it, too, and this time he captures both. The serial killer storyline pulls the story along, but its heart is in the longing for an era gone by, for youth flown, even with all its sorrows and insecurities. When drugs and sex were novelties still, part of a process of discovery rather than avoidance, and it felt – before viruses, the internet, climate change and all the other infinite horrors – like anything was possible. Shards of hope.The Shards is on Disney+Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewRyan MurphyBret Easton EllisDramareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hunt for the Wilderpeople review – Sam Neill is warm and wise in Taika Waititi’s goofily tremendous film | Movies | The Guardian
description: Waititi’s eccentric drama sends the late actor into the New Zealand wilderness with his young charge, angry authorities in hot pursuit
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Waititi’s eccentric drama sends the late actor into the New Zealand wilderness with his young charge, angry authorities in hot pursuit
Content: Distinctive irony … Sam Neill in Hunt for the Wilderpeople.Photograph: Kane Skennar/Piki Films/AllstarView image in fullscreenDistinctive irony … Sam Neill in Hunt for the Wilderpeople.Photograph: Kane Skennar/Piki Films/AllstarMoviesReviewHunt for the Wilderpeople review – Sam Neill is warm and wise in Taika Waititi’s goofily tremendous filmWaititi’s eccentric drama sends the late actor into the New Zealand wilderness with his young charge, angry authorities in hot pursuitPeter BradshawThu 6 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe recent sad loss of Sam Neill is a great opportunity to revisit one of his greatest roles, in this tremendous family film from 2016, a goofy mix of Butch and Sundance and Chaplin’s The Kid. It’s arguably the masterpiece of its writer-directorTaika Waititi, who adapted the 1986 bestseller Wild Pork and Watercress by New Zealand author Barry Crump, bringing his distinctive irony, comedy and quirk (Waititi has a droll cameo as a wacky vicar), but wisely lets the story and performances do the real work, so the movie continues to win the hearts of audiences.Neill plays Hector, a grouchy old buzzard who works on a farm on New Zealand’s North Island just below the vast forested wilderness of the breathtakingly beautifulTe Urewera. The property is owned by his big-hearted wife Bella (Rima Te Wiata) who works as a foster parent, regularly taking in troubled kids, and Hector is under no illusions that she married him in the same charitable spirit. But glum, taciturn Hector is not best pleased when Bella takes in the toughest and most recalcitrant teen the state authorities have ever dealt with. This is Ricky, played by Maori actor Julian Dennison, and Rachel House gives an amusing performance as Paula, the child welfare worker who is on Ricky’s case.Bella has a tactless habit of referring cheerfully to Ricky’s size, but the boy can certainly sense her kindly and wise nature and it actually seems as if this unlikely new foster family is going to live together happily. But then an awful fate intervenes and Hector and Ricky go on the run together in the jungle, being tracked by the pitiless forces of the state who want to put the boy into “juvie”. Bad-tempered, self-reliant Hector, for all his impatience, is darned if he’s going to let these bullies push the boy – or him – around. A nationwide manhunt gets under way for this odd couple, who are now living on pure instinct, moving across tough terrain like a human version of wildebeest, and the general public, hearing about them on breathless TV news reports, begin to feel that they are the underdog heroes.The sentimental possibilities of the drama are amusingly undercut by Waititi, particularly with a series of gags which make it look as if Hector is going to seem like a child molester; there’s some funny stuff too for the hatchet-faced Paula who quarrels with Ricky when she comes face to face with him in the undergrowth. She compares herself to the Terminator, and Ricky crossly claims that he is the one who is like the Terminator, at which point Paula petulantly snaps that Ricky is more like “Sarah Connor ... from the first movie, before she could do chin-ups.” Neill gives a lovely, gentle and wise performance.Hunt for the Wilderpeople is in UK and Irish cinemas from 7 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsSam NeillTaika WaititiNew ZealandComedyAsia PacificreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Practical Magic review – Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock’s 90s witchy fantasy still enchants  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Preceding a long-awaited sequel, Griffin Dunne’s supernatural suburban romance gets a big-screen rerelease. With its romcom quirk, buttery cinematography and stabs of black comedy, it remains a zany gem
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Preceding a long-awaited sequel, Griffin Dunne’s supernatural suburban romance gets a big-screen rerelease. With its romcom quirk, buttery cinematography and stabs of black comedy, it remains a zany gem
Content: The Witches of Eastwick meets Thelma & Louise … Practical Magic.Photograph: Warner Bros./AllstarView image in fullscreenThe Witches of Eastwick meets Thelma & Louise … Practical Magic.Photograph: Warner Bros./AllstarMoviesReviewPractical Magic review – Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock’s 90s witchy fantasy still enchantsPreceding a long-awaited sequel, Griffin Dunne’s supernatural suburban romance gets a big-screen rerelease. With its romcom quirk, buttery cinematography and stabs of black comedy, it remains a zany gemPeter BradshawThu 6 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith a sequel shortly to make an appearance – Nicole Kidman,Sandra Bullock, Stockard Channing and Dianne Wiest (but not Evan Rachel Wood) all reprising their roles – the original Practical Magic from 1998 is now getting a rerelease. This is Griffin Dunne’s smalltown supernatural goof-fest, adapted from a bestseller by Alice Hoffman; the sequel is based on her own follow-up, The Book of Magic. A zanier adventure in occult romance can hardly be imagined, and the elements of grown up noir violence only make it weirder – it is as if The Witches of Eastwick took on something of Thelma & Louise with a decaffeinated David Lynch. Meanwhile, cinematographer Andrew Dunn bathes the daytime scenes in a golden, buttery light.In a suburban American anytown, buttoned-up residents and frowning soccer moms are disapprovingly obsessed with the fact that the local Owens family womenfolk are witches. There is an amusing “prelude” scene showing a Salem-style public hanging of one of their ancestors; a stark stab of black comedy. In the present day, the Owens sisters Sally and Gillian, played by Bullock and Kidman, are intensely aware of their magical inheritance, as personified by naughty maiden aunts Frances and Bridget, played by Channing and Wiest.But the two women could hardly be more different. Sally is more sensible, a widowed mother whose late husband tragically fell victim to the curse that awaits any man with whom an Owens woman falls genuinely in love. Single Gillian is a wild child; a rock’n’roll badass who left home as a young woman and fell in love (or lust) with sexy Jimmy Angelov (Goran Visnjic), who turns out to be a psychopathic abuser. Sally and Gillian did what they needed to do to be rid of him, by natural and supernatural means, and now a certain law enforcement official is coming around, asking questions; this is sensitive dreamboat Gary Hallet (Aidan Quinn), who feels the magic of love stirring the moment he sets eyes on his prime suspect, Sally. Bullock then goes into the alluring klutz routine that was her Kitemark for years.It’s an amusing, if very 90s, movie; the kind that has its own endless afterlife on home entertainment. It’s also interesting to see a small part for stalwart supporting actor Margo Martindale, as one of the sympathetic town women – the kind of character she often played before getting more interesting roles in her silver years.Practical Magic is in UK and Irish cinemas from 7 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmRomance filmsComedy filmsScience fiction and fantasy filmsSandra BullockNicole KidmanFilm adaptationsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Thirst by John Robins audiobook review – an ex-drinker’s darkly funny journey | Books | The Guardian
description: The comedian and broadcaster narrates the heartfelt and at times self-lacerating account of his relationship with alcohol
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The comedian and broadcaster narrates the heartfelt and at times self-lacerating account of his relationship with alcohol
Content: Sage advice … John Robins.Photograph: Pål Hansen/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSage advice … John Robins.Photograph: Pål Hansen/The GuardianAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewThirst by John Robins audiobook review – an ex-drinker’s darkly funny journeyThe comedian and broadcaster narrates the heartfelt and at times self-lacerating account of his relationship with alcoholFiona SturgesThu 6 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmemoir chronicling the comic and broadcaster John Robins’s life in alcohol and his subsequent path to sobriety, Thirst is structured around the drinks that changed his life. There’s the bottle of Jacob’s Creek wine left out on a kitchen worktop which he helped himself to at the age of seven, secreting it into his orange juice, and the beer given to him at scout camp which he drank alone. There’s also his stomach-churning recreation, while on a comedy tour of Australia, of the white russians drunk by the Dude in The Big Lebowski using a gallon of milk, a litre of vodka and a bottle of Kahlua.As an adult, Robins, who is best known for his shows on Radio X and on BBC5 Live, romanticised pubs, which he saw as places of peacefulness and refuge. He even co-hosted the podcast The Moon Under Water where he invited guests to describe their ideal pub. Robins reveals that what kept him drinking for so long was the lie that he was in control. That he could, on occasion, get through a Dry January convinced him he couldn’t be an addict, although he got a wakeup call when a GP told him to “sort your fucking life out”.Robins is our narrator and his reading, much like his prose, is heartfelt, darkly funny, sometimes self-lacerating and full of sage advice born from bruising experience. Currently sober, he must now grapple with the depression from which alcohol was shielding him. “I can thank alcohol for trying to step in,” he notes “but remind it that its services are no longer required, that I’ll take it from here.”Thirst: Twelve Drinks That Changed My Life is available via Penguin Audio, 11hr 36minFurther listeningThe Land and Its PeopleDavid Sedaris, Little, Brown, 7hr 26minThe latest essay collection from the humorist was recorded live in front of an audience in Massachusetts and features reflections on his late mother, an anti-Trump protest in New Hampshire and the trials of looking after his partner, Hugh, after a hip operation.The Book of RecordsMadeleine Thien, Granta, 13hr 50minRichard Lam, Athena Karkanis and Scott Turner Schofield are among the narrators of the fourth novel from the Dogs at the Perimeter author. It sees an ailing father and his daughter reflect on their past as they arrive at a remote migratory outpost called “the sea”.Explore more on these topicsBooksAudiobook of the weekAlcoholismAlcoholHealthreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like if John Sayles directed Forrest Gump’: the incredible life of historian Howard Zinn | Books | The Guardian
description: The life of the hugely influential ‘people’s historian’ is explored in a wide-ranging new book that brings in everything from wars to civil rights to Matt Damon
Author: Martin Pengelly
Headline: The life of the hugely influential ‘people’s historian’ is explored in a wide-ranging new book that brings in everything from wars to civil rights to Matt Damon
Content: ‘He finds himself at these incredible pivots and yet also has this incredible history and perspective and leadership ability through his years as an organizer’ … Howard Zinn in 1984.Photograph: Marilyn Humphries/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘He finds himself at these incredible pivots and yet also has this incredible history and perspective and leadership ability through his years as an organizer’ … Howard Zinn in 1984.Photograph: Marilyn Humphries/AlamyBooks‘Like if John Sayles directed Forrest Gump’: the incredible life of historian Howard ZinnThe life of the hugely influential ‘people’s historian’ is explored in a wide-ranging new book that brings in everything from wars to civil rights to Matt DamonMartin PengellyThu 6 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMatt Damon may play a great hero inThe Odyssey, but one of the star’s own heroes is also set for his time in the spotlight. In Massachusetts in the 1970s and 80s, Damon grew up close toHoward Zinn, now the subject ofThe People’s Historian, a biography by Dave Zirin.“Frankly,” Zirin said, “the fact that he’sMatt Damonand oh by the way is now in the biggest movie perhaps since Titanic, it makes it a nice little bauble for the book that I got to interview him.“But honestly, I would have interviewed anybody who hadMatt Damon’s perspective of being young and knowing Howard Zinn as this kind of elder, because the dynamics of their relationship to me really say something about Zinn, from him being willing to go to little Mattie’s public high school to do a talk, as a favor to the family, to being a friend and a sounding board, not behaving like some unapproachable elder, but at the same time it being pretty clear that other adults really respected this guy.”Howard Zinn obituaryRead moreMany did, worldwide. After an epic career in academia and progressive politics, Zinndiedin 2010, aged 87. Damon has carried lessons from him through his own career.Good Will Hunting, his breakthrough hit from 1997, containsmentionof Zinn’s seminal work, A People’s History of the United States: “That book’ll fuckin’ knock you on your ass.” Damon has sought to bring Zinn to the screen, including via the documentaryThe People Speak, from 2009.But despite such adult endeavors, Zirin said the star’s “child’s perspective on Howard Zinn” was most useful when it came to writing his book. After all, plenty of American schoolchildren continue to come to know Zinn through A People’s History,first published in 1980, often updated, now with more than 4m copies sold. The story of America from “1492-Present”, it is explicitlynotthe story of the great white men of tradition, from Christopher Columbus to the founders and on through the civil war, the Gilded Age and the long 20th century. Inevitably, it has long been a target for angry rightwingers.View image in fullscreenMatt Damon, Howard Zinn and Ben Affleck in 1999.Photograph: Vinnie Zuffante/Getty Images“Our children are instructed from propaganda tracts, like those of Howard Zinn, that try to make students ashamed of their own history,” Donald Trumpsaidat the National Archives in September 2020, laying the ground for the presentassault on revisionist history.When asking historians or biographers what their subject might have made of Trump, it often pays to be circumspect. Not when talking to Zirin, who is sports editor of the Nation, the progressive magazine founded in 1865. In his introduction, Zirin considers what Zinn would have thought about the politics of the 2020s, including the pursuit of racial justice and its rightwing backlash. Furthermore, Zirin knew Zinn well, having written his ownA People’s History of Sports in the United States, and having moderated events with Zinn towards the end of his life.“He wrote so much and he lectured so much to the end of his life, that we have more than breadcrumbs” about what Zinn would think, Zirin said. “We have full loaves of bread. When you read what he was writing about the Bush administration and the endless wars and the growth of the surveillance state, he could very much be talking about Donald Trump, in terms of his acidic humor about having this dullard in the White House, to the growth of tyranny … he had a perspective on history and how one weathered the ups and downs of history, and in those statements you get a kind of broad view that I think is universal and can apply to 2026 as much as to 1949.”Zinn was born in 1922, in Brooklyn, New York, to poor Jewish immigrants from Russia and Austria-Hungary. At 17, he went to work in the Brooklyn Navy Yard. Swiftly, he became a union organizer, beginning a political journey that would land him in the sights of the FBI in the red scare and after. In 1944, he metRoslyn Shechter, another leftwing firebrand who became his wife. Joining the US Army Air Corps to fight fascism, Zinn became a bombardier. In April 1945, he took part in a raid over the French coast, an early use of napalm. His horrified realization of what he helped do to the town of Royan would shape his decades of activism and protest.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Penguin Random HouseZinn was a leading voice against the Vietnam war, where napalm was heavily used. In an extraordinary chapter, Zirin retells the story of thearduous, hazardous journeyZinn and thepriest and peace activist Daniel Berrigantook to Hanoiin 1968, to secure the release ofthree US airmen, battling absurd army bureaucracy and Washington machinations. Another key passage of The People’s Historian concerns the early to mid-60s, years when Howard and Roz Zinn worked on the ground in the American south, in the thick of the civil rights struggle. Academic politics intrudes too, including stories of how Zinn ran afoul of conservative authorities at Spelman College in Atlanta and at Boston University, where he taught for decades. Given such rich subject matter, Zirin’s book sometimes reads less like a biography of a historian than as the basis for a novel or screenplay, written (in fantasyland) by Joseph Heller or Philip Roth.Zirin found himself thinking cinematically, sometimes “of the Woody Allen characterZeligor or even the Tom Hanks character ofForrest Gump: people who find themselves unintentionally at these incredible pivot points in history. And yet the difference between Howard Zinn and Zelig or Forrest Gump is that Zinn is also a working-class, Ivy League-trained historian [he studied at NYU and Columbia after the war], so he finds himself at these incredible pivots and yet also has this incredible history and perspective and leadership ability through his years as an organizer. It’s incredible. It would be like ifJohn Saylesdirected Forrest Gump.”Zirin clearly looked up to Zinn, much as Damon did before. Nonetheless, the portrait in Zirin’s pages is unsparing.“There’s a sign over my desk that says ‘hagiography’ with a line through it,” Zirin said. “I looked for the warts, hard, because the fear going in was given my respect for the work and the fact I got to know him at the end of his life,” a need to celebrate the man and his work might take over.Zinn’s commitment to protest and rise to national fame was hard onRozand their children, Jeff and Myla. When times got tough for Zinn, Zirin said: “What I found was that if you want to call it his drug of choice, he was able to live through these times when he was also able to lecture in the classroom, about all sorts of topics from the history of civil liberties to the Gilded Age. He taught social sciences at different points, and then saw his students be able to go out and apply it, then come back to the classroom. He lived through times when people were living history. He was able to teach that history, and then see history being made.”The People’s Historian: The Outsized Life of Howard Zinn, published by Dutton, isout now.Explore more on these topicsBooksHistory booksHistoryMatt DamonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sky City by Jacqueline Crooks review – an ambitious, lyrical portrait of trauma | Books | The Guardian
description: A young woman is haunted by her childhood in this forcefully imaginative and unapologetically bleak novel from the author of Fire Rush
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: A young woman is haunted by her childhood in this forcefully imaginative and unapologetically bleak novel from the author of Fire Rush
Content: Poetic ambition … Jacqueline Crooks.Photograph: Katherine Anne Rose/The ObserverView image in fullscreenPoetic ambition … Jacqueline Crooks.Photograph: Katherine Anne Rose/The ObserverBook of the dayBooksReviewSky City by Jacqueline Crooks review – an ambitious, lyrical portrait of traumaA young woman is haunted by her childhood in this forcefully imaginative and unapologetically bleak novel from the author of Fire RushEmma LoffhagenThu 6 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 02.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world of Sky City never quite settles beneath your feet. The action of Jacqueline Crooks’s second novel unfolds in a recognisable 1990s London, yet everything seems subtly untethered from reality: a council estate suspended above the city, voices drifting in and out through pirate radio, ghosts walking beside the living. The narrative floats just above the surface of the everyday, a world where trauma transforms the mundane into something uncanny.We first meet protagonist Jaycee as a child, trapped in a west London housing estate she calls the Cyborg House. Her stepfather subjects her to horrific sexual abuse while her mother turns a blind eye, exercising her own brand of cruelty. Families, Jaycee comes to believe, are “dangerous places … like nests of poisonous spiders, huddled in dark, undisturbed corners, their venom, a single drop enough to rot the body inside out”. Eventually taken into care, she finds an unlikely lifeline in Ella-G, another damaged girl whose exuberance masks wounds as profound as Jaycee’s own; both feel “on the outside of the world”. The care home turns out to be similarly brutal, and the pair survive together, forging a friendship that becomes the novel’s emotional anchor.As adults, Jaycee and Ella-G could hardly seem more different. Jaycee retreats into solitude in her high-rise council flat in Sky City, an estate perched above a shopping centre in north London where Crooks herself once lived. “Being alone is what it means to be at peace,” she tells herself. In a near-perennial state of dissociation, she imagines herself transformed by trauma into something less than fully human. Ella-G, meanwhile, propelled by her restless charisma, heads to the bright lights of New York’s music scene.Through a conversation between past and present, Jaycee’s childhood seeps into the contemporary narrative in shards of memory and recurring visions, her adult life continually interrupted by the child she once was. Crooks sketches this psychic dislocation with extraordinary imaginative force. The abuse reverberates through Jaycee’s consciousness in fragments. She is haunted by Obsidia, a spectral child who comes to represent a version of herself.double quotation markCrooks’s prose is deeply musical – sentences swell and eddy in a dreamlike, rhythmic fashionThe present-day narrative gathers momentum when Jaycee unexpectedly reconnects with Sol, a boy who offered her a rare glimpse of tenderness at secondary school before circumstance tore them apart. Their reunion carries the promise of romance, yet Crooks is after something more subtle than a conventional love story. Sol becomes another lost soul searching for belonging, his own fractured identity mirroring Jaycee’s.As in her 2023 Women’s prize-shortlisted debut,Fire Rush, music provides the novel’s connective tissue and emotional scaffolding. An obscure blues record by a forgotten singer drawsJaycee into a quest that eventually takes her and Ella-G to Atlantic City in the search for a missing father, which becomes inseparable from Jaycee’s search for self.Crooks’s prose, too, is deeply musical. Sentences swell and eddy in a dreamlike, rhythmic fashion, looping back on to recurring images before resolving into clarity. It takes a while to acclimatise, and at times the lyricism threatens to overwhelm the narrative. The novel’s momentum can sag beneath the weight of its own poetic ambition.Sky City is also unapologetically bleak: there is a near constant effluvium of loneliness, hanging over the novel like the weather. Much of the narrative, as Crooks notes in the acknowledgments, is autobiographical. It feels as though she is refusing to soften or redeem her trauma for the reader’s comfort. It is a reminder that adversity can be an enduring condition, not a narrative device on the way to catharsis.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFire Rush announced a singular literary talent: a novelist capable of fusing the propulsive rhythms of dub music with the spiritual inheritance of African spiritualism, defying conventional realism. Sky City is, in many ways, even more ambitious. It is a haunting, polyphonic meditation on trauma and belonging that hovers between realism and dream, asking how a person might rebuild a self after childhood has shattered it.Sky City by Jacqueline Crooks is published by Jonathan Cape (£18.99).
