title: Nazis and Happy Feet collide in Penguin Colony, a psychological horror game set at the world’s end | Games | The Guardian
description: Explore Antarctica as a flightless bird – and dodge some earthly monsters – in this surreal adaptation of HP Lovecraft
Author: Sarah Thwaites
Headline: Explore Antarctica as a flightless bird – and dodge some earthly monsters – in this surreal adaptation of HP Lovecraft
Content: PS2-style aesthetic … Penguin Colony.Illustration: Fellow TravellerView image in fullscreenPS2-style aesthetic … Penguin Colony.Illustration: Fellow TravellerSummer games previewsGamesNazis and Happy Feet collide in Penguin Colony, a psychological horror game set at the world’s endExplore Antarctica as a flightless bird – and dodge some earthly monsters – in this surreal adaptation of HP LovecraftSarah ThwaitesThu 6 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile watching the 2006 animated film Happy Feet with his daughter, Origame Digital founder Naphtali Faulkner noticed something interesting. “[In the movie], they see the digger fall into the ocean, and it has an almost eldritch quality,” he says. Over time, and with plenty of iteration, Faulkner’s inspirations coalesced, from HP Lovecraft to the 1982 version of The Thing and the works of David Lynch. “I’m a big fan of horror that sits in your head rather than in your stomach,” says Faulkner.In Penguin Colony, players body-switch between species of flightless birds, piecing together cryptic cosmic clues as they tail a Nazi expedition to Antarctica. In the process, Origame Digital draws on Lovecraft’s novella At the Mountains of Madness. “I’d always wanted to do a creature that’s a manifestation of colonial thought, energy and power, and the idea of it resting and then regrowing,” says Faulkner. “I was looking through the history of Lovecraft and him being agigantic racist, and this idea of the Nazis sort of came out,” he adds.View image in fullscreenPenguin Colony.Illustration: Fellow TravellerThe visual style of Penguin Colony pays homage to the low-poly aesthetics of the PS2, a period Faulkner calls romantic, owing to the era’s limited technical capabilities, which led to impressionist designs. “We’re not a rich studio,” he says. “There was just a games crash; publishers aren’t funding anything, everyone seems to be out of money. So why don’t we make something very cheap to make?” It started with the game’s isolated setting, followed by a decision to have humans in the game appear as soldiers; their uniform bodies could be duplicated with only their heads swapped out. “Repetition pays its weight in gold sometimes because you aren’t having to be so meticulous. You can paint with broad strokes and really build something out.”Penguin Colony’s Antarctic setting is predominantly open-world, allowing Origame Digital to hide enigmatic notes, photographs and soundbites across the frigid tundra. “We wanted to play into the Lovecraftian fear of the unknown,” Faulkner says. As such, instead of relying on a user interface, players are guided by their intuition.This stylistic choice was also inspired by Dark Souls directorHidetaka Miyazaki, whose intentional vagueness evokes a distinctly pre-internet sense of discovery. “Certain things are in an alien language that players will need to decipher if they want to know what’s being said,” says Faulkner. By investigating, players also emulate the Nazi expedition’s archaeological activity. “[Later] you’ll come across some hieroglyphics, and we’ve made sure those image files contain no metadata, so players will actually have to look at them and try to decipher what it’s saying in context.”This cryptic touch isn’t the only homage to FromSoftware. Penguin Colony features an insight system comparable to Bloodborne, which lets players interpret the game’s otherworldly aspects with greater clarity based on how they play. “I don’t want to spoil exactly what,” adds Faulkner. “But, in a dark area, if you have enough insight, you can hear something walking around behind you.”Despite its surreal surroundings, Penguin Colony’s narrative draws on real history. “I did my research on this group calledthe Ahnenerbe, which was tasked with finding the Spear of Destiny and other Christian artefacts,” says Faulkner. “Nazi relic hunting went all around the world,” he continues. “They would find things with barely any connection to anything, and invent histories that don’t actually exist, and that was used as their justification for the colonial annexation of Europe.”It’s a confronting topic, but Faulkner feels this kind of conversation belongs in games, especially since they are one of the few art forms in which audience participation is mandatory. He recalls a conversation with his mentor about playing in the grey, where you place ideas side by side and explore the feelings they can evoke. “There are people out there who, the moment you say colonisation, freak out and start stomping their feet. [That’s] not my audience … I think of it like this: if this game reaches someone who hadn’t thought about this [topic] before and they change the way they think about it, just a little bit, then it was worth it.”Penguin Colony is coming soon to PC andNintendo Switch 2.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCNintendo Switch 2featuresShareReuse this content

title: Metroid at 40: happy birthday to Samus Aran, gaming’s greatest badass and my personal heroine | Games | The Guardian
description: Being a woman who loves video games has often felt lonely, like being on a hostile planet – but Metroid’s female space hunter has been with me all the way
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Being a woman who loves video games has often felt lonely, like being on a hostile planet – but Metroid’s female space hunter has been with me all the way
Content: Fearless, intelligent, devoted, determined … Samus Aran in Metroid Prime 4.Photograph: NintendoView image in fullscreenFearless, intelligent, devoted, determined … Samus Aran in Metroid Prime 4.Photograph: NintendoGamesMetroid at 40: happy birthday to Samus Aran, gaming’s greatest badass and my personal heroineBeing a woman who loves video games has often felt lonely, like being on a hostile planet – but Metroid’s female space hunter has been with me all the wayMaddy MyersThu 6 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s 1986, and you’re playing a brand-new game. (You’re in Japan in this scenario, by the way; the game in question, Metroid, won’t come to North America and Europe until later.) Anyway, this new game has you in its grip. You are a lone astronaut exploring a hostile alien planet full of ancient, mysterious structures. This astronaut looks human enough – but this distinctly alien place is full of objects that power up their spacesuit’s capabilities. Each new ability allows you to explore a new area, and as you do, you realise that the entirety of the planetary base you’re exploringis one, massive, interconnected maze.Whoa.Hours later, you finally defeat Mother Brain and set off a timed self-destruct sequence. Upon your escape, you’re treated to an endgame screen: the little astronaut faces you as text on screen implores you to “pray for peace in space”.View image in fullscreenSamus is you … Super Metroid.Illustration: ArcadeImages/AlamyBut then, the astronaut’s suit starts flashing rapidly – pink, green, orange. Suddenly, the suit disappears. What remains is … awoman!And a hot one, at that. Her pixelated hourglass figure has been lovingly rendered; her low-cut red leotard matches the dot of red lipstick that denotes her mouth. She’s looking right at you, the player, and she’s waving, as if to say,Congratulations, big boy! And if you beat the game even faster, I’ll strip down to just a bikini.This reveal lacked the consideration that a woman or girl might be the oneplayingthe game. (The concept of a queer female player was also almost certainly not on any developer’s mind, either.) By 1986, video games were already “for boys”. As reporter Tracey Lien outlined in her extensive feature on how and whenvideo game marketing shifted towards targeting boys, the video game crash of 1983 was followed by a marketing reset for several companies. The Nintendo Entertainment System, on which Metroidmade its debut to non-Japanese audiences, “was targeted toward boys under 10. If you look at the Super NES five years later, it starts targeting boys ages 10-15,” Jesse Divnich, former vice president of insights and analysis for Electronic Entertainment Design and Research, told Lien.The reveal of Samus Aran’s red bikini demonstrated that, in 1986 at least, if a game was going to have a female protagonist, she needed to be presented as a sex object to be enjoyed by the (presumed male, straight) player. That trend continued … for decades, unfortunately. But Samus Aran herself complicated the narrative. Sure, she was wearing increasingly skimpy outfits underneath that battle suit, but she also had spent the entire game up to that point performing extraordinarily badass feats. Well, technically, you – the player! – had performed them, as her. You were her, after all. Metroidtried to make you forget that, right at the end, by having her present herself to you as an object. But prior to that moment; she had been you, and you had been her, with all the personhood that implies.It’s hard not to project personality traits on to the largely blank slate that is Samus. She must be fearless, venturing into space completely alone. She must be intelligent; she’s mapping out this entire mazelike structure as she goes along. She must be devoted, determined, working for herself alone as a bounty hunter – a solitary job. Theinstruction bookletsays that Samus “is the greatest of all the space hunters and has successfully completed numerous missions that everybody thought were absolutely impossible”. This is the hyper-competent hero whose space boots you’re stepping into, and yeah, once again, she’s a woman.View image in fullscreenShe’s just so cool … Samus in Metroid Prime 4: Beyond.Illustration: NintendoIt’s for all of these reasons that I love the original Metroid so much. Its design and concept, iterated and improved upon in its sequels, would go on to inspire countless other games (and one of gaming’s most famousgenre terms). I always enjoy environmental puzzles and exploration in games, but it’s Samus Aran herself that I truly love – the version of Samus I created in my own head, as I played these games and projected myself on to her.Just like Samus Aran, I am 40 years old. My birthday is just one month prior to hers; I appreciate that I did not have to live in this world for very long without her. Because, like Samus, my journey has often been a lonely one. I didn’t start playing Metroid games until I was 21 and had just gone through a bad breakup; we had shared an apartment, and now suddenly, I was living alone. At that time, I was a college student and an unpaid intern at the Boston Phoenix, and I had yet to get any of my article pitches approved. I had been playing video games ever since getting a Game Boy as a young child, but I had mostly played games with male characters in them. After all, that’s what video games were, most of the time. But I always knew there were some exceptions, like Lara Croft in the Tomb Raider series, or Jade in Beyond Good and Evil. And of course, Samus Aran in Metroid.View image in fullscreenShe’s fearless, bold, intelligent … Metroid Dread.Photograph: NintendoIn a post-breakup depressive fugue, I rented and played through a bunch of Metroidgames, totally out of order. Like a baby bird seeking her mother – or more relevantly, like a baby Metroid – I glommed on to Samus Aran with a fervour that has yet to really end. I began to seek out other games with female characters, and spaces online where other female gamers and queer gamers hung out. Through these spaces, I learned what feminism actually was (turns out, it’s not “hating men,” as I had been assuming prior to that point). Starting out as a video games journalist, I clung on to this small community I found.Writing about games as a queer woman in the 2000s and 2010s came with a lot of harassment and blowback. Often I felt very alone – but I would tell myself I was like Samus Aran, on a hostile planet. I kept on going, kept on exploring, kept on building up my abilities. After all, like Samus on Zebes, the hostile place I was exploring was also actually my home. I had a right to be there. Those space pirates – or the bigots sending me death threats, whatever – did not belong. The blank slate of Samus, especially in the earliest Metroidgames, let me infuse as much of myself and my own personality into her journey as I wanted.View image in fullscreenA shared trauma for the Metroidfandom … Metroid Other M.Illustration: NintendoThere have been many Metroid games since, some of which have depicted versions of Samus with a bit more personality. Most notoriously, Metroid: Other M serves up a fearful and traumatised Samus who refuses to question Galactic Federation orders, even when those orders make no sense and put her in danger. This version of the character clashed so heavily with many players’ perceptions of her that it has since become something like a shared trauma for the Metroidfandom. I thought the game was so bad thatthe only solution for Metroidgoing forward would be a full reboot.But that’s not what happened. Instead, fully seven years after Other M, we got Samus Returns, MercurySteam’s 2017 remake of Metroid 2. It was a reminder of the power of the original Metroidgames – Metroid, Metroid 2, and Super Metroid. (These games actually make up a trilogy, albeit with a minimalist narrative.) It was a reminder of the Samus I remembered and loved: fearless, intelligent, devoted, determined. And unlike in Other M, whose camera’s gaze was unafraid to slide slowly over Samus Aran’s clingy zero suit, Samus Returns was not objectifying Samus or distancing her from the player. It was much easier to remember, instead, that Samus is you.You should want to be Samus Aran. You can’t even help it, right? She’s just so fucking cool! And that part at the end of the first few Metroidgames where she performs for you as a sex object is not, really, the important part; it’s dissonant, actually, a fourth-wall breaking moment that doesn’t reflect the core of what Metroidis. The important part is the whole rest of the game, whereyou get to be Samus– who happens to be a woman. And a person, just like you.Explore more on these topicsGamesNintendoAdventure gamesAction gamesLGBTQ+ rightsFeminismfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Feisty, funny and for real – how new opera the Galloping Cure puts drama at its heart  | Opera | The Guardian
description: Missy Mazzoli’s bold new work is about the opioid crisis. The director of its world premiere staging tells of bringing it to life, from tragic arias to blood rehearsals – and a flock of singing sheep
Author: Tom Morris
Headline: Missy Mazzoli’s bold new work is about the opioid crisis. The director of its world premiere staging tells of bringing it to life, from tragic arias to blood rehearsals – and a flock of singing sheep
Content: ‘You didn’t tell me it was going to be funny’ … the chorus of Scottish Opera rehearse The Galloping Cure by Missy Mazzoli.Photograph: Christopher BowenView image in fullscreen‘You didn’t tell me it was going to be funny’ … the chorus of Scottish Opera rehearse The Galloping Cure by Missy Mazzoli.Photograph: Christopher BowenOperaFeisty, funny and for real – how new opera the Galloping Cure puts drama at its heartMissy Mazzoli’s bold new work is about the opioid crisis. The director of its world premiere staging tells of bringing it to life, from tragic arias to blood rehearsals – and a flock of singing sheepTom MorrisThu 6 Aug 2026 07.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 08.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘We’re not telling this story to impress a tiny crowd of insiders!” There is steely ambition in the eyes of the composer Missy Mazzoli. “Whether you like The Tiger King, Lady Gaga, Poor Things or Cirque de Soleil I’m writing this for you.”We’re not pitching to HBO at the height of the streaming boom. We’re sipping coffee with librettist Royce Vavrek in the Jonathon Porritt Library at leafy Hawkwood House in Gloucestershire, where maverick impresarioJohn Berryhas sent us to work on the structure of an unusual new opera commissioned by his new charityOpera Ventures.Since Timothée Chalamet whistled away his Oscar prospects bytrash-talking the traditional European art forms, the airwaves have been pungent with feisty opera chat. International opera bigwigs have defended their programmes, but there is still a sense that something has to change, and a hunger to find it. Berry has taken the opera world to task for failing to commission storytellers from TV and film and ignoring the social media marketing expertise that might connect it with the new audience it craves. This opera, he tells us will give them the chance to get it right. Thanks for that, John. No pressure there. We drink deep into our coffee.The Galloping Cureis triggered by the opioid crisis. Seeking to honour friends who have died from addiction, Mazzoli and Vavrek sent Kafka’s storyA Country Doctorto the novelistKaren Russelland asked her to respond with a provocation for a new opera.double quotation markNew opera can be boring because we’ve forgotten that our job is to entertain peopleMissy MazzoliRussell gave us a story in which a fairground hawker captivates the inhabitants of a depressed industrial town with an exhilarating ride. But once galloping, they can’t stop. Its tone veers from Trainspotting to Sweeney Todd with occasional hints of the madder bits of The Rocky Horror Show.It has vivid characters, sweeping tragic arias and (as of today) a flock of singing sheep and two domesticated dogs. Vavrek, pen in hand, is never more than two scribbles away from a bout of giggles. “You didn’t tell me it was going to be funny,” splutters Berry in the lunchbreak.Within the world of opera, Mazzoli and Vavrek are superstars. Between them they share a Pulitzer prize (Vavrek, forAngel’s Bone), three Grammy nominations (all Mazzoli) and a rare Met world premiere (Lincoln in the Bardo)later this year. What they say about the future of opera counts. But what is the root of the problem that all these fizzing opera folk are trying to address?Sitting at the piano having written the first sketch of a banging tune for the hawker Lucky Mack, Mazzoli tries to explain. “New opera is sometimes boring because we’ve forgotten that our job is to entertain people.” She recallsAnna Nicole, composed by Mark-Anthony Turnage to a libretto by Richard Thomas (Jerry Springer: The Opera) as a rare exception. “One composer who I admired told me it wasn’t really an opera,” she says, her engine revving again. Why? Because it has singable tunes and is based on a story from popular culture?Is there self-censorship in the opera world? Do writers hold back from tunes, bold stories and jokes for fear of not giving the opera hierarchy what they think it wants? Mazzoli thinks the answer is simpler. “During all my time in the American development system, no one ever told me that my job as a composer was to be a dramatist.”To the backdrop of Gloucestershire birdsong, a small penny starts to drop. Wagner, Verdi and Puccini all saw themselves as dramatists. Handel and Britten were dramatists. “If you want spectacle, humour, tragedy, opera is the place to find it. But it doesn’t happen by itself,” Mazzoli continues. “We need a theatrical development process applied to opera instead of pretending that the art form is about music in the abstract, and that story and acting don’t matter.”So my job is to bring a theatrical development process to this new opera.View image in fullscreen‘If you want spectacle, humour, tragedy, opera is the place to find it’ … Justin Austin (Lucky Mack) and Susan Bullock (Ivona Kowalski) in The Galloping Cure.Photograph: Antonia BainSix months later I’m in Glasgow with a group of singers looking at the first draft of act two. We’re testing its story and characters just as I would in a workshop for a theatre show. But the boldness of Mazzoli and Vavrek’s writing keeps forcing to me to change route.Patrick Radden Keefe’s Empire of Pain portrays Arthur Sackler (patriarch of the dynasty who made and marketed OxyContin) as both a salesman and a physician moved to moral outrage at the poor treatment of mentally ill patients. We started out pitting a dedicated country doctor against a diabolic fairground hawker. But the evolving libretto and music bring moments of kindness and doubt to the hawker, making the relationship between doctor and salesman compellingly tangled. It’s as if the characters represent two different sides of Sackler’s personality. As we work I realise the story is compelling because we’re trapped in the middle of it. Some of the houses where the opera will be performed have been funded by the Sacklers. Mazzoli’s story isn’t interested in demonising the villains and declaring victory. As we dig into it, her extraordinary work starts to question the very economic structures within which these injustices and these works of art are produced.Meanwhile, designer Rebecca Ringst, whose work with Calixto Bieito has put her among the opera’s most cherished enfants terribles, is creating galloping horses which seek to evoke the allure of a “miracle drug”. “If the audience wants to jump into the show and have a ride, I will have done my job,” she says with a twinkle.There is a bravery and a freedom in this opera process that commercial theatre finds hard to achieve. Tomorrow, at Mazzoli’s request, we are meeting the celebrated Wagnerian soprano Susan Bullock to try out material for a new character, Iwona Kowalksi, an elderly patient whose chronic pain is so excruciating that she would happily give everything she has to be rid of it. In a horrific newly written scene, Lucky Mack will aim to make her dreams come true by inviting her to give her body to science. “Would science want my body?” she asks Lucky. “Science is desperate,” he replies.View image in fullscreen‘The most beautiful art form’ … Justin Austin in The Galloping Cure.Photograph: Christopher BowenRehearsals move into the theatre and Ringst’s horses are flying for the first time. Bullock’s husband, Richard, walks into a blood rehearsal (yes, a blood rehearsal) for her big scene in act three. “This is one of the craziest and most wonderful things I have ever seen,” he says and immediately we find ourselves pondering whether her character’s throughline ends in joy or despair.I find a love letter which I had asked Russell to write from Iwona to her dead husband, explaining how Lucky Mack has changed her life. It expresses the deep longing that sits at the heart of the opera, right alongside Mazzoli and Vavrek’s incandescent fury at the Sacklers and the culture they worked in. The tone is complex and won’t settle until it meets an audience.“Opera is the most beautiful art form and the most frustrating,” says Mazzoli. “It is at its most beautiful when everything – music, libretto, design and performance are all harnessed together.” And now, as opening night approaches, the thing that excites me most is that its ambiguities can’t be resolved except in the response and discussions it might provoke in its audiences.The world premiere ofThe Galloping Cureis at the Festival theatre, Edinburgh, part of the Edinburgh international festival, from 9-12 August.Explore more on these topicsOperaEdinburgh festival 2026Classical musicScottish OperaEdinburgh festivalFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Carlos Acosta: Myths and Modern Masters review – superstar returns with style, the Stones and his daughter | Dance | The Guardian
description: Mixing contemporary, Cuban and classical works, Acosta has charisma to burn and is accompanied by an impressive cohort
Author: Sanjoy Roy
Headline: Mixing contemporary, Cuban and classical works, Acosta has charisma to burn and is accompanied by an impressive cohort
Content: Great presence and depth … Carlos Acosta in Nosotros, from Myths and Modern Masters.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGreat presence and depth … Carlos Acosta in Nosotros, from Myths and Modern Masters.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianDanceReviewCarlos Acosta: Myths and Modern Masters review – superstar returns with style, the Stones and his daughterRoyal Opera House, LondonMixing contemporary, Cuban and classical works, Acosta has charisma to burn and is accompanied by an impressive cohortSanjoy RoyThu 6 Aug 2026 07.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a bit of a stretch to call this undoubtedly enjoyable programme Myths and Modern Masters but granted, it sounds better than Miscellany. Carlos Acosta – superstar dancer, now director ofBirmingham Royal Balletand Cuban company Acosta Danza – has picked and mixed dancers from both companies to offer a very eclectic spread of dance, and added himself into the mix.At 53, Acosta may not have the physical prowess of his youth, but he brings great presence and depth – and some great dancing, too. That serves very well in José Limón’s landmark 1949 work The Moor’s Pavane, a distillation of Shakespeare’s Othello which boils down the story to four characters – Othello (Acosta), Desdemona (Beatrice Parma), Iago (Max Maslen) and Emilia (Miki Mizutani) – and contains their drama of deception, jealousy and revenge within a stately composition of measured steps and stylised gestures, set to courtly music by Purcell.View image in fullscreenPatterns of give and take … Carlos Acosta and Amisaday Naara in Nosotros at the Royal Opera House.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianNosotros, an intimate duet by Cuban choreographers Beatriz García and Raúl Reinoso, also benefits from Acosta’s gravitas and experience. Backed by plangent piano and cello, Acosta and Amisaday Naara enact the complex yet everyday dynamics of a longstanding couple: patterns of give and take, small gestures of tenderness or neglect, physical enactments of impeding, supporting, mirroring, clasping or evading.In his ownNutracker in Havana Suite, Acosta casts himself as a fatherly magician to young Clara (Aila Acosta Holland – yes, his own daughter), conjuring up exotic scenes of delight familiar from Act 2 of the traditional Nutcracker. It’s nicely danced and choreographed, has zero qualms about any orientalist overtones, adds in a slightly weird party scene and ends with the classic pas de deux as if to say: there’s your pinnacle.View image in fullscreenA virtuosity only youth can provide … Katherine Ochoa and Yasiel Hodelín Bello in Diana and Actaeon.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianThe programme proceeds to top that with a show-stopping performance of Agrippina Vaganova’s 1935 Diana and Actaeon pas de deux, Katherine Ochoa and Yasiel Hodelín Bello almost superhuman in their whirls, bounds and balances; you surrender to a virtuosity only youth could achieve. Acosta is well out of this one.The evening closes withChristopher Bruce’s perennially popular Rooster, an effervescent crowd pleaser set to songs by the Rolling Stones. It’s the one piece that doesn’t quite play to Acosta’s strengths, though he dances impressively and gives great attitude, because the choreography itself is fired by the freshness of youth, yet to be weathered by experience. Acosta has moved beyond that.AtRoyal Opera House, London, until 9 AugustExplore more on these topicsDanceCarlos AcostaRoyal BalletBirmingham Royal BalletRoyal Opera HouseBalletThe Rolling StonesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Fame the Musical review – stardom seekers light up the stage like a flame | Theatre | The Guardian
description: This exuberant revival fizzes like a shaken can of soda, capturing the round-the-clock toil of aspiring performers
Author: Holly O'Mahony
Headline: This exuberant revival fizzes like a shaken can of soda, capturing the round-the-clock toil of aspiring performers
Content: Talia Palamathanan and Amonik Melaco (front) in Fame the Musical at Theatre Royal Plymouth.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenTalia Palamathanan and Amonik Melaco (front) in Fame the Musical at Theatre Royal Plymouth.Photograph: Johan PerssonTheatreReviewFame the Musical review – stardom seekers light up the stage like a flameTheatre Royal PlymouthThis exuberant revival fizzes like a shaken can of soda, capturing the round-the-clock toil of aspiring performersHolly O'MahonyThu 6 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a real-life cohort of performers head to Edinburgh hoping to achieve recognition at the fringe, at the opposite end of the UK a revival of David De Silva’s film turned musical breathes fresh life into its own story of fame-hungry students.With a book by Jose Fernandez, music by Steve Margoshes and lyrics by Jacques Levy, this is a production pumped with guts and gusto. It erupts like a shaken can of soda and comfortably fills the vast stage atTheatreRoyal Plymouth, where Fame received its UK (and European) stage premiere in 1995. It’s directed and choreographed by Tom Jackson Greaves, soon to choreograph the West End’s much-anticipated revival of Rent, and fuelled by an exuberant cast, most of whom fulfilled their own dreams of performing on the professional stage several credits ago and are now flourishing.View image in fullscreenDriving force … Shanay Holmes in Fame the Musical.Photograph: Johan PerssonShanay Holmes, though a shade young to play Miss Sherman, is the driving force whose narration carries the class – and us – through a four-year cycle at a prestigious performing arts school in New York City, while her vocals are the show’s dynamite.Storylines have been tweaked and songs cut, but the production captures the round-the-clock toil and sheer determination of these aspirants. Early number Hard Work sets the scene with movement filling every corner as the gaggle stretch, practise their scales and pirouette across the stage.Richard Howell’s lighting visualises the sense that the students’ whole world is a stage by casting a giant spotlight on the fortress of Soutra Gilmour’s school set, while life beyond remains in shadow, unknown and unappealing. Nods to the 1980s come in the shape of leg warmers and the sound of squealing tape recorders being rewound.It doesn’t shy away from the story’s grittier moments, including the fate of the initially spunky Carmen (Talia Palamathanan), but as in a Greek tragedy, they take place offstage and are reported back.It’s when the students pool their talents – for the boisterous canteen scene and flashmob to the title track (written by Dean Pitchford and Michael Gore), with its flying jumps and mid-air splits – that it beams brightest. That’s when Miss Sherman’s message to her students, that success is not a solo endeavour but something to achieve together, rings truest.AtTheatre Royal Plymouthuntil15 August.Explore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsActingDancereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Chris Smith obituary | Photography | The Guardian
description: Sports photographer for the Observer and the Sunday Times who sought to capture human drama and emotion
Author: Greg Whitmore
Headline: Sports photographer for the Observer and the Sunday Times who sought to capture human drama and emotion
Content: Chris Smith’s image of Cassius Clay taking on the Beatles, from left to right, George Harrison, Ringo Starr, John Lennon and Paul McCartney, in Miami, during the run-up to his title fight against Sonny Liston, 1964.Photograph: Chris Smith/Popperfoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChris Smith’s image of Cassius Clay taking on the Beatles, from left to right, George Harrison, Ringo Starr, John Lennon and Paul McCartney, in Miami, during the run-up to his title fight against Sonny Liston, 1964.Photograph: Chris Smith/Popperfoto/Getty ImagesPhotographyObituaryChris Smith obituarySports photographer for the Observer and the Sunday Times who sought to capture human drama and emotionGreg WhitmoreThu 6 Aug 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the Beatles waltzed unannounced into the 5th Street Gym in Miami Beach in 1964, the sports photographer Chris Smith seized the moment. He was there to record Cassius Clay (laterMuhammad Ali) in training for his fight with Sonny Liston, but when the Fab Four began hamming it up with the Greatest, he captured the five most famous faces on the planet in one memorable shot.Ali went on to furnish Smith with many unforgettable images over the years, and the photographer seemed always to be in the right place at the right time to document the host of larger-than-life sporting characters who peopled the last four decades of the 20th century, includingGeorge Best,Seve Ballesteros, Frank Bruno, Martina Navratilova andLester Piggott.View image in fullscreenChris SmithWhether at niche events or the world’s greatest amphitheatres, Smith, who has died aged 88, sought to photograph human drama and emotion. He wanted to portray the moment when dreams are broken as well as when they are realised. As the sportswriterHugh McIlvanney, with whom Smith worked extensively throughout his career, wrote in an essay in Smith’s 1987 book Sport in Focus: “He is a master of composition, but the flow of feeling through his pictures is almost invariably more important than the deployment of shapes, human or inanimate.”When the boxerBarry McGuigan fought Steve Cruzfor the world featherweight title in Las Vegas in 1986, it was 43C (around 110F) in the ring. The fighter from Clones, Northern Ireland, was struggling in the furnace and towards the end of the fight Smith caught a glimpse of McGuigan in his corner and knew what he had to do. At the end of the 13th round, Smith switched to a longer lens and captured what McGuigan would later call “the picture of me with the dead eyes”. The boxer ended up in hospital with heat exhaustion and dehydration.At the British Open in Sandwich in 1985, Ballesteros was a long way behind the leaders. When a squall momentarily whipped Seve’s waterproof across his body, Smith shot one frame that immortalised the Spaniard’s crushing disappointment and frustration. The image of the Golfing Matador won an award and Ballesteros said: “Good photograph. It says how I felt. It makes me remember.”View image in fullscreenSeve Ballesteros during the British Open golf championship at the Royal St George’s club, Sandwich, 1985.Photograph: Chris Smith/Popperfoto/Getty ImagesSmith would always turn up to events early, to try to outwit his photographic opposition. At the 100m at the Moscow Olympics in 1980, which featured the Scottish sprinter Allan Wells, Smith made the courageous decision to position himself alongside the start line. He focused on Wells and, when the starter fired his pistol, Smith fired his shutter. The explosion of Wells from the blocks screams animal instinct and determination.Though he was adept in the use of colour, it was black and white photography that showed the best of Smith. The play of light in his pictures would often accentuate the beauty and significance of landscape – where an ordinary steeplechase at Newbury takes on the extraordinary or pictures of golfers become studies in loneliness.Photographs of drama and emotion – the career of Chris SmithRead moreSmith was one of the most admired and decorated sports photographers that Britain has produced – he won Sports Photographer of the Year four times and individual Sports Picture of the Year twice. He also won a special award in the SSF World Sports Photo Contest in 1995. In 2012, Smith’s Ali photographs were exhibited at Alon Zaikam Fine Art gallery in London and there was a major retrospective of his work, Gods of Sport, at the National Heritage Centre for Horseracing and Sporting Art in Newmarket, Suffolk, in 2017. A collection of his Ali pictures,The Greatest, was published in 2024. In addition to his talent, it was his gentle, humble nature and his willingness to help his colleagues that made him an inspiration to a generation of sports photographers.Smith was born in Hartlepool, County Durham, to Jennie (nee Vale) and Thomas Smith, a dock worker. After leaving school at 16, Smith joined the local evening newspaper, the Hartlepool Mail, as a trainee. He knew nothing about photography but mixed chemicals, printed, swept the floor and learned his craft. When it was quiet he would wander the streets of his home town with a plate camera, taking pictures of the docks, fishing fleet and steelworks. He remained at the Mail for three years and, during that time, as well as the obligatory local flower and dog shows, he began to cover sports events because, he recalled, “nobody else wanted to be out in all weathers on a Saturday”.View image in fullscreenNational Hunt racing at Newbury in the 1970s.Photograph: Chris Smith/Popperfoto/Getty ImagesAt 19, Smith served his two years of national service in the Grenadier Guards and, with a busby atop his 6ft frame, he cut an imposing figure on guard duty outside Buckingham Palace. When he left the army, he returned to Hartlepool but longed to work in what he described as “the mecca of journalism for newspaper people” – Fleet Street. A tour of London newspaper offices in 1959 resulted in an offer to join the Daily Herald (which became the Sun in 1964) as a junior. It was there, despite beginning to specialise in sports photography, that Smith picked up his first award – News Picture of the Year – for a shot taken at the dress rehearsal ofPrincess Margaret’s wedding in Westminster Abbey in 1960.After eight years at the Herald, and a short stint freelancing, he was offered a contract at the Observer in 1968. At the Sunday newspaper – which had been home to one of his great inspirations, the sports photographerGerry Cranham– Smith’s talent was trusted to provide pictures for the front page as well as the back. He was sent not only to Wembley and Lord’s but to New York and Prague to cover the funerals of Robert Kennedy in 1968 and Jan Palach in 1969. Smith’s work also appeared regularly in the Observer magazine.In 1976 he became chief sports photographer for the Sunday Times, where he remained for 24 award-sprinkled years. While there, he shot what, when pressed, he said was his favourite photograph. He had never seen Italian football’s “ultras” before and when he witnessed their flares, smoke grenades and fireworks at the European Cup final between Roma and Liverpool in Rome in 1984 he jumped into the crowd to get a shot that is as much a dramatic news picture as a startling sports picture.In 1964 he had married Sylvia Phillipson, who worked as a flight attendant for BOAC before having children. After Sylvia suffered a stroke 20 years ago, Chris put down his camera and devoted himself to caring for her at home.He is survived by Sylvia, their sons, Dan and Josh, four grandchildren, and by his sisters, Barbara and Kathleen.Christopher Smith, photographer, born 27 December 1937; died 28 June 2026Explore more on these topicsPhotographyNewspapersobituariesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We were ahead of our time!’: Charly Clive and Ellen Robertson AKA sketch duo Britney on their new TV fame and word-of-mouth hits | Comedy | The Guardian
description: With TV shows Rooster and Vladimir under their belts, the sketch stars and best friends since school have withstood tumours, nerdy perfectionism and US success. So why are they so eager to get back to the fringe? Explore the rest of our Edinburgh festival 2026 coverage
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: With TV shows Rooster and Vladimir under their belts, the sketch stars and best friends since school have withstood tumours, nerdy perfectionism and US success. So why are they so eager to get back to the fringe? Explore the rest of our Edinburgh festival 2026 coverage
Content: Hats off … Britney, AKA Charly Clive (left) and Ellen Robertson.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearView image in fullscreenHats off … Britney, AKA Charly Clive (left) and Ellen Robertson.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearComedyInterview‘We were ahead of our time!’: Charly Clive and Ellen Robertson AKA sketch duo Britney on their new TV fame and word-of-mouth hitsRachel AroestiWith TV shows Rooster and Vladimir under their belts, the sketch stars and best friends since school have withstood tumours, nerdy perfectionism and US success. So why are they so eager to get back to the fringe?Explore the rest of our Edinburgh festival 2026 coverageThu 6 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 08.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere has always been a lot of overlap in the lives of Charly Clive and Ellen Robertson. After bonding on a school trip 20 years ago, the pair have spent the past decade performing sketch comedy together and were flatmates for almost as long.Recently, though, the similarities have bordered on the spooky. In December 2024, Clive was told she had been cast as Steve Carell’s professor daughter in the HBO campus comedyRooster. Soon after, Robertson found out she was also getting a new superstar parent: she’d be playing Rachel Weisz’s lawyer daughter in Netflix’sVladimir, another smart, funny show set at a US university. Both series debuted in March to enthusiastic reviews and viewing figures in the millions.“It was bonkers,” says Robertson, who recalls the pair digesting the news of their coincidental castings on a rooftop over a bottle of wine. Clive, however, maintains she was “very unsurprised” they’d both managed to land such high-profile gigs after years of small TV roles and near-breakthroughs (Clive led the Channel 4 OCD dramaPurein 2019). “I thought it was pretty inevitable, genuinely.” Whenever Robertson fretted about their professional futures, Clive would assure her it was “happening, baby! Then, thank God, it did.”Despite having significantly upped their respective profiles, Clive and Robertson, both 33, are not abandoning their lo-fi sketch roots. This year, under their joint moniker Britney, they’re taking a new show to the Edinburgh fringe (well, two actually: they’ll spend their lunchtimes acting in a Robertson-penned play called Jitters, in which Clive plays her comedy partner’s stepmum-to-be, and their evenings performing their latest sketch show Holy Mackerel!).View image in fullscreenBoard silly … Charly Clive in Rooster.Photograph: Katrina Marcinowski/Warner BrosIt’s June when we meet for lunch in an east London restaurant, but the duo are in no rush to prepare for the festival: I saw a preview of Holy Mackerel! in February and it was pretty much flawless. There’s clearly a level of nerdy perfectionism involved in a Britney production; Clive describes their shows as “meticulously prepared – so it’s even sadder when it’s not funny!”.That won’t be an issue: Clive and Robertson have an incredible knack for finding hilarity in unexpected places. Their last Edinburgh show, 2022’s Friends and Nothing More, managed to extract an impressive number of laughs from a banal Stephen King quote. This time around, they’ve transformed an inadvertently weird headline from the Guardian’s TV section into one of the funniest sketches I’ve seen in years. I don’t want to give too much away, but the fashion designer Karl Lagerfeld and serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer both feature.The pair clearly keep a lookout for jokes hidden in plain sight. “Do you know what’s funny about that menu?” Clive observes after we order. “It said: house trout. Like, house red, house white, house trout. That will be our new sketch – you can find inspiration anywhere!” Occasionally, however, the pair’s references can be a little too niche. They are considering dropping a sketch about B*Witched’s 1998 chart-topper C’est la Vie. Older audiences don’t get it, neither do younger ones: previewing it to a nonplussed gen Z crowd recently “was gutting”, says Robertson. Both agree that in an ideal world they’d perform solely to millennial women. The intended vibe of a Britney show is: “I don’t need to worry about the state of the world, I can sit down and be taken care of by two year-aboves, who are gonna be nice to us for one hour,” says Clive.View image in fullscreenParental guidance … Ellen Robertson with Rachel Weisz in Vladimir.Photograph: NetflixThe pair first bonded at their Oxfordshire all-girls school in year nine, when they found themselves sitting together on a coach to the first world war battlefields of Ypres. They had never spoken before: Clive, who was bullied at school for “being gay” due to her cropped hairstyle (an attempt to get rid of recurring nits; she is straight), thought: “Ellen was very cool, she had really nice hair and boyfriends – which is so funny because she’s the gayest woman in town.”Fleabag at 10: did Phoebe Waller-Bridge usher in a wave of female-fronted series – or straitjacket them?Read moreBy the time they arrived at their destination, they were firm friends – “laughing our heads off around Ypres”. Back at school, they’d “just walk around doing funny voices to each other” at lunchtime. What did their classmates think of their comedy stylings? “It’s hard to know. I think they were like: well, those guys are weird,” says Robertson. Clive has a characteristically self-confident take: “I think they thought we were funny. We were a bit ahead of our time – I think people were jealous!”Robertson went on to Cambridge, where she performed with the Footlights, while Clive studied drama in New York. After graduating, they began entertaining the idea of taking a sketch show to the fringe. Then Clive was diagnosed with a brain tumour.Robertson suggested they base the show on the diagnosis because Clive was “being so funny about it”, thinking it would also be a way to provide her friend with some positive memories of an awful year. “And I said: absolutely not,” says Clive. Eventually, shechanged her mind; the resulting show, titledBritney– also the nickname they’d given Clive’s tumour to give it a glamorous spin – was a word-of-mouth hit.View image in fullscreenOops, they did it again … Britney.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearThe following year, after initial surgery, Clive’s tumour began growing again, meaning that she needed radiotherapy. The pair decided it was a good excuse to revive Britney, the show (now also the name of their double act), “slightly more lucratively” in London. It won the attention of the BBC, which adapted it into a2021 pilotco-starring My Parents Are Aliens’ Tony Gardner, an early champion of the Edinburgh show. Making the pilot was “the most fun I’ve ever had”, says Robertson. “We obviously really hoped they’d want it for a series. And then they didn’t.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRooster review – Steve Carell and a naked college president add wisdom to this cringe comedy dramaRead moreThe rejection was “tricky and strange”, partly because of the deeply personal subject matter and partly because of all the gruelling promotion they’d done. “We had interview after interview with someone saying: so just tell us again about the worst period of your life,” says Clive. Once they’d accepted it was going no further, “we were like OK. We did everything the way we wanted to do it. That goes to bed now.”UK TV’s loss was ultimately the US’s gain. Why do they think so many British actors are landing the sorts of roles in the US that have eluded them here? “Americans seem more interested in us for whatever reason … are we cheaper?” wonders Robertson.View image in fullscreenFringe concern … Britney: Friends and Nothing More at Edinburgh in 2022.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian“Almost definitely – God, I’d do it for free. Don’t print that,” jokes Clive. Another possibility is the risk-averse nature of homegrown TV. While UK broadcasters are still trying to find the next Fleabag, in the US “they’re like: ‘How can we wow everybody again with something as successful as Fleabag, but that isn’t Fleabag?’” says Clive.Vladimir review – Rachel Weisz is unswervingly brilliant in a TV show you’ll admire for years to comeRead moreThanks to Vladimir and the already recommissioned Rooster – plus various other acting projects (Clive recently played Sally Phillips’s sister inRelicsat the Lyric Hammersmith; Robertson will appear in Caryl Churchill’sCloud 9at the National Theatre in London from November) – Britney is now more of a passion project than something the pair are relying on for a career breakthrough. They don’t covet online clout – in fact, they don’t share any sketches on social media: Robertson thinks pumping out skits for Instagram would feel like “drudgery”. They aren’t particularly bothered about critical success, either. Some comedians have told them a positive review in a broadsheet can inflate the average age of the crowd “by, like, 40 years” – a disaster for the B*Witched material.Instead, they want to ensure Britney always feels like a treat. “Because it’s not the only thing we do, I think we’re allowed for it to be a really special thing for us,” says Clive.“Working on a strange little hour of comedy is our dream,” agrees Robertson. Twenty years on, the unadulterated joy of those year nine lunch breaks is clearly still going strong.Holy Mackerel!is at the Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh,to 21 August;Jittersis at Old Lab at Summerhall, 6 to 30 August.Explore more on these topicsComedyTheatreTelevisionEdinburgh festivalEdinburgh festival 2026featuresShareReuse this content

title: Arlene Smith obituary | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Singer with one of the first ‘girl groups’, the Chantels, whose 1950s hit Maybe sold more than a million copies
Author: Richard Williams
Headline: Singer with one of the first ‘girl groups’, the Chantels, whose 1950s hit Maybe sold more than a million copies
Content: Arlene Smith, far right, with other members of the Chantels in New York, 1957.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenArlene Smith, far right, with other members of the Chantels in New York, 1957.Photograph: Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesPop and rockObituaryArlene Smith obituarySinger with one of the first ‘girl groups’, the Chantels, whose 1950s hit Maybe sold more than a million copiesRichard WilliamsThu 6 Aug 2026 08.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost before the five Bronx schoolgirls who called themselves the Chantels had finished their unaccompanied delivery of a song called The Plea in his office on Broadway one day in 1957, the record label owner George Goldner was fishing in his desk for a contract they could take home and show their parents. Within months the group were high in the charts with a ballad calledMaybe, featuring the powerful lead voice of the 16-year-old Arlene Smith.The Chantels set the pattern for the success of such “girl groups”, as they became known, as theShirelles,the Crystals, the Chiffons,the Ronettes, and many more.Smith, who has died aged 84, had formed the group four years earlier, recruiting fellow members of the choir at the St Anthony of Padua school in the Bronx, New York. With the school choir, she recalled singing in Latin, practising harmonies, and singing Gregorian chant. But with Jackie Landry, Renee Minus, Lois Harris and Sonia Goring, she moved into secular territory, singing standards such as Autumn Leaves and Summertime, to the nuns’ distress.After growing up with parents who played Duke Ellington and Sarah Vaughan records at home, Smith widened her listening to include such R&B singers as Shirley Gunter andEtta James. Listening to the boys in her neighbourhood practising their doo-wop harmonies on the street corners, and knowing that a local group called the Chords had made the national Top 10 withSh-Boomin 1954, she felt the urge to match them.“My thing was, ‘The guys are not the only ones who can do this,’” she told Laura Flam and Emily Sieu Liebowitz, the authors of But Will You Love Me Tomorrow? (2023), an oral history of girl groups. Their name was adapted from that of another local Catholic school, St Frances de Chantal.View image in fullscreenSmith performing in New York, 2005.Photograph: Bill Tompkins/Getty ImagesThey were not the very first of the girl groups. The Hearts, also from the Bronx, had an R&B hit with Lonely Nights in 1955, and the Bobbettes, from East Harlem, made the Top 10 of the pop chart with Mr Lee in 1957. But something about the ardour of Smith’s voice, and the richness of the group’s harmonies, set a template for what would become one of the most beloved of pop music’s sub-genres.“I never wanted to sing girl songs and I never wanted that typical girl sound – my thing wasn’t cutesy,” Smith said. Shirley Owens of the Shirelles, Judy Craig of the Chiffons, Barbara Alston of the Crystals andVeronica Bennett (later Ronnie Spector)of the Ronettes were among those who took the lesson to heart. The finest girl-group records, although dedicated to the ups and downs of teenage romance, possessed an enduring emotional resonance.After winning local talent contests, the group decided to go in search of Frankie Lymon, the 13-year-old singer who, with his group the Teenagers, had just enjoyed a smash hit withWhy Do Fools Fall in Love?. Instead they found his manager, Richard Barrett. When they sangThe Pleato Barrett, he thought they had “an angelic sound – I thought it would be really good to put a sound like that in rock and roll.”It was he who introduced them to Goldner, on whose label their first records would appear: He’s Gone, written by Smith, and then Maybe, credited to Barrett and Goldner, which sold more than a million copies. A classic four-chord 12/8 doo-wop ballad, Maybe focused on what would become the classic girl-group theme, the desperate yearnings of the young heart.Under Barrett’s supervision, the song took many takes to record, but after being given the initial impetus of Goldner’s expert use of payola, bribing radio programme directors and disc jockeys to give it airtime, it made a legitimate claim on the public’s imagination and went on to reach No 15 on the pop charts and No 2 on the R&B list.On the strength of their hit, the group went on a nationwide tour. In the deep south, they found themselves playing a show to a white audience in the main auditorium followed by a second show for their black fans in the basement. Barrett, who travelled with them, did not allow them to mingle with older fellow artists, locking the doors to their dressing rooms and hotel bedrooms.Each member was given a $20 a week allowance, but at the end of 1959 they were told that the record company was going out of business and that the earnings supposedly put aside for them did not exist. Goldner had gambled it away. “If you want to see the Chantels’ money,” Smith said, “go to the racetrack.”She announced that she was leaving the group to start a solo career, which never caught fire, despite the release in 1961 of a song called Love Love Love produced by the 21-year-oldPhil Spector. The others continued without her, but there would be no more significant hit records. Her former bandmate Minus commented: “My feeling is that the public fell so in love with all five of us and our sound together. Things were never the same after the split.”Smith resumed her music studies at the Juilliard conservatory in New York. In 1973 she formed a version of the Chantels with two new members before taking a master’s in education and teaching music in Bronx schools until her retirement. It was at one of them that she was filmed for Heart & Soul (2023), Kenny Vance’s doo-wop documentary, in front of pupils astonished to discover who she had once been.Arlene Smith, singer, born 5 October 1941; died 29 July 2026Explore more on these topicsPop and rockobituariesShareReuse this content

title: David Queensberry obituary | Ceramics | The Guardian
description: Designer of ceramics who displayed a keen sense of shape in tableware and its appeal to a mass market
Author: Tanya Harrod
Headline: Designer of ceramics who displayed a keen sense of shape in tableware and its appeal to a mass market
Content: As the 12th Marquess of Queensberry, he observed: ‘I come from quite a grand family but inherited absolutely nothing apart from a lot of old plates.’Photograph: Matt InwoodView image in fullscreenAs the 12th Marquess of Queensberry, he observed: ‘I come from quite a grand family but inherited absolutely nothing apart from a lot of old plates.’Photograph: Matt InwoodCeramicsObituaryDavid Queensberry obituaryDesigner of ceramics who displayed a keen sense of shape in tableware and its appeal to a mass marketTanya HarrodThu 6 Aug 2026 06.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Queensberry, who has died aged 96, was an adventurous designer with the highest aesthetic standards, an acute business sense and a deep, informed love of ceramics. With regard to his title of the 12th Marquess of Queensberry, he observed: “I come from quite a grand family but inherited absolutely nothing apart from a lot of old plates which were made for them in the late 18th century. So, it’s fortunate that I should be very interested in ceramics.” And love them he did, from industrial mocha wares to raku and stoneware, and the work of his students at the Royal College of Art in London, where he was professor of ceramics from 1959 until 1983.WithMartin Hunt, in 1966 he co-founded the design consultancy Queensberry Hunt, and together they bridged the frequently insuperable gulf between good design and commercial success.Their tableware had a global reach, and included the sculpturalConceptrange (1976) for Hornsea Pottery, andTrend(1983) for Rosenthal Thomas. Trend exemplified tableware designed for modern informality – symbolised by the pasta plate, a hybrid between a plate and bowl, now a standard form.Trend was followed byLoft(1999), based on Queensberry’s consciousness of the increasing fashion for Asian cuisine, in which square and rectangular plates are traditionally used. For Loft, high-tech isostatic dust pressing – ceramic dust pressurised into metal moulds – was used to make non-round shapes at low cost. Other successful ranges includedCocobone china for Jamie Oliver in 2009, andChoices(2017), a fine translucent porcelain for Portmeirion in collaboration with the Sri Lankan porcelain factory Dankotuwa.View image in fullscreenQueensberry Hunt’s Concept range for Hornsea Pottery, 1976.Photograph: Martin Hunt/Queensberry HuntQueensberry Hunt’sCupolaandConcavebone china continues to sell at John Lewis, and their porcelain is a mainstay at the North American chain Crate & Barrel. If Hunt, John Horler andRobin Levien, all of whom worked with Queensberry Hunt, were fine designers, Queensberry was the ideas man, aware of changing dining habits and the obsolescence of formal dinner services. In effect he helped transform the look of the ceramic scene, keeping decoration to the minimum – “we are shape guys – that is what we do,” he said.His paternal background might have seemed unpromising. The eldest son of Francis Douglas, 11th Marquess of Queensberry, a stockbroker, David was born in London and went to Eton college, followed by national service as a Guards officer. But the Eton drawing school underWilfrid Bluntincluded pottery and, after studying in London at Chelsea School of Art, David went on to the Central School of Arts and Crafts, where he initially saw himself as a studio potter.Deciding he did not want to make work for the few but wishing to reach a mass market, he got on his motorbike and travelled to the heartland, Stoke-on-Trent, still in those postwar days a hive of industrious production. His mother,Cathleen Mann, the second of Francis’s three wives, was a respected portrait painter, while his maternal grandmother, Florence Pasley, was an interior designer, who put him in contact with the H & R Johnson Tiles factory, where he was offered a junior laboratory role researching glazes – he made his own work in the evenings and weekends.View image in fullscreenDavid Queensberry’s Fine Shape series for the Stoke-on-Trent firm of Midwinter, 1962, proved to be a bestseller.Photograph: Neil Baylis/AlamyIn the 1950s Queensberry threw himself into life in the six towns of Stoke-on-Trent, assisting with the last firings of the Crown Staffordshire bottle kiln, where he witnessed the vitrification of the bone china being tested tacitly by sight and sound rather than by scientific pyrometers, attending North Staffordshire Technical College, forming local friendships and drinking in the roughest of pubs. He was also part of the 50s “youth quake” of talent along with designers such asMary Quantand his friendTerence Conran(Queensberry Hunt later sold at Conran’s Habitat stores).Queensberry – who until his father’s death in 1954 was styled Viscount Drumlanrig – briefly set up Drumlanrig & Melbourne with Colin Melbourne in 1952, producing plates with two abstract “atomic” designs sold byMilo Parmoor’s Flavian Trading Company. He designed for Crown Staffordshire, the work selling at Heal’s department store in London, and later for Midwinter, for whom he created the best-selling Fine Shape in 1962.Over time he was to witness and mourn the gradual shrinkage of production at Stoke, and, as manufacturing bases shifted, Queensberry Hunt became active in south-east Asia – principally in Bangladesh and Sri Lanka. Visiting a factory with Queensberry was a delight, so deep was his empathy with the workforce and his knowledge of both traditional processes and cutting-edge technologies.In 1959 Queensberry returned to London and the Royal College of Art. There he ran a department where art, studio ceramics and advanced industrial design could flourish, bringing in the studio potterHans Coperand the artistEduardo Paolozzias tutors. The atmosphere in the department was tolerant and inspiring, with his brilliant studentElizabeth Fritsch’s little son made welcome, reminding his students that this was a place that did not operate conventionally.Although he worried that so many students were drawn to what he called “para-art activity” rather than design for industry, the department produced figures of the stature of Fritsch, Glenys Barton, Alison Britton, Jennifer Lee, Dame Magdalene Odundo and Jacqui Poncelet, Queensberry forming long friendships with them all. His students knew they were at the best place at the best time.Hunt was another of his most brilliant pupils, a superlative craftsman and model-maker. Initially they ran Queensberry Hunt within the department, later moving to studios in Brook Mews North across Hyde Park from the college. Queensberry also recruited Levien and Horler, former students, and for a while the practice was named Queensberry Hunt Levien.He helped another of his students, David Grant, launch Highland Stoneware in 1975 in Lochiver, Grant riding pillion as they motorbiked into the City to raise funds. Highland Stoneware became something of a busman’s holiday for Queensberry, taking his children to the Highlands over the summer and right up until his death working on Highland Stoneware’s Geological Glaze project, inspired by the geological formations of the north-west Highlands.His life was recorded during 2003-04 for National Life Stories at the British Library. A substantial collection of Queensberry Hunt ceramics are in the collection of the Victoria & Albert Museum.View image in fullscreenDavid Queensberry with the souvenir mug that he designed for the wedding of Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer in 1981.Photograph: Chris Ware/Getty ImagesA visit to his house in London was always a delight, as likely to involve a discussion of poetry as a stern quizzing on tri-axial glazes, the walls hung with paintings by his mother and his grandfatherHarrington Mann, with Paolozzi plates for Wedgwood propped on shelves. Though Queensberry made little of his ancestry, it was the 9th marquess who had denounced Oscar Wilde because of his connection with his third son, Lord Alfred Douglas.Once Queensberry was able to sit in the House of Lords (after the passing of the Peerage Act 1963, which granted that right to Scottish hereditary peers), he offered his support to the sexual offences bill, making it the subject of his maiden speech. This became the Sexual Offences Act of 1967, which decriminalised sex between men over 21 in private – the beginnings of proper reform.Queensberry is survived by his third wife, Chun Liao, whom he married in 2000; their daughter, Beth, died in 2008. He is also survived by three daughters, Emma, Alice and Victoria, and a son, Abimbola, from his first marriage, to Ann Zane (nee Sinnett-Jones), which ended in divorce; two sons, Sholto and Torquil, and a daughter, Kate, from his second marriage, to Alexandra Wyndham, which also ended in divorce; a son, Ambrose, from a relationship with Ann Carey; 16 grandchildren and four great-grandchildren; and his half-brother, Gawain. Another son, Milo, from his second marriage, and four grandchildren predeceased him.David Harrington Angus Douglas, 12th Marquess of Queensberry, born 19 December 1929; died 22 July 2026Explore more on these topicsCeramicsobituariesShareReuse this content

title: I am sometimes overwhelmed by feelings of nostalgia. Is this a bad thing? | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: There’s a difference between longing for the past and assuming it was better, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. The trick is knowing which you’re feeling
Author: Eleanor Gordon-Smith
Headline: There’s a difference between longing for the past and assuming it was better, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. The trick is knowing which you’re feeling
Content: ‘Some amount of longing to go back is inevitable for mortal creatures like us, who can only travel one way through time.’ Painting: Classical Ruins at Sunset by Pierre Pequignot.Illustration: piemags/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Some amount of longing to go back is inevitable for mortal creatures like us, who can only travel one way through time.’ Painting: Classical Ruins at Sunset by Pierre Pequignot.Illustration: piemags/AlamyLeading questionsAustralian lifestyleI am sometimes overwhelmed by feelings of nostalgia. Is this a bad thing?There’s a difference between longing for the past and assuming it was better, writes advice columnistEleanor Gordon-Smith. The trick is knowing which you’re feelingRead moreLeading questionsEleanor Gordon-SmithThu 6 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 20.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs nostalgia a negative emotion? I often feel nostalgic these days. It is a background noise that I am trying to ignore.It was especially present during the pandemic, when my nostalgia seemed to spread into a species of grief for lost places and activities. I find myself thinking sadly about places I won’t be able to visit for a very long time.I am nostalgic for odd things, like an old Hovis bread sign on a shop that is now a kebab shop. I feel such longing for my old haunts that I often go on virtual trips using Google Street View.It is becoming an overwhelming emotion, and I don’t know whether to suppress it or go with it.Eleanor says:One of the smartest people I know says grief has two parts: one for missing the thing you lost, and one for feeling like you didn’t hold it quite right when you had it. If you’re right that nostalgia is grief for things past, I wonder whether it’s like that too: one part for wanting those things back, and another for wanting to go back, now you know what it’s like to miss them. Once more wandering to the shop to buy a loaf, once more doing nothing for an afternoon at that house, once more hearing those people chatter in a different room. Breathing it all in properly this time.My job provides financial stability but my passion has gone. What do I do? | Leading questionsRead moreSome amount of longing to go back is inevitable for mortal creatures like us, who can only travel one way through time. But, as you say, that feeling can become overwhelming. I think the trick is knowing the difference between our sadness that we can’t go back, and sadness that Things Were Better Back Then. Only one really holds up.The part of nostalgia that’s telling the truth says: you can’t go back. You can’t have time twice. This justispoignant; I don’t know of any philosophy that fully solves how it feels to slowly let go of things we love. The homes you know get washed away; the worlds and people you’d love to see again crossfade to existing in memory alone. It starts to feel very important that they stay alive there, if memory is the only place they live: to hold on to the photographs and re-run the anecdotes. Watching parts of your life leave the physical world makes you want to insist on reminiscence. I don’t think there’s anything necessarily negative about this part of nostalgia. “Going back” in imagination – walking around old haunts, revisiting them on Google Maps – is also warm and comforting contact with the elements of these things thatcan’tbe lost, not completely.But nostalgia can turn negative and misleading when it feels like things werejust betterback then. Memory presents a sepia-toned composite of a past. We can mistake that image for a true depiction of the whole. Didn’t things then seem simpler, nicer? Wasn’t I better, stronger? This can yield the profound conservatism of wanting to go back for the past’s own sake, thinking what came before is ipso facto better. This is such a common confusion, it’s a trope: “in my day”. We experienceour ownfeeling of decay and moving too fast through time, and confuse it for evidence that the worlditself is in decay and moving too fast. “I wish I could go back” becomes “that was better than this”.Aside from probably being wrong about the past, that thought will also cost you the present. Someday you will be nostalgic for this time right now too. And then you’ll have the same feeling you do now – not just the wish to go back, but the wish to breathe it in properly while you have it.Ask Eleanor a questionShare your questionTell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose.
