title: Can one multi-styler really do it all? Shark’s Glossi 2-in-1 hot tool comes close | Hair care | The Guardian
description: Love a blow dry but not the salon cost? Shark’s versatile brush styles wet and dry hair, making it ideal for refreshing your look between wash days
Author: Lise Smith
Headline: Love a blow dry but not the salon cost? Shark’s versatile brush styles wet and dry hair, making it ideal for refreshing your look between wash days
Content: One for all: the Glossi combines wet and dry styling in a single, easy-to-use brush.Photograph: Lise Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOne for all: the Glossi combines wet and dry styling in a single, easy-to-use brush.Photograph: Lise Smith/The GuardianThe FilterHair careReviewCan one multi-styler really do it all? Shark’s Glossi 2-in-1 hot tool comes closeLove a blow dry but not the salon cost? Shark’s versatile brush styles wet and dry hair, making it ideal for refreshing your look between wash daysThe best hot brushes, testedLise SmithThu 6 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Not just a pretty brush (although it definitely also is that), Shark’s Glossi is a well-designed styling tool that aims to streamline your routine. It combines wet-to-dry air styling for blow-drying freshly washed hair with a dry styling mode for smoothing and refreshing between wash days.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Hybrid wet-and-dryhot brusheshave become increasingly popular in recent years: current competition includesDyson’s super-premium Airwrap multi-styler, and the Glossi upgrades Shark’s own discontinued SmoothStyle brush.All these dual-mode hot brushes promise faster, simpler styling at home, but can the Glossi really replace yourhairdryerand straightening brush in one neat tool?View at SharkNinjaView at AmazonHow I testedView image in fullscreenFrom wet to dry: the styling modes were tested for speed, ease of use and finished results.Photograph: Lise Smith/The GuardianThe Glossi has two styling modes: one for wet hair and one for dry hair. For the former, I used the Glossi’s wet mode after washing my medium-length curly hair, using my usual heat-protection and styling products. I also styled from wet and then immediately followed with dry mode for a sleeker finished style. The dry mode was tested a day or two after washing. In all cases, I tested in the morning before work to see how the finished style would hold during a day of typical wear.I compared the Glossi’s speed, ease of use and overall results with Shark’s previous SmoothStyle hot brush, as well as the other hot brushes I’ve tested for the Filter. Along the way, I assessed how long it took to create a finished style, how my hair looked and felt after styling, and how easy the brush made it to get my desired look.What you need to knowView image in fullscreenTake control: independently adjustable heat and airflow provide nine wet-mode combinations.Photograph: Lise Smith/The GuardianView at SharkNinjaView at AmazonThe Glossi is Shark’s follow-up to its SmoothStyle dual-mode styling brush, and the core concept is the same: you can use it like a blow-dry brush on damp hair after washing or like a straightening brush on dry hair for a smoother finish. The Glossi has a distinctive teardrop shape, with blow-dry vents and bristles on the wider side, and heated ceramic fins on the narrow side. The heated fins operate only in dry mode.In wet mode, the Glossi pushes air through the vents to dry and shape simultaneously. There are three independent heat and three airspeed settings in wet mode, giving nine combinations suitable for almost any hair type. The higher settings will be effective on thicker and coarser hair, while finer hair will prefer the gentler low settings.Once you’ve blow-dried with wet mode, you have the option to switch to dry mode. This reduces the airflow and activates the heated ceramic plates on the narrow side of the brush. These work more like a straightening brush to smooth down frizz and give an overall sleeker finish. Once again, there’s a choice of three heat settings in dry mode, up to 210C for thicker hair.As well as a smaller and lighter design (see below), Shark has upgraded the hardware too–the Glossi’s 1,250W motor is a step up from the SmoothStyle’s 900W, so there’s more power for faster styling, and the new brush uses smart heat sensors to keep the temperature consistent between passes of the brush. That means less chance of damaging the hair with overheating and more consistent styling, as the brush doesn’t cool down between passes.It comes in four fun colours – I tried raspberry, a bold metallic hot pink, but there’s also lychee, juniper and liquid goldfrom which to choose.Shark Glossi specificationsPower:1,250WTemperature settings:three (wet mode); three (dry mode) plus cool shotSpeed settings:three – independent of heatWeight:710g (including cable & plug adapter – main brush unit alone is 440g)Cord length:2.4mWhat we loveView image in fullscreenSmooth operator: rolling the brush inwards creates softly curved ends without needing a separate styling tool.Photograph: Lise Smith/The GuardianThe Glossi builds on the SmoothStyle’s promise of versatile wet-or-dry styling with a more powerful motor along with independently adjustable heat and airflow. The stronger airflow means you can choose one of the lower heat settings, and it will still dry your hair effectively, reducing the risk of dehydration and heat damage.On my hair, I found that a fast airspeed and medium heat combo was good for rough-drying and starting the process of styling. I then finished with the medium airspeed and cooler heat setting. To switch between temperature and speed settings, simply press the button at the base of the handle – it’s easy to choose a gentler speed or temperature when styling shorter and more delicate sections of hair.The Glossi is noticeably smaller and neater than the SmoothStyle, too. The new size is lighter than the SmoothStyle and feels nice and balanced to hold. It’s easy to manoeuvre it around the head and right up to the roots. This makes the Glossi effective on shorter hair, where styling around the roots is more noticeable.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs with other round blow-dry brushes, using the Glossi in wet mode gives the hair quite a bouncy, voluminous finish, with lifted roots and movement at the ends. This was good for a simple daytime look, and the style lasted all day and into the evening when I styled my hair using wet mode (and my usual styling products). While this straight look didn’t stay completely intact overnight, my roots and lengths were still noticeably smoother than usual the next day.double quotation markMy hair felt soft and healthy after stylingThe final look depends on how much you roll and hold the hair around the brush as you style – hold it taut for a straight finish, or let it fall into a loose ringlet to curl. Rolling the brush inwards towards the face will curl the ends softly under, and rolling the brush away from the face will give more of a Farrah-Fawcett-meets-Sabrina-Carpenter flicked look.I then tried wet mode followed by dry for a sleeker look. To activate dry mode, simply slide the switch on the handle and wait a few seconds for the ceramic fins to heat up. You use the brush in the same way, rolling it through sections of hair, but with dry mode activated, the ceramic fins work like a straightener to smooth frizz and flyaways. Dry mode can be used straight after blow-drying on wet mode, but it’s also good for quick touch-ups to already-dry hair.My hair felt soft and healthy after styling in either mode, and following wet mode with dry mode gave it a definite shine. It’s an attractive brush, too: the four bright colour options offer a fun alternative to all the typical white and silver styling tools out there.What we don’t loveDry mode alone wasn’t enough to completely straighten my locks – I needed to roughly blow-dry damp hair straight on wet mode first. If you have looser curls or waves than my type-3 hair, though, you may find you can straighten with dry mode alone. I found dry styling much more successful the day after I’d washed and blow-dried using wet mode – my hair stayed somewhat straight overnight, so it was easy to smooth it out completely.double quotation markIf you have very long or thick hair, you may prefer a larger brushAt just under £160, the Glossi is more of an investment than rival models such as theBaByliss Air Power(£49.99 at the time of writing) andRevlon’s OneStep(£50)–although it’s also more budget-friendly thanGHD’s Duet Blowdry(£379).I’ve noted that the more compact Glossi brush is good for precision around the roots and is especially good for shorter hair. For related reasons, if you have very long or thick hair, you may prefer a larger brush, such as theBaByliss Air Power, to deal with lots of hair efficiently. And if you definitely want to style your hair straight rather than curled, you might find a hot brush with an oval or paddle shape suits your needs better.Should I buy it?View image in fullscreenBuilt to last: the Glossi feels solid, well balanced and thoughtfully designed.Photograph: Lise Smith/The GuardianView at SharkNinjaView at AmazonOverall, Shark’s Glossi is a neat and simple-to-use hot brush that leaves hair feeling as good as it looks. I was impressed with the speed and quality of the styling in wet mode, and the glossy finish of my hair after using dry mode. The build quality of the brush is good – it feels well designed, with intuitive controls built into the handle. Because it can be used on wet or dry hair, the Glossi is more versatile than most hot brushes, too.All of that said, if you’ve bought a blow-dry brush in the past couple of years and you’re happy with it, the Glossi might not be a significant enough improvement to warrant an upgrade. But if you don’t have a hot brush already – or your existing brush has seen better days – this is a great product at a not-too-hefty price.If it’s time to upgrade any of your old electrical beauty tools, you can useCloud Nine’s recycling schemeto recycle products from any brand, or checkRecycle Your Electricalsto find your nearest electrical equipment recycling centre.For more hair stylingtips and tricks from the Filter, read:Dyson Airwrap Co-anda 2x reviewThe best hot brushes, testedThe best hair straighteners for foolproof stylingLise Smith is a writer with more than 15 years of experience covering beauty, lifestyle, parenting and the performing arts. She loves any beauty tool or product that can guarantee an extra 10 minutes in bedExplore more on these topicsHair careThe FilterWomen's hairBeautyGadgetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Côtes Catalanes: the wine with the renegade spirit  | Wine | The Guardian
description: From a wild corner of southern France, these crisp, minerally whites and silky red blends are unforgettable wines
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: From a wild corner of southern France, these crisp, minerally whites and silky red blends are unforgettable wines
Content: These mineral-rich wines offer deep flavours and encourage drinkers to be inquisitivePhotograph: Yana Iskayeva/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThese mineral-rich wines offer deep flavours and encourage drinkers to be inquisitivePhotograph: Yana Iskayeva/Getty ImagesWineCôtes Catalanes: the wine with the renegade spiritFrom a wild corner of southern France, these crisp, minerally whites and silky red blends are unforgettable winesMina HollandThu 6 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.We all have our coming-of-age story: a transition to adulthood defined by emotional growth. I’ll let my friends be the judge of whether mine’s happened, but in wine terms, I can pinpoint my coming of age to the day I first tasted a white from Côtes CatalanesIGP. Whatwasthis nectar? I’d spent a lifetime chugging things I liked (from Um Bongo to supermarket Macon), but this was not a chugger. The bottle was Domaine Gauby’s Les Calcinaires Blanc 2010, a blend of muscat, chardonnay, macabeu and vermentino from the eastern foothills of the Pyrenees in French Catalonia. I had to take my time over something this good, and that felt very grown up indeed.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The Côtes Catalanes IGP (Indication Géographique Protégée) sits within a nook of Languedoc-Roussillon in the very south of France. As an IGP, it is a less prestigious designation than AOP (Appellation d’Origine Protégée), but one that gives winemakers greater freedom to flex their muscles. Where wines from Côtes de Roussillon AOC have to be particular blends with particular proportions, winemakers in the Côtes Catalanes can produce single-varietal wines with a greater range of grapes; many are organic or biodynamic. They have a renegade spirit I’m sure you can taste in wines that are mineral, full of complex fruit and often have notes ofgarrigue– Mediterranean scrubby herbs such as thyme and rosemary.After that first time, I had it in my head that Côtes Catalanes was my thing. The appellation has seldom let me down with its sun-soaked, almost elemental whites, made with macabeu, grenache gris and blanc, or velvety, herbal reds made with cinsault, carignan and grenache, often blended with international varieties such as sauvignon blanc or syrah respectively. Many of these decades-old vines are like eccentric Boomers, producing rich and characterful fruit, especially in tandem with the region’s singular geography.With its dry and drought-prone climate, this wild and immensely beautiful landscape is not the easiest place to practise viticulture, but it sure pays off. Here you find lots of conditions that make wines interesting: 300 days a year of sunshine and very little rainfall, hot days and cool nights, and strong winds, in this case, the Tramontane from the north-west. What’s more, “we have an amazing mosaic of terroirs,” says Thibault Ponthier of Domaine Le Roc des Anges – soils with almost every geological formation in southern France (schist, marl, clay, limestone, granite) concentrated into less than 5,000 hectares of vines. These make for the kind of intensely mineral, concentrated wines that implore drinkers to reach for the bottle in fervent curiosity – as that first one did me.As my picks today testify, these are not the cheapest wines, but they quite possibly offer the best value in France. Forget bangs, these are an explosion for your buck and promise emotional growth – of sorts.L’apprentie Sorcièredu Clos des Fees Rosé 2025£14.75 Yapp, 13%. Bewitching, characterful young vine rosé – richer (and cheaper!) than Provencal iterations.Le Roc des Anges Segna de Cor 2023£16–£20 Vinum, 13%. Cor by name and cor by nature – long, velvety and mineral red that sings of Côtes CatalanesTramontane Côtes Catalanes Macabeu 2021£17.10 Amathus, 13%. Named after the wind that cools the old vines at night after hot days – fresh and aromatic with notes ofgarrigueMon P’tit Pithon Blanc 2025£14.41 Vinatis, 12.5%. Crisp, golden and intense, this macabeu blend is a biodynamic blinder and great gateway to the region’s whitesUn Vent de Folie 100+£22 Laithwaites, 14.5%. Luscious, long and made in tiny proportions, as you might expect from a grenache-carignan blend from vines that are more than 100 years oldDanjou-Banessy Coste 2024£46 Dynamic Vines, 12.5%. OK, a gawp-worthy price, but consider this exquisite 100% macabeu for a special occasion. There is nothing I’d rather drinkExplore more on these topicsWineFrench food and drinkFoodCatalonia holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Light, sweet and easy to eat – why melons and other cool fruits rule August | Food | The Guardian
description: The Mediterranean’s best beach ritual, plus melons, cucumbers and cold soups to keep us cool this summer
Author: Itamar Srulovich
Headline: The Mediterranean’s best beach ritual, plus melons, cucumbers and cold soups to keep us cool this summer
Content: A perfect beach day is not complete without a “perfectly chilled” watermelon, Itamar and Sarit write.Photograph: Pictor International/AlamyView image in fullscreenA perfect beach day is not complete without a “perfectly chilled” watermelon, Itamar and Sarit write.Photograph: Pictor International/AlamyFeastFoodLight, sweet and easy to eat – why melons and other cool fruits rule AugustThe Mediterranean’s best beach ritual, plus melons, cucumbers and cold soups to keep us cool this summerSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastItamar SrulovichandSarit PackerThu 6 Aug 2026 07.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 07.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Everyone who grew up by the Mediterranean Sea knows that a lazy day on the beach requires a certain level of planning. You should pack everything you’ll need, or may need, and get there early to secure a good spot. But the first thing you need to do when you get there – even before you spread out your blankets and put that sunscreen on – is to drop a watermelon in the sea, so that, by noon, when it’s so hot your skin feels as if it’s about to blister, it is ready for you, all cool and sweet. It’s just about the only thing capable of quenching your thirst and your hunger, while also cooling you downandgiving you the sugar you need.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The other important bit about the watermelon – the part that separates wisdom from wishful thinking – is that you also need to tie a piece of string around it, complete with an empty plastic bottle at the other end, so that it bobs above the waves and marks the spot. This is something you learn the hard way – or at least we did. There is a very particular kind of disappointment that comes from standing waist-deep in the sea, staring into the blue, convinced that a whole watermelon cannot simply disappear. We searched. We dived. We accusedpassing currents. We briefly entertained the idea that another family had found it and were, at that very moment, enjoying our perfectly chilled watermelon. Then again, perhaps it is still out there somewhere, floating towards Sicily …View image in fullscreenPerfect for summer … Yotam Ottolenghi’s cucumber, yoghurt and peanut soup.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianThis is the season of the cool fruits: cucumber, melon and watermelon are all at their peak and are perfect for the weather. They are light, sweet, easy to prepare and to eat, and, most importantly in August, cooling. They also don’t need to be cooked, unlike their autumnal cousins, pumpkins, squash and gourds. (If you do want to cook with them, though, the possibilities are almost endless. They are all especially good companions for salty things – feta, parmesan, anchovies, olives,prosciutto, the list goes on.)Feta and watermelonis a classic combination for a reason, and the cheese also works incredibly well withother kinds of melons, as well as with chilli heat, such as in Anna Jones’shoneydew and green chilli salad(incidentally, that same piece also suggests a spicy grilled watermelon salad that looks just as punchily refreshing for a hot day). If your melon is sweet enough, you can crank up the chilli levels quite high – we speak from experience.If cold soups are your thing in the summer – as they are for us – Yotam Ottolenghi has you covered withthese two perfect summery numbers. Those, along with some mint, are everything you need to keep cool this August. Other than maybe a piece of string.Our week in foodView image in fullscreenArt … chef’s knives.Photograph: Noctiluxx/GettyBlades of glory|If you love your chef’s knives as much as we love ours, see them as a living work of art, as we do, and believe they deserve to be displayed with pride:these wooden knife magnetsfrom Etsy will change your life. Your knives will never have looked so good.Bargain hunt|The August sales are when we splurge on treats for our kitchens that we don’t actually need but really, really want. Department stores are still the best places to look for bargains, but there are some good things to be had online. We’re already on the hunt forMauviel copper pansand cutlery fromSabre Paris– yes, they are expensive, even when discounted, so the trick is to divide the cost between the years of use and joy that you and your heirs will get from them. Then, magically, they seem a bit of a bargain.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn a pickle|On a recent trip to the US, we developed a fondness forTrader Joe’s dill pickle mustard. It definitely falls under the group of “hideoulicious” things we like yet are deeply ashamed of, but we’re admitting this publicly because we desperately need a top-up, should anyone happen to be flying back from the US any time soon …If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastFruitSummer food and drinkSaladTomatoesnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for pasta with red peppers and anchovies or goat’s cheese | Food | The Guardian
description: The skins may be pesky to peel away, but the result is this velvety and vibrant, flavourful pasta dish
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: The skins may be pesky to peel away, but the result is this velvety and vibrant, flavourful pasta dish
Content: Rachel Roddy's pasta with red peppers and anchovies or goat's cheese.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachel Roddy's pasta with red peppers and anchovies or goat's cheese.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianA kitchen in RomeFoodRachel Roddy’s recipe for pasta with red peppers and anchovies or goat’s cheeseThe skins may be pesky to peel away, but the result is this velvety and vibrant, flavourful pasta dishRachel RoddyThu 6 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s no two ways about it: charring and then peeling red, yellow or orange peppers is a messy business. Just out of the oven (if they haven’t burst while baking), roasted and blackened peppers are not unlike mini balloons; the hot juices, which have collected in the cavity, gushing out as the collapsed pepper is manoeuvred from the baking tray to the bowl. Once they have steamed under a plate, and cooled a little, the peppers might be easier to handle, but the thin scales of charred skin are still pesky to peel away, and however hard you try to flick them into the bin, they will stick to forearms and foreheads, as do the slippery white seeds. Having peeled peppers, it is not unusual to find a seed stuck to the back of my upper arm six hours later. Messy and annoying, but also worthwhile, because a strip of peeled pepper freed from its cellophane skin is a wonderful thing: fleshy with velvet texture and a deep, sweet, smoky flavour.I was taught to char peppers on the stovetop by a friend’s Greek mum, balancing them on the gas ring directly over the naked flame and turning regularly. It is sometimes hard to get them to balance and they often wobble off, but if you use a barbecue regularly, that is another option, as is the oven, and apparently the air fryer, too. Whichever method you use, the aim is flesh that is almost completely or well-patched black, and cracked like bark – a bit shocking the first time, but rest assured that the more charred they are, the redder the flesh underneath.Thick strips of tricolour peppers dressed with olive oil, red-wine vinegar and a little of the juice that gushed from the cavity (and hopefully caught in a bowl) are gorgeous just so, or topped with anchovy fillets and black olives, or crumbled feta, as a side dish. They also make a good topping for rounds of toast spread with goat’s cheese or mashed beans, alternatively, they can be paired with pasta, an idea borrowed from Ottavio Cavalcanti’s La Cucina Calabrese and Elizabeth David. I like to blend a third of the peppers into a cream, while ripping the rest into strips, short and slim enough to mix and cling to the pasta (most shapes work). You then have two options for additions: anchovy fillets or crumbled goat’s cheese, neither of which are messy or annoying.Pasta with red peppers and anchovies or goat’s cheeseWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appServes44 red peppers,or a mix of red and yellowOlive oil2garlic cloves,peeled; 1 left whole, 1 minced1 small fresh or dried red chilli300g tomatoes,peeled (plunge into boiling water for three minutes, then into cold water), or tinned4-6 anchovies(optional)450-500gpasta(fusilli, penne, radiatori, mezze maniche)Basil1 roundgoat’s cheese(optional)Put the peppers on a baking tray and in a 200C (180C fan)/390F/gas 6 oven for 30-40 minutes, turning them once or twice, or until they are charred all over and starting to collapse. Carefully lift the peppers into a bowl and cover with a plate for 20 minutes, so they steam and cool enough to handle. Working over the bowl to catch the juices, rub the charred skin from the peppers and tear into thick strips, brushing away the seeds and pith. Put the clean strips on a plate.Take a third of the pepper strips and, working in a food processor, blend them until smooth, seasoning with a little salt. Tear the remaining peppers into small strips that will toss well with pasta.In a large flying pan, warm five tablespoons of olive oil with the whole garlic clove and chilli. Once the garlic is fragrant, add the tomatoes and cook for about 12-15 minutes, pressing down with the back of a spoon to break them up into a sauce. Add the anchovies, if you are including them, stirring so they break up in the sauce.Bring a large pan of water to the boil, salt it, and cook the pasta according to the packet instructions. Add the pepper strips to the tomatoes, along with the minced garlic, stir, then add the blended peppers.When the pasta is al dente, lift from the water into the sauce and stir vigorously, along with a handful of basil and the crumbled goat’s cheese, if you are adding it.Explore more on these topicsFoodA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkPastaMain courseCheeserecipesShareReuse this content

title: From shrekking to cookie-jarring: how well do you know the latest dating terms? | Dating | The Guardian
description: In an app-based era, new dating tactics emerge rapidly and while you may have deployed one or been subject to one, how many of the following are real?
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: In an app-based era, new dating tactics emerge rapidly and while you may have deployed one or been subject to one, how many of the following are real?
Content: Composite: Getty/Alamy/PRView image in fullscreenComposite: Getty/Alamy/PRDatingFrom shrekking to cookie-jarring: how well do you know the latest dating terms?In an app-based era, new dating tactics emerge rapidly and while you may have deployed one or been subject to one, how many of the following are real?Tim DowlingThu 6 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the age of app-based romance, fresh dating trends seem to emerge every week. Many of them – in the mould of ghosting and catfishing – are profoundly antisocial, while some are defensive strategies against toxic suitors. More than a few are but new names for disgraceful behaviours as old as time. You may have been the victim of one – or you may have unwittingly deployed one – but how many can you identify? Which of the following are genuine trends, and which are not?1.Breadcrumbing. In this strategy, the toxic romantic prospect offers an admirer a sparse trail of attention – intermittent texts, occasional flirtations and “likes” of social media posts; just enough to maintain a level of continuing interest without personal investment or commitment.TrueFalseReveal2.Ghostlighting. An unholy combination of ghosting and gaslighting: to disappear from a romantic partner’s life suddenly and completely, only to reappear months or even years later, as if nothing untoward had occurred, with the intention of picking up where things left off.TrueFalseReveal3.Floodlighting. The practice of oversharing personal emotional baggage – on a first date, or even sooner – in order to seem vulnerable and engineer a quick route to intimacy. The apparent vulnerability on offer is, in this case, a ruse.TrueFalseReveal4.Process doppelganging. A narcissistic strategy to exploit the patience of a prospective love interest by deliberately sabotaging a second date: changing the venue at the last minute, drinking too much, behaving boorishly all evening and refusing to apologise. The next day, you claim your evil identical twin tricked his way into taking your place. But really it was just you with your hair parted a little differently.TrueFalseReveal5.Cuffing. As in “handcuffing” – figuratively shackling yourself to a partner by entering into a monogamous relationship not out of love, but to avoid being single for a specific period, and without admitting the attachment is temporary and will cease as soon as it’s served its purpose.TrueFalseReveal6.Cookie-jarring. This is when someone keeps you in reserve as a back-up dating option, occasionally reaching out – the way they might for a cookie in a jar – when they’re feeling bored or insecure about their main relationship, or rejected by the person they’re actually pursuing.TrueFalseReveal7.Pocketing. If your new partner is trying to keep your relationship a secret – from friends and family, on social media or in public – then you’re probably being pocketed. There may be non-toxic reasons for this, but it’s a definite red flag.TrueFalseReveal8.Shrekking. Choosing to date someone you find physically unattractive, either in the belief that appearance is not as important as what’s on the inside, or in the hope that someone who is punching above their weight will treat you better out of gratitude.TrueFalseReveal9.Collie-modelling. A bid to imitate the good-natured, eager-to-please energy of a pet collie, with the express intention of becoming someone’s lovable, uncomplicated boyfriend. Alternatively, the conscious search for just such a boyfriend.TrueFalseReveal10.Wildflowering. Essentially this is a repudiation of all the other trends out there: dating on your own terms, without specific expectations or goals in mind. It’s the strategy of not having a strategy – you just let things happen, and see where they lead.TrueFalseReveal11.Choremancing. An ultra low-key form of dating where people meet up to exercise, run errands, effect repairs or some other thing you were going to do anyway, the idea being that life is a chore and only someone you can enjoy mundane activities with is worth considering for the long-term.TrueFalseReveal12.Monkey-barring. The disreputable habit of starting a new relationship before you’ve quite ended the previous one – like a monkey swinging between bars, with a hand still on both – either out of caution, or sloth, or both.TrueFalseReveal13.Reckfulness. A sharp return to a cautious, painfully slow approach to dating, based on the hard-won wisdom that being alone, sad and unfulfilled is still better than spending the weekend with some idiot you met on Hinge.TrueFalseReveal14.Chalance. An approach to dating that emphasises enthusiasm, engagement and a refusal to play it cool, ie the opposite of nonchalance. If you really want to win someone’s heart, the advice is don’t be casual, aloof, or indifferent – be chalant.TrueFalseReveal15.Wanderlove. In theory, an openness to the possibility of romance in exotic locales; in practice, a willingness to use dating apps to find hookups while on holiday.TrueFalseReveal16.Clear-coding. Being honest and forthcoming about your dating intentions and goals – whether it’s a long-term relationship, a quick fling or just someone to gaslight for the rest of the summer – instead of relying on those old romantic standbys, guesswork and the occasional mixed signal.TrueFalseReveal17.Lime-biking. Dumping someone abruptly, unceremoniously and at your convenience, as soon as the charge has gone out of a relationship.TrueFalseReveal18.Zip coding. As the American word for postcode implies, this means limiting your search for love to your immediate area, either to keep things local or – depending on your actual postcode – to restrict your dating matches to people who live in the same exclusive neighbourhood as you do.TrueFalseReveal19.Thermocoupling. A new fashion for arranging first dates in saunas, on the grounds that you can never really tell if a person is right for you until you’ve seen them naked and sweating profusely, in the company of other naked sweaty people.TrueFalseReveal20.Banksying. The act of planning a breakup meticulously and over time, while pretending to be as enthusiastic about the relationship as ever, so that the split appears without warning for the other person, like a Banksy on a brick wall in the night.TrueFalseRevealExplore more on these topicsDatingQuiz and trivia gamesRelationshipsquizzesShareReuse this content

title: You be the judge: my partner confronts bad drivers. Should he stop? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Riya says her boyfriend has road rage, but Declan insists he never loses his temper. You decide if needs to put the brakes on his motormouth
Author: Georgina Lawton
Headline: Riya says her boyfriend has road rage, but Declan insists he never loses his temper. You decide if needs to put the brakes on his motormouth
Content: Illustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Igor Bastidas/The GuardianYou be the judgeLife and styleYou be the judge: my partner confronts bad drivers. Should he stop?Riya says her boyfriend has road rage, but Declan insists he never loses his temper. You decide if needs to put the brakes on his motormouthFind out how to get a disagreement settled or become a jurorInterviews byGeorgina LawtonThu 6 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 10.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheprosecution: Riyadouble quotation markEvery time Declan chooseskicking off over de-escalation, he compromises our safetyMy boyfriend, Declan, has bad road rage. In day-to-day life he is mild-mannered. But the roads in London, where we live, seem to transform him, and he gets a kick out of being heard.I’ve watched him go from perfectly calm to furious in seconds, and swear at people for cutting him up or for driving aggressively. Most of the time I agree that the other driver is in the wrong. But being right doesn’t make confronting strangers a sensible idea.I grew up in London and people are insane on the roads here. But I don’t ever respond because I like to save my energy. I don’t think shouting back or getting out of the car ever helps.As a woman of colour, I also don’t have the privilege of reacting when I’m by myself because it’s not safe, whereas Declan is a 6ft 3in white man.When people cut us up, beep impatiently or drive as though they’re the only person that matters, it can be scary or infuriating, but Declan just goes off on one.double quotation markI was furious – Declan turned an annoying situation into a big confrontation that could have ended badlyThe worst incident happened when another driver dangerously overtook us. Declan accelerated to catch up with them at the traffic lights and shouted through the window about how reckless they’d been. The other driver got out of his car and kicked off. Thankfully, after I shouted at Declan to drive away, he did. Afterwards, I was furious – he’d turned an annoying situation into a big confrontation that could have ended badly.Another time, after a driver flipped me off, Declan started yelling again. I know he was trying to defend me, but I don’t need defending if it means putting us both at risk. Every time Declan chooses confrontation over de-escalation, he compromises our safety over a stranger’s bad behaviour.Declan is a great partner and we usually see eye to eye when it comes to how to handle conflict. He just has a strong sense of injustice, which seems to come out on the roads. I know he likes to be vindicated, but I’d prefer him to let it go.Thedefence: Declandouble quotation markI don’t believe people should get away with dangerous or disrespectful drivingRiya and I have fundamentally different approaches when it comes to driving. I don’t lose my temper for no reason, I react when people behave recklessly. Unfortunately that happens a lot in London.I don’t believe people should get away with dangerous or disrespectful driving. Why should the person in the wrong get to drive off thinking their behaviour is acceptable?The incident with the driver who dangerously overtook us proves my point. They could have caused a serious accident. Impatient people like that are a danger to everyone. I caught up with him at the lights because I wanted him to know he’d put lives at risk, not because I was looking for a fight. Yes, he got out of his car, but as soon as it became clear things were escalating, I drove away. If I’d wanted a confrontation, I would have got out of the car, but I didn’t want to put our lives in danger.My frustration comes from seeing people behave selfishly and never face any consequences. I know I can’t police the roads, but I don’t think calling someone out automatically makes me irrational or angry.double quotation markRiya overlooks the fact that I’m reacting to bad behaviour rather than causing the problemsThe same goes for people being rude to Riya. If someone shouts abuse or makes an aggressive gesture, my instinct is to stand up for her, so why do I get called angry? I’d rather she knew I’d defend her than sit silently while someone treats her badly.Could I express myself more calmly? Probably. I’ll admit I can get heated in the moment. I never start it or go looking for fights, but I do like to have the last word. I could be less reactive. But I think Riya overlooks the fact that I’m reacting to bad behaviour rather than causing the problems myself. There’s a difference between someone making an honest mistake and someone driving dangerously.It’s unfair to label me as someone with road rage. I don’t drive aggressively or intimidate other motorists. I’m a careful, competent driver who gets frustrated when other people put lives at risk.Names have been changedskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe jury of Guardian readersPutting his girlfriend at risk isn’t protecting her, and Declan’s road rage isn’t making roads safer. Riya is telling him his behaviour makes her feel unsafe, but he doesn’t listen, which seems to indicate it’s more about ego than justice. Declan needs to think about the irony of his justifications.Paula, 43I get Declan’s frustration; there are too many bad drivers. But he needs to respect Riya’s feelings – she’s uncomfortable – and rein it in when they’re in the car together. Justified or not, Declan is directing his anger at people who don’t care and Riya’s feelings are more important.Lucille, 55The incident at the traffic lights shows what can happen. Taking out his frustrations might be therapeutic for Declan in the moment, but if it escalates into confrontation he (and Riya) could come off worse …Katherine, 52Declan says he wants to defend Riya, but he sped them both into a confrontation in the worst incident. Angry men are scary in a way I suspect most other men don’t appreciate – Declan must listen to Riya and cool his temper.Kathryn, 40If Declan behaves the way he does on the road because he cares about Riya, then he should listen to what she wants. Staying in your car does not necessarily mean that you are behaving well.Lucy, 34Now you be the judgeIn our online poll, tell us: should Declan stop driving Riya round the bend?The poll closes on Wednesday 12 August at 9am BSTLast week’s resultsWe asked, shouldDaniella’s brother stop hogging the living roomwhile he’s staying with her?77%of you said yes –Seamus is guilty23%of you said no –Seamus is not guiltyExplore more on these topicsLife and styleYou be the judgefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I have an ego that needs to be put in check’: ex-Gawker editor AJ Daulerio on life after addiction | Media | The Guardian
description: After his fall from grace, media’s former enfant terrible is now sober and helping others with his addiction recovery newsletter and podcast, The Small Bow
Author: John McDermott
Headline: After his fall from grace, media’s former enfant terrible is now sober and helping others with his addiction recovery newsletter and podcast, The Small Bow
Content: Media‘I have an ego that needs to be put in check’: ex-Gawker editor AJ Daulerio on life after addictionAfter his fall from grace, media’s former enfant terrible is now sober and helping others with his addiction recovery newsletter and podcast, The Small BowJohn McDermottThu 6 Aug 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.37 EDTShareView image in fullscreenAJ Daulerio: ‘The Small Bow is a living amends for whatever version of me came before on the internet.’Photograph: Storm Santos/Contour RA by Getty ImagesEvery other Tuesday, AJ Daulerio wakes up at 5.30am and meditates for five to 20 minutes before beginning his multistep daily journaling protocol: reading a selection from a poetry anthology, then a passage from one of his daily wisdom readers (his go-to is a heavily annotated copy of Leo Tolstoy’sA Calendar of Wisdom); writing his Fear of the Day and gratitude list, then sharing his spiritual takeaway in a note to his three kids.After a banana and coffee, Daulerio trains Brazilian jujitsu before hitting a 9.45am meditation at Besant Lodge – a community center just below the Hollywood sign that once served as a meeting place for mid-century mystics – immediately followed by him leading a recovery meeting of his own through Zoom.He goes to personal therapy at 11.15am, picks up his kids in the afternoon and spends the rest of the evening with them and his wife, giving him just a few hours at night to work on his advicecolumnfor Slate and the two books he’s writing.double quotation markI know there’s a good way of self-promoting, I’m just wary of my intentions a lot of the timeAJ DaulerioThis is in addition to emotional sobriety step work (cultivating inner peace after the drinking stops) on Zoom on Wednesday nights, an Adult Children of Alcoholics meeting every Friday morning, Alcoholics Anonymous on Sundays, couples therapy every other week, and a quarterly meeting with his psychiatrist to refine his cocktail of psychotropic medications, including a mood stabilizer (Lamictal) and an antipsychotic (Zyprexa), to treat his bipolar disorder.“I have an ego that needs to be put in check all the time,” Daulerio tells me. “Half of my recovery is dedicated to that.”Daulerio celebrated 10 years of sobriety this July, a joyous capstone to a tumultuous decade-plus that saw Daulerio go from digital media visionary as editor of Gawker to broke, disgraced and the man most responsible for the site’s demise.Daulerio has re-emerged in recent years, again as a media innovator – not as the cutthroat, traffic-obsessed editor reputation he garnered at Gawker, but as the gentle, deeply pensive and contrite author ofThe Small Bow,the newsletter he created in 2018 to chronicle his recovery from drug and alcohol addiction, and his attempts to reclaim his life as a changed man.Today Daulerio maintains a rigorous recovery regimen to battle the twin demons that once fueled his self-destructive impulses: the lonesomeness that led him to seek companionship in dive bars among other strange drunks, and the ego that convinced him he had it all under control, despite signs to the opposite.I spent 22 years as a problem drinker. Here are 10 things I’ve learned since I quitRead moreDaulerio has built a devout following by writing about his recovery program in unsparingly honest, vulnerable first-person essays in The Small Bow, and he now wants to grow the company into a multiplatform media company that provides wisdom and guidance to people struggling with addictions of all kinds.But therein lies Daulerio’s existential dilemma: how to build a successful media business without sacrificing the spiritual practice that made his second act possible.“It’s something I have to get comfortable with and better at, because I do believe in what we’re doing,” Daulerio says between bites of his cheeseburger. “I know there’s a good way of self-promoting, I’m just wary of my intentions a lot of the time.”One needs a certain amount of irrational self-confidence to start any business, especially in print media, an industry that has been in steady decline since Daulerio first became a journalist in 2000. Then there’s the self-promotion required to grow a business, even as it risks inflating the ego that fueled his fall from grace and that he’s worked so hard to keep in check.That The Small Bow is built almost entirely around Daulerio’s personal experience makes this all the more difficult.In Daulerio’s favor is his unmatched skill at growing digital media properties. It’s what propelled him to success as the editor of the now defunctGawker Media– and also what led to his and the company’s downfall.The Small Bow uses lots of religious iconography in its branding: pen and colored pencil illustrations of demons and angels drawn by Edith Zimmerman, a writer and artist whohas also found sobriety– and they serve as an easy metaphor for the tension between Daulerio’s professional ambitions and his personal recovery: the demon whispering in one ear to revert to his old tricks and grow The Small Bow by any means necessary, and the angel whispering in the other to preserve what’s made The Small Bow so resonant with readers undergoing their own struggles.“How do you sell something that is supposed to be genuine?” he asks me rhetorically. As with his sobriety, all he can do is forge ahead and attempt to achieve this seemingly irreconcilable balancing act, one day at a time. “What are the other options?”The last 10 years of Daulerio’s life have been an exercise in being humbled. Few figures in recent history have had their rise and fall scrutinized as intensely by the media. His exploits have been the subject of two Netflix documentaries, glossy magazine profiles, and countless reports and thought pieces on sound journalistic practice and the limits of first amendment freedoms.double quotation markI had the ability to get people to tell me things they weren’t supposed toAJ DaulerioBut long before he was media’s enfant terrible, he was one of the most promising young talents in 2000s digital journalism.Daulerio started in journalism in 1998, covering city council meetings for the East Brunswick Sentinel in New Jersey. His initial dream was to be a music producer – he was simultaneously interning at a recording studio – or, saving that, a music critic. But he quickly exhibited a preternatural talent for landing scoops, a skill that would become his MO as he ascended the highest echelons of the digital publishing industry.“I had the ability to get people to tell me things they weren’t supposed to,” Daulerio says. “Because I didn’t have strict deadlines, I could hang out with the council members.” A former college classmate of Daulerio’s worked the same beat for a competing newspaper, and Daulerio delighted in beating him to stories. “I loved it. I was weirdly competitive in a way that’s good for reporting. I’ve never been competitive in anything else.”Despite being a diehard Philly sports fan, Daulerio was a feckless athlete himself, much to the embarrassment of his father (a topic Daulerio frequently visits in his Small Bow columns). “I grew up playing sports, but I never knew how to win. In the journalism world, I knew how to win.”Daulerio shuffled through writing and editing gigs in New York and Philadelphia – including stints at the trade publications Bond Buyer and American Lawyer Media; men’s lifestyle newsletter Thrillist; and Philadelphia magazine – before landing a senior editor job at Deadspin, Gawker’s sports vertical, in 2008. Just months later, he was promoted to editor for the entire site.Then Daulerio published photos of former New York Jets quarterback Brett Favre’s penis, and his life trajectory was forever altered.In August 2010, Daulerio published a Deadspin post alleging that Favrehad sent lewd voicemails and pictures of his penisto the Jets sideline reporter Jenn Sterger. Two months later, Dauleriopublished the illicit photos, purportedly from Favre, in a video montage, with Favre’s voicemails providing the soundtrack.The story generated millions of page views for Deadspin and months of headlines across the wider sports media ecosystem, cementing the three-person sports blog as a player on the national stage and Daulerio as a fearless journalist on the vanguard of a new era of digital journalism. “So many NFL reporters had known about [Favre’s behavior] the whole time and wouldn’t cover it,” Daulerio says. (Favre admitted to leaving the voicemails but denied sending lewd photos.)Professional and personal accolades showered over Daulerio. He did the Today show (while drunk, stoned and on Adderall). Nick Denton, Gawker Media’s founder and CEO, rewarded Daulerio with a raise, three more Deadspin staff writers and a freelance budget.double quotation markI would go to a bar on Thursday and come out of it on MondayAJ DaulerioDaulerio was spotlighted in aGQprofile and became a star of the New York City media scene. “A friend of mine from high school came to a Gawker office rooftop party,” Daulerio recalls. “He watched me walk into this place and he was like, ‘I feel like I’m with Don Corleone.’”It was the success and recognition Daulerio had always coveted. He had dreamed about having his glossy portrait photo featured in Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list. And yet all the attention – and criticism – made him uncomfortable. “I did not like my full-time job to be a punching bag for all the heels on the internet,” he says. “On the other hand, I had been treading water for 10 years in online journalism, and now I had attention and career options.” After the GQ story, “there was no reversing who I was.”As he climbed the ranks of the media industry, Daulerio was also feeding a drinking habit that would land him in rehab. He drank six nights a week, rotating through a familiar circuit of bars near work in the Bowery (Congee Village, Professor Thom’s) and, on weekends, in Williamsburg (Dardy Bar). Some Saturdays he would post up at a bar at 11am, down 10 beers and five shots, stay until close and then do cocaine with his newly formed friends. “I would just live in these places,” Daulerio says. “I was a binger. I would go to a bar on Thursday and come out of it on Monday … There was never really a plan other than to stay for as long as I possibly could.”Drinking was a way to treat the “free-floating loneliness” Daulerio had lived with since he was a child, he says. “It was fun to do cocaine with strangers until 4.30 in the morning. That felt like home to me … It would be silly to blame [my addiction] on anything other than I never felt normal or at ease, and I’m always battling that and probably always will.”He was one of the most successful editors in the burgeoning digital publishing industry, but he couldn’t afford an apartment because his credit was so bad. He bounced between friends’ couches.His cavalier editorial philosophy came under fire at the same time. To critics, Gawker became emblematic of a new wave of digital journalists who prioritized the almighty click and page view without any consideration for journalistic ethics or basic human decency.Publishing the Favre story, for instance, meant burning Sterger, the recipient of the reportedly unsolicited “dong shots” (Daulerio’s words), who had explicitly asked to not be included in the story. (Daulerio bought the photos and voicemails from a third party for $12,000.) He even published Sterger’s request to leave her out of it.Daulerio now says he wishes he had broken the Favre scoop without mentioning her.Later, when the Gawker empire imploded, a narrative emerged that Daulerio’s alcohol and drug use was largely to blame for the editorial decisions that led to its collapse, a premise Daulerio wholly rejects. “A lot of good things were happening when things were bad,” he says.The rise and fall of Deadspin: how ‘jerks in Brooklyn’ changed sports journalismRead moreSuch as Deadspin’s immense growth. In just three years under Daulerio’s tenure, Deadspin’s traffic tripled, as the site continued to break raunchy, irreverent scoops – former New York Jets head coachRex Ryan filming foot fetish videosstarring his wife; photos of Texas Rangers outfielderJosh Hamilton drunk and shirtless, licking whipped cream off a woman’s breasts in a Tempe, Arizona, bar, despite supposedly being sober; andESPN Horndog Dossier, a collection of unconfirmed rumors about rampant illicit sexual behavior at “the Worldwide Leader in Sports”.There was even some genuine investigative reporting mixed in with the scuzzy gossip, such asleaked financial documentsexposing the creative accounting techniques that Major League Baseball franchises employ to boost profits.Denton named Daulerio editor ofGawker.com, Gawker Media’s flagship site, in late 2011. The following fall, Daulerio approved publication of a sex tape starring the professional wrestler Hulk Hogan. Hogan filed an invasion of privacy lawsuit against Gawker just two weeks later, a legal action that would bankrupt Gawker and force its sale, and temporarily ruin Daulerio’s life and career. (It was later revealed that Hogan’s suit was financed by the billionaire venture capitalist Peter Thiel, who harbored a grudge against Gawker Media ever since itouted him as gay in 2007.)Hogan won a $140m judgment in March 2016 against Gawker, including $100,000 in punitive damages for Daulerio, a verdict that was largely blamed on Daulerio and hiscallouseditorial ethos. (Gawker settled with Hogan for $31m, and Daulerio didn’t have to pay the $100,000.)During the trial, Hogan’s attorneys brought up how Daulerio once published a separate sex tape of two people who were not public figures, and how Daulerio initially dismissed the woman in the video when she requested its removal. (Daulerio implored her to “not make a big deal out of this”.)The post was eventually deleted, and Daulerio says publishing it was the most regrettable moment of his career.The most damning moment in the trial was when Hogan’s attorneys showed the courtroom a videotaped deposition of Daulerio from October 2013, in which a Hogan attorney asked Daulerio: “Can you imagine a situation where a celebrity sex tape would not be newsworthy?”“If they were a child,” Daulerio replied.The lawyer pushed: “Under what age?”“Four.”The exchange sent “a palpable sense of shock” through the courtroom,according to the New York Times. There wereaudible gasps and groans. Daulerio says the comment was a sarcastic joke, “a defense mechanism” after getting frustrated with the interrogation, but it supported the plaintiff’s portrayal of Daulerio as a heartless gossip-peddler who trafficked in the sordid details of people’s personal lives, even when they had zero news value.Adding to Daulerio’s embarrassment, the trial revealed he hada net worth of negative $35,000. The court froze the $1,500 he had in his bank account. The 2017 Netflix documentary Nobody Speak: Trials of the Free Press about the Hogan trial opens with Daulerio laughing as he reads a bank email informing him a $230m hold had been placed on his bank account.Daulerio can’t recall how he felt during the trial. He dissociated. “It was so big and overwhelming, I just felt like I was a character in this thing,” he says. The only part of the experience he can latch on to is the photo of him from theNew York Timesarticle. “I feel like I know what that expression is: really helpless, but also in trouble.”As Daulerio’s professional life was put on trial, he was also trying to get sober. He first entered rehab in August 2015, seven months before the trial began, but quickly relapsed. “Two months later, I was back at it pretty hardcore,” he says.Daulerio fully committed to sobriety on 15 July 2016, a month after Gawker filed for bankruptcy and put itself up for sale. “July 15, 2016, was simply the day I decided to stop resisting and give up the warped idea that I could do my own modified version of sobriety, something akin to what I liked to call ‘advanced moderation’,” he wrote ina recent Small Bow essayabout his 10th anniversary of sobriety.What Daulerio still longed for in his early days of recovery was a way to process the experience the best way he knew how: through writing.The first piece Daulerio published after the trial wasa 2017 first-person essay about his fraught relationship with his fatherfor the now shuttered men’s publication Mel.The piece had the pugnacious writing that made Deadspin so popular; Daulerio opens the essay recounting a physical fight with his father. But it also had the emotional vulnerability of an adult man trying to heal his daddy issues, told through the prism of past Father’s Days. (I was a staff writer at Mel at that time, but did not work with Daulerio).“The piece was masculinity and neuroses laid bare, not in a self-pitying, ‘woe is me’ way, but in a curious way,” former Mel editor-in-chief Josh Schollmeyer says. “If there’s any difference between the pre- and post-trial AJ, it’s AJ falling in love with his own mythology versus being who he really is, which is a master storyteller. That humility was apparent from the jump.”The naked confessional style would become The Small Bow’s signature. In the newsletter, Daulerio recounts his various sobriety efforts – AA meetings, therapy, meditation, psychiatry, stoicism, Buddhism – in oftentimes painful, but always heartfelt honesty.Earlier this year, he wrote aboutmoving his elderly mother into an assisted living facilityin Florida near where he went to rehab. He also frequently writes about the spiritual blessings of being a family man; Daulerio and screenwriter Julieanne Smolinski married in 2018, and they have three children together in Los Angeles.double quotation markHe has been through the level of public shame that I have. Few people have experienced thatJenn StergerSome of the most powerful Small Bow entries are about Daulerio making amends – steps eight and nine in 12-step programs – to those he wronged during his years actively in addiction, such as making peace with Sterger.Ina January 2020 essay, Daulerio revealed he and Sterger incidentally reconnected when he adopted a dog for his growing family. Sterger just so happened to work at the dog shelter Smolinski emailed, resulting in Daulerio and Sterger meeting at the LA diner House of Pies.She admitted that there are still uncomfortable days and awkward moments stemming from the Favre ordeal. There’s still a version of her that exists in the internet’s memory hole where she will never be a real person; she’s just a plot point without context, without skin. But the thing that I did was more vicious. You see, I knew she was a real person – and I did what I did anyway. I didn’t care if I destroyed her. That’s just the type of person I was back then.I don’t remember how long we actually talked, but I remember we both walked out of there a little relieved like we’d both just found a therapist who finally understood the excavation tools required to break new ground. Some hurts were still unreachable, though. Time takes time.Sterger agreed to meet him out of curiosity: she wanted to understand why Daulerio betrayed her wishes and upended her life. “I found a guy that had looked at himself in the mirror and really done a lot of hard work on himself – really examined why he had done the things that he had done, and realized the hurt that he had caused people,” Sterger says.The two got along so well that they developed the unlikeliest of friendships. “He has been through the level of public shame that I have,” Sterger says. “Few people have experienced that.” Sterger later appeared on The Small Bow podcast, where she and Daulerio publicly buried the hatchet.“There’s a concept in recovery of a living amends,” Daulerio says. When a direct amends might inflict even more pain on the injured party, addicts in recovery are instructed to atone by simply living a good life. “The Small Bow is a living amends for whatever version of me came before on the internet.”The newsletter has amassed 20,000 subscribers – about 2,000 of them paid, making him $72,000 a year – including some celebrities that have embraced the publication as a platform to discuss their own sobriety.Fans of the CBS talkshow The Talk and the Barstool Sports podcast Pardon My Take know Jerry O’Connell as a happy-go-lucky actor with a goofy sense of humor, but on The Small Bow podcast in April, O’Connellrevealed he’s been in recovery from alcoholismfor 13 years.Going public about his sobriety took some convincing. O’Connell got sober under the old-school AA mentality that treats anonymity as sacrosanct – “it’s right there in the title,” he says – but made an exception because Daulerio had been so important to his own recovery. The two connected during the pandemic over their shared sobriety after O’Connell, a longtime Deadspin fan, reached out.“AJ has a new-school way of thinking, and that’s why this venture is interesting,” O’Connell says of Daulerio’s willingness to bare it all. “This is all uncharted territory.”“I was publicly drunk, so being publicly sober makes sense to me, and I like to talk about the many methods I go about to stay that way,” Daulerio recently wrote in The Small Bow. “But recovery is a personal thing – how someone chooses to do it isn’t my business.”double quotation mark[Daulerio is] very self-effacing in a way that is honest, not trying to win brownie points by being self-effacingAlex WinterActor and documentarian Alex Winter has a routine meetup with Daulerio at House of Pies, where they discuss recovery and fatherhood. Winter, too,discussed his recovery on an episode of The Small Bow, the only time he has appeared on a recovery podcast.“I’ve always bristled a little bit at these kinds of recovery-forward podcasts,” Winter says. “I always worry about people getting very enthusiastic about getting sober. … Recovery is delicate. It’s fragile. So I just feel for the people who expose themselves that way and hope that they’re OK.” What separates Daulerio, Winter says, is his radical candor. “He’s very self-effacing in a way that is honest, not trying to win brownie points by being self-effacing.”The day after Hogan died last July,Daulerio penned a Small Bow essaypartially thanking the Hulkster for body-slamming his life and career. “Without that experience, there is no Small Bow, probably,” Daulerio says. “That’s how I choose to think about it.”“I forgot to brush my teeth,” Daulerio announces to The Small Bow production team, as he prepares to tape a new episode.Between fatherhood and his recovery routine, Daulerio’s is more structured than ever, but chaos seeps in at times. After nearly three decades as a writer, he still gets bothered by commenters. He recently senta snarky email responseto a reader who criticizedone of his Slate advice columns.double quotation markWhat I want to create a dialogue about is: you can stop drinking just because you don’t like itRyan O’ConnellA current focus in his recovery is on improving his sleep. A night owl, Daulerio typically gets only five hours of sleep a night, staying up until the wee hours to watch violent action movies, often starring Jason Statham. He has started using a sleep mask and soothing ASMR sounds to help lull him into slumber.The podcast is integral to Daulerio’s strategy for growing The Small Bow. His larger vision is something akin to a trade magazine for the recovery industry. He wants to sell subscriptions to recovery facilities – hospitals, clinics, rehabs, halfway houses – whose patients would then be able to access, and even contribute to, The Small Bow’s archive of addiction-related content. “A farm system for The Small Bow,” he says, not unlike how Gawker recruited the wittiest contributors in its comments section to become paid staff writers.Daulerio piloted such a program with Divided Sky, the Ludlow, Vermont, drug rehab facility co-founded by the Phish frontman Trey Anastasio, whoseappearance on The Small Bow podcastis the show’s most popular to date.How the rivalry between Gawker and BuzzFeed drove a social media boom – and bustRead moreAs The Small Bow has attracted more contributors, its scope has widened to include a broader array of addictions and mental health issues: sex, shopping, gambling, weed, depression, bipolar disorder. The internet itself.Today’spodcast tapingis with writer Ryan O’Connell, who’s promoting his essay collection,Inspiration Porn– a welcome development for Daulerio, who wants The Small Bow to be a requisite stop on the memoir promotion circuit. Daulerio’s own books, a compilation of essays about recovery called The Small Book, a play on AA’s Big Book, and a memoir about his life post-Gawker trial, are scheduled to publish in 2027.Ryan O’Connell’s relationship with alcohol falls into the expanded definition of sobriety. He never hit “rock bottom” because he quit before he could get there. “It’s the only substance you get shamed for quitting,” he says. “What I want to create a dialogue about is: you can stop drinking just because you don’t like it. AJ is expanding recovery conversations to be about so much more.”I ask Daulerio what success looks like to him now. On a personal level, it’s spending quality time with his family, the spiritual opposite of when he would stay out all night to avoid going home.Professionally, success means rediscovering his love of writing, doing it consistently, and serving the recovery community he’s cultivated.“I’m never going to have the notoriety I had, but I really enjoy what I do know and learning how to write again,” he says. “It’s the best work I’ve ever done.”

title: Summer on the Baltic: a laidback coastal adventure in Lithuania | Lithuania holidays | The Guardian
description: With great beaches, culture and nature, the resort town of Palanga and the wild Curonian Spit offer an affordable – and cooler – alternative to the Med
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With great beaches, culture and nature, the resort town of Palanga and the wild Curonian Spit offer an affordable – and cooler – alternative to the Med
Content: Palanga, Lithuania’s most popular beach resort.Photograph: Aleksandar Tomic/AlamyView image in fullscreenPalanga, Lithuania’s most popular beach resort.Photograph: Aleksandar Tomic/AlamyLithuania holidaysSummer on the Baltic: a laidback coastal adventure in LithuaniaWith great beaches, culture and nature, the resort town of Palanga and the wild Curonian Spit offer an affordable – and cooler – alternative to the MedSarah RodriguesThu 6 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe water off Palanga’s sandy white beach is tinged pale green – the colour of the feathery clouds ofFurcellaria lumbricalisthat occasionally brush against my calves. Underfoot, the Baltic seabed is ridged, the sea so clear and shallow that every ripple is visible. The water deepens very gradually – making it ideal for families. I’m quite far from the coast, but still only thigh deep, the sea still cool as I duck beneath the surface.Elsewhere in Europe, another heatwave has prompted health warnings and school closures. But here in Lithuania, children scamper on the sand and splash in the shallows as temperatures remain, if not cool, bearable. I’ve come to explore some of the Baltic beaches – here and on the Curonian Spit – which are fast gaining popularity as the Med heats up and prices in southern Europe remain stubbornly high.Palanga has been drawing Lithuanian holidaymakers since the wealthy Tiškevičiai family transformed it into a seaside resort in the mid-19th century. Today, there is a certain rowdy seaside vibe in parts: the central beach can get crowded and the promenade is on the kitsch side too, with many of the historic wooden buildings – demolished or damaged in the Soviet era – replaced by brash signage, entertainment venues and raucous restaurants.Nonetheless, the main beach is reassuringly devoid of construction and characterised primarily by its distinctive 19th-century L-shaped pier, a popular sunset-catching spot. Away from the shore, you need only stroll the 100-hectare (250-acre)botanical garden, home to the 19th-century Tiškevičiai Palace and amber museum, with its thousands of prehistoric exhibits, to witness a different past. A bronze sculpture of Feliksas Tiškevičius stands just outside the park; legend has it that if you rub his foot with yours and kiss his cheek, good luck will follow.View image in fullscreenTiškevičiai Palace and botanical gardens.Photograph: Jurgita Vaicikeviciene/AlamyJust a 10-minute cycle ride away from the pier, my hotel, theGradiali(B&B doubles from €118), is another peaceful oasis. From here, a 500-metre walk through aromatic pine forest leads to an uncrowded section of Palanga beach, where €75 (£64) gets you all-day use of a curtained cabana, complete with a bottle of prosecco and a mountain of ice-cream. (I’ve paid at least double that on the Greek island of Mykonos – and that was just for the bed.)There are other ways to get into the water around Palanga, including wakeboarding at the313 Cable Park(from €20), about 2.5 miles (4km) from the town, or plunging into one of the 16 leisure and mineral pools at theAtostogų Parkas complex(from €30), about 4 miles away. But I’m on a mission to explore Lithuania’s more untamed side – the Curonian Spit, a protected 61-mile stretch of dense forest and Blue Flag beaches accessed only via the modern port city of Klaipėda, a half-hour drive away. Trains run to Klaipėda from the capital, Vilnius, too – and electrification of the train line next year will reduce the 205-mile journey time by 30 minutes to four hours.double quotation markThe Curonian Spit is Lithuania’s more untamed side –  a protected stretch of dense forest and Blue Flag beachesWith its waterfront setting, compact old town and restoredcastle complex, Klaipėda makes for a pleasant afternoon stop – but I’m eager to board the ferry (approximately €1.70), which has me on the spit within 10 minutes. Threaded by bike and walking trails, this narrow stretch of sand peninsula – flanked by the Baltic Sea on one side and the Curonian Lagoon on the other – is occupied in the south by Russia. Observation decks near the border allow glimpses of a similarly forested landscape, but one punctuated by watchtowers.View image in fullscreenThe Curonian Spit is flanked by the Baltic Sea on one side and the Curonian Lagoon on the other.Photograph: Pavel Dudek/AlamyAs fascinating as this off-limits area is, it’s the older stories about the spit that bewitch me. Legend has it the giant Neringa formed it by pouring sand from her apron to create a protective break between the irascible Baltic Sea and her people. The amber fragments, which still wash up on the peninsula’s beaches, are said to be the debris from an underwater amber castle, shattered in rage by the thunder god Perkūnas when Jūratė, goddess of the sea, fell in love with a mortal.But some of the area’s most haunting tales are not mere myth. On an evening trip in a traditionalflat-bottomed fishing boatfrom the harbour in Nida – the spit’s largest town – our skipper Aurelijus Armonavičius speaks of the vagaries of shifting sands and the 18th-century felling of forests, which led to the slow burial of 14 villages and two cemeteries on the spit. Only through the building of a sand ridge and concerted reforestation efforts has this – now Unesco-listed – landscape been preserved.My accommodation,Hotel Nidus(B&B doubles from €119), lies between lagoon and beach, and features basic, comfortable rooms and expansive gardens. I head to the harbour for dinner atNidos Prieplauka, watching the sunset and sampling the cold, kefir-based beetroot soup – a traditional Lithuanian dish so adored that there’s an annual springtimefestivalheld for it in the capital.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe following day, I meet Angelina Ivanova, from Nida’s tourism centre, to bike to Vecekrugas Dune. At 67 metres (220ft) above sea level, it is the spit’s highest point: the flatness of the landscape, as well as its pine needle-strewn bike paths, make it manageable for even the least experienced cyclists. As we walk from our bikes to the peak, the ground is scarred with furrows of dark earth; the work of wild boar. Clusters of mushrooms stud the soil; foraging is a beloved Baltic activity – although the protected status of the Curonian Spit means that it is off limits in certain areas, such as the Nagliai nature reserve, about 11 miles from Nida.View image in fullscreenThe spit’s dunes are popular with birdwatchers and can easily be reached by bike.Photograph: Image Professionals/AlamyThe area is also a migratory path for millions of birds such as peregrine falcons and red kites. This being high summer, we see mostly gulls and cormorants. “The shoulder seasons are our busiest for twitchers,” says Angelina, as we reach the top of the dune. And, with water on both sides – at points separated by as little as 400 metres – the spit sustains not only these migratory birds, but also the fishing traditions that have traditionally shaped life here.We continue on to Preila, about a mile away. A tiny village on the lagoon, it is home to a row of smoke-fishing shacks. “Everybody has their favourite,” says Angelina, as we peruse that day’s offerings: hers is Rimo Žuvis, owned by the parents of her schoolfriend. Eel, considered a delicacy, is the most expensive dish on the menu, but we opt for sea perch and turbot, which we eat at picnic tables overlooking the water, accompanied by bread, fresh tomatoes and cold beer. Later, we will end the day back in the sea at Nida, with the midsummer sun hanging high in the sky and temperatures still hovering pleasantly in the 20s.The trip was provided by theNeringa,Klaipėda,PalangaandKretingatourism offices, with accommodation atHotel NidusandHotel GradialiExplore more on these topicsLithuania holidaysEurope holidaysBeach holidaysSummer holidaysFamily holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Thursday news quiz: Feral paws, language laws and a public Ariana pause | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Test yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare?
Author: Martin Belam
Headline: Test yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare?
Content: This cat has got some questions for you …Photograph: Amrita Chandradas/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThis cat has got some questions for you …Photograph: Amrita Chandradas/The GuardianThursday quizLife and styleThursday news quiz: Feral paws, language laws and a public Ariana pauseTest yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare?Martin BelamThu 6 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo Andy Burnham questions this week because – Shock! Horror! – a man with a family has taken a summer holiday with his family. But the Thursday quiz has done no such thing. Fifteen new questions await you on topical news, general knowledge and popular culture. There are no prizes, but you can boast about your score in the comments.
