title: ‘It can make you psychotic or give you a cardiac arrest’: why are so many children vaping the ‘prison drug’ spice? | Vaping | The Guardian
description: Parents and teachers worry about the number of kids who vape cannabis. But many of them are using something far more dangerous – without even realising it
Author: Amy Fleming
Headline: Parents and teachers worry about the number of kids who vape cannabis. But many of them are using something far more dangerous – without even realising it
Content: The effects of spice vaping ‘can come on fast and strong’.Photograph: AleksandrYu/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe effects of spice vaping ‘can come on fast and strong’.Photograph: AleksandrYu/Getty Images/iStockphotoVaping‘It can make you psychotic or give you a cardiac arrest’: why are so many children vaping the ‘prison drug’ spice?Parents and teachers worry about the number of kids who vape cannabis. But many of them are using something far more dangerous – without even realising itAmy FlemingThu 6 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIbumped into an old acquaintance the other day. Updating me on his children’s ages, he said, with an eyeroll of resignation: “My daughter’s 15 now; just found a cannabis vape in her room.” It’s an increasingly common and concerning situation for parents – with no way of telling if a vape does in fact contain weed (which comes with its own risks, just like vaping tobacco) or something much worse.Instead of the natural cannabinoids THC or CBD, these vapes can contain a much cheaper substitute: the “prison drug” spice. Last year scientists from the University of Bath analysed 1,923 vapes that had been confiscated from children in 114 schools in England, andfound that13% contained spice. In London and Lancashire it was 25%. And this is among vapes of all kinds, nicotine included, not just those that purported to contain cannabis. As for vapes labelled as containing THC, CBD or cannabis, when the drug-testing service Wedinos (part of Public Health Wales) examined 297 samples received in the year up to March 2025, it found that 39% contained spice.Chris Pudney, professor of applied biochemistry at the University of Bath, said researchers also found that these vapes are “overtly and blatantly available on the major social media platforms”, which hold huge sway over young people. A recent report for ITV’s Good Morning Britain featured a boy who was incredulous that, at the age of 12, he had become addicted to spice vapes advertised on social media as THC – which he “bought for a tenner” – and ended up in a coma with a collapsed lung.View image in fullscreenHundreds of vapes were confiscated from schoolchildren this year.Photograph: Plan Shooting 2/Imazins/Getty Images/ImaZinS RFScientists aren’t allowed to buy drugs from dealers to test them, so to get an idea of how many supposedly THC products advertised on social media contain spice, Pudney used his experience with testing vapes seized by schools to “visually triage” them (more on how to spot a spice-containing vape later) and estimated that 68% of those bought via TikTok contained spice, compared with 12% bought via Facebook.If, as a concerned adult, you look up spice on the internet, it’s hard not to panic. You will find aheartbreaking BBC News clipabout the drug turning users in north Wales into “zombies”, along with reports of it causing deaths amonghomelessandprisonpopulations. “It’s not considered a drug like heroin that causes a lot of death,” says Pudney, and is not to be confused with the mass killer fentanyl and other, even stronger, emerging synthetic opioids. But, he says, “it can have acute health outcomes, depending on dosage”.Spice has a dissociative affect, “so it makes you feel like you’re not in your body – which is why you can imagine people who are in prison or homeless like it – but it can also make you psychotic and potentially make you aggressive and give you a hypertensive crisis. At the worst end, it can give you seizures or cause a cardiac arrest.” There’s also a risk of serious accidents arising as a result of being incapacitated, which can easily happen because the effects can come on fast and strong.Spice isn’t one drug – it’s a catch-all name for a range of chemicals that are often referred to as synthetic cannabinoids. “I think over 250 have now been recorded,” says Pudney. New variations were developed in quick succession as existing versions were made illegal, “in the same way we’re seeing with synthetic opioids at the moment, that are changing all the time,” he says. “ThePsychoactive Substances Act[2016] was there to stop that sort of whack-a-mole. We now ban things based on a whole class of molecules, so all synthetic cannabinoid receptor agonists fall under the Psychoactive Substances Act.”View image in fullscreenChris Pudney from the University of Bath tests vapes with his spice detector.Photograph: University of Bath/PACannabis itself was often viewed as a fairly harmless entry-level illegal drug in the 1990s. But in this century, a type of high-potency cannabis called skunk became the norm. Cultivated for a very high concentration of THC (the chemical that makes you feel stoned and potentially paranoid), it has barely any of the more calming CBD. Smoking lots of skunk in adolescencecan increase the risk of psychotic illnessfivefold, according to a paper in the BMJ.It’s wrong, says Pudney, to view spice as synthetic cannabis. Where the THC in natural cannabis partially binds to certain receptors in cells, spice binds much more strongly to them. “It’s what’s called a full agonist, so it has a much stronger effect, and the structure of the molecule is completely different.” How does it compare to high-dose THC as found in skunk? “There is no comparison,” he says. “It’s vastly more harmful than cannabis.” In 2015, the Global Drugs Surveyfoundthat the risk of needing emergency medical treatment when using spice was 30 times greater than when using skunk.double quotation markThe spice vapes have no real smell. This makes it easier for children to use them and become addicted“There are relatively regular media reports of children collapsing in school after vaping spice,” says Pudney. Spice is also addictive. “When you’re addicted to a really strong drug like spice, you simply don’t have any choices left in your life,” says Pudney. “Kids start stealing from their parents. When you’re addicted to a drug like that, it puts you in the pocket of the drug dealer. So my real concern is that spice is so remarkably addictive that it places people, young people who are already vulnerable, in very risky situations.” As with most poor health outcomes, those affected by poverty, trauma and lack of family support are at far greater risk.Spice flew through the prison system because it was easily smuggled in, soaked on to paper that could then be smoked without incriminating odours. Similarly, it can be vaped in school without detection. “When we’re speaking to schools about it, they’ve got absolutely no idea if this is just a normal vape or a spice vape,” says Annabelle Johnson, of the health and social care charity Change Grow Live. “That’s one of the reasons why we’re finding so much of it in school.”Jack Spicer, senior lecturer in criminology at University of Bath, has been speaking to young people who use spice as part of his own research. “The spice vapes have no real smell,” he says. “This makes it easier for children to use them and become addicted.” Spicer says this cautiously, “not wanting to overstate it and whip up a moral panic around it. But, at the same time, there are legitimate reasons to be concerned.”Spice is cheap and easy to produce, and there is serious money to be made from it. Most forms in the UK are made from one of two molecules, says Pudney, and kits containing the components for these can be bought from China. Approximately £1,000 to £1,500 will get you enough to make a kilogram of spice – “but if you can sell it all in vape liquid, it will be worth about £1m”.View image in fullscreenVapes are sold in colourful packaging.Photograph: Oksana Lyskova/AlamyIt’s in the last three to five years that vape devices have become “the new method of consumption” for children, says Chris Henniker, children and young people’s cluster manager for Change Grow Live. Originally, he’d hear of THC vapes being bought for £30 to £40. “Then we started to hear more and more young people saying they were buying ‘THC vapes’ for £10, £15. And then we started to hear these anecdotal adverse reactions, people being hospitalised.”Once it became clear that these supposed THC vapes were spice vapes, usage died down among young people, “because there was a lot of stigma attached to spice use,” says Henniker. More recently, however, he says that young people haven’t seemed as concerned about the stigma. “They were willing to throw caution to the wind and see what happens. A number of them will try to ensure that it is THC they’re using, buying from what they have classed as trusted sources, but we also know there are a significant number of young people who are just buying whatever is being sold, with the hope it’s THC, but if it’s not, it’s not: ‘And we’re still going to use it anyway.’”Some concerned teens buy cheap urine tests online that claim to identify spice once you’ve taken it. However, Pudney, who first developed his test for prison use, says “there’s no urine test you can buy on the market that’s going to be accurate for picking up spice.” Vape testing can’t be carried out locally, says Henniker. The only way to define what’s inside vapes is to send them for laboratory testing.double quotation markMore and more young people were buying these vapes for £10, £15. Then we started to hear about them being hospitalisedHaving tested so many at the University of Bath, Pudney has some guidelines for recognising spice v cannabis in a vape in the first instance. Along with the often telltale pricing mentioned above, “you can know very easily whether it’s a THC vape because it will stink of cannabis, whereas spice vapes don’t smell of anything other than vape liquid,” he says.Much of what’s sold on social media comes in unlabelled vape liquid refill bottles, and there’s a “high chance” that what you’re buying is spice, says Pudney. His analysis found that spice doesn’t tend to get mixed with genuine THC; it’s usually one or the other.Dealers will often post menus of cannabis vape options alongside their other products. Spicer says you often see branded vapes “mimicking the legitimate ones that are being sold in jurisdictions where they are legal, in the US and Canada. Most young people are pretty alive to the fact that they probably aren’t legit, but still, in some way, buy into the branding. There’s some sort of materialism around it.”Clarissa (not her real name), 21, from the north-west of England, who vapes THC in the evening because she feels it helps manage her panic attacks, says she can tell the difference by the effect of the drug. “With normal THC, you get the munchies and you’re still aware of what’s going on. But with the synthetic ones, it makes you very zombie-ish. It makes it very easy to fall asleep and it can take away your appetite.” In the past, she disposed of these, but recently she has been keeping them, to use if she can’t sleep. “I don’t use them on nights when I know I’ve got work the next day. I only use it on the weekends when I’m really struggling to sleep, and I use the THC on weeknights.” She works full-time and says she’s never had problems with spice: “But I know I’m taking a risk, whereas kids don’t know that they’re buying that.”View image in fullscreenVapes have become ‘the new method of consumption’ for children.Photograph: Charinporn Thayot/Getty ImagesShe has friends who knowingly use spice vapes more frequently and “struggle with tiredness”. When one went cold turkey, she vomited for days “and she had headaches”, Clarissa says.Spice is so lucrative that dealers will always find ways to reach children, but Pudney is campaigning for more action to be taken about the presence of vapes on social media. Under the Online Safety Act, tech firms are required to tackle this themselves, but drug content still slips through the net. Pudney and his colleaguespresented their findings to MPsin November 2025 during Evidence Week – an event set up eight years ago in Westminster to discuss how evidence is used and scrutinised – but gaining traction for further action is frustratingly slow. He has called for Ofcom to penalise social media firms for failing to uphold their duty. “If the regulator won’t enforce the law, we end up in the situation we’re in at the moment,” he says. “They haven’t found the evidence we’ve provided sufficient to warrant them taking any action. So we’re having a continuous dialogue with them.”Meta – the owner of platforms including Facebook and Instagram – didn’t respond to the Guardian’s invitation to comment, but according to TikTok, 99.8% of all the videos removed from the platform for violating its “policies on regulated goods and services” were taken down before anyone had reported them. An Ofcom spokesperson said: “We’ve been pressing tech firms on what they’re doing to comply with their duties, and we’ve shown we’ll take action where companies fall short. Insights from academics like Prof Pudney are crucial to our work in enforcing the act, and we remain open to receiving further evidence on this matter.”Meanwhile, says Pudney, “very vulnerable young people are at risk.”Explore more on these topicsVapingDrugsCannabisHealthChildrenYoung peoplefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Plushies, Labubu dolls and Pokémon collectibles: claw machine craze sweeps Hong Kong | Hong Kong | The Guardian
description: Claw machine shops have proliferated in the territory in recent years, filling vacant spaces left behind by businesses that closed during the pandemic
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Claw machine shops have proliferated in the territory in recent years, filling vacant spaces left behind by businesses that closed during the pandemic
Content: Claw machines in Hong KongHong KongPlushies, Labubu dolls and Pokémon collectibles: claw machine craze sweeps Hong KongClaw machine shops have proliferated in the territory in recent years, filling vacant spaces left behind by businesses that closed during the pandemicJessie Pang in Hong Kong. Photography by Billy H C Kwok.Wed 5 Aug 2026 20.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTShareIn Hong Kong’s neon-lit arcades, a maze of claw machines illuminates the prizes of the day: plushies, Labubu dolls and an array of Pokémon collectibles.Across the city, claw machine shops have proliferated in recent years, now surpassing more than 2,500, many filling vacant spaces left by businesses that closed during the pandemic.View image in fullscreenClaw machines glow in the dark in Kwai Chung Plaza, Hong Kong.The venues, some of them open 24 hours a day, attract players of all ages.“Visiting a claw machine shop is like escaping!” says Hiu-ching, a 28-year-old radiographer who became so enthralled with the game that she decided to rent a machine and operate her own small stall.“I can’t resist playing the claw machine all the time. Because I lack skill, I usually play the claw machine with a lucky draw, which is similar to rolling dice.”View image in fullscreenSome venues in Hong Kong are open 24 hours a day.Some players are happy with any prize, while others are enticed by the possible resale value of some of the rare collectibles on offer.Every month, friends Jerry and Parco meet to play claw machines together, something they have been doing since last year. Parco says he once spent more than HK$4,000 ($510) playing claw machines floor by floor at the Dragon Centre, a small arcade in Hong Kong’s Sham Shui Po.View image in fullscreenJerry, 27, a property management officer, plays a claw machine in Kwai Chung Plaza.To most, claw machines are a bit of fun but there are concerns about people spending too much time on them. In May, Hong Kong’s home and youth affairs bureau proposed stricter regulations, including displaying addiction risk warnings.View image in fullscreenClaw machines are unregulated in Hong Kong, raising concerns they could lead to addictive behaviour.A 2022 court ruling exempted claw machines from public entertainment licences, leaving them unregulated in Hong Kong.Some serious claw machine players have gripes with operators, claiming they use bamboo toothpicks, needles, as well as plastic and metal strips to narrow the hole and slow down the machine’s crane, making it harder for people to win.View image in fullscreenHong Kong’s consumer council said complaints about claw machines surged from 16 in 2023 to 138 last year.“As someone who loves to play claw machines, I am quite unhappy about the current trend, as there are many ways to narrow or seal the hole,” says Parco.In June, Hong Kong’s consumer council said complaints about claw machines surged from 16 in 2023 to 138 last year, with players alleging operators altered settings to lower winning odds.But for many Hongkongers, claw machines are a cheap way to relieve stress.Ming Lee, a 38-year-old school cleaner, plays claw machines to relax. Over the past two years she has collected around a hundred plush toys from playing the machines.“It’s the thrill of successfully grabbing a prize that attracts me,” she says.View image in fullscreenFor many people, claw machines are a cheap way to relieve stress.Ki Kwong, a 25-year-old kitchen worker and a claw machine owner, says playing the machines is “a joy”. A message placed on one of his machines filled with plush toys reads: “Remember to be happy”. He also gives away the plushies he wins to his customers, if they don’t win themselves.View image in fullscreenClaw machine players can win anything from plushies to Labubu dolls and Pokémon collectibles.“After playing claw machines for so long, I want to share with others … I want to let people experience that playing the claw machine is not a pressure but a joy.”Kwong says he also sees claw machines as a way to connect with young people.“They are under a lot of pressure, and this is a stress-relieving activity.”

title: Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials say | Ebola | The Guardian
description: Cases have passed 4,000 and health watchdog plans to go door to door to find patients in major response escalation
Author: Kat Lay
Headline: Cases have passed 4,000 and health watchdog plans to go door to door to find patients in major response escalation
Content: Members of a Congolese Red Cross team with the coffin of a woman suspected of having died from Ebola virus in Bunia last June.Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMembers of a Congolese Red Cross team with the coffin of a woman suspected of having died from Ebola virus in Bunia last June.Photograph: Jospin Mwisha/AFP/Getty ImagesEbolaEbola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials sayCases have passed 4,000 and health watchdog plans to go door to door to find patients in major response escalationKat LayGlobal health correspondentThu 6 Aug 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe virus causing a massive outbreak of Ebola in theDemocratic Republic of the Congocould be mutating, health officials fear, as confirmed cases pass 4,000.Africa’s public health watchdog said the time for incremental action was over as they announced plans to scale up every aspect of the response and go “door to door” looking for patients.TheEbolaoutbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, was first reported on 15 May, although there are suspicions the disease could have been spreading since January.There have been3,973 cases and 1,801 deathsrecorded as of 4 August, according to the DRC’s national public health institute. Speaking on Thursday, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), told a press briefing cases had topped 4,000.The outbreak is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. There are eight times more cases, and six times more deaths than were recorded 11 weeks into the West Africa Ebola outbreak in 2014-18, which infected more than 28,000 people and killed at least 11,000.Kaseya said he had spoken to the director general of the World Health Organization, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, and they planned studies “to check if there is no additional issue, or maybe if the virus is not mutating. Because thelevel of severityof this Bundibugyo outbreak is unprecedented.”More than two-thirds of Ebola deaths are happening in the community rather than in treatment centres. In a treatment centre run by MSF in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province, 90% of admitted patients do not appear on authorities’ lists of contacts of known cases. Both factors indicate high levels of untracked transmission.Kaseya said contact tracing in the DRC was insufficient, with only 10 contacts identified for every Ebola patient, when about 40 would be the expected number.Ebola is a viral haemorrhagic fever that can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, organ damage and internal bleeding. The outbreak is centred on the conflict-affected mining province of Ituri, but has spread to Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo. There were 20 cases recorded in neighbouring Uganda before itbrought its outbreak under control.Dr Wessam Mankoula, acting head of emergency preparedness and response at Africa CDC, said response teams planned a shift “from contact tracing to active case search”, which would mean community health workers “moving from door to door” asking households if they had anyone sick with Ebola symptoms.He added: “I think the time for incremental action is over and we’re starting now the phase for scaling up.”Kaseya promised a “village-centered response” that would involve communities, more use of digital tools and greater action in the camps for people who have been internally displaced by conflict in affected provinces.Officials also said they planned to begin using antiviral remdesivir on a compassionate use basis to treat patients. They will also start testing whether Ervebo, a vaccine licensed for use against a different strain of Ebola, should be offered in the affected province, after receiving data suggesting that Bundibugyo caused less serious disease and “zero death” among people who had received that jab.“Seeing the expansion of this outbreak, only the public health measure will not be enough to quickly control or stop this outbreak,” said Dr Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC director of research, clinical trials and innovation.DRC authorities said they were investigating a suspected Ebola death on a boat heading to the capital, Kinshasa, from the north-east of the country, and that the other passengers on board would be quarantined and tested.Unicef warned that essential healthcare was being disrupted by the outbreak as fear of infection and service disruptions kept families away from clinics. In the outbreak’s centre, the mining town of Mongbwalu, the proportion of children receiving their first measles dose has fallen 69%.Explore more on these topicsEbolaDemocratic Republic of the CongoAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum | US foreign policy | The Guardian
description: State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon
Content: The closures are the latest in a process of cutbacks overseen by Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe closures are the latest in a process of cutbacks overseen by Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesUS foreign policyUS to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuumState department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and CameroonRobert Taitin WashingtonThu 6 Aug 2026 11.41 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 15.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and theCaribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China.The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada.The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the departmentfired more than 1,300 employees,including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants.More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to theAmerican Foreign Service Association.Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China.“China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” saidJeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee.“The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added. “Is that worth pulling back from these places whereChinais present?”The decision to close the consulate in Winnipeg has come in for criticism inCanada, on which Trump recently announced the imposition of 50% tariffs on a range of goods.Opened in 2001, the Winnipeg consulate has served to facilitate trade and investment issues mainly relating to the province of Manitoba, of which Winnipeg is the capital.Brad Kirbyson, a former political specialist who worked at the consulate for 20 years,told the Canadian broadcaster CBCthe closure could harm US interests.“I’m sure it’ll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there,” he said. “The United States found that it was a very long way between the US consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto.“It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world.”A spokesperson for the Canadian embassy in Washington said: “Canada and the US have a long history of collaboration on areas of shared interest, including through our foreign offices in both countries.”China does not have a diplomatic mission in Winnipeg, but it has a presence in St George’s, Nagoya and Medan. The US mission in St George’s, the capital of the Caribbean island ofGrenada, has full embassy status, while the Douala facility is defined as an “embassy branch office”.A state department spokesperson said: “The department is committed to following congressional notification procedures including post closures. We have nothing further to report at this time.“We are focused on ensuring our diplomatic footprint is efficient, effective and delivers results for the American people.”In a later statement, issued after this story was first published, a department spokesperson countered the assertion that the closures would benefit China.“Claims that China is filling a diplomatic vacuum is [sic] inherently false and we recommend that individuals who subscribe to this propaganda take a look at the so-called help China had in the recent earthquakes in Venezuela or to address the Ebola outbreak,” the spokesperson said.The White House’s office of management and budget has argued for a much more extensive closure program of up to 30 foreign missions.Democrats, supported by national security and foreign policy specialists, have countered that such moves will dangerously reduce the US’s diplomatic footprint and global influence, especially when combined with last year’s dismantling of USAID, the main overseas development body, which was drastically reduced in size before being bundled into the state department.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policyChinaCameroonIndonesiaJapanGrenadaCanadanewsShareReuse this content

title: Top Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stones | Soccer | The Guardian
description: David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone
Content: David Owori was described as ‘an inspiration to a generation’ by the Federation of Uganda Football Associations.Photograph: SC VillaView image in fullscreenDavid Owori was described as ‘an inspiration to a generation’ by the Federation of Uganda Football Associations.Photograph: SC VillaSoccerTop Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stonesDavid Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phoneCarlos MureithiThu 6 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatally injured during a robbery in the capital, Kampala, on Tuesday night.David Owori, who captained Sports Club Villa, a Uganda Premier League club, and represented the national team, was attacked after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings near his home in Makindye division.Racheal Kawala, a spokesperson for the Kampala Metropolitan police, said he was found unconscious by ​passersby, who took him to a nearby hospital. He was ​transferred to another hospital, where he was pronounced dead on Wednesday.Witnesses said attackers hit the footballer with paving stones before robbing him and fleeing, leaving him unconscious,the BBC reported.Owori, 27, was a right-back and midfielder for SC Villa. He helped the team win a record 17th Uganda Premier League title in 2024.He started his senior career in 2016 at the Uganda Premier League side Vipers Sports Club and had stints in Europe with Vélez CF in Spain and Utsiktens BK in Sweden.He played for the national team in the qualifiers for the 2021AfricaCup of Nations.SC Villasaid: “It is with profound sorrow that we announce the untimely passing of our captain, Owori, who had been receiving treatment at Case Clinic following an attack by suspected thugs. Our deepest condolences and prayers are with his family.”The Federation ​of Uganda Football Associationssaid: “David was not just a footballer. He was ​both a leader and an inspiration to a generation. As ​Captain of SC Villa, he led with courage, humility and passion. In the Uganda Cranes jersey, he carried the hopes of a nation.”It added: “We have lost a son, a leader and a star. His light on and off the pitch will never be forgotten.”The Ugandan parliament observed a minute of silence in Owori’s honour on Wednesday.In June Sydney Gongodyo, a Ugandan rugby international, ​died after a mob attacked him in Kampala, mistaking him for a thief, police said.Uganda’s National Council of Sports said: “Sadly, ​Ugandan sport has been hit with many such ​tragedies lately, and we hope for justice and a lasting solution.”Explore more on these topicsFootballUgandaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Nigerian security forces free more than 300 hostages in ‘largest single-day recovery’ | Nigeria | The Guardian
description: President hails operation to rescue captives held in dense forests of Kainji Lake national park in north-central region
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: President hails operation to rescue captives held in dense forests of Kainji Lake national park in north-central region
Content: More than 160 of the freed abductees had been kidnapped in a February attack on Woro, Kwara state, pictured.Photograph: Light Oriye Tamunotonye/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMore than 160 of the freed abductees had been kidnapped in a February attack on Woro, Kwara state, pictured.Photograph: Light Oriye Tamunotonye/AFP/Getty ImagesNigeriaNigerian security forces free more than 300 hostages in ‘largest single-day recovery’President hails operation to rescue captives held in dense forests of Kainji Lake national park in north-central regionEromo Egbejulein Abidjan and agenciesThu 6 Aug 2026 08.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigerian security forces have rescued more than 300 abducted people in what the president, Bola Ahmed Tinubu, hailed as the largest single-day hostage recovery in the country’s history.The release was announced on Wednesday after a joint operation, conducted by the military, police and counter-terrorism units, freed victims held captive in the dense forests of the Kainji Lake national park in the north-central region.Among those who regained freedom were 163 people abducted in February duringa deadly raidon thevillage of Woroin Kwara state, and 145 others seized primarily from the neighbouring Niger state. Both states are flanked to the west by Benin, where militant attacks have been surging in recent times. Officials confirmed the survivors are receiving medical evaluations at an army installation before being reunited with their families.View image in fullscreenA woman walks past debris, burnt structures and damaged shops after the February attack on Woro.Photograph: Light Oriye Tamunotonye/AFP/Getty Images“The successful execution of this intelligence-led operation demonstrates the growing efficiency and collaboration among our security services,” Tinubu said ina statementon the presidency’s website. “I commend our gallant men and women in uniform for their bravery and unwavering commitment to safeguarding Nigerian lives.”The government spokesperson Bayo Onanuga said the rescue operation was part of the president’s resolve to “restore lasting peace across every corner of the nation”.‘They killed my sons’: chief of Nigerian village where jihadists massacred hundreds recounts night of terrorRead moreIn the last decade, kidnapping for ransom has become endemic in Africa’s most populous country, especially in the north where different armed groups includingbandit gangsand jihadists roam large unoccupied forests and shrublands.Between July 2024 and June 2025, at least 4,722 people were kidnapped across 997 reported incidents, leading to at least 762 deaths, according to a report by the Lagos-based geopolitical advisory SBM Intelligence. In that 12-month period, abductors demanded ₦48bn ($35m or £26m) in payments, with families and communities ultimately handing over at least ₦2.57bn in ransom to secure the release of their loved ones.Ahead of January’s presidential election in which Tinubu is seeking a second four-year term, the government has been ramping up reforms and rescue operations as insecurity worsens.The latest rescue was announced in the same week the army declared the governor ofIslamic StateWest Africa Province, Abu Musa al-Mangawi Baa Shuwa, and his deputy, Amirul Jaish Muhammad Jidda, wanted. The duo run the Islamic State-affiliated Boko Haram offshoot operating primarily around the Lake Chad basin, which straddles Cameroon, Chad, Niger and Nigeria.View image in fullscreenTeachers and students went to Lagos in June to call for the release of those abducted from a school in Oyo state. Security services freed at least 40 students and teachers in July.Photograph: Emmanuel Adegboye/EPAIn July, security services freed at least 40 students and teachers who had been kidnapped in Mayfrom a school in Oyoin south-western Nigeria.Last week, the presidencyannounced a salary increaseworth 30% to 80% for thousands of soldiers, the largest hike in years for an army once seen as one of the continent’s most powerful but now derided as underfunded and unequipped to handle concurrent insurgencies across Nigerian territory.Explore more on these topicsNigeriaBoko HaramIslamic StateAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Morocco feels emboldened’: Trump’s influence in spotlight after Ceuta disaster | Morocco | The Guardian
description: Washington-Rabat ties under scrutiny as questions swirl over what led to deadly influx into tiny Spanish territory
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Washington-Rabat ties under scrutiny as questions swirl over what led to deadly influx into tiny Spanish territory
Content: Morocco’s foreign minister, Nasser Bourita, sits next to Donald Trump as he holds up the signed founding charter of his Board of Peace in January.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMorocco’s foreign minister, Nasser Bourita, sits next to Donald Trump as he holds up the signed founding charter of his Board of Peace in January.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesMorocco‘Morocco feels emboldened’: Trump’s influence in spotlight after Ceuta disasterWashington-Rabat ties under scrutiny as questions swirl over what led to deadly  influx into tiny Spanish territoryAshifa Kassamin MadridThu 6 Aug 2026 05.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe cosy relationship between Washington and Rabat has long been flaunted by both sides, from Morocco’s announcement this year that it would be the first African state to join Donald Trump’sBoard of Peaceto the congratulatory message recently sent by Trump to mark King Mohammed VI’s 27 years in power.The latest example landed this week. As Spain grappled with the aftermath ofthe sudden influx– and swift return – of more than 70,000 people into Ceuta, Morocco’s monarch confirmedhe had nameda $1bn highway flanking the disputed territory of Western Sahara after Trump.The deepening ties have come under renewed scrutiny as questions continue to swirl over what exactly led to the deadly mass border crossing into the tiny Spanish territory in northAfrica.“I think there’s enough evidence to hypothesise or claim thatMoroccois behind this,” said Riccardo Fabiani, the north Africa project director for the International Crisis Group. “But there was no clear trigger for this, and this is what is puzzling for everyone.”0:44Migrants in Spain’s Ceuta enclave escorted back to Morocco – videoObservers have suggested Spain’s recent rapprochement with Rabat’s archrival, Algeria, could have set off Morocco. But another, perhaps more plausible explanation pointed towards the US, said Fabiani.“It’s obviously impossible to demonstrate,” he said. “But in terms of plausibility, I don’t think it’s impossible to imagine that Morocco might have done something to earn brownie points with its allies, given that Morocco and this particular administration in Washington do have a very close, excellent relationship.”While Morocco had probably not “masterminded” the surge into Ceuta, he said, its relationship with the Trump administration – along with the Moroccan king’s desire to keep its claim to Ceuta in the spotlight – may have affectedhow it respondedto fast-spreading online rumours about the Spanish border being thrown open.View image in fullscreenA young person is escorted by Spanish security forces after attempting to cross into Ceuta on Saturday.Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters“For sure the Moroccan security forces were monitoring those conversations,” said Fabiani. “They saw that and there was probably some conversation where they decided to do nothing and see where this goes.”What followedmade headlinesacross the globe as tens of thousands of people swam or waded across one of the EU’s two land borders with Africa. As Spain scrambled to cope, far-right voices seized on the images.In the US, the vice-president, JD Vance, and the state departmentblamedthe influx on the Socialist-led government of Spain, while Trump warned that electing Democrats would make what happened in Spain “look small-time”. At no point did any of them mention Morocco or the potential role it might have played.Trump and his administration have long been open about the deep antipathy they feel for Pedro Sánchez, the Spanish prime minister, whoserefusalto allow the US to use its airbases during the Iran war,rejectionof the 5% defence spending target andvociferous criticismof Israel’s actions in Gaza have arguably made Spain the administration’s least favourite EU country.The American response seemed to be a triumph for Rabat, whose relationship with the US president traces back to his first term,when Morocco agreedto normalise ties with Israel in exchange for Trump’s recognition of its sovereignty claim over the disputed territory ofWestern Sahara.Since then, Morocco’s all-powerful monarch had doubled down on outreach efforts, said Fabiani. “The Moroccans have really made extra efforts to cultivate every single major decision-maker within the administration, including the president himself, to make sure that this administration will support, until the end, the Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara.”A hint that the relationship could help Morocco lay claim to more than Western Sahara came in a recent US congressional reportthat appearedto be sympathetic to Morocco’s refusal to recognise Ceuta as Spanish territory, describing it as “Spanish-administered” rather than a part of Spain, as it has been since 1580.Days after the influx, interest in Ceuta remained heightened among those close to both Trump and the Israeli government, said Haizam Amirah-Fernández, the director of the Madrid-based Centre for Contemporary Arab Studies. “They haven’t stopped talking about Ceuta for several days in a row, which is quite striking.”View image in fullscreenRed Cross personnel distributing food at  Trampolín beach in Ceuta this week.Photograph: REDUAN/EPAWhat had been laid bare was Rabat’s willingness to use “hybrid tactics to achieve political objectives”, said Amirah-Fernández, drawing a parallel with May 2021 when Rabat loosened border controls toallow more than 8,000 peopleto cross into Ceuta in a show of anger over Madrid’s decision to allow a Western Sahara pro-independence leader to travel to Spain to be treated for Covid-19.This time around, as nearly 10 times more people crossed into Ceuta, it set off a bout offinger-pointingacross the EU rather than any kind of concerted effort to push back using the bloc’s status as Morocco’s largest trading partner and largest foreign investor. “The reaction of several governments in the EU was, in the end, what the White House was looking for – the erosion of solidarity between European partners,” said Amirah-Fernández.Senior officials in Morocco havepushed back against accusationsit was in any way complicit.View image in fullscreenKing Mohammed VI and Trump in 2018.Photograph: Ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty ImagesAt the Rabat-based Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis, there was little doubt that relations between Morocco and the US were in their “golden era”. Even so, the country’s approach to the Trump administration remained pragmatic, said Said Saddiki, a senior fellow at the institute.“Moroccan policymakers are well aware of President Trump’s transactional style and have sought to preserve Morocco’s strategic autonomy,” Saddiki said in an email, citing efforts to maintain partnerships with the EU, China and the Gulf states, among others.“The relationship with the Trump administration has strengthened Morocco’s international position, but so far it has not come at the expense of its relations with Spain or the European Union.”For Fabiani, the events in Ceuta served to underscore the perils of Europe’s reliance on north African states to control migration flows. “This has made Europe entirely vulnerable and dependent on the goodwill of a country like Morocco,” he said. “Morocco is a partner, but at the same time it has its own interests. This vulnerability was on show.”This weakness could become more of an issue as time passed, given Morocco’s perception that the issue of Ceuta remained unsettled, Fabiani warned. “And Morocco feels emboldened, and there is an administration in Washington that is willing to back it up,” he said. “I don’t think Europe is ready for what comes next because it could get much more complicated.”Explore more on these topicsMoroccoDonald TrumpUS foreign policySpainMigrationRefugeesMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Mamma mia!’: Trump tariffs refund ignites 53% profit spike at Nintendo | Nintendo | The Guardian
description: Profit jump fuelled largely by unknown US refund amount as Japanese video game firm records quarterly sales drop
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Profit jump fuelled largely by unknown US refund amount as Japanese video game firm records quarterly sales drop
Content: Nintendo said sales of its Switch 2 console, which was released last summer, maintained strong momentum but overall sales dropped 10%.Photograph: Richard A Brooks/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNintendo said sales of its Switch 2 console, which was released last summer, maintained strong momentum but overall sales dropped 10%.Photograph: Richard A Brooks/AFP/Getty ImagesNintendo‘Mamma mia!’: Trump tariffs refund ignites 53% profit spike at NintendoProfit jump fuelled largely by unknown US refund amount as Japanese video game firm records quarterly sales dropKalyeena MakortoffThu 6 Aug 2026 07.11 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNintendo has reported a jump in profits, as the Japanese game maker’s earnings were buoyed up by a long-awaited refund on Donald Trump’s tariffs.The company said profits surged 53.5% to ¥147.4bn (£694m) over the three months to June, substantially beating expert forecasts for ¥77.8bn.Nintendo said sales of its Switch 2 console, which was released last summer, “maintained strong sales momentum”, while popular games such as Yoshi and the Mysterious Book, Star Fox, and Pokémon Pokopia “performed steadily”. However, that did not make up for an overall drop in sales compared with the same period last year, with revenue down by 10% to ¥517.8bn.‘Let’s-a go!’ The story of Nintendo – podcastRead moreInstead, Nintendo said profits were aided by a refund on US tariffs, after the country’ssupreme court ruledin February that Donald Trump’s sweeping “liberation day” trade levies were illegal.TheTrump administrationhas refunded about $100bn from the tariffs charged before the court ruling, representing 60% of the total $165bn collected. Trump has continued to pitch tariffs as a solution for the US economy, bringing back domestic production, securing better trade deals and closing the deficit in the federal budget.Nintendo’s Tokyo-listed shares were up 2.87% on Thursday after the earnings release.The companyfiled a lawsuitweeks after the US supreme court ruling, demanding a full refund from the White House that would cover what it spent on tariffs, plus interest.While a refund now appears to have come through, Nintendo stopped short of confirming the full amount, at a time when it is still appears to be resisting calls to pass those refunds on to consumers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLast month, Nintendo was hit with aclass action lawsuit on behalf of customers, which claims the company hiked its prices because of tariffs but later benefited from the refunds. Nintendo’s lawyers described the lawsuit as “meritless”, and that the price customers paid represented “the purchase price of the goods they wanted and received.”Last month, Trump imposed afresh round of tariffson more than 80 countries, including Japan, in a move that is likely to pose further problems for companies such as Nintendo. However, a coalition of 25 US statesare now suing the Trump administration over the levies, potentially opening the door to another round of refunds for beleaguered exporters.Explore more on these topicsNintendoTrump tariffsNintendo Switch 2GamesJapanTariffsInternational tradenewsShareReuse this content

title: Starbucks Korea raided by police after ‘Tank Day’ campaign sparks public outrage | South Korea | The Guardian
description: Coffee chain has faced backlash over marketing promotion tied to anniversary of Gwangju massacre
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Coffee chain has faced backlash over marketing promotion tied to anniversary of Gwangju massacre
Content: Protesters call for a boycott of Starbucks Korea outside the company’s headquarters in Seoul.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters call for a boycott of Starbucks Korea outside the company’s headquarters in Seoul.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesSouth KoreaStarbucks Korea raided by police after ‘Tank Day’ campaign sparks public outrageCoffee chain has faced backlash over marketing promotion tied to anniversary of Gwangju massacreAssociated Press in SeoulThu 6 Aug 2026 03.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouth Korean police have raided the headquarters of Starbucks Korea as part of an investigation into a marketing campaign accused of trivialising the country’s 1980s pro-democracy movement.Investigators searched the building in southern Seoul on Tuesday, police said on Wednesday. No further details were released, although South Korean media reported that officers also searched the homes of theStarbucksKorea executives.How a Starbucks marketing stunt spiralled into mass boycotts in South KoreaRead moreThecoffee chain triggered a public outcryafter launching a range of stainless-steel reusable tumblers it called “SS Tank” and declaring 18 May “Tank Day”. The date marks the anniversary of the 1980 Gwangju uprising, when pro-democracy demonstrators were brutally suppressed by South Korea’s then military-backed government.The campaign also used the slogan “Thwack it on the table!”, which many interpreted as a reference to a notorious 1987 police claim that the student activistPark Jong-chuldied after investigators “hit the desk with a thwack”. Authorities had falsely used the phrase to conceal the fact that Park had died by torture during an interrogation.The backlash over the coffee chain’s marketing campaign prompted Shinsegae Group, which owns a 67.5% stake in Starbucks Korea, to cancel the promotion within hoursand dismiss the company’s chief executive. The Shinsegae chair, Chung Yong-jin, later issued a televised apology.Starbucks Koreaclosed all of its stores nationwideon 22 June for mandatory training in history and social awareness.The police investigation was launched after complaints from relatives of victims of the Gwangju crackdown, in which, official records say, about 200 people were killed.South Korea’s transition to democracy gained momentum in 1987, when the authoritarian president Chun Doo-hwan, whose government had overseen the Gwangju crackdown, accepted constitutional reforms introducing direct presidential elections after months of nationwide pro-democracy protests.Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreaStarbucksAsia PacificFood & drink industryRetail industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We expected it, but now it’s here’: on the frontline of Australia’s bird flu outbreak, people are distressed  | Bird flu | The Guardian
description: As Australia prepares for the H5 bird flu to potentially rip through hundreds of species, residents of the Limestone Coast are already seeing the impacts
Author: Petra Stock
Headline: As Australia prepares for the H5 bird flu to potentially rip through hundreds of species, residents of the Limestone Coast are already seeing the impacts
Content: A dead greater crested tern found at Pelican Point on the Limestone Coast in South Australia.Photograph: Veronica MillerView image in fullscreenA dead greater crested tern found at Pelican Point on the Limestone Coast in South Australia.Photograph: Veronica MillerAustralian climate and environmental reportingBird flu‘We expected it, but now it’s here’: on the frontline of Australia’s bird flu outbreak, people are distressedAs Australia prepares for the H5 bird flu to potentially rip through hundreds of species, residents of the Limestone Coast are already seeing the impactsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSupported byAbout this contentPetra StockThu 6 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 17.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has only been three weeks sinceH5 bird flu was detectedon South Australia’s Limestone Coast and already encounters with sick or dead birds are becoming commonplace.Maureen Christie, who lives in the seaside town of Carpenter Rocks, has been observing and protecting birds in the region for decades. She is now witnessing many stricken and suffering.“It’s just awful,” Christie said, who helped establish the Friends of Shorebirds SE more than 20 years ago. “We expected it but, now it’s here, it’s just traumatic.”The state’s south-east is renowned for its bird life, she said, which includes resident hooded plovers and oyster catchers, along with fly-ins from other countries, such as double-banded plovers, red-necked stints, sanderlings and ruddy turnstones.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailLocals have been following state government advice to “avoid, record and report”, she said. Christie said many people have been getting in touch by email and phone to relay their own sightings and reports. “Everybody’s feeling distressed, but everybody’s trying to be supportive of one another.”Since thefirst casein a local Australian seabird – a greater crested tern – was detected in early July, the region has seen dozens more suspected and confirmed cases, including the first confirmedmass mortalityevent atBaudin Rocks, a group of islets about 8km from the coastal town of Robe.“Robe has a very special and unique environment that the local community knows, uses, celebrates and cares for,” the president of Friends of Little Dip Conservation Park and Robe Coast Care, Roland Wells, said. There’s everything from migratory, coastal and inland birds, wombats, wallabies and echidnas, as well as marine mammals such as sea lions, seals and dolphins.He said people have undertaken conservation work over many decades to support shorebirds, which makes the recent arrival of bird flu “very upsetting”.The situation has escalated considerably over the past week. Council officers from Robe district council have been identifying and reporting sick and deceased birds almost daily, mainly greater crested terns and some silver gulls.Penguins and dolphins among nearly 400 Australian species under threat from bird flu as ‘true extent of disaster’ revealedRead moreA spokesperson for South Australia’s primary industries department said crested terns – which make up many of the bird flu cases – “commonly commingle” with other species like cormorants, gulls, grebes, ducks and other tern species. This increases the potential for transmission.“From a conservation perspective, several threatened and priority species have been identified as high risk, includingfairy terns,” the spokesperson said. “Marine mammals are also being closely monitored, with Australian sea lions and long-nosed fur seals among the species considered most vulnerable to potential impacts from the virus.”Wildlife carers and clinics – now required to don personal protective equipment and undertake strict cleaning and quarantine measures when dealing with other wild birds injured by cars, in dog and cat attacks or entanglement – have been calling on the state government for support.Mish Simpson, from SKER wildlife veterinary centre, said the clinic was already at capacity before bird flu. But now, more wild birds are being brought in because other vets have stopped accepting them, partly due to the additional requirements and the risk of exposure for other animals.Simpson is concerned there is not enough emphasis on slowing the spread, which would give vets, carers and the community more time to prepare. For example, she said, the dead bodies of infected birds are often being left in the environment, where they pose an infection risk to other wildlife, particularly scavengers.As the federal environment minister, Murray Watt,observed on Monday, the events rapidly unfolding in the south-east, and around Australia, are “the beginning of what is likely to be a long, difficult journey in terms of the impacts on wildlife”.InVictoria, the chief veterinary officer, Dr Graeme Cooke, said recent aerial and ground surveillance near Portland and Nelson has already shown “a clear increase in the number of dead terns along that part of the coast”, consistent with deaths in South Australia.“Last week we talked about individual detections; the first cases of the H5 bird flu in Victoria. We are now seeing a change.”What that means for hundreds of native species and the people who care for them remains uncertain.Explore more on these topicsBird fluAustralian climate and environmental reportingSouth AustraliaVictoriaWildlifeBirdsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Minns said he wouldn’t ‘gloat’ about Icac hearings into the Liberals. Instead, he’s quietly taking out the trash | New South Wales politics | The Guardian
description: Amid revelations that could damage the opposition’s state election hopes, the NSW government dropped key documents on three contentious issues
Author: Penry Buckley
Headline: Amid revelations that could damage the opposition’s state election hopes, the NSW government dropped key documents on three contentious issues
Content: The NSW premier Chris Minns has defended his government’s timing in releasing controversial reports.Photograph: Gaye Gerard/AAPView image in fullscreenThe NSW premier Chris Minns has defended his government’s timing in releasing controversial reports.Photograph: Gaye Gerard/AAPNew South Wales politicsAnalysisMinns said he wouldn’t ‘gloat’ about Icac hearings into the Liberals. Instead, he’s quietly taking out the trashPenry BuckleyAmid revelations that could damage the opposition’s state election hopes, the NSW government dropped key documents on three contentious issuesFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastThu 6 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.11 EDTShareDuring the first week of the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s Operation Rosny’shearings into allegationsagainst people associated with the New South Wales Liberal party, Chris Minns took the high ground.“There’ll be no gloating or taking political advantage,” the NSW Labor premier told reporters. “It’s an important process and ultimately, hopefully, it makes all political parties cleaner and sends a message to anyone who’s thinking of breaching the laws or committing a corrupt act, that someone is watching.”There’s a less generous way to describe what the Labor government has quietly gone about doing during Icac’s second of at least eight weeks of hearings: “Taking out the trash.”This week the NSW government dropped key documents on not one but three contentious issues, burying them – intentionally or not – amid revelations that could damage the election hopes of state Liberal and opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, who was not an MP at the time of the alleged wrongdoing being investigated by the corruption watchdog.Texts suggest Angus Taylor ‘paid money to the Reformers … or was refusing to’, Icac inquiry hearsRead moreThe first document, a long-awaited report into hate speech laws by the former supreme court justice John Sackar, was tabled by the attorney general, Michael Daley, during an Icac appearance by Liberal leader in the upper house, Damien Tudehope.Tudehope, as shadow attorney general, had been leading a fight for the release of the Sackar review, which had been gathering dust since November – and which the government had argued was “cabinet in confidence”. The Labor ministerJohn Graham was suspendedover the government’s refusal to release it in May.Giving evidence on Tuesday morning Tudehope defended talks he gave at conservative Liberal events, including one against the Safe Schools program, which had a stated aim of keeping gay and transgender students safe.View image in fullscreenNSW Liberal member of the Legislative Council Damien Tudehope (right) arrives to give evidence during the Icac Operation Rosny hearings.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPOn Tuesday afternoon, Daley announced that the government would not implement the Sackar review’s key recommendation, to expand a controversial offence for inciting hatred on the grounds of race to other protected attributes, including religion, sexual orientation and gender identity, because it raised “complex questions”.But rather than the focus being on the government’s report, Tudehope, who is not named in Icac’s allegations and has stepped aside from his shadow cabinet roles during the inquiry,found himself making headlines. After the admission that he had leaked a confidential parliamentary report to conservative Liberal factional group the Reformers, his future as shadow attorney general is now uncertain.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailOn Wednesday, with the Liberals still reeling from Tudehope’s testimony and Icac hearing evidence from the younger brother of former Liberal premier, Dominic Perrottet, Jean-Claude Perrottet, the government released two more documents.At a press conference on Wednesday on the government’s response to the inquest into the Bondi Junction attack, amid questions about why it had only committed “in principle” to a recommendation to provide short- and long-term accommodation for people experiencing mental health issues and homelessness, Daley rejected the suggestion the government had buried the Sackar report the previous day.“A few weeks ago we were getting criticised for not releasing the report. Now we’re getting criticised for releasing the report,” he said. “What day would have been better? Sunday be better?”That same afternoon, Daley tabled legal advice sought in response to a committee report which had found the state’s top prosecutor, the director of public prosecutions, Sally Dowling, lied under oath to an inquiry.The allegations relate to a decision by the DPP to pitch a story about an Indigenous child who performed an acknowledgment of country during a sentencing hearing.Dowling admitted her office had pitched the storyto radio station 2GB but denied she had authorised it. The DPP has rejected the committee’s findings.The tabled advice from former Bar Association president Noel Hutley SC said there was no “no positive basis” to reject Dowling’s account “and find that she, in fact, gave false evidence”. “For such a serious finding to be substantiated, something more than mere disbelief of the director’s evidence was required,” Hutley wrote.The committee had written about the difficulty it experienced after other ODPP witnesses did not appear following a court of appeal decision in favour of the premier’s chief of staff, which removed the upper house’s power to compel witnesses to appear before inquiries – another issue Tudehope had been prosecuting. But on Wednesday, Daley said he considered the committee’s findings “closed”.The Australian high court will hear an appeal by the upper house against the court of appeal decision later this year.Despite his claims of not taking “political advantage”, the premier has not resisted delighting in the Liberals’ troubles.The Icac spotlight has shone on Dominic Perrottet’s brother – and it won’t be the last we hear from his familyRead moreAs Tudehope gave evidence to Icac on Tuesday, Minns used a speech in question time to reference the shadow attorney general, “who is in the news at the moment”. He also referenced Chris Rath, another Liberal frontbencher in the upper house caught up in the Icac inquiry.Last week, after the Sydney Morning Herald revealed Rath had helped members of the Reformers evade summons to appear before a 2023 parliamentary inquiry, the premier used it as a pretext to reject calls for the restoration of witness powers. Rath, who is not named in Icac’s allegations, has apologised after receiving a caution from the parliamentary privileges committee.Minns told a press conference: “I think this is exhibit 400 as to why the upper house shouldn’t be given extraordinary police powers. They’re desperate to get the power of arrest.”On Thursday, criticising an upper house amendment which would increase the number of political staffers in crossbench and opposition offices, Minns took open aim at Tudehope.“This is happening at the same time as the Icac is reporting incredibly concerning details of political staff [allegedly] not being used for taxpayer purposes, but for internalLiberal partypurposes,” he said.“One of the people who would get extra staff as a result of this amendment is Damien Tudehope. I think it’s extraordinary.”On Thursday, Minns defended the timing of the release of the Sackar report, nine months after it was tabled: “[Icac] goes for eight weeks. If … we went by that logic, we couldn’t do anything.“It wasn’t released at midnight and on Sunday. It was during work hours, at the beginning of the work week. It had been asked for by the crossbench repeatedly.”But even with the Labor taking out the trash while the Liberals stare down scandal, neither could end up winners – as Minns himself acknowledged.Last week, as One Nation rose in the polls, Minns said the Icac inquiry was not “necessarily the big boon for our political party that many believe”.“My concern is that people say, ‘Well I’ve seen Labor at Icac, and I’ve seen the Liberal party at Icac. I’m going to vote for a third party this time.’”Explore more on these topicsNew South Wales politicsIndependent Commission Against CorruptionChris MinnsNew South WalesLiberal partyLabor partyanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Can Australia make housing affordable while avoiding a major market crash? We may soon find out | Housing | The Guardian
description: Politicians’ fever dreams of ‘sustainable price increases’ – where values keep rising, but by less than wages – could happen
Author: Patrick Commins
Headline: Politicians’ fever dreams of ‘sustainable price increases’ – where values keep rising, but by less than wages – could happen
Content: Less generous tax settings for property investors has made betting on rising home prices less attractive. Where this will settle is impossible to predict.Photograph: Diego Fedele/AAPView image in fullscreenLess generous tax settings for property investors has made betting on rising home prices less attractive. Where this will settle is impossible to predict.Photograph: Diego Fedele/AAPHousingAnalysisCan Australia make housing affordable while avoiding a major market crash? We may soon find outPatrick ComminsPoliticians’ fever dreams of ‘sustainable price increases’ – where values keep rising but by less than wages – could happenFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastThu 6 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 20.18 EDTShareThe Reserve Bank has hiked interest rates and the property market is in retreat. So far, so normal.Or is it?There is a sense that this year’s fall in home prices feels different from previous episodes. The data tells another story.Over the past four decades there have been seven property market downturns of varying length and depth, according to analysis put together by Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist.They are often triggered by interest rate hikes, which make home loans more expensive, but they also occur during crises and policy changes.Graph showing a history of property price declinesFor instance, there was a short-lived fall from April 2020 during the Covid-19 pandemic lockdowns, when the average capital city home value fell by 1.5% over three months.Two years later, and at the tail end of a massive boom, there was a much steeper decline after the RBA started its rearguard battle against roaring inflation.Between April 2022 and January 2023, prices dropped by 8.1%.The largest downturn in property prices in recent memory started in September 2017, when average capital city home values declined by 8.2% – albeit over a much longer 19 months. That time it was a regulatory crackdown on investor lending in an attempt to squash some of the speculative fervour that had gripped the market.Which brings us to today.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailOliver forecasts that average prices across the capital cities will keep falling until about April next year, capping a 7.8% drop from top to bottom.That would certainly make it among the steepest falls in the past four decades – UBS says the average since the early 1990s has been a 5% decline over 13 months.Oliver says this year’s home price declines started with the three straight interest rate hikes but are now more about the shift in sentiment triggered by the government’s changes to property investor taxes – a psychological twist that makes it harder to predict how things will turn out from here.“So far it looks similar to past cyclical downturns, but I think it’s early days yet,” he says.It’s also worth noting that the downturn looks very different depending on where you are in the country, as analysis from NAB shows.For example, the bank’s economists predict the peak-to-trough declines in Sydney and Melbourne will be in the order of 10%, versus 2% to 4% falls across the mid-sized capitals. And looking at performance by calendar year – instead of just the periods where prices are falling – values in Brisbane, Perth, Adelaide and Hobart are predicted to be higher in 2026.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTable showing property price changes in Australian state capitalsThey expect prices to level out in early 2027 before beginning to grow “modestly” through the second half of next year thanks to lower interest rates and improving sentiment.“Ultimately, we see house prices continuing to be well supported by the imbalance of supply and demand,” they note.Still, change is in the air. Less generous tax settings for property investors has changed the maths and made betting on rising home prices less attractive. Where this will settle is impossible to predict.Interest rates are expected to be structurally higher than they were before the pandemic. That means mainstream politicians’ fever dreams of “sustainable price increases” – where values keep rising but by less than wages – may happen.NAB forecasts pretty stagnant property price growth next year. Will that be the new normal? And if it is, surely that is a step in the right direction on the long, long road to achieving a more affordable property market without a major crash?In the meantime, expect the government to cop plenty of flak for “attacking aspiration” or “deliberately crashing Australians’ wealth”. But as Oliver says, despite all the angst and outrage, politicians of all stripes profess to want more affordable homes.Slashing immigration, turbocharging building or hiking taxes – or some combination of these – all lead to a situation where house prices would come off and be more stagnant over time.That may well be where we are heading now. It’s hardly a solution to our housing mess but it’s a start.Patrick Commins is Guardian Australia’s economics editorExplore more on these topicsHousingInterest ratesReserve Bank of AustraliaAustralian economyAustralian politicsTaxanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Leipzig drone bomb was found near Ukrainian plane carrying ammunition, say police | Germany | The Guardian
description: Germany investigating whether foreign state involved as minister says ‘ripped’ detonator stopped device going off
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Germany investigating whether foreign state involved as minister says ‘ripped’ detonator stopped device going off
Content: A bomb disposal robot and forensic technician at Leipzig airport on Wednesday.Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/APView image in fullscreenA bomb disposal robot and forensic technician at Leipzig airport on Wednesday.Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/APGermanyLeipzig drone bomb was found near Ukrainian plane carrying ammunition, say policeGermany investigating whether foreign state involved as minister says ‘ripped’ detonator stopped device going offEurope live – latest updatesDeborah Colein BerlinThu 6 Aug 2026 11.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 16.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA catastrophe with multiple casualties was possibly narrowly averted by the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, German officials said, as they examined whether a foreign state could be behind the plot.One of the Ukrainian aircraft next to where the bomb drone was found was loaded with military ammunition, according to a classified police report quoted by the public broadcasters WDR and NDR and the Süddeutsche newspaper.The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, who said on Wednesday Germany faced a“new level of danger”, said only an apparently “ripped” detonator had prevented the device going off near Ukrainian cargo planes on the tarmac at the shipping and military hub.View image in fullscreenPolice officers search an area at Leipzig airport after the discovery of the drone.Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/APThe highly explosive Ukrainian cargo, with a tank filled with jet fuel, had apparently been transported from France to Leipzig shortly beforehand and was presumably intended for onward transport, the report said.The airport is about 12.5 miles (20km) from the centre of Leipzig, a city of more than 600,000 people. The facility hosts a major cargo processing centre that employs hundreds of people round the clock and is adjacent to two busy autobahn routes.The Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for EuropeRead moreThe Bild newspaper reported that the drone found near the Ukrainian plane had a handmade remote detonator that did not work, and investigators hoped it could offer clues as to its origin and the culprits.Leipzig airport’s status as a Nato and German military logistics hub, as well as the the base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines in Europe, has directed suspicion toward Russia, which German and European authorities say has carried out repeated sabotage attacks.The German government and authorities have stopped short of pointing the finger at Moscow for whatmarked a clear escalation of the threat level in Europe.But Dobrindt said investigators were treating the incident as part of a “professional hybrid threat scenario” with a focus on “foreign powers” as likely perpetrators.View image in fullscreenThe airport is a Nato and German military logistics hub and the base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines in Europe.Photograph: Axel Schmidt/ReutersRoderich Kiesewetter, a member of the German parliament’s intelligence committee, blamed Russia directly. “I consider the threat toGermanyposed by hybrid attacks orchestrated by Russia to be serious,” said Kiesewetter, a member of the co-ruling Christian Democrats.“I also believe that the attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport was a targeted hybrid attack – in other words, an attempted act of terrorism – orchestrated byRussia.”An airport staff member discovered the drone shortly before midnight on Tuesday, “hovering” near the ground between two Antonov Airlines An-124 cargo airplanes, among ​the world’s biggest freighters.Police said a drone defence sensor system at the airport, considered “critical infrastructure” by Germany, had not picked up the drone. They now believe based on security footage it had been on site for several hours before it was found.Dobrindt told reporters that the drone seemed to have been modified to circumvent electronic detection. It was attached to a package of explosives roughly the size of a fist, according to the WDR-NDR-Süddeutsche report, and investigators said the substance inside was believed to be semtex, a powerful plastic explosive.The discovery of the drone led the airport to suspend air traffic, forcing a DHL cargo plane from Marseille on its approach to take off again. It then collided with what is believed to have been a second drone.The media report said that plane had also been carrying unspecified “dangerous goods” before it made an emergency landing in Hanover, about 155 miles north-west, with minor damage.Bild said the drone that hit the DHL plane had a camera used to film the attack.Air traffic had been diverted on Wednesday from the airport’s southern runway but was back to normal on Thursday with no additional security measures reported.Ukraine has been using Leipzig airport as an alternate location for the transport of military goods since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to official records. German defence ministry officials said its armed forces were not conducting military transport operations at the airport at the time of the incident.The airport has previously been targeted. A firebomb, posted via DHL, exploded at the facility in July 2024 while a second was sent to the UK andcaught fire at a warehouse in Birmingham. Two similar packages were also found in Poland.A subsequent pan-European investigation identified 22 suspects in Lithuania and Poland who were suspected of having been employed by Russian intelligence.Testimony this week at a trial in Lithuania of five people suspected of mailing the incendiary devices showedhow narrowly the plane from Leipzig avoided being set on fire in mid-flight.A DHL company representative told the court the parcel ignited on the ground at its logistics centre at Leipzig airport shortly before loading, rather than during the flight, because the plane was delayed.Explore more on these topicsGermanyRussiaUkraineDrones (military)EuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ceuta residents ‘sad, helpless, anxious’ as up to 5,000 migrants remain in the city, president says – as it happened | Europe | The Guardian
description: Juan Jesús Vivas has been briefing EU lawmakers on the ‘humanitarian emergency’ and says updated death toll now lies at least 100 people
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Juan Jesús Vivas has been briefing EU lawmakers on the ‘humanitarian emergency’ and says updated death toll now lies at least 100 people
