Content: 08.21 EDTCeuta residents 'sad, helpless, anxious' as up to 5,000 migrants remain in the city, president saysOver in Brussels,Ceuta’s conservative president Juan Jesús Vivas is briefing European lawmakers on the situation in the city in the aftermath of last week’s migration crisis with Morocco.Police officers guard a group of migrants at El Trampolin beach in Ceuta, Spain.Photograph: REDUAN/EPAHe tells MEPs thatthe incident amount to “an invasion”defined as “an anomalous or ir regulation occupation of a specific place.”He says3,000 to 5,000 people migrants of the 80,000 who he says crossed the border still remain in the city,which “in no way allows us to say that our city has returned to normal.”“We have a situation wherethe influx has led to a humanitarian emergency of enormous proportions,compounded by disturbances to public order and a high risk to public safety.”He warns lawmakers that “our people feel sad, helpless, anxious, fearful and worried,and they have good reason to, because it is inevitable to wonder whether this will happen again at some point.”Vivas also says that “it has become evident” that “our security and integrity are in the hands of a third country, Morocco, that does not recognise our sovereignty.”He calls upon Spanish national authorities to “adopt whatever measures necessary to restore the normality,” including “immediate expulsion” of all people who crossed the border irregularly.He also laments the death of some 100 people who died during the crisis.ShareUpdated at08.22 EDT

title: Nearly 50 asylum seekers deported under ‘one in one out’ scheme have returned to the UK | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Figure raises questions about deal with France despite UK ministers insisting repeat arrivals will be removed
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Figure raises questions about deal with France despite UK ministers insisting repeat arrivals will be removed
Content: Migrants clamber on to a UK Border Force vessel.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/GettyView image in fullscreenMigrants clamber on to a UK Border Force vessel.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/GettyImmigration and asylumNearly 50 asylum seekers deported under ‘one in one out’ scheme have returned to the UKFigure raises questions about deal with France despite UK ministers insisting repeat arrivals will be removedDiane TaylorThu 6 Aug 2026 09.32 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost 50 asylum seekers deported using the “one in one out” scheme have been recorded as returning to the UK a second time, the Guardian has learned.In addition to the returnees detained by theHome Office, an unknown number are believed to have arrived in the UK undetected.The scheme, which began last September, allows the UK government to return people arriving on small boats toFrance, in exchange for a similar number of asylum seekers being brought to the UK legally. The aim is to deter asylum seekers from crossing the Channel in small boats.The Guardianpreviously revealedthat the first asylum seeker who returned to the UK a second time did so last October, a few weeks after being forcibly returned to France. But until now the number of people returning to the UK after forced return was not known.So far this year small boat crossings havereducedby about 43%. This fall is likely to be due to a variety of factors, including bad weather and a reduction in migrants arriving in Europe overall by about a third, as well as efforts by UK and French authorities to disrupt people smugglers.The rationale for sending a proportion of small boat arrivals back to France is that France is a safe country. Asylum seekers who have subsequently returned to the UK have argued that they faced threats from people smugglers in France, or feared being returned by French authorities to their home countries or to countries they passed through.Has the UK government’s strategy on small boat crossings been effective?Read moreAbout4% of small boat arrivalshave been returned to France so far under the “one in one out” deal.According to the Home Office, as of 30 June 2026, there were 1,117 individuals transferred to the UK and 1,087 individuals returned to France under “one in one out”. Officials say the treaty between UK and France has been amended so that second-time returnees to the UK will be once again returned to France.One asylum seeker who returned to the UK a second time in a lorry was eventually returned to France after spending five months in detention. He said he was accommodated for only a few days by French authorities. “There is nowhere for asylum seekers to go and be safe and have peace inEurope,” he said. “I’m sleeping on the streets of Paris because France wants to send me back to Bulgaria where I was fingerprinted. I was better off in a UK detention centre.”Griff Ferris, of Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants, said: “People fleeing war, persecution and climate destruction are forced to take incredibly dangerous routes to cross the Channel and get to the UK because there is no other way. We must let everyone access the same safe routes to travel that are open to so many, like the daily ferries between Calais and Dover.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Home Office spokesperson said: “Anyone looking to return to the UK after being removed under the UK-France agreement is wasting their time and money – and will be removed again. Under our payment by results returns agreement with France, we have removed more than 1,000 illegal migrants from British soil.“Hundreds of enforcement actions, including arrests, investigations, and sanctions have been pursued against migrant smuggling networks since the election, and we’ve returned or removed almost 70,000 illegal migrants.”France’s interior ministry has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeMigrationFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Danish pupils will have to orally defend essays in attempt to combat AI cheating | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Government introduces several measures, including monitoring of computers, for pupils aged 16 to 19
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Government introduces several measures, including monitoring of computers, for pupils aged 16 to 19
Content: Upper secondary schools will be required to monitor how computers are being used for written exams.Photograph: Posed by models; Solskin/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUpper secondary schools will be required to monitor how computers are being used for written exams.Photograph: Posed by models; Solskin/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Danish pupils will have to orally defend essays in attempt to combat AI cheatingGovernment introduces several measures, including monitoring of computers, for pupils aged 16 to 19Europe live – latest updatesMiranda BryantNordic correspondentThu 6 Aug 2026 07.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDanish teenagers will have to make an oral defence of their written essays to combat AI cheating, the government has announced.Pupils aged 16 to 19 at upper secondary school (known inDenmarkasgymnasiet) will also be encouraged to do written assignments at school under controlled conditions, including monitoring of their computer screens, rather than at home.The measures, announced on Thursday as pupils prepare to go back to school next week after the summer break, will come into immediate effect after Magnus Heunicke, the country’s education minister, demanded urgent action.“Unfortunately, we have a problem with AI cheating in upper secondary schools,” he said. “Action is needed now.”AI had posed a growing challenge to teaching and exams, the education ministry said. It is hoped the new measures will help to establish clearer guidelines for when pupils are not permitted to use it.The government is also preparing a comprehensive national strategy for AI use in all schools and the wider education sector.Heunicke said he would speak to schools, teachers and students to “ensure that AI does not undermine students’ competencies, professionalism and, not least, the ability to think for themselves”.The first measure to be introduced is the oral defence of exam assignments written at home. About 9,000 upper secondary school students each year write a big assignment (known asstørre skriftlige opgaveor SSO), which they will now have to defend orally. The ministry said it would speak to schools about the best way to do this.Upper secondary schools will also be required to use monitoring tools to oversee how computers are being used for written exams. They are required to install firewalls to filter what is available on the school network during exams and teaching.The third measure is a plea to schools to encourage pupils to do more of their written assignments at school under controlled conditions, to “follow the students’ work process, provide relevant feedback and create a more accurate basis for assessment”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe ready availability of AI tools is upending education around the world for teachers and pupils, leaving governments scrambling to assess if and how they should intervene.In neighbouring Sweden, a study found that the number of students suspended or warned for unauthorised AI use rose by 688% between 2023 and 2025. The government has commissioned a review into how schools are tackling AI cheating, which will report back in April.Announcing the review, Lotta Edholm, the Swedish minister for upper secondary school, said in January: “There is no reason to turn a blind eye to cheating students. Cheating is completely unacceptable regardless of what form. It risks affecting grades that should reflect students’ knowledge and in the long term, students are not actually learning what they should.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)DenmarkEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Nato to ‘urgently’ get air defences for Ukraine, as Zelenskyy warns of surge in Russian missile production  | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: After Ukraine failed to shoot down a single ballistic missile fired by Russia on Wednesday, the president urged allies to increase supplies of Patriot interceptors
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After Ukraine failed to shoot down a single ballistic missile fired by Russia on Wednesday, the president urged allies to increase supplies of Patriot interceptors
Content: Rescuers work at the site of a Russian missile strike on a goods storage in Kyiv on Wednesday.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAView image in fullscreenRescuers work at the site of a Russian missile strike on a goods storage in Kyiv on Wednesday.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAUkraineNato to ‘urgently’ get air defences for Ukraine, as Zelenskyy warns of surge in Russian missile productionAfter Ukraine failed to shoot down a single ballistic missile fired by Russia on Wednesday, the president urged allies to increase supplies of Patriot interceptorsGuardian staff and agenciesWed 5 Aug 2026 22.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNato is working to get Ukraine the air defences it “urgently needs”, its secretary general has said, after Kyiv failed to shoot down a single Russian missile in an attack on Wednesday, and asVolodymyr Zelenskyywarned that Moscow was seeking to significantly boost missile ⁠production ahead of winter.Speaking at a National Security and Defense Council meeting on winter resilience, the Ukrainian president did not rule out the idea that stalling missile supplies from western allies were “aimed at makingUkraine, so to speak, more willing to compromise” in peace talks with Russia.Ukraine war briefing: Cut-price Patriot among options in desperate search for missile defenceRead moreAfter meeting Nato’s Mark Rutte, Zelenskyy said: “It is important to cut through all red tape and make the necessary political decisions. Literally every day, people’s lives here in Ukraine depend on the resolve of our partners inEuropeand the United States.”Russia launched24 ballistic missiles in an overnight attack on Wednesday, killing at least 17 people. Preliminary data from the Ukrainian air force showed its defences shot down 98 of the 115 drones fired byRussiaovernight, but none of the ballistic missiles.On Wednesday, Zelenskyy said that in the first half of 2026, supplies of air defence missiles from Ukraine’s allies had fallen to a third of their 2025 level.View image in fullscreenUkrainian service members view a Patriot air defence system in 2024.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersThe president also warned that Moscow was looking to significantly increase ballistic missile ⁠production as winter neared, when it is expected to renew its campaign against Ukraine’s energy sector.Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine’s president on the development of defence technology, estimated thatRussiawas capable of launching 100 ballistic missiles every month to attack logistic ​hubs, industrial facilities, food stores and warehouses. “The war of attrition has entered its next phase,” he said on the Telegram app.Ukraine has been short on US-made Patriot interceptors capable of downing Russian ballistic missiles since the ⁠start of the war. But in recent weeks, anacute shortage has come into focus, with Moscow pummelling Kyiv, on ​average, every three days in July alone. Zelenskyy said the shortage of interceptor missiles was mainly caused by the war in the Middle East.Patriot missile systems are the only system in Ukrainian service able to intercept the Russian Iskander-M, S-400 and Zircon missiles, according to the Ukrainian air force.Russia often combines ballistic missiles with cruise missiles, drones and decoys, forcing defenders to track many threats and ration scarce interceptors, but Ukraine says it has too few batteries and interceptors to properly protect itself.View image in fullscreenUkrainian firefighters work to put out a fire following a massive Russian ballistic missile and drone strike on Kyiv.Photograph: Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP/Getty ImagesThe interceptor shortage has become more acute as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran, which hasconsumed large numbers of Patriot and other interceptors. An analysis by the Associated Press estimated that the US Patriot inventory had fallen by at least 65% since before the war. The Pentagon claims it retains a deep arsenal of supplies.Production cannot immediately close the gap. Lockheed Martin delivered more than 600 of the newest model of interceptors in 2025 and is working toward annual capacity of 2,000 by the end of 2030. But according to some estimates, Gulf statescollectively fired more than 1,100 interceptorsin the first three months of the Iran war.Nato says Europe’s first Patriot missile production facility is expected to open in September in Germany.Political signals from Washington have also shifted. At a Nato summit last month, Donald Trump said the US would giveUkraine a licence to produce Patriots. About three weeks later,he said he had not made a final decision. Even with a licence, officials and experts estimate that starting production in Ukraine would take years.Despite Trump casting doubt on the deal last month, the US is pressing ahead with talks on allowing Ukraine to make Patriot interceptors, according to reports from Reuters.The discussions ⁠include an option for Ukraine to ⁠build some components for final assembly elsewhere in ​Europe, according to the report.Explore more on these topicsUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyUS foreign policyEuropeRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran says a deal with Oman to reopen the strait of Hormuz is close to being finalised – as it happened | US-Israel war on Iran | The Guardian
description: This live blog is now closed.
Author: Taz Ali
Headline: This live blog is now closed.
Content: 04.21 EDTTehran would control Hormuz strait's inbound traffic in deal, according to reportsWelcome to our live coverage of the latest in the ongoing Middle East crisis.Iran said a deal with Oman to reopen the strait of Hormuz is close to being finalised,with reports suggesting Tehranwould have control over ships entering the Gulfthrough the strategic waterway.Both countries, which sit on opposite ends of the narrow strait, have been engaged in talks to jointly manage the key shipping route, which has been effectively closed since the start of the war in February. Iran has insisted the strait would not operate as it did before the conflict, as an open international waterway that carried about a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply, as it seeks greater control over the flow of maritime traffic through the channel. Several media reports, citing sources familiar with the talks, suggest Oman would oversee outbound shipping through the strait.A drone view shows vessels in the strait of Hormuz.Photograph: ReutersBut despite reports of potentially one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran, Reuters news agency said Iranian sources⁠rejected US President Donald Trump’s claims that a deal to reopen the strait was imminent,saying important details ​were still to be agreed.“The concession has already been made regarding some form of control over Hormuz,” one of the sources said.Iran has also said that reopening the strait would hinge on the US lifting its blockade of Iranian ports.Trump told Fox News earlier this week that talks over the strait were “moving along nicely”, adding that the strait “is going to be open very soon”.Here’s our full report from last night on the proposed deal between Iran and Oman:Understanding reached on coordinates for shipping route through Hormuz, Iran saysRead moreInYemen, meanwhile, the Iran-backedHouthissaid yesterday they had attacked two Saudi oil tankers with ballistic missiles, amid the group’s maritime blockade of the kingdom.In other developmentsTwo Israeli reserve soldiers were killed and four seriously injured in an explosion southern Lebanon, the military said this morning – the first Israeli deaths since the fragile truce between Israel and the Iran-backed militantHezbollahin June. An Israeli military official told the Associated Press that “an explosion was detonated” when the soldiers entered a site in the village of Majdal Zoun and that the nature of the explosive was under review.One person was killed and 12 wounded in an Israeli strike in the southern Lebanese town of Tebnine, Lebanon’s health ministry said. The Israeli military earlier told residents of the southern Lebanese village of Mansouri to evacuate – the first such order in more than a month – saying it was in response to a Hezbollah ceasefire violation.Forest fires sweep through the outskirts of the southern Lebanese village of Kfar Shouba as a result of Israeli shelling on Wednesday.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesThe escalations came despite ongoing US-backed talks in Rome aimed at ending hostilities. Israel requested that yesterday’s talks withLebanonend three hours early, a source told AFP, saying the Israeli delegation’s head had blamed alleged “misleading leaks” by the Lebanese side. But the talks are expected to resume today for a third and final day.A Houthi military spokesperson said its latest attacks targeted the eighth and ninth Saudi oil tankerssince the start of its blockade last month. Saudi authorities had no immediate comment.Shipping traffic through the Hormuz and ⁠Bab-el-Mandeb straits – the key maritime chokepoints in the Gulf – reduced significantly yesterdayfrom the ⁠previous ​day, shipping data showed.Share

title: Israel charges West Bank settler over death of renowned Palestinian activist | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Yinon Levi faces trial for reckless manslaughter related to the 2025 killing of Awdah Hathaleen
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Yinon Levi faces trial for reckless manslaughter related to the 2025 killing of Awdah Hathaleen
Content: A demonstrator holds a photo of Awdah Hathaleen during an August 2025 protest in Tel Aviv over his death.Photograph: Tamir Kalifa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA demonstrator holds a photo of Awdah Hathaleen during an August 2025 protest in Tel Aviv over his death.Photograph: Tamir Kalifa/Getty ImagesWest BankIsrael charges West Bank settler over death of renowned Palestinian activistYinon Levi faces trial for reckless manslaughter related to the 2025 killing of Awdah HathaleenReuters in JerusalemThu 6 Aug 2026 10.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli prosecutors have charged a Jewish settler over the killing of a Palestinian community leader in the occupiedWest Banklast year – the ⁠first such indictment in nearly three years.In papers filed by the state attorney’s office, Yinon Levi is charged with reckless manslaughter in the death of Awdah Hathaleen, a prominent ⁠activist who was involved in the 2025 Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land.The charges against Levi also include armed trespassing and malicious property damage during a July 2025 incident in which settlers operated ⁠a large excavator in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair, setting off a confrontation with residents.Hathaleen filmed the moment ​he was shot during the confrontation. Footage released by ‌the Israeli rights group B’Tselem shows ‌Levi draw a weapon and fire in Hathaleen’s direction. Hathaleen is then heard moaning as he falls to ‌the ground.0:53Palestinian activist recorded moment he was killed by settler in West Bank – videoLevi, whom the UK and EU have placed under sanctions over violence against Palestinians, has previously denied firing the shot that killed Hathaleen. Reuters was not able to reach his lawyer for comment.Thursday’s indictment is the first since the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks that set off Israel’s war in Gaza and led to a sharp rise in settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, B’Tselem said.Israeli soldiers and settlers have since killed at least 1,100 Palestinians in the West Bank, among them at least 240 children, according to UN data.My sweet friend Awdah Hathaleen was murdered by a West Bank settler. May his memory be a revolution |  Emily GlickRead more“The decision to indict Yinon Levi is the ​exception that proves the rule. The impunity Israel grants to soldiers and settlers who harm Palestinians is not a failure of the system. It is a central component of a policy designed to allow the violence to continue and escalate,” B’Tselem said.Israel’s military says it investigates instances of wrongdoing by its soldiers and that it and the Israeli police take steps ⁠to crack down on settler violence.Hundreds of thousands of Israelis have settled among millions ​of Palestinians in land that Israel ​captured in a 1967 war, and which ​Palestinians seek as the core of an independent future state.UN bodies, Palestinians and most countries ​view the settlements as illegal ‌under international conventions ​and a major obstacle to ​peace. Israel disputes that view, saying a Jewish presence has existed in the West Bank for thousands of years.Eighteen Palestinians have been killed in incidents linked to settler attacks so far this year, compared with 17 in the whole of 2025, according to UN figures.Explore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineIsraelMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s Gaza Board of Peace issues first building contract – for a military base | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Louisiana firm awarded tender to build rudimentary outpost to house Moroccan troops
Author: Aram Roston
Headline: Exclusive: Louisiana firm awarded tender to build rudimentary outpost to house Moroccan troops
Content: Palestinians use a digger to recover bodies under the rubble in devastated Gaza City earlier this year. The Board of Peace is no longer talking of reconstructing the whole strip.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPalestinians use a digger to recover bodies under the rubble in devastated Gaza City earlier this year. The Board of Peace is no longer talking of reconstructing the whole strip.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesGazaTrump’s Gaza Board of Peace issues first building contract – for a military baseExclusive: Louisiana firm awarded tender to build rudimentary outpost to house Moroccan troopsAram Rostonin WashingtonThu 6 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s Board of Peace, which wasset up in January to oversee the reconstruction of Gaza, has finally issued its first construction contract in the devastated territory: a project to build a rudimentary 150-person military outpost to house Moroccan troops, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian.The contract, which has not yet been finalised, was awarded to Arkel International, a Louisiana-based firm that has previously carried out work with the US government in countries such as Iraq.The Board of Peace is chaired by the US president and led by a team that includes his son-in-lawJared Kushnerand friend Steve Witkoff.In an email, a Board of Peace official said the board and a group of Palestinian technocrats installed to oversee Gaza “are in the final stages of preparing several contract awards. None have been finalised.” The Palestinian group is known as theNational Committee for the Administration of Gaza.The official said “one prospective contract concerns facilities to support the international stabilisation force (ISF), which will assist in implementing the roadmap’s security and governance arrangements”.They added: “This contract will be one of many that are essential for the future ofGaza.”Trump’s Board of Peace plans to grant itself sweeping immunity, documents showRead moreThe award comes just days after Trump announced that Hamas had agreed to disarm, though there are considerable questions about how the group would give up its guns.Israel has opposed the plan, andincreased airstrikes in Gaza after Trump’s announcement.The Guardian reported in July that the board’s original Gaza reconstruction had shrunk dramatically froman ambitious blueprintto rebuild the whole territory toa small pilot project in the south of the strip.The base now being planned is just 100 metres by 120 metres and is intended to house a contingent of Moroccan troops, who would rotate from a base in Israel, the source said. It would lie in the 60% of Gaza’s territory that the Israeli army directly controls.Israeli forces have also created a buffer zone beyond that area.The source said the base was about a mile from the Israeli border and would have a “quick extraction route” in case the small force came under attack.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump’s original grandiose vision of a reconstructed Gaza is displayed by the president at the World Economic Forum meeting at Davos on 22 January.The UN resolution authorising the Board of Peace had approved establishing an “international stabilisation force” for Gaza, and there have been varying reports on which country would provide these troops. Morocco has promised a small contingent, but the legal framework for the ISF has yet to be finalised, and it is not clear when the deployment would begin.In earlier contract plans seen by the Guardian, the 150-person base was the first phase ofa plan to build a 5,000-person military base in Gaza for the ISF.This base would have included “vehicle fighting positions” and a perimeter berm – or raised defensive bank – and would have rudimentary facilities suitable for short-term deployments. The earlier contract said the first phase would consist of “tents and cots for forces to sleep, as well as chemical toilets and handwashing stations. At this phase, this is what we would consider habitable.”Trump announced in February 2025that the US would “take over” and “own” Gaza, although the agreement that set up the Board of Peace fell short of that.At the board’s first meeting in January, Kushner unveiled a “master plan” to build “New Gaza” with an expansive waterfront city with gleaming mixed-use towers. “It could be a hope, it could be a destination. A lot of industry,” he said.At least 80% of Gaza’s buildings were damaged or destroyed in the war. Ten months after the ceasefire, most of the territory’s 2 million people are still living in makeshift and unsanitary camps.Explore more on these topicsGazaIsraelDonald TrumpPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaJared KushnerTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Top Democrats accuse Trump officials over Israeli settlers’ ‘unbridled violence’ | US foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Letter says lifting of sanctions sent ‘clear message’ settlers can use deadly force in West Bank without consequences
Author: David Smith
Headline: Letter says lifting of sanctions sent ‘clear message’ settlers can use deadly force in West Bank without consequences
Content: A burned car and building after a reported attack by Israeli settlers on the outskirts of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA burned car and building after a reported attack by Israeli settlers on the outskirts of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty ImagesUS foreign policyTop Democrats accuse Trump officials over Israeli settlers’ ‘unbridled violence’Letter says lifting of sanctions sent ‘clear message’ settlers can use deadly force in West Bank without consequencesDavid SmithWashington bureau chiefThu 6 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 10.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSenior Democrats have accused Donald Trump’s administration of giving a green light toviolent Israeli settlersin the occupied West Bank, warning that its policies created “a climate of impunity and unbridled violence” that endangers both Palestinians and US citizens.In a letter seen by the Guardian, a group of 19 Democratic senators and representatives call for the restoration of sanctions against extremist settlers and demand independent US investigations into thedeaths of nine US citizenskilled in the West Bank since 2022.The letter, signed by the Massachusetts senatorElizabeth Warrenamong others, is addressed to Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general, Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, and Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary.It argues that Trump’s promise last year that “I will not allow Israel to annex the West Bank” has been undermined by events on the ground. “In practice,” theDemocratswrite, “violent settlers and the [Benjamin] Netanyahu government have proceeded to rapidly extend Israeli control over civilian populations in the region.”They urge the administration to use “all the diplomatic and economic tools at its disposal, including restoring sanctions, to end this violence and expansion of settlements”.The Democrats argue that Trump’s decision on his first day back in office torescind sanctions imposedon more than 30 settlers and organisations linked to violence has had profound consequences.“Ending sanctions against those individuals and entities associated with West Bank extremism sent a clear message,” they write. “Settlers can use violent and deadly force with impunity against Palestinians and Americans while seizing land … and no one will face consequences.”The letter cites UN figures showing1,835 attacks on Palestinian communitiesand property during 2025, the highest number since records began, and says the UN has reported that the pace of settler attacks this year is higher than in any year on record.It highlightsrepeated attacks on Turmus Ayya, a Palestinian town where the majority of residents are US citizens, including the burning of a family home belonging to Americans from Massachusetts and Washington state.The elected officials also focus on what they say has become an increasingly dangerous environment for Americans. Since Trump returned to office, they write, four US citizens have been killed by Israeli settlers or security forces in the West Bank, bringing the total since 2022 to nine.The victims include the Palestinian American journalistShireen Abu Akleh, 14-year-oldAmer Mohammed Rabea, 17-year-olds Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohammad Ahmed Mohammad Khdour and 20-year-old Sayfollah Musallet, as well as Omar Assad, a 78-year-old Palestinian American, and the Turkish American activist Aysenur Ezgi Eygi.The letter says the justice department “has the authority to independently investigate the killing of Americans abroad” but “has reportedly not opened investigations into any of the killings since 2025. Israel has yet to indict a single person involved in these incidents.”The Democrats also express concern over the detention of US citizens by the Israeli military including 20-year-oldSama Safi, whose access to vital medication was allegedly interrupted after her arrest, andMohammed Ibrahim, who they say was detained for nine months while aged 15. They urge the administration to secure Safi’s immediate release and “push for the end of unjust and arbitrary detentions in the territory”.The senators and representatives argue that the violence extends beyond Palestinian communities, pointing to repeated attacks on Taybeh, described in the letter as “the last entirely Christian village in the West Bank”.Although the US ambassador to Israel,Mike Huckabee, described an earlier attack there as “an act of terror” and pledged that those responsible would be prosecuted, the senators and representatives note that “no one has been arrested in connection with these crimes”. Huckabee is an evangelical Christian who has supported Jewish claims on the occupied land that settlers call Judea and Samaria.The letter is signed by Warren, Ed Markey, Jeff Merkley, Patty Murray, Jack Reed,Bernie Sanders, Brian Schatz, Adam Schiff, Chris Van Hollen, Peter Welch and Ron Wyden. The House of Representatives signatories are Katherine Clark, Richard Neal, Jim McGovern, Seth Moulton, Ayanna Pressley, Jake Auchincloss, Stephen Lynch and Lori Trahan.It concludes that Israeli security forces and settlers have attacked and displaced Palestinians in the West Bank “at an unprecedented rate” since theTrump administrationtook office and argues that Washington’s “deference to the Netanyahu government has contributed to a climate of impunity and unbridled violence towards civilian populations and religious minorities”.It demands answers by 17 August on investigations into attacks on Americans, the lifting of sanctions and the treatment of US citizens detained by the Israeli military.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policyIsraelPalestineDonald TrumpMiddle East and north AfricaTrump administrationDemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli strike that killed journalist in Lebanon was war crime, say rights groups | Israel | The Guardian
description: Investigation by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty and Legal Agenda shows Israel deliberately attacked Amal Khalil and colleague Zeinab Faraj knowing they were civilians
Author: William Christou
Headline: Investigation by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty and Legal Agenda shows Israel deliberately attacked Amal Khalil and colleague Zeinab Faraj knowing they were civilians
Content: Killing of Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil was a war crime, say rights groups.Photograph: Mohammed Zaatari/APView image in fullscreenKilling of Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil was a war crime, say rights groups.Photograph: Mohammed Zaatari/APRights and freedomIsraelIsraeli strike that killed journalist in Lebanon was war crime, say rights groupsInvestigation by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty and Legal Agenda shows Israel deliberately attacked Amal Khalil and colleague Zeinab Faraj knowing they were civiliansSupported byAbout this contentWilliam ChristouThu 6 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Israeli strike that killed Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil and injured her colleague Zeinab Faraj in April was a war crime, three rights organisations said on Thursday.Investigations from Human Rights Watch (HRW),Amnesty Internationaland Legal Agenda showed that Israel deliberately and directly attacked Khalil and Faraj, with apparent knowledge that they were civilians. The organisations called for the attacks to be investigated as war crimes, while HRW called for states to halt arm sales to Israel and put targeted sanctions on Israeli officials responsible for ongoing crimes.Deliberate attacks on civilians, which both journalists were, is a war crime. Israel has killed at least 15 journalists in Lebanon and 210 in Gaza since 2023, according to theUN human rights office.The reports also indicated that Israel delayed Lebanese ambulances from reaching Khalil and Faraj for hours – at one pointing dropping stun grenades on Lebanese Red Cross workers and firing on their ambulances.The delay in rescue might have led to Khalil’s death, as hospital reports indicate that she might have still been alive hours after an Israeli strike toppled a building on top of her and Faraj.“The evidence is clear that the Israeli military knew, or should have, that Faraj and Khalil were civilians, but attacked them anyway, and then prevented paramedics from rescuing them for hours,” said Ramzi Kaiss,Lebanonresearcher at Human Rights Watch.Israel said it “regrets any harm caused to journalists,” and that the journalists were killed “as part of a series of events” during which two Hezbollah military operatives were killed. There was about two hours between the initial strike that killed the two men Israel said were in Hezbollah, and a second strike that targeted a building the journalists were sheltering in.Amal Khalil was a 42-year-old journalist working for al-Akhbar, a Lebanese newspaper, while Zeinab Faraj was a 21-year-old freelance camerawoman and photojournalist. Both had been active in covering the war in Lebanon over the last three years.View image in fullscreenZainab, the sister of Amal Khalil, mourns over her coffin in Baysariyeh, southern Lebanon.Photograph: Mohammed Zaatari/APOn 22 April 2026, the pair drove to the village of al-Tiri, south Lebanon, to verify reports that Israeli troops had left the area. They drove behind a car carrying Ali Nabil Bazzi, a municipal official of the city of Bint Jbeil, as well as Mohammed Hourani, a friend of the mayor.Al-Tiri was in what Israel calls its “security zone” in southern Lebanon, which its troops occupy. Amnesty said that despite the Israeli military calling it a military zone and barring people from going there, it is still required to distinguish between civilians and combatants.At 2.25pm, after entering al-Tiri, the car carrying Bazzi and Hournai was struck, killing the men. Khalil called the Lebanese civil defence and requested assistance.The civil defence drove to the entry of the village, where they were told to stop at a military checkpoint while they waited for authorisation from the Israeli military to enter the village safely.Rescue crews operating in areas of south Lebanon where fighting is taking place or which the Israeli military occupies must coordinate with the “mechanism”, a deconfliction channel, to get safe passage. Among others, the Israeli military must give approval for requests for civil defence to get safe passage.By 5pm, the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon had given a safe route for civil defence to follow to enter the town, but Israel had not yet given its approval.While waiting for the civil defence to arrive, Faraj and Khalil left their car and sought shelter elsewhere. Israeli quadcopters circled low overhead while the two journalists waited, Faraj said.“The drones came extremely close through the roof, less than a metre from my face and Amal’s,” she said.At 3.31pm, a member of the Lebanese civil defence called Khalil and urged her to get into her car and drive out of the village, as he had not yet received permission from the mechanism to enter the village. Around nine minutes later, Israel struck the journalists’ car, injuring both women.“Glass and debris flew towards us. My ear felt like it burst. She [Amal Khalil] was bleeding heavily from the nose and head and had shrapnel wounds in her arm and thigh; she couldn’t move her leg,” Farj said.The two women crawled into a nearby building for shelter. They both continued calling people, asking for assistance, but were told they could not be rescued until authorisation was given from the mechanism.At 4.25pm, Israel conducted a third strike, bombing the building where they were sheltering, collapsing it and burying both women under the rubble.At 5pm, permission was given to the Lebanese Red Cross to enter the village. They were able to evacuate Faraj, who had a fractured skull, severe injuries to her right leg and eye, and a crushed hand. Rescuers could not rescue Khalil, who was trapped under rubble.The rescuers came under attack by an Israeli quadcopter, which dropped a stun grenade near them. Witnesses also said they heard bursts of gunfire during the evacuations, and HRW reviewed photographs of bulletholes in the ambulances consistent with small arms fire.The rescuers were forced to withdraw with only Faraj.The Israeli military finally granted the request for rescue crews to re-enter the town at 8.15pm. Khalil’s body was recovered at 11pm.An examination of her body at the nearby Tebnine hospital showed that she probably died at 7pm – two-and-a-half hours after she was struck for the last time. She was trapped under the rubble during that time, waiting to be rescued, while the Israeli military prevented rescue crews from saving her life.All three organisations have demanded accountability for Khalil’s killing, and described it as part of a larger pattern of impunity by the Israeli military towards civilians.“The impunity enjoyed by Israeli forces for the killing of journalists and other civilians in Lebanon over the past three years has enabled the Israeli military to continue with its unlawful airstrikes, including direct attacks on civilians,” said Heba Morayef, director for theMiddle East and north Africaat Amnesty International.“It is well past time that the international community impose a comprehensive arms embargo on Israel,” Morayef added.Explore more on these topicsIsraelRights and freedomWar crimesMiddle East and north AfricaLebanonJournalist safetyHuman rightsAmnesty InternationalnewsShareReuse this content

title: India-Bangladesh relations hit new low over exiled PM’s speech to press in Delhi  | Bangladesh | The Guardian
description: Dhaka accuses India of giving platform to a ‘convicted genocider’ by allowing Sheikh Hasina to address journalists
Author: Redwan Ahmed
Headline: Dhaka accuses India of giving platform to a ‘convicted genocider’ by allowing Sheikh Hasina to address journalists
Content: Journalists listen to the virtual address by Hasina, hosted by the Foreign Correspondents' Club of South Asia in New Delhi on Wednesday.Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/ReutersView image in fullscreenJournalists listen to the virtual address by Hasina, hosted by the Foreign Correspondents' Club of South Asia in New Delhi on Wednesday.Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/ReutersBangladeshIndia-Bangladesh relations hit new low over exiled PM’s speech to press in DelhiDhaka accuses India of giving platform to a ‘convicted genocider’ by allowing Sheikh Hasina to address journalistsRedwan Ahmedin Dhaka andPenelope MacRaein DelhiThu 6 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBangladesh has lashed out at India for allowing the ousted prime ministerSheikh Hasinato address journalists in New Delhi, plunging already strained bilateral relations to a fresh low.Dhaka accused India of giving a platform to a fugitive it labelled a “convicted genocider” and of undermining efforts to repair ties, afterHasina vowed to return to Bangladesh in Decemberdespite facing a death sentence on charges of “crimes against humanity”.The angry response late on Wednesday came hours after Hasina, speaking on the second anniversary of the massivestudent-led uprisingthat led to her flight to India, declared: “Whatever fate awaits me, I will return to my people.”Exiled PM vows to return to Bangladesh despite execution threatRead moreBangladesh’s foreign ministry said it was “outraged” Hasina had been allowed to participate in the event, where it said she and her allies launched “venomous vitriol” againstBangladeshand its people.“This interaction by Hasina on Indian soil stands as an affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh,” the ministry said. Dhaka also renewed its demands forIndiato extradite Hasina.India earlier distanced itself from the news conference – Hasina’s first sincefleeing Bangladesh in 2024, saying it had no role in organising it and would not endorse any political views voiced.Hasina said she was ready to face whatever fate awaited her in Bangladesh, where her Awami League party is now banned. “They may put me in a cell. They may kill me. Anything may happen, but I still have to go,” the 78-year-old said via audio link.“My life moved beyond calculations of personal safety long ago.”After 15 years in power, Hasina fled to India in 2024 following weeks of student-led protests. Her government was accused of misusing state institutions to entrench its hold on power and stamp out dissent, including through the killing of opposition activists.In her speech, she dismissed criminal cases against her as politically motivated and accused Bangladesh’s new government, led by Tarique Rahman, of economic mismanagement, political repression and persecution of her supporters.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHasina was sentenced in absentia to death by hanging over her government’s deadly crackdown on the uprising. She said she wanted to return in December because it marked Bangladesh’s “month of victory”, commemorating Pakistan’s defeat in the 1971 independence war.She claimed thousands of Awami League activists had been killed or jailed since her downfall.Her son Sajeeb Wazed Joy stoked the diplomatic row by extolling India’s hospitality. “She’s being treated very well and has been provided with the full services and security accorded to a head of state,” he said. “Prime Minister Modi’s government has shown her the utmost respect.”Hasina was joined at the event by Shakib Al Hasan, a former national cricket captain. Hours later unidentified attackers hurled petrol bombs and smashed windows at his home in Bangladesh, but no one was hurt, police said. Shakib, elected to parliament as an Awami League candidate, has remained outside Bangladesh since Hasina’s overthrow.Explore more on these topicsBangladeshIndiaSheikh HasinaSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: High-profile Indian journalist jailed for 10 years for raping colleague | India | The Guardian
description: Tarun Tejpal, ex-editor of Tehelka magazine, was initially acquitted in 2021 in case that drew nationwide attention
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tarun Tejpal, ex-editor of Tehelka magazine, was initially acquitted in 2021 in case that drew nationwide attention
Content: Tarun Tejpal’s acquittal in 2021 was challenged by the Goa government.Photograph: Frédéric Soltan/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTarun Tejpal’s acquittal in 2021 was challenged by the Goa government.Photograph: Frédéric Soltan/Corbis/Getty ImagesIndiaHigh-profile Indian journalist jailed for 10 years for raping colleagueTarun Tejpal, ex-editor of Tehelka magazine, was initially acquitted in 2021 in case that drew nationwide attentionAgence France-Press in MumbaiThu 6 Aug 2026 07.47 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 04.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Indian court has sentenced a high-profile former editor of an investigative news magazine to 10 years in prison after convicting him of raping a junior colleague, overturning his acquittal in a case that drew nationwide attention.Tarun Tejpal, 63, the founder and former editor of Tehelka magazine,was accused of raping a journalist in the lift of a five-star hotelin the western coastal state of Goa during an event in November 2013. He was arrested and spent seven months in jail until the supreme court granted him bail.A court in Goa acquitted Tejpal of charges including rape, sexual harassment and wrongful restraint in 2021.The government of Goa challenged the acquittal before the Bombay high court, which set aside the trial court’s verdict and sentenced him to 10 years in jail on Thursday.“He has been convicted to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment. He has been given two weeks’ time to surrender,” the police investigator Sunita Sawant, who led the case against Tejpal, told reporters.The court also ordered him to pay a £3,900 fine, he said.Tejpal, 63, said he would challenge the conviction in the supreme court.He had initially blamed the assault on “a lapse of judgement” but later alleged the case against him was part of a vendetta by the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) government in Goa.“For the past 13 years, they have been pursuing me as a part of a political vendetta,” he said after conviction.Sawant told reporters: “This is a sentence where a girl has stood up for her rights … so this judgment is very important for women who are working in any sector.”The case emerged at a time when India’s handling of sexual assault cases was under intense scrutiny afterthe gang-rape and murder of a 23-year-old student on a Delhi busin December 2012.That attack triggered nationwide protests and international outrage, and prompted the government to strengthen the country’s rape laws.Tejpal’s case severely damaged the authority and credibility of Tehelka, which had historically championed women’s rights and social justice.The magazine continues to operate under new leadership, but it has failed to regain the influence it had before the 2013 case.Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK,Rape Crisisoffers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 inScotland, or 0800 0246 991 inNorthern Ireland. In the US,Rainnoffers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at1800Respect(1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found atibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsIndiaRape and sexual assaultViolence against women and girlsSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It is British life’: No 10 vows to stop councils trying to limit standing in pubs | London | The Guardian
description: Westminster council has recommended banning ‘vertical drinking’ or ordering at the bar in new draft licensing policy
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Westminster council has recommended banning ‘vertical drinking’ or ordering at the bar in new draft licensing policy
Content: The prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the chancellor, John Healey, at a London pub in July.Photograph: Richard Pohle/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the chancellor, John Healey, at a London pub in July.Photograph: Richard Pohle/AFP/Getty ImagesLondon‘It is British life’: No 10 vows to stop councils trying to limit standing in pubsWestminster council has recommended banning ‘vertical drinking’ or ordering at the bar in new draft licensing policyHelena HortonThu 6 Aug 2026 17.07 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo 10 has vowed to confiscate powers from local councils which try to restrict customers from standing up while drinking in pubs or ordering at the bar.It comes after the Guardianrevealed on Thursdaythat Westminster council in central London recommended not allowing “vertical drinking” or ordering at the bar in itsnew draft licensing policy.The draft document, now out for consultation, recommends that pubs applying for new licences allow only table service rather than bar ordering. It also suggests new pubs in popular nightlife areas including Soho call last orders at 10pm, to reduce noise and disturbance.A Downing Street spokesperson said: “Busy pubs full of people talking to each other is not a public nuisance, it is British life, and it is thousands of jobs.“The government is devolving new licensing powers to the mayor [of London] to help support pubs and nightlife. Soho did not become world famous by taking last orders early, switching the lights off at 10 o’clock.“The prime minister encourages local leaders to work with the industry so that pubs can continue to thrive.”Diageo to nearly double Guinness production and cut jobs in turnaround planRead moreThe government is due to grant new powers to the London mayor,Sadiq Khan, allowing him to “call in” local council decisions he opposes.Khan said of the proposals on X: “You can’t run a world-famous nightlife district with a village-hall mindset.”A spokesperson for the mayor previously said he was against “restrictive and anti-growth policies” and said he hoped to use new powers to be granted to him by the government to stop councils from overreaching.The draft policy says pubs should “discourage excessive drunkenness and encourage the provision of more seating in premises that serve alcohol for people to sit and enjoy a drink and order food by table service in place of open bar space that caters for high-volume vertical drinking”.It goes on to recommend that sales of alcohol and food should be “by waiter or waitress service only”.Operators of pubs and bars in Soho have criticised what they see as overly restrictive licensing policies and said the proposals could kill off West End nightlife.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPaul Swaddle, the Conservative leader of Westminster council, denied the plans amounted to a ban on “vertical drinking”.He told the Press Association that newspapers had carried “confusing stories” about the document and added: “I want to be straight with people. There is no plan, and never has been, to ban drinking while standing up in a Westminster pub.”Responding to Khan’s criticism, he said: “We don’t need lectures from city hall on backing hospitality when they have directed the police to object to every new licence application as their solution to curbing crime in the West End.”The council also plans to ban the opening of new pubs and bars in what it terms the “cumulative impact zone”, encompassing Soho and large parts of the West End.Areas such as Victoria and Mayfair will also face restrictions on new openings if the draft policy is made official.Explore more on these topicsLondonLocal governmentFood & drink industryHospitality industryPubsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dons call for Cambridge leaders to take blame for Jason Arday appointment | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Academics call for inquiry, saying university must be held accountable for ‘grotesque racism unleashed’
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Exclusive: Academics call for inquiry, saying university must be held accountable for ‘grotesque racism unleashed’
Content: Jason Arday at the time of his appointment to a professorship at Cambridge University in 2023.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJason Arday at the time of his appointment to a professorship at Cambridge University in 2023.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianJason ArdayDons call for Cambridge leaders to take blame for Jason Arday appointmentExclusive: Academics call for inquiry, saying university must be held accountable for ‘grotesque racism unleashed’Richard AdamsEducation editorThu 6 Aug 2026 15.54 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 14.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe University of Cambridge’s leaders deserve blame for the “grotesque racism unleashed” by Jason Arday’s appointment as professor, according to academics calling for the university to hold an independent inquiry.The Guardian understands that senior dons at Cambridge are circulating a joint letter calling for an inquiry into the processes and circumstances around Arday being given the position, with many suggesting the university wanted a “quick fix” to improve the diversity of its staff.Arday was appointed as professor of sociology of education in 2023 at the relatively young age of 37 and despite a slim track record of research and publications compared with those appointed to similar chairs at Cambridge.Arday resignedon Wednesday after more than a week of public questions involving plagiarism in his PhD thesis and other publications, allegations of exaggerating his academic appointments, mounting controversy over his claims to have raised millions of pounds for charity, and lurid statements involving masked attackers and even a pig’s head delivered to his parents’ home in London.Arday is preparing to publish his memoir in the US and UK in the coming days and told the Guardian that its publisher,Simon & Schuster, is to pay him “1.4 million”for his extraordinary backstory, which includes being unable to speak until he was 11 years old.The group of Cambridge academics want any inquiry to include external members and be given independent status. They point to concerns over the appointment committee for Arday’s post, and to previous disputes within the university’s faculty of education where Arday was based.Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge’s English faculty and one of the group organising the letter, said: “An independent investigation must scrutinise how such an early-career appointment to a very senior and prestigious professorial chair was made and what both the faculty of education and university management may have got very badly wrong.”She added: “Whatever the results of any investigation, the university bears no little responsibility for the grotesque racism which this whole business has unleashed, and for the harm done both to the individual in the line of fire, to Black academics as a group, and the broader field of critical race studies.“This requires accountability now from those responsible, not a cover-up.”Other academics who spoke to the Guardian said they had been surprised by Arday’s appointment in 2023, with one sociologist admitting to never having heard of Arday before: “When it was announced I looked for his body of work, and it was disappointing to say the least.”Gopal said Cambridge had been too tempted to “cut corners on the hard work of fostering equality and inclusion” by opting for a media-friendly appointment.“The extent to which this appointment wasparaded in the mediaby the university … raises questions about whether the university sought public kudos for itself rather than teaching and research from this appointment.“It is highly unusual, to say the least, to appoint such an early-career academic to a very senior post,” Gopal said.“Academic misconduct also needs more robust and transparent procedures in place, as more than one case at Cambridge indicates.“The university must also pay attention to the consequences of putting young people of colour in highly visible places to carry the burden of representation before they are ready to withstand scrutiny.”Playbooks, plagiarism and a pig’s head: new claims surrounding a star Cambridge professorRead moreWhen the controversy first erupted, the university briefed journalists that it stood by its appointment process, and publicly defended Arday as “the victim of a vile campaign” to discredit him.But on Wednesday night the university abruptly announced that it wouldopen a fresh investigationafter receiving “new information” about his qualifications and appointments.Shortly afterwards Arday said he would resign, adding: “I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgment.”The university and other organisations have since distanced themselves from Arday by deleting webpages and excising references, which one academic described as “wiping away the traces”.Jesus College, Cambridge, and the university’s faculty of education have taken down Arday’s staff profiles.Arday had signed up to speakers’ bureaus and, since his Cambridge appointment, has addressed a number of commercial organisations, including the annual conference of the Association of British Insurers in 2025.Simon & Schuster’s speakers bureau lists Arday as “an internationally sought-after speaker for industry conferences, corporate events, university lectures, and more, and has travelled across the United States for speaking engagements”.In 2024 Arday was a keynote speaker at US National Association of Funeral Directors international convention in New Orleans. His subsequent appearances, however, may dry up: an appearance in Arizona promised for October this year has also been removed.Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayUniversity of CambridgeHigher educationRaceAcademicsPlagiarismUniversitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Covent Garden victims stabbed in the back with pair of scissors, court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Stella Gollovena, 47, has been charged with four counts of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Stella Gollovena, 47, has been charged with four counts of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm
Content: Police cordoned off the area in London’s West End on Wednesday after the attack.Photograph: Tayfun Salcı/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolice cordoned off the area in London’s West End on Wednesday after the attack.Photograph: Tayfun Salcı/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockUK newsCovent Garden victims stabbed in the back with pair of scissors, court hearsStella Gollovena, 47, has been charged with four counts of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harmPress AssociationThu 6 Aug 2026 14.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman has appeared in court accused of stabbing four men in the back with a pair of scissors in one of London’s busiest tourist districts.Stella Gollovena, 47, is accused of attacking Patrick De Barr, Thomas Harding, Adrian Lovett and Mantas Jankus during the attack in Covent Garden on Wednesday lunchtime.She has been charged with four counts of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm and one count of possession of an offensive weapon, a pair of scissors, in a public place.Gollovena, of no fixed address, faced the five criminal charges for the first time in a hearing at Highbury Corner magistrates court on Thursday afternoon.The hearing was told police were flagged down in Endell Street, a popular tourist area filled with bars, theatres and restaurants, at about 12.25pm by one of the injured victims. He and a second man reported being stabbed, before the suspect was chased and Tasered.The court heard police took statements from four men who were treated in hospital for stab wounds to their backs, while a fifth person said at the scene that they had also been stabbed but did not want to give a statement to police. It is alleged Gollovena had a pair of scissors – also described as a “pair of shears” – on her when she was arrested.The deputy chief magistrate, Tan Ikram, remanded Gollovena in custody until the next hearing at Snaresbrook crown court on 3 September. Gollovena spoke to confirm her identity but did not enter any pleas to the charges.An air ambulance helicopter landed in a packed Trafalgar Square on Wednesday afternoon after the stabbings and London ambulance service said it had “treated four patients at the scene and took them all to a major trauma centre as a priority by road”.The Met said the four men – aged 34, 39, 42 and 56 – had stab wounds but had since been discharged from hospital as their injuries were not deemed life-threatening or life-changing.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Norfolk police arrest two men after officers injured during unrest over asylum plans | UK news | The Guardian
description: Homes of people believed to be asylum seekers attacked during two nights of violence in Thetford
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Homes of people believed to be asylum seekers attacked during two nights of violence in Thetford
Content: Protests have been held over plans to house asylum seekers on the RAF Barnham site near Thetford.Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtests have been held over plans to house asylum seekers on the RAF Barnham site near Thetford.Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty ImagesUK newsNorfolk police arrest two men after officers injured during unrest over asylum plansHomes of people believed to be asylum seekers attacked during two nights of violence in ThetfordMatthew WeaverThu 6 Aug 2026 14.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo men have been arrested after police were injured as they intervened to protect men believed to be asylum seekers from angry mobs trying to break into their homes.The arrests followed two nights of unrest in Thetford, Norfolk, involving more than 100 people protesting against plans to house asylum seekers in former military barracks near the market town.The unrest followed the circulation online of a list of properties whose landlords have contracts with a government contractor to provide homes for asylum seekers.Policing powers in Norfolk were boosted in Thetford on Thursday evening and public safety measures have been imposed.Norfolk police said on Wednesday one of its officers was struck by a rock, another officer was bitten and a third was spat at while responding to reports of protesters trying to break into a home in the north of the town. The injured officers were taken to hospital.One man in his 40s, who was arrested on suspected public order offences, remains in custody. A second man, Brian Thompson, 68, has been charged with possession of an offensive weapon, a wooden bat. He is due to appear at Norwich magistrates court on 25 August.View image in fullscreenDamage caused to a house in Thetford where protesters allegedly tried to break into the homes of people believed to be asylum seekers.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAOn Tuesday night, officers intervened to protect five men who were being threatened by dozens of protesters, some of whom tried to break into a property, smashed a window, and damaged a fence and letterbox. Police were responding to a report that between 30 and 50 people were trying to enter a house in the west of Thetford.Video footage of the incident showed the men being escorted to safety by officers as dozens of protesters jeered and shouted abuse at police and the men. Shouts of “refugees not welcome”, “get out” and “bye” could be heard. In another video of the unrest, a man could be heard shouting: “They don’t want the white man any more, they want to swap us.”Later on Tuesday, officers responded to reports of residents being threatened at two homes in the south of the town. Police believed some of those involved had been present at the earlier attempted break-in.At one of the homes, windows were smashed. At another, a resident was forced out and had their mobile phone stolen when a small group forced entry.A man in his 30s who was arrested over Tuesday’s night’s unrest on suspicion of a public order offence had since been released and issued with a conditional caution, police said.The local Labour MP, Terry Jermy, who has previously criticised plans to use the former barracks at nearby RAF Barnham to house up to 1,000 asylum seekers, condemned the violence and what he called “mob rule”.View image in fullscreenThe arrests followed two nights of unrest in Thetford involving more than 100 people protesting against plans to house asylum seekers at the RAF Barnham site (pictured).Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty ImagesJermy said protesters were targeting a list of houses of multiple occupation used by Serco to house asylum seekers. “There doesn’t seem to be protests at all of the properties known about thus far, so the potential for increase and escalation is clearly there,” he said.“I’ve had constituents contact me of mixed ethnicity who are terrified that they will be misidentified as asylum seekers and what that might mean for their families.”Jermy said he recognised many of the protesters as local people in the videos of the unrest, but that he believed tensions were being “whipped up by outside forces”.In a statement, Jermy said: “The ugly scenes in Thetford over the past few days have been difficult to watch and are deeply concerning.“People have been pulled from their homes – a place of safety – and forcibly removed, with reports of members of the public breaking into homes, taking property and smashing windows.“I do not know the immigration status of the people placed in these properties or their legal status, but I know they are human beings that must be afforded the same rights that we all expect in this country.“Whatever our own individual views on immigration – mob rule and vigilantism is not acceptable.”View image in fullscreenUnder the proposals, the RAF Barnham site could house 1,000 asylum seekers.Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty ImagesNorfolk police also condemned the violence. The assistant chief constable Julie Dean, who is overseeing the response to the unrest, said: “We will always facilitate and support the right to peaceful protest. However, no matter how strongly those views are held, there is no place for violence, intimidation or criminal behaviour.“We will not stand by and allow violence to take place, whether that is directed towards members of the public, local residents or police officers carrying out their duties.”Policing powers in Norfolk were increased in Thetford on Thursday evening.Public safety measures have been imposed, including people being required to remove a face covering if asked to do so by officers. Police will also be permitted to direct anyone committing, or whom they suspect may commit, antisocial behaviour to leave the area.The measures are in place from 6pm on Thursday until 7am on Friday. Anyone who refuses to remove a face covering when asked to do so may be arrested, the force said.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Foster + Partners cleared over man’s death when window fell from London penthouse | London | The Guardian
description: Court rules architecture firm not responsible for fatal incident but project managers and engineers found guilty of safety breaches
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Court rules architecture firm not responsible for fatal incident but project managers and engineers found guilty of safety breaches
Content: Mick Ferris was killed when a 130kg window fell from the Corniche, a luxury block of flats on the Albert Embankment, central London, in October 2018.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAView image in fullscreenMick Ferris was killed when a 130kg window fell from the Corniche, a luxury block of flats on the Albert Embankment, central London, in October 2018.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PALondonFoster + Partners cleared over man’s death when window fell from London penthouseCourt rules architecture firm not responsible for fatal incident but project managers and engineers found guilty of safety breachesMatthew WeaverThu 6 Aug 2026 14.06 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 09.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe architecture firm founded byNorman Fosterhas been cleared over the death of a man killed by a window that fell 90 metres from a newly constructed London penthouse.Foster + Partners (F+P), the practice behind some of the world’s most recognisable buildings such asthe Gherkinandrevamps of the British Museumand Germany’s Reichstag, were not held to be responsible forthe death of Mick Ferris, a 53-year-old coach driver, in 2018.However, St James, the project managers of the building where the incident took place, and the project’s engineers, Lindner Prater, were found guilty of safety breaches over the death by a jury at InnerLondoncrown court.Ferris was killed instantly when the 130kg (287lbs) window fell from the penthouse of the Corniche, a luxury tower block development on Albert Embankment, on to the street below.View image in fullscreenThe jury was told the designers should have considered the risk of the outward-opening, side-hung windows.Photograph: Nick Ansell/PAThe court heard that just over a year earlier a window panel had also fallen from the same development. “Miraculously” no one was hurt but no changes were made to the designs as a result of that incident, the court heard.The prosecution, which was brought by the Health and Safety Executive, said Ferris’s death was foreseeable and the designers had ignored concerns about the proven danger of outward-opening windows.After more than 11 hours of deliberation the jury cleared F+P and the building’s design engineer, Wintech. But it found St James and Lindner Prater had failed in their duty to keep the public safe under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974.The prosecutor Gordon Menzies told the jury it “wasn’t an accident waiting to happen … it was an accident that had already happened in August 2017. The prosecution say it was an accident waiting to happen again.”Ferris was killed by the falling window which had been blown off its hinges when the building was almost complete, the court heard. A woman coming towards him, who was pushing a wheelchair, narrowly missed being hit, jurors were told. A restrictor put in place to prevent the window being blown off had been removed, they heard.The designers had failed to consider the “catastrophic” consequences if something went wrong with this restrictor, the prosecution said. They also failed to take into account the fulcrum effect of an 85cm (33in) window being prised off its hinges, the prosecution said.Jurors were told that after the first window panel fell from the building the designers failed to use the incident as a reason to “go back to the drawing board”. The jury was told of 12 “missed opportunities” where the designers should have considered the risk of the outward-opening, side-hung windows.View image in fullscreenBillboards outside the new development in March 2017.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianAll four defendants denied the charges and claimed they did all that was reasonably practicable to ensure safety.Menzies told the court: “The wind was sufficiently strong to blow the window open further than 8 and a half inches and the oversailing glass clashed with the frame and, as a result, the hinges were prised off.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOriginally the windows had been designed to open inwards, but the design was changed to avoid them clashing with an internal ceiling coffer containing wires and pipes that they would have cleared, the court was told.It was only after Ferris’s death that the window design was changed back to inward-opening, the court heard. The prosecution said F+P should have known such risks due to its specialist knowledge of glass-covered buildings including the Gherkin.Lawyers for F+P said the firm’s role was limited and it was not involved in technical issues. They said it was there to focus on the visual aspects of the design.A spokesperson for F+P said: “Our thoughts remain with Mr Ferris’s family, as they have since October 2018. We note the court’s decision and are grateful to the jury for the time and care they have taken in considering this matter.”A spokesperson for Wintech said: “While the court has reached its conclusion, the tragedy of what happened remains. It is vital that we continue to reflect and learn, and as an industry, remain committed to strengthening standards and practices to help prevent such incidents in the future.”A spokesperson for St James said: “The death of Mick Ferris in 2018 was tragic. Our thoughts remain with his family and friends. We acknowledge today’s verdict and will carefully consider its implications.”Lindner Prater has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsLondonArchitectureConstruction industryBerkeleyNorman FosterEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump administration plans overhaul of antipoverty program for children | US news | The Guardian
description: While officials say proposed revisions will encourage more enrollment, advocates say it will undermine the program
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: While officials say proposed revisions will encourage more enrollment, advocates say it will undermine the program
Content: Children play during aftercare for the Head Start program at Easterseals South Florida in Miami in 2025.Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/APView image in fullscreenChildren play during aftercare for the Head Start program at Easterseals South Florida in Miami in 2025.Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/APUS newsTrump administration plans overhaul of antipoverty program for childrenWhile officials say proposed revisions to Head Start program will encourage more enrollment, advocates say it will undermine the programAssociated PressThu 6 Aug 2026 19.27 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 22.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Trump administration has said it plans to overhaul Head Start, tossing out many of the regulations that are the hallmark of the early education program for the nation’s neediest children.Officials from the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the federally funded preschool program, said on Thursday the proposed changes would encourage more local decision-making, but the proposal has sparked alarm across the Head Start community, where advocates say it threatens the backbone of the antipoverty initiative.Rural Americans who rely on Head Start worry about its future: ‘Without free childcare I couldn’t work’Read moreThe public will have 60 days to weigh in before it goes into effect, though it could face legal challenges that might delay implementation.Head Start centers serve around 700,000 of the nation’s most vulnerable children, including those who are homeless, in foster care or disabled. That wouldn’t change under the overhaul, though some of the changes could make it more difficult for out-of-work or homeless parents to enroll their children.Alex JAdams, an assistant secretary at health and human services, said the department is hoping to give Head Start centers the flexibility to change the way they operate. That means eliminating most of Head Start’s regulations, such as standards for low staff-to-student ratios or requirements to provide services to preschoolers’ families.“Federal mandates can certainly hinder local decision-making, drive up costs and limit the program’s reach,” Adams said on a call with reporters.
