He highlighted a decade-long decline in Head Start enrollment. “If we get this proposed rule right, we will grow the number of Head Start slots.”On a call previewing the proposed changes,Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, spoke reverently about Head Start, which was started by his uncle Sargent Shriver during the administration of president Lyndon B Johnson.“It’s a program that works for the most vulnerable of the poorest kids in our society, and it’s really important we protect it,” Kennedy said.But the changes would undermine many of the things that make Head Start distinct from other early education programs, according to current and former Head Start leaders.“This version of Head Start is a shell of the program,” said Khari Garvin, who oversaw Head Start under Joe Biden, the former Democratic president. “This is a deeply diluted version of the program, which, in my view, will cause child and community outcomes to wane.”Head Start, which began in the 1960s as part of Johnson’s “war on poverty”, is currently governed by more than 100 pages of regulations. Those require centers to have low staff-to-student ratios and a research-backed curriculum, among other things, and they ensure centers are providing wraparound services that are critical to children in poverty, including medical and dental screenings and parent coaching.The Trump administration wants to toss out nearly all of that rule book, erasing some 1,400 regulations. Instead, Head Start’s operators – which include nonprofits and school districts – would look to state and local childcare licensing requirements for guidance, including on matters of child safety and class sizes. The proposal also scraps detailed requirements on preventing lead exposure in Head Start facilities.Other aspects of the program would be scrapped entirely. Operators would no longer be required to provide robust family support services spelled out in current regulations that help parents move toward financial independence. They would no longer have deadlines for providing regular health screenings or evaluating children for developmental delays. Gone, too, is a mandate that children brush their teeth at school.While the proposed rules largely loosen requirements, Adams emphasized centers have the option to continue to operate as they had in the past. He estimated the new rules could generate more than $2bn in savings and potentially allow Head Start to serve more children.Head Start advocates called the changes out of touch and unrealistic. Many Head Start preschools are under financial pressure, facing rising labor, healthcare and supply costs. And they aren’t likely to get more money: the Trump administration hasn’t called for increasing the program’s $12bn in annual funding. So without regulations for class sizes and services, advocates worry operators would be forced to make tough choices, laying off staff or forgoing traditional offerings such as developmental screenings.Alongside the deregulation, the proposal would add some new requirements. Staffers would have to deliver all instruction in English, except in tribal communities that run immersion programs in native languages. There would be a 5% cap on administrative expenses, down from 15%. The proposal also includes a requirement for 30 minutes of physical activity – outside if the weather permits – for every three and a half hours of the program. New nutrition standards, championed by Kennedy, would require programs to provide more nutrition education for families, including warning them of “the negative health consequences of sugar-sweetened beverages and grain-based desserts”.In a call with reporters, Kennedy said he believes Head Start is effective. He cited research showing its graduates have fewer law enforcement encounters, do better in school and have better jobs than their peers. He added that he tried to shield Head Start from many of the cuts that hit the rest of his agency.Still, the Trump administration succeeded last year in laying off much of Head Start’s support staff and closing half of its regional offices.Explore more on these topicsUS newsChildrenRobert F Kennedy JrPovertynewsShareReuse this content

title: Judge approves $106m settlement over deadly 2019 Hard Rock Hotel collapse | New Orleans | The Guardian
description: Settlement ends years-long legal battle over collapse of 18-story hotel that was under construction in New Orleans
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Settlement ends years-long legal battle over collapse of 18-story hotel that was under construction in New Orleans
Content: A view of the Hard Rock Hotel after a fatal partial collapse in New Orleans on 12 October 2019.Photograph: Gerald Herbert/APView image in fullscreenA view of the Hard Rock Hotel after a fatal partial collapse in New Orleans on 12 October 2019.Photograph: Gerald Herbert/APNew OrleansJudge approves $106m settlement over deadly 2019 Hard Rock Hotel collapseSettlement ends years-long legal battle over collapse of 18-story hotel that was under construction in New OrleansAssociated PressThu 6 Aug 2026 19.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 19.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA judge approved a $106m settlement on Thursday that ends a years-long legal battle over the deadly 2019 collapse of a Hard Rock Hotel that was under construction inNew Orleans.The 18-story hotel project partially collapsed in October 2019 , killing three people and damaging nearby property. A grand jury ultimately decided against indicting anyone in the deadly collapse, but lawsuits were filed, including one brought by the city of New Orleans in August 2020 naming the building owners, their partners and contractors.The various lawsuits were consolidated into one case that includes a total of 490 plaintiffs, including injured workers and businesses affected by the collapse, against 21 defendants, according to Mark Glago, co-lead counsel for the plaintiffs. The case has been pending for more than six years, Glago noted.The combined $106m settlement was approved by Orleans parish civil district court judge Kern Reese on Thursday, according to Glago and Court records.“This will be an honor to, you know, these claimants that have been through so much,” Glago said of the settlement. “We are very, very happy with this $106m.”The settlement funds will eventually be distributed by a special master.Explore more on these topicsNew OrleansnewsShareReuse this content

title: Most Americans view rising living costs as biggest barrier to a better life, survey finds | US economy | The Guardian
description: When asked to detail what would make a better life in three to five years, 60% of US adults said greater financial security
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: When asked to detail what would make a better life in three to five years, 60% of US adults said greater financial security
Content: Groceries and food costs in particular are causing financial distress, with 90% of survey respondents listing it as their top cost-of-living concern.Photograph: Jeff Greenberg/Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGroceries and food costs in particular are causing financial distress, with 90% of survey respondents listing it as their top cost-of-living concern.Photograph: Jeff Greenberg/Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesUS economyMost Americans view rising living costs as biggest barrier to a better life, survey findsWhen asked to detail what would make a better life in three to five years, 60% of US adults said greater financial securityGaya GuptaThu 6 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmericans may seem increasingly divided on beliefs and values, but in a new survey of more than 30,000 adults from across the country spanning generations and economic classes, a majority of Americans agree there’s a significant barrier to achieving a better life: the rising cost of living.When asked to describe what a better life in three to five years would look like, 60% of Americans said they wanted greater financial security, according to a survey that was conducted by the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility and the WK Kellogg Foundation in mid-April.In interviews that accompanied the survey, respondents often defined financial security as being able to afford basic necessities without worry.“A better life for me and my family would look like being able to buy a home, and being able to afford all the basic necessities, rent, utilities, car, food, healthcare – as well as being able to have enough left over to save for the future for retirement and vacations,” said a 35-year-old respondent from Dearborn Heights, Michigan.Though it may appear to be a simple goal, many Americans believe it’s out of reach. Forty per cent of respondents described themselves as either “getting by but financially vulnerable” or “struggling to meet basic needs”. Groceries and food costs in particular are causing financial distress, with 90% of respondents listing it as their top cost-of-living concern, followed by housing, transportation and healthcare.One survey respondent, a 49-year-old father in Philadelphia, said that success to him was not about extravagant living, rather it was being able to afford his child’s field trips for school or help a family member struggling with their bills. “I just want to be comfortable,” he said.The survey is the latest illustration of how the rising cost of living is the defining challenge for many Americans today. Between higher gas prices, growing electricity bills and a housing market that feels out of reach, many everyday expenses have turned into everyday frustrations for Americans whose paychecks aren’t keeping up with rising inflation. A recentHarris pollthat found 95% of Americans believe the country is undergoing an affordability crisis.This experience seems out of step with other parts of the economy, like the US stock market reachingrecord highsand the seemingly unstoppable rise of AI investment, that are growing.“While we spend a lot of time discussing some of these macroeconomic indicators – from the jobs report, to quarterly GDP growth, to what’s happening with interest rates – they alone can’t help us understand how people are actually experiencing the economy in their day-to-day lives,” said JP Julien, a partner at McKinsey involved in the research, during a news briefing.While Americans largely agreed that affordability was a key barrier to achieving a better quality of life, they diverged on what needs to be improved. Rural respondents were likely to say they needed better jobs and career pathways, while urban respondents said they wanted to see more affordable housing and improved safety.A majority (60%) of respondents said local, state and federal government was responsible for helping people get ahead – 20% more than other institutions including faith organizations, banks, non-profits and schooling systems.But only 30% reported that government institutions have been helpful. Instead, respondents ranked friends and family as the top group helping them get ahead, followed by employers.With this gap in support from the government and employers, community connectedness was a key indicator of how respondents felt more broadly about their outlook. Respondents who said they felt strongly connected to their communities were more than twice as likely to say they were in control of their lives and future and nearly four times as likely to say their lives had “momentum”. Only one-third of respondents, however, reported feeling this strong sense of community.“We’re not too connected with our community and neighborhood,” said a 61-year-old respondent from Los Angeles. “There are a few people that we know, but for the most part, most people keep to themselves.”Explore more on these topicsUS economyEconomicsFoodnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Mamma mia!’: Trump tariffs refund ignites 53% profit spike at Nintendo | Nintendo | The Guardian
description: Profit jump fuelled largely by unknown US refund amount as Japanese video game firm records quarterly sales drop
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Profit jump fuelled largely by unknown US refund amount as Japanese video game firm records quarterly sales drop
Content: Nintendo said sales of its Switch 2 console, which was released last summer, maintained strong momentum but overall sales dropped 10%.Photograph: Richard A Brooks/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNintendo said sales of its Switch 2 console, which was released last summer, maintained strong momentum but overall sales dropped 10%.Photograph: Richard A Brooks/AFP/Getty ImagesNintendo‘Mamma mia!’: Trump tariffs refund ignites 53% profit spike at NintendoProfit jump fuelled largely by unknown US refund amount as Japanese video game firm records quarterly sales dropKalyeena MakortoffThu 6 Aug 2026 07.11 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNintendo has reported a jump in profits, as the Japanese game maker’s earnings were buoyed up by a long-awaited refund on Donald Trump’s tariffs.The company said profits surged 53.5% to ¥147.4bn (£694m) over the three months to June, substantially beating expert forecasts for ¥77.8bn.Nintendo said sales of its Switch 2 console, which was released last summer, “maintained strong sales momentum”, while popular games such as Yoshi and the Mysterious Book, Star Fox, and Pokémon Pokopia “performed steadily”. However, that did not make up for an overall drop in sales compared with the same period last year, with revenue down by 10% to ¥517.8bn.‘Let’s-a go!’ The story of Nintendo – podcastRead moreInstead, Nintendo said profits were aided by a refund on US tariffs, after the country’ssupreme court ruledin February that Donald Trump’s sweeping “liberation day” trade levies were illegal.TheTrump administrationhas refunded about $100bn from the tariffs charged before the court ruling, representing 60% of the total $165bn collected. Trump has continued to pitch tariffs as a solution for the US economy, bringing back domestic production, securing better trade deals and closing the deficit in the federal budget.Nintendo’s Tokyo-listed shares were up 2.87% on Thursday after the earnings release.The companyfiled a lawsuitweeks after the US supreme court ruling, demanding a full refund from the White House that would cover what it spent on tariffs, plus interest.While a refund now appears to have come through, Nintendo stopped short of confirming the full amount, at a time when it is still appears to be resisting calls to pass those refunds on to consumers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLast month, Nintendo was hit with aclass action lawsuit on behalf of customers, which claims the company hiked its prices because of tariffs but later benefited from the refunds. Nintendo’s lawyers described the lawsuit as “meritless”, and that the price customers paid represented “the purchase price of the goods they wanted and received.”Last month, Trump imposed afresh round of tariffson more than 80 countries, including Japan, in a move that is likely to pose further problems for companies such as Nintendo. However, a coalition of 25 US statesare now suing the Trump administration over the levies, potentially opening the door to another round of refunds for beleaguered exporters.Explore more on these topicsNintendoTrump tariffsNintendo Switch 2GamesJapanTariffsInternational tradenewsShareReuse this content

title: One potential breakout star for each Premier League club this season | Premier League | The Guardian
description: A crop of young players emerges every season in the Premier League. Who will make the grade this year?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A crop of young players emerges every season in the Premier League. Who will make the grade this year?
Content: The young players who could make their names this season.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe young players who could make their names this season.Composite: Getty ImagesOpta AnalystPremier LeagueOne potential breakout star for each Premier League club this seasonA crop of young players emerges every season in the Premier League. Who will make the grade this year?ByOpta AnalystRyan Benson, Aryan Jolly and David SegarThu 6 Aug 2026 08.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 08.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal: Marli SalmonDowman is old news by now, so we’re going to look at someone four months older than him. Much like the fish of the same name, Salmon has risen quickly. The defender became the fourth-youngest player to represent Arsenal last season when he came off the bench against Club Brugge in the Champions League in December at the age of just 16 years and 102 days.Salmon made four appearances for the first team last season, while also featuring 14 times for their Under-21s inPremier League2. He won an impressive 71.8% of his duels in PL2 (56 of 78); of defenders to contest at least 50 duels, only two players had a better success rate. Salmon – who can play right-back or centre-back – has signed a pre-agreement to commit his future to the club when he turns 17 later this month, and it would not be surprising to see him given more opportunities by Mikel Arteta.View image in fullscreenAston Villa: Brian MadjoAston Villa signed Madjo from Metz in January for about £10.5m but were not able to register him. He is available now and has been involved regularly during pre-season. The giant 17-year-old centre-forward’s movement and power are reminiscent of Erling Haaland.He has caught the eye in Villa’s recent friendlies, scoring four times. Pre-season only counts for so much, of course, but you can only score against what’s in front of you.Bournemouth: Veljko MilosavljevicAfter the departure of Marcos Senesi, Bournemouth have a position in the centre of defence up for grabs and Milosavljevic could be the man to claim it. Milosavljevic joined the club last summer from Red Star Belgrade. Although he didn’t feature prominently, making just seven appearances in all competitions, the 19-year-old is clearly a promising defender.He made more clearances than any other Bournemouth player on his Premier League debut in September, before going on to make his full international debut for Serbia in October. Marco Rose may want more experience at centre-back, especially given how youthful some of Bournemouth’s other defenders are, but Milosavljevic will hope to take another step forward this season.Brentford: Antoni MilamboMilambo had a difficult introduction to English football last season. Signed from Feyenoord for around £21m last year, he suffered a season-ending ACL injury on international duty in October. He was obviously set back but will be confident he can force his way into Keith Andrews’ thinking this term.He became Feyenoord’s youngest ever player in 2021, when he made his debut as a 16-year-old, but Milambo rose to prominence in 2024-25 as a forward-thinking, box-to-box midfielder who was technically good and could be a threat in attack. No other Eredivisie player under the age of 21 bettered his 14 goal involvements in all competitions that season. He could be a dynamic asset in the very useful midfield Andrews has built.View image in fullscreenBrighton: Zadok YohannaYohanna will need a little patience as he’s still quite raw but, if he is given opportunities at Brighton this season, he will catch the eye. The 19-year-old Nigerian has joined from AIK for around £21.5m, a record sale for Swedish football, despite playing just 13 league games for the club. It was enough to convince Brighton, who have been impressed by his direct style and fearless dribbling.A left-footed winger who plays on the right side of the attack, Yohanna was attempting more dribbles per 90 minutes than any other player in the Allsvenskan this year before his move was confirmed in June. He also tallied the most take-ons driving into the box (six), take-ons inthe box (15) and the joint-most take-ons followed by a shot (three), despite playing significantly fewer minutes than many other players. His end product needs work, but he will get bums off seats.Chelsea: Reggie WatsonChelsea always have a conveyor belt of young talent waiting for a chance – the issue is many seem to get lost in the crowd. But, after losing Rio Ngumoha to Liverpool a couple of years ago, the club have apparently made a greater effort to keep hold of emerging homegrown talents, and one of those they were especially keen to tie down was Reggie Watson.A towering defensive midfielder, Watson, 16, has impressive physical attributes but is also tidy on the ball, appears to have good spatial awareness and plays with considerable personality for one so young. It’s easy to see why he’s been tentatively compared with Rodri.Xabi Alonso has also spoken about being “really impressed” with his impact in pre-season. Given the uncertainty around other midfielders – such as the fitness issues of Roméo Lavia and Dário Essugo – Watson could get minutes this season.Coventry City: Kai AndrewsWith survival being the name of the game for Coventry City season, giving minutes to young players may not be Frank Lampard’s top priority. There is one youngster who could force his way into Lampard’s plans, though: Andrews. The 19-year-old midfielder made 10 appearances for Coventry last season before joining Hibernian on loan.While Andrews failed to make his mark in Scotland, he ended the campaign on a high as he made his first start for Wales in a friendly against Romania. He acquitted himself well in the match, making nine passes in the final third, the third most of any player, and winning two fouls. Andrews will need to decide whether to stay at Coventry and fight for a place or go out on loan for regular minutes.Crystal Palace: Joél Drakes-ThomasDrakes-Thomas became Crystal Palace’s youngest Premier League player last season and will hope to play a more prominent role this campaign. The wideman made his Palace debut in the Conference League when he was just 16 years old and he shone against Finnish side KuPS. He attempted seven crosses during the match, the most of any player, and he created two chances, the joint-most. The appointment of Pierre Sage has signalled the start of a new era at Selhurst Park, and Drakes-Thomas has the ability to be a figurehead of any future success.Everton: Tyrique GeorgeGeorge looked promising at Chelsea, but his first few months at Everton after initially joining on loan in February were something of a settling-in period, as he started just one game for David Moyes’ side. With a full pre-season under his belt, George could burst into life this season.Quick, dynamic and eager to run at full-backs, the 20-year-old could be the one to benefit most from Jack Grealish returning to Manchester City after his loan. George has started three of Everton’s four pre-season friendlies in the absence of Iliman Ndiaye, who is reportedly the subject of interest from abroad. With Grealish gone and Dwight McNeil dropping down the pecking order, George has a big opportunity.View image in fullscreenFulham: Farhaan Ali-WahidThe 19-year-old will be hoping to make his debut for Fulham this season, having already impressed for their Under-21s. He signed his first professional contract with the club last summer and went on to score 10 goals in PL2. The left winger also added seven assists, proving he can create as well as find the net himself.Only Chelsea’s Shumaira Mheuka (19) and Liverpool’s Kieran Morrison (18) recorded more goal involvements than Ali-Wahid (17) in the PL2 last season, while just 10 players created more chances from open play than his 26. He was nominated for the PL2 Player of the Season award and the new Fulham manager, Álvaro Arbeloa, has been picking him in pre-season.Hull City: Charlie HughesHughes was Hull’s defensive lynchpin last season. The 22-year-old centre-back started 36 games in the Championship and played every minute of their successful playoff campaign. He has a remarkable willingness to put his body on the line. Last season, he made 1.54 blocks per 90 minutes, the most of any regular player in the Championship. He also made more clearances per 90 minutes (7.62) than any of his teammates (1,000+ mins). Hull may struggle in the Premier League, but Hughes could be a diamond in the rough.Ipswich Town: Tudor Mendel-IdowuMendel-Idowu, who spent most of his youth development at Chelsea before a year at Anderlecht, was snapped up by Ipswich in the summer of 2024, though he is yet to make his first-team debut. The winger is an intelligent fellow; he appeared on a TV show called Child Genius when he was eight years old and went on to become a King’s Scholar at Eton College.He has not only thrived in academia, but also on the pitch. He recorded 15 goal involvements in 17 PL2 games for the Ipswich’s Under-21s last season (nine goals, six assists); only three players managed more in the league. On top of that, only three players created more chances from open play than his 33, and just two won possession in the final third more than him (21).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLeeds United: Jayden LienouChances were at a premium last season for young players under Daniel Farke. The youngest player to play for Leeds was 21-year-old Facundo Buonanotte, who had already made his debut for Argentina, and even he only played a fleeting role in the second half of the season.But Lienou may just be winning Farke’s trust. The 18-year-old defender started all but one of Leeds’ PL2 games last season and won possession 5.4 times per 90 minutes, the second most in the side. He was the only youth-team player to feature in Leeds’ first three pre-season games, and he was called into the senior Wales squad by Craig Bellamy in June, showing he is impressing coaches for both club and country.View image in fullscreenLiverpool: Trey NyoniWith a new manager comes a new opportunity to impress, and Trey Nyoni hastaken that chance in pre-season. The midfielder had to be patient after joining Liverpool from Leicester in 2023. Arne Slot gave him limited minutes last season, with Nyoni making 14 appearances in all competitions, only two of which were starts, both in the League Cup. With Andoni Iraola now in the dugout, the 19-year-old has been able to stake his claim and has been Liverpool’s standout midfielder in pre-season.One of the most impressive aspects to his game is his verticality. Nyoni wants to get the ball forward as often as possible, though he’s not careless in possession. In his three friendlies this summer in the US – against Sunderland, Wrexham and Leeds United – Nyoni attempted 154 passes, completing 141 of them (92%). Just looking at forward passes, he completed an impressive 44 out of 54 (81%). With Curtis Jones potentially leaving, and most of Liverpool’s transfer funds seemingly going on attackers, the path may open up for Nyoni.Manchester City: Ryan McAidooMcAidoo has shone in City’s extremely competitive academy. The winger impressed in the PL2 last season, with only Reigan Heskey (15) registering more goal involvements than him (12) for City. McAidoo made his first-team debut last season, and he marked the occasion by scoring the ninth goal inCity’s 10-1 drubbing of Exeter Cityin the FA Cup.More recently, the 18-year-old caught the eye with his one-v-one ability in City’s pre-season friendly against Inter. He also had the second-most touches in the opposition’s box (13). Enzo Maresca raved about McAidoo’s performance, calling him “the type of winger I love”.View image in fullscreenManchester United: JJ GabrielGabriel is undoubtedly the biggest hope in Manchester United’s academy. He apparently nearly left at the end of the 2024-25 season until senior club figures stepped in and his reputation has only continued to grow since. Then, aged 14, he had already become the youngest player to represent United’s Under-18s, scoring twice on his debut. After turning 15 in October, he was soon involved in first-team training.Nevertheless, his focus remained the Under-18s, for whom he scored 23 goals – a tally bettered by only one player – in the 2025-26 U18 Premier League campaign, winning the competition’s Player of the Season award.Where all 20 Premier League clubs should strengthen before the seasonRead moreA skilful attacker who can play out wide or through the middle, Gabriel is brave, expressive and confident. He showed these traits when he came on as a late substitute in United’s pre-season friendly against Atlético Madrid at the weekend.The record for youngest Premier League player is out of reach, but Gabriel has a good chance of becoming United’s youngest player in the Premier League; that honour currently belongs to Angel Gomes (16 years, 263 days).Newcastle United: Park Seung-sooFor all the good he did at Newcastle, some supporters think Eddie Howe could have done more to bring young talent through. Now he’s gone and Newcastle are in a transition period, several of their young players will fancy their chances of stepping up. Park, 19, is one of them. The South Korean left-winger was signed last summer and spent the season adapting to English football in PL2. He averaged 4.7 dribble attempts per 90 minutes in that competition and caught the eye with his energetic displays and tidy footwork.With Anthony Gordon gone, there may well be chances available on the left flank, especially ifnew signing Bazoumana Tourédoes not get off to a flying start. Park has impressed in pre-season and a step up to top-flight football might not be far down the line.Nottingham Forest: Kalum ThompsonThompson signed for Nottingham Forest from Northern Irish club Linfield last July and, despite being 16 at the time, he went on to spend the majority of 2025-26 playing for the club’s Under-21s. The left winger was the youngest player to feature for Forest Under-21s last season and yet only four players – three of whom are now 20 – tallied more minutes than him (1,090).The 17-year-old won the club’s scholar of the year prize at the end of the season. A tricky and purposeful player, Thompson’s 4.7 dribble attempts per 90 ranked highly in the PL2 and his six goal involvements were the most of any Forest player.Sunderland: Nilson AnguloAlthough Angulo reportedly cost £15m in January and is already 23 years old, he just about fits into the potential breakout player category. After joining from Anderlecht, Angulo’s impact at Sunderland wasn’t exactly explosive. There were flashes of his flair but he was clearly still pretty raw.Nevertheless, those first few months gave him time to adapt and, after a fairly encouraging World Cup with Ecuador, he’ll now hope to kick on. He has the ability and he has an athletic build which should help him once his game has been refined a little more.Sunderland will hope the Angulo of Anderlecht comes to the fore a little more this season. Prior to his move last season, he’d attempted more dribbles (111) than any other player in the Belgian Pro League, while only Christos Tzolis (17) – now at Arsenal – bettered his 11 goal involvements. If he keeps progressing, Angulo will be a very useful weapon for Régis Le Bris.Tottenham: Lucá Williams-BarnettSpurs seem to have exciting young talents breaking through every other season, and now it’s Williams-Barnett’s turn to see if he can make his mark. Williams-Barnett started last season playing Under-18s football but quickly broke into first-team contention. He made one senior appearance but featured on the bench semi-regularly throughout the campaign.He was one of Spurs’ standout players in the PL2 despite only playing 10 games. Williams-Barnett recorded an astounding 1.25 combined goals and assists per 90 in the PL2, ranking him fourth among all players (500+ mins). The 17-year-old attacking midfielder also created 0.8 big chances per 90 last season, again ranking him fourth (500+ mins). He has featured heavily in pre-season, building great momentum which he can hopefully take into the season.This is an article byOpta AnalystExplore more on these topicsPremier LeagueOpta AnalystfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tour de France Femmes: Reusser stays ahead as Le Court savours stage win | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Kim Le Court won the sixth stage of the Tour de France Femmes in Tournon-sur-Rhône while Marlen Reusser retained the overall lead
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Kim Le Court won the sixth stage of the Tour de France Femmes in Tournon-sur-Rhône while Marlen Reusser retained the overall lead
Content: Kim Le Court shows her delight as she crosses the finish line to win the stage.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKim Le Court shows her delight as she crosses the finish line to win the stage.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesTour de France FemmesTour de France Femmes: Reusser stays ahead as Le Court savours stage winMauritian rider outsprints Kerbaol and Pieterse‘Winning a stage in a Tour de France is very special’Jeremy Whittlein Tournon-sur-RhôneThu 6 Aug 2026 13.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 20.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarlen Reusser retained the overall lead in theTour de France Femmesfrom rival Demi Vollering after another broiling stage through central France saw Kim Le Court take the second Tour stage win of her career in Tournon-sur-Rhone.The Mauritian rider Le Court recovered from a mechanical problem earlier in the stage on the climb of the Col de Lalouvesc to join the day’s breakaway group and outsprint Cédrine Kerbaol of France, and Queen of the Mountains classification leader, Puck Pieterse.“I was on the limit,” Le Court said of her winning sprint. “I can’t believe I still had the legs to sprint. It was really hard, this close, before I could give up. I will never give up after the big effort my team did.”Tour de France Femmes 2026: Kim Le Court wins stage six sprint after breakaway – liveRead moreLe Court had originally been considered a contender for final victory but lost ground after Tuesday’s individual time trial. “I’ve been really struggling since the time trial day but I think this really makes our Tour,” she said.“We’ve still got ambitions for the general classification, but winning a stage in a Tour de France is very special. People don’t really remember top 10 or top five riders in Tour, but they do remember stage winners.”Le Court’s success is a popular one, after a difficult season in which she has dealt with serial injuries. But she has also shown considerable sportsmanship, stopping to help Kasia Niewiadoma after the 2024 Tour Femmes winner crashed heavily in Milan-San Remo.Despite missing out on the stage victory, it was a successful day for Pieterse as she now has 47 points in the mountain classification, the highest total ever recorded in the history of the Tour de France Femmes.“I wanted to win the stage of course,” Pieterse said, “but I think I did everything else today. I decided to gamble, but Kim was still the strongest in the sprint, so I don’t think I can be too sad.”As the heatwave continued, the peloton raced over six classified climbs into the Ardeche, with Friday’s ascent of Mont Ventoux now very much in their thoughts.After three days she will want to forget, defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prevot arrested the decline in her form and finished the stage in the group of favourites alongside Reusser, Vollering and Niewiadoma. She is still languishing in 15th place overall, five minutes behind race leader Reusser, and on Wednesday had conceded that: “It’s over.”However, while her deficit seems almost insurmountable, her rivals will have taken note of her improved performance and of her experience of the Ventoux, which she first rode in 2021.“I think it’s the most iconic climb in France,” Ferrand-Prevot said of the Provençal mountain. “Everyone knows about it, even if you’re not a cyclist.”The inclusion of the Ventoux in the Tour de France Femmes is the latest indicator of a race growing in stature, year by year.“We try to align with the most mythical summits,” Tour de France Femmes director Marion Rousse said. “They’re part of the history of the Tour and the history of the sport.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBoth Vollering and Niewiadoma have prior experience of the mountain, but not at this level of racing, and only from the less demanding north side, rather than the more daunting southern ascent. However, there is no doubt that the ascent of the Ventoux, by a women’s peloton that only a few years ago was derided by some for its abilities, will be a Rubicon moment.One rider who never shared those doubts is current race leader Reusser. “It’s proof that human beings aren’t always such a smart species,” she said of those who had disparaged the women’s peloton.View image in fullscreenMarlen Reusser shows her delight at retaining the lead.Photograph: Alex Broadway/Getty ImagesIn terms of past exploits by women on the “Giant of Provence” Nicole Cooke’s solo attack over the Ventoux, which took her to overall victory in the 2006 Grande Boucle Feminine, is perhaps the most memorable.“I don’t suppose anybody wanted to chase me all the way up the Ventoux,” Cooke recalled. “The heat was a big factor. People don’t want to chase on a day when the heat is so debilitating.”Cooke won the stage by four minutes and the race overall by more than six. “After the finish, we went to a cafe and had ice-creams,” she said. “It was one of the special days.”At that time, women’s cycling had little profile and media coverage was almost nonexistent. Cooke’s achievement never really got the recognition it deserved, due to what she considered to be media’s preoccupation with the prevalence of doping in men’s cycling. The rebirth of the Tour de France Femmes however has dramatically reversed that trend. The heat will also be big factor in toFriday’s stage to the Ventoux, 20 years after Cooke’s own moment in the sun. But the inclusion of a climb that the French still call the “killer mountain”, is a total vindication of the quantum leap achieved by the women’s peloton.Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It just means more’: Black college gymnasts competing in a divided south | College sports | The Guardian
description: Nyla Aquino’s rise at the University of Georgia reveals the tensions facing Black athletes as the SEC thrives while DEI programs and voting rights come under attack
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Nyla Aquino’s rise at the University of Georgia reveals the tensions facing Black athletes as the SEC thrives while DEI programs and voting rights come under attack
Content: Nyla Aquino of the Georgia Bulldogs reacts after competing in vault during the NCAA women's gymnastics championship in April.Photograph: Chris Swann/NCAA Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNyla Aquino of the Georgia Bulldogs reacts after competing in vault during the NCAA women's gymnastics championship in April.Photograph: Chris Swann/NCAA Photos/Getty ImagesCollege sports‘It just means more’: Black college gymnasts competing in a divided southNyla Aquino’s rise at the University of Georgia reveals the tensions facing Black athletes as the SEC thrives while DEI programs and voting rights come under attackCaroline PriceThu 6 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 12.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a February Friday night at the University of Georgia, but Stegeman Coliseum is alive.Situated in the center of the sprawling southern campus in Athens, the towering arena has hosted Georgia Bulldogs basketball, volleyball and gymnastics teams for more than six decades. On 22 February 1964, Stegeman Coliseum hosted its first athletic event and, concurrently, its first win.Six decades later, on 20 February 2026, then-19-year-old Nyla Aquino salutes the judges before a sold-out crowd of more than 10,000 spectators. The No 6-ranked Bulldogs are in the final stretch of a close battle with Southeastern Conference rival No 4 Florida, and Aquino needs to deliver. Settling into her opening pose, the sophomore nonchalantly smiles, winks at her teammates and begins.Just three years before Stegeman Coliseum opened its doors, Aquino, a Black student athlete from Boston, would have had to fight to attend UGA. In 1961, the university admitted its first two Black students only after judicial order, and a mob of roughly 1,000 locals and Klan members rioted. Sixty-five years later, Aquino leads Georgia’s charge against Florida during Black History Month.The NAACP’s boycott call is a wake-up moment for the American Black athlete | Howard BryantRead moreAs the crowd rustles, Hollywood Swinging by Kool & The Gang cuts through the noise andAquino takes off. The NCAA All-American launches into a massive tumbling pass, nearing the rafters and landing with a stick, a smile, and a roar.Aquino soars through her routine, every move exuding confidence. She leaps to a track by Lil Jon & The East Side Boyz, tumbles to DMX and hits her final pose to Jay-Z. As she salutes the judges, Stegeman erupts. Her teammates swarm Aquino with hugs and the crowd breaks into chants for a “perfect 10”. The arena is living, breathing – alive, all because of Nyla. She scores a 9.925 for the highest mark of the night.Though Georgia fall just short of upsetting Florida, Aquino’s ovation doesn’t stop in Stegeman. Online, Aquino’sode to Black culturetook flight, collecting more than 3m views on ESPNW’s TikTok.On the floor, Aquino is one of the University of Georgia’s brightest stars, leading the Bulldogs to a resurgent sixth-place finish at this year’sNCAAchampionships. But beyond the 60-year-old Coliseum doors and into the south, she faces a starkly different reality.While Black athletes perform, tumble and win for the Southeastern Conference, state lawmakers fight to redraw district lines and strip diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs from the very universities they represent.The SEC ‘just means more’From Athens to Baton Rouge, the SEC has built something that doesn’t exist anywhere else in women’s college gymnastics: an undeniable culture.“People who are SEC fans are usually diehard SEC fans,” Aquino reflects. That mentality extends to gymnastics. “You see a lot of loyalty coming from the fans [and] alumni ... no matter what sport they’re originally supporting or coming from, they are going to be diehard for you as well.”All nine SEC programs rank in the national top 20 for attendance. This March, Arkansas set the all-time SEC attendance record with 15,512 fans. “I love competing at Arkansas,” Aquino tells me. “That energy, that connection, and that community is something that you really only get when you’re competing in the SEC.”This culture also wins – a lot. Five of the eight teams at the 2026 NCAA championships came from the SEC, and 28 of the sport’s 45 all-time team titles (62%) belong to schools now in the conference. While the Oklahoma Sooners dominate the 21st-century title race, the sport’s winningest program is none other than Georgia.For national title-contending recruits like Aquino, the choice of program had long been limited to the SEC, UCLA, Utah – or a program with a marginal shot at a national title. While Aquino was heavily courted by UCLA as a teen, the SEC’s southern drawl pulled her in. “As I got older and my family was more in tune with the SEC, I knew that the SEC was somewhere that I really wanted to be.”“There’s so much culture – who doesn’t want to be in the SEC, right?”Dr Amira Rose Davis, assistant professor and historian at the University of Texas-Austin, understands the appeal. Her cousin played women’s basketball at LSU, so she witnessed the cultural immersion first-hand. “There is a certain swag in the community … there’s nothing like being on campus watching their fans turn out.”She says the SEC’s culture is uniquely fitted to amplify women’s sports. “In SEC spaces, [sports] matter socially in the fabric of those communities in a different way,” Davis says. From gymnastics to basketball, SEC women’s sports draw the crowds and headlines that other conferences don’t.“You’re merging a kind of inherently southern culture and fandom that draws from a huge cross section of the community.” The SEC doesn’t just “mean more”, to quotethe conference’s long-running slogan– its schools “do it different”, Davis adds. However, doing it differently inevitably has drawbacks.View image in fullscreenNyla Aquino of the Georgia Bulldogs competes on the floor during a meet against the Auburn Tigers in February 2025.Photograph: Stew Milne/Getty ImagesConditional loveWhen Aquino’s floor routine went viral, overwhelming support flooded in. The performance to an all-Black musical lineup during Black History Month made waves in online communities. “She represented. Being unapologetically Black during OUR month in a predominantly white setting is so next level,” one user wrote.Not everyone who showed up to Stegeman – or engaged on TikTok – joined the ovation. While Aquino, a young Black athlete, delivered a winning performance for her Georgia teammates, she also delivered for a demographically mismatched donor base.“These flagship SEC schools run on boosterism and donated dollars,” Davis says. “Courting booster money means you are dealing with older alumni who might have very strong opinions about if you have hip-hop in your gymnastics routine.”While the online support was plentiful, it also offered counters. “75% dancing like we’re in a club. 25% actual gymnastics. I miss the old days when gymnastics was actually an art,” a user complained. Comments from anonymous users criticized Aquino’s choice of music and artistic expression.On a night where Aquino delivered her team’s top score , her performance still received pushback. Should she or one of her Black teammates make a mistake, the outcome can be far worse. “No matter how well I do, someone’s going to be racist,” she says.That reality has come to light across the SEC in recent years, as majority-Black athletes and teams deliver winning results for white donors. That dichotomy is contentious. “Anytime you have the demographics of a fanbase not necessarily matching up with the demographics of the athletic laborers, you set yourself up for some of these tensions,” Davis attests.In 2018, a top Mississippi donor sent photos of Black women on Oxford Square to a former dean. The alum complained that the college town was being “overtaken by the wrong elements”, using derogatory language and arguing the image did not represent the traditional culture of the university or town. “Goddamn, this is literally like being in the Congo jungle,” the donor wrote, per theMississippi Free Press.At Texas, alumni threatened to pull funding in 2021 after Longhorn athletesdisavowedthe Eyes of Texas fight song. According to theTexas Tribune, the song was historically performed at campus minstrel shows and its title was linked to a saying from Robert E Lee.“My wife and I have given an endowment in excess of $1 million to athletics. This could very easily be rescinded if things don’t drastically change around here,” one donor wrote to the university. “Has everyone become oblivious of who supports athletics?”These donors disparage the same athletes they bankroll. The Texas football team, which reached the College Football Playoff in 2023 and 2024, has a majority-Black roster. Of the nine Georgia gymnasts who made the All-SEC team this year, five are Black.Yet, after nearly two decades of competing as a Black female athlete in a predominantly white sport, Aquino is accustomed to emotional whiplash. She has learned to channel distraction into action. Aquino’s identity is a point of pride, not a financial talking point.“The whole point is to revolutionize,” she says. “I deserve to display my Blackness on a pedestal, whether it makes you uncomfortable or not.”The disappearing scaffoldingWhile Aquino and Black athletes lead with pride on the floor and field, administrators struggle to offer support as they face mounting sociopolitical roadblocks. Davis has witnessed the structural collapse. Presently, it feels like the scaffolding is collapsing around her.In 2023, Texas Governor Greg Abbott signedSenate Bill 17, prohibiting public institutions of higher education from engaging in “specified diversity, equity, and inclusion activities”. In 2025, the Trump administration directed federal agencies to eliminate equity-related grants and DEI offices, pushing the Department of Justice toinvestigateuniversities’ diversity programs.In just the past few years, UT-Austin has lost its Multicultural Engagement Center, the African and African Diaspora Studies department and countless supporting staff and administrative workers.Full departments, resources, careers: gutted. Davis and her colleagues feel much the same. Also lost are relevant courses, cultural resources and support for the university’s Black athletes. While the courses often attract significant interest from Black students, the instructors’ syllabi face rapidly intensifying scrutiny.“They’re going through [our courses] with a fine-tooth comb,” she attests.A simple stroll through campus from the Gordon-White Building, home to the Black Studies program, paints a sobering picture. “It feels like two different worlds,”Davis confesses. “It’s hard to walk through this campus and watch our department and other programs and services being taken away while they announce millions of dollars in investment to other corners of campus.”When you reach Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium, the contrast becomes blinding. While Davis and her colleagues face roadblock after roadblock, donors park rows of shiny vehicles to entice recruits. On the other side of town, historically Black Austin neighborhoods become further siloed from the institution at its center.Though she pushes on, Davis and her colleagues across the nation feel suffocated. At the moment, the light at the end of the tunnel is dim. “It’s hard to imagine support systems ... they’ve been eradicated and I haven’t seen them rebuilt.”An avid gymnastics supporter, Davis watched with excitement in 2022 as Fisk University in Nashville announced the nation’s first gymnastics program at a historically Black college or university (HBCU). The move made headlines, and two more HBCUs – Talladega College in Alabama and Wilberforce University in Ohio – soon created programs of their own.For the first time, Black gymnasts could bring their gymnastics talents to an HBCU. Shortly after, nationally ranked recruit Morgan Price decommitted from Arkansas, choosing instead to join Fisk. Price made history for the Bulldogs, becoming the first HBCU gymnast to score a perfect 10 and win a national title.But after just three seasons, Fisk cut its program, citing “considerable challenges to schedule competitions and build a robust recruiting pipeline”. Talladega fell after just one year of competition. For a fleeting moment, HBCU gymnastics was a dream realized. Though Aquino and many top Black recruits chose to attend predominantly white institutions (PWIs), the announcement was still devastating. “I was so hurt,” Aquino reflected.“Fisk represented opportunity, and it built on incredible history. It was all about visibility – about proving that Black athletes belong in gymnastics.”View image in fullscreenThe Georgia Bulldogs are introduced before the NCAA championships in April.Photograph: Chris Swann/NCAA Photos/Getty ImagesOut of boundsFor Aquino and Black athletes, visibility is power. So what happens when they choose to withhold it? In May, the NAACP’s “Out of Bounds” initiativecalled onBlack athletes across the SEC to do just that. Launched in response to April’s landmarkgerrymandering rulingin Louisiana v Callais, the organization called on Black athletes and their supporters to withhold athletic and financial support from public universities in states that suppressed Black voting representation.The campaign’s message lands with particular weight this week: Thursday is the 61st anniversary of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, the very law at the center of the NAACP’s argument.‘A Jackie Robinson moment’: Jeffries echoes NAACP calls for college sports boycott over voting rightsRead moreThe NAACP named eight priority states targeted in its initiative, directly calling out the state’s flagship public universities for their reliance on Black athletic talent. Among the schools targeted were 11 SEC universities, including the University of Georgia and University of Texas.The call urged Black athletes to “encourage” their institutions to “publicly oppose racial vote dilution and affirm that Black athletes’ civic power matters beyond their athletic performance”. It also urged them to reconsider attending the “priority” schools, offering HBCU alternatives.In addition, the NAACP demanded the states adopt a state Voting Rights Act, repeal maps that dilute Black voting power, restore districts reflecting Black population strength and commit to transparent redistricting. “You can’t have one without the other. Profiting off of Black athletes while suppressing their vote is out of bounds,” the organization wrote. The NAACP did not respond to a request for comment.While the announcement generated headlines at a point of political tension, the message met mixed reviews from multiple parties, Davis among them. Davis’s conflict stems from the implication for young Black athletes.“I don’t fundamentally disagree with looking for leverage points at a time of crisis,” Davis says. Understanding that Black athletic labor sustains – and built – modern institutions, she says, “is a really apt observation.” Her hesitation lies elsewhere.“As far as I can tell this is a call that has not [been] done with input or voices of athletes,” she says of the “Out of Bounds” movement. While the movement may have been well-intended, Davis argues that the execution places greater burden on vulnerable young adults.At the time of the announcement, the transfer portals for men’s basketball and football – the campaign’s target revenue sports – had closed. With current SEC athletes largely unable to act, the announcement put the onus of a life-changing decision on teenage recruits. For a Black gymnast with NCAA title ambitions, walking away from the SEC means walking away from more than half of the sport’s championship contenders.“It’s laying the burden of saving this moment on the backs [of athletes],” Davis adds. “It’s just exploiting labor in a different way.”While she disagrees with the NAACP’s execution, as a Texas resident with deep roots in the Mississippi Delta, she understands the sentiment. “I personally don’t love when folks go to Ole Miss. I have walked that campus. I’ve given talks at that campus. I understand the ghost that exists on that campus,” she admits.Some understandably run from the ghosts. Davis wants to confront and build despite them. Though the past few years of legislation dismantled years of progress, she and her colleagues remain committed to rebuilding and sustaining support infrastructure.She recognizes promise at Missouri, where Black students and community members have been collectively mobilizing for more than a year. “The conversations that ensued between organizers and athletes ensured a way to merge those movements,” she says. “This is the infrastructure we have built.”Those in the hardest of spots are often the ones “who move the most ground in terms of building a better future”, she reflects.View image in fullscreenGeorgia fans look on during last spring’s NCAA championships in Fort Worth, Texas.Photograph: C Morgan Engel/NCAA Photos/Getty ImagesStructural v cosmeticAs another academic semester approaches and fall sports begin to ramp up, gerrymandering efforts continue across the South and Black athletes, recruits and families face yet another wave of difficult decisions.“I think this is a time where we have to be the most discerning about what’s structural change and what’s cosmetic,” Davis advises. For Black athletes and their families in the college search, this means isolating the “bells and whistles” from concrete support systems.Instead of focusing on the often-ephemeral name, image and likeness (NIL) deals, brand partnerships and merchandise, ask structural questions. Ask about the process behind selecting those deals. Talk to current students. While it may no longer fall under the designation of a “DEI” issue, discuss specific concerns that a Black child could have.For Davis, this advice hits home. Her daughter – a talented musical theater performer – recently concluded her own college search. Much to her family’s initial concern, many of the nation’s top theater programs sit within the sprawling cornfields of in staunchly conservative states.While their first visits to the campuses were jarring, Davis vowed not to dismiss her daughter’s opportunity. Like NIL deals, the cornfields are cosmetic. Before ruling out the institution, she and her daughter asked structural questions.Are you going to be isolated from family – or does the area simplylookisolating? Are you going to be the first or one of the few Black women on the team, or is there already a cohort of folks there? If the infrastructure doesn’t exist, what is the institution doing to circumvent any bottlenecks?Attention to detail can make all the difference, Davis says. Back in the 1970s, Penn State’s predominantly white Happy Valley had no salons that could provide haircuts for Black students. Hoping to attract more Black recruits, Penn State athletic recruiters located the nearest suitable salons and began organizing regular bus tripsIt went unnamed at the time, but this was DEI.“That was somebody realizing we don’t have the infrastructure here ... so we’re going to organize a bus ride. That is diversity, equity, inclusion, whether or not you give it that label,” Davis says.Looking ahead“We don’t need a taskforce … we don’t need a meeting to form a panel to think about a taskforce. We need boots-on-the-ground conversations,” Davis concludes. These conversations are exactly the kind Aquino intends to keep having long after her floor music ends.Aquino enters her junior year coming off a historic season. With Cécile Canqueteau-Landi and Laurent Landi, the former coaches of Simone Biles, at the helm and recruits flocking to Athens in droves, Georgia are widely considered top contenders for the 2027 NCAA title.Already a two-time All-American and NCAA Regional champion, Aquino is expected to be a massive part of the program’s push for its first team crown since 2009. Her floor routine will remain one to watch – and rest assured, she’s not dialing it back for anyone.And while she’s ready to battle, that fight carries her far beyond the walls of Stegeman Coliseum. After she finishes her undergraduate degrees in sociology and criminal justice, she has sights set on law school.“If I can help a young Black child who has a court case and is being tried as an adult, I’m doing that. If I can help juveniles [by] understanding their social behavior and getting them the resources and advocating for them … I’m going to do that.”The SEC just means more. For Black athletes like Nyla Aquino, that couldn’t be more true. “No matter what I do and where I do it, it has to mean more.”Explore more on these topicsCollege sportsGymnasticsUS sportsNCAAfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Uefa maintains World Cup boycott still stands despite Fifa’s backing for Infantino | Uefa | The Guardian
description: Uefa is not standing down in its fight with Fifa, saying ‘conditions have not been met’ for it to call off its current boycott of competitions
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Uefa is not standing down in its fight with Fifa, saying ‘conditions have not been met’ for it to call off its current boycott of competitions
Content: The Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, with his Fifa counterpart, Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenThe Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, with his Fifa counterpart, Gianni Infantino.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAUefaUefa maintains World Cup boycott still stands despite Fifa’s backing for InfantinoEuropean body says Fifa statement ‘changes nothing’Fifpro condemns ‘profound abuse of presidential power’Nick AmesandMatt HughesThu 6 Aug 2026 10.45 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUefa has doubled down on itsthreat to boycott Fifa-run competitionsand reiterated its loss of confidence in Gianni Infantino’s presidency.The latest damning intervention from European football’s governing body came as criticism of Infantino continued to rain in from several angles. The global players’ union, Fifpro, condemned “a profound abuse of presidential power” while the South American confederation, Conmebol, usually a strong Infantino ally, was moved to chastise “repeated unilateral actions taken without resorting to dialogue”.It is Uefa’s continued stance, though, that may damage Infantino most severely. In a statement it saidFifa’s public backing of Infantinoon Wednesday night “changes nothing” and explained it was not convinced repeats of the past nine days’ crisis will not occur.Uefa planning to check if Infantino tried to sell stakes in World Cup on cheapRead moreLast week Uefa’s 55 member associations agreed to boycottFifatournaments if Infantino did not withdraw his privately funded Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme and, although the plan was scrapped last Friday, it said the terms necessary to avert the boycott have not been met.“Uefa’s associations were very clear about the conditions attached to their non-participation inFifacompetitions,” it said. “First, the proposals to sell off the major competitions had to be withdrawn and, secondly, assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again.“These conditions have not been met. In addition, Uefa made it abundantly clear in its statement on Saturday that it has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino’s presidency. That position holds. Yesterday’s announcement that some people employed by the Fifa president (and whose careers depend on his favour) agree with him changes nothing.”It heightens the turmoil enveloping football’s governance. If no accord is reached before the Under-20 Women’sWorld Cup, which begins in Poland on 5 September, that would be the first tournament subjected to a Uefa-led boycott.Uefa remains hopeful it can exploit divisions within Fifa’s leadership despite the Infantino-led show of unity following Wednesday’s meeting of some of its management board in Rabat.There were several notable absentees, however, and it is understood that Arsène Wenger declined an invitation to travel to Morocco in his capacity as Fifa’s chief of global development because of a desire to distance himself from Infantino. The former Arsenal manager hadlaunched a scathing attackon the World Cup sell-off plans, saying it was “absolutely necessary and beyond question” that they were scrapped.In contrast to Wenger, Fifa’s chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, who had described the proposals as “the project of one person”, was not invited to the summit in a development that will raise further questions over his future. Additionally Jill Ellis, the chief football officer, and Sarai Bareman, the chief women’s football officer, were not present in Rabat.While Fifa has sent apologies to the Fifa council and member associations for their exclusion from the FFE process, it is believed that those sentiments failed to sway a large percentage of council members.Infantino is getting his karmic kicking, but why did football take so long to rebel against Fifa? | Jonathan LiewRead moreA handful of Uefa federations have withdrawn letters of support for Infantino’s re-election for a fourth term, although the early rush to make such declarations has slowed. The Football Association has now written to Fifa formally retracting its backing.Uefa’s repeat of its boycott threat was followed by a scathing release from Fifpro. Before theWorld CupFifpro signalled its intention to work with Fifa by signing a memorandum of understanding but that has proved the briefest of truces.Alongside the criticism, Fifpro wrote to Fifa making a series of demands, including giving players voting rights on the Fifa council, which is supposed to be the main decision-making body but has often been bypassed by Infantino.“Fifa Forward Enterprise is gone, but the abuse of power that produced it is not,” Fifpro said. “Governance reforms, not a cover-up, are urgently needed. The withdrawal of FFE was inevitable. But withdrawing the proposal does not erase what it revealed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“A plan capable of permanently altering the ownership and governance of the Fifa World Cup … was conceived in secrecy, negotiated behind closed doors and brought to the brink of agreement before the Fifa council, the member associations, players and football’s recognised stakeholders even knew it existed. That is not merely a governance failure. It is a profound abuse of presidential power.”Conmebol, three of whose members are in line to host matches at the 2030 World Cup, had waited more than a week to comment publicly. While its disapproval was clear it stopped short of pushing for immediate change.In a statement it said the Conmebol council “unanimously expresses its concern regarding the repeated unilateral actions taken without resorting to dialogue or to the institutional mechanisms established to address situations of this nature”.While Uefa is leading efforts to unseat Infantino before Fifa’s election in March, Conmebol pointed out the timeline for the process has already been set. “Accordingly, Conmebol will not support any action or procedure that disregards or departs from those institutional mechanisms,” it said.Earlier on Thursday the Jordan Football Association president, Prince Ali bin al-Hussein, said Fifa had paid bonuses owed from last December’s Arab Cup but clarified he would still oppose Infantino.The money appears to have materialised after Prince Aliaccused Fifa of “blackmail”, saying the governing body had threatened to withhold funds if Jordan refused to back Infantino’s re-election.“Thank you to the Fifa administration for suddenly this morning delivering what was owed to our players and coaching staff, for the Jordan national team’s accession to the final of the Fifa Arab Cup in Qatar last December,” he wrote.“This was funding that should have been received eight months ago … It is symptomatic of those exact difficulties that we all face, and that are usually linked to the Fifa presidential elections. And it does not change my clear position concerning the leadership of Fifa: my FA and I will not endorse president Infantino, nor will we vote for him.”Meanwhile on Thursday, the executive committee of the African confederation (Caf) unanimously confirmed its support for Infantino. In a statement it said: “The CAF executive committee unanimously endorses the joint update by the Fifa president and secretary general on the FFE and will continue to focus on making African Football amongst the best in the world and adhering to governance and transparency global best practices.”Explore more on these topicsUefaGianni InfantinoFifaWorld CupWorld Cup 2026Football politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal hopes dashed after Vinícius Júnior extends Real Madrid contract to 2032 | Vinícius Júnior | The Guardian
description: Vinícius Júnior has ended summer speculation over his future by agreeing a new six-year contract with Real Madrid
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Vinícius Júnior has ended summer speculation over his future by agreeing a new six-year contract with Real Madrid
Content: Vinícius Júnior has been at Real Madrid since joining the club as an 18-year-old in July 2018.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenVinícius Júnior has been at Real Madrid since joining the club as an 18-year-old in July 2018.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAVinícius JúniorArsenal hopes dashed after Vinícius Júnior extends Real Madrid contract to 2032Brazil international has agreed a new six-year deal‘Eight years at the Bernabéu are too few,’ says ViníciusAgenciesThu 6 Aug 2026 18.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVinícius Júnior has ended summer speculation over his future by agreeing a new six-year contract with Real Madrid. Arsenal had been heavily linked with a move for the Brazil international, who had entered the final 12 months of his deal at the Bernabéu.A tumultuous 2025-26 campaign in which Real failed to win a trophy and initial uncertainty after the arrival of José Mourinho in Madrid alerted the Premier League champions, but Vinícius has now committed his long-term future to the Spanish club.Barcelona step up Rodri interest after Real Madrid talks with Manchester City star stallRead more“Real Madrid and Vinícius Júnior have agreed on the extension of our player’s contract, which links him to the club until 30 June 2032,” a club statement read.“Vinícius Júnior joined Real Madrid in July 2018 at the age of 18. In his eight seasons wearing our jersey, he has played 375 matches, scored 128 goals, and won 14 titles: two Champions Leagues, three Club World Cups, two Uefa Super Cups, three La Liga titles, one Copa del Rey, and three Spanish Super Cups.“His contribution to all these titles has been pivotal due to his gameplay, assists, and goals.”Vinícius wrote on Instagram: “Eight years at the Bernabéu are too few … six more years, and for ever!”The 26-year-old had hinted at extending his association with Real during an in-house interview on Tuesday where he spoke about Mourinho wanting him to be “happy” and “joyful” after a difficult spell.A shock last-16 World Cup exit in America with Brazil also added to a frustrating 12-month period for Vinícius, but with his future settled the former Flamengo prospect will aim to help Real get back to competing for major honours again under Mourinho.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTying down ‌Vinícius represents another significant ​step in an ​active summer for Real. The club have also strengthened their squad withthe arrivals of winger Yan Diomande, midfielder Bernardo Silva, centre-back Ibrahima Konaté, left-back Marc Cucurella and wing-back Denzel Dumfries.Explore more on these topicsVinícius JúniorReal MadridArsenalTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Caitlin Clark and A’ja Wilson headline stacked USA roster for Fiba World Cup | Fiba Women's Basketball World Cup 2026 | The Guardian
description: Clark, Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers will make their World Cup debuts as members of the US women’s national team for next month’s tournament in Berlin
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Clark, Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers will make their World Cup debuts as members of the US women’s national team for next month’s tournament in Berlin
Content: Caitlin Clark and A’ja Wilson will team up on the US squad for the Fiba World Cup next month.Photograph: Ethan Miller/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCaitlin Clark and A’ja Wilson will team up on the US squad for the Fiba World Cup next month.Photograph: Ethan Miller/Getty ImagesFiba Women's Basketball World Cup 2026Caitlin Clark and A’ja Wilson headline stacked USA roster for Fiba World CupAngel Reese, Paige Bueckers to make World Cup debutsAmericans seek fifth consecutive tournament titleWorld Cup will be held in Berlin from 4-13 SeptemberAssociated PressThu 6 Aug 2026 10.53 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 14.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCaitlin Clark, Angel Reese and Paige Bueckers will make their World Cup debuts as members of the US women’s national team next month.The trio will try to help the US win their fifth consecutive Fiba World Cup title. The young stars will be joined by Olympic medalists A’ja Wilson, Breanna Stewart, Napheesa Collier, Chelsea Gray, Jackie Young, Kahleah Copper and Kelsey Plum. Rhyne Howard and Aliyah Boston will also be making their World Cup debuts to round out the team.WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert has a hard job. Here's how to make it easier | Jordan RobinsonRead more“I’m so excited to announce the 2026 USABasketballWomen’s National Team,” Sue Bird, USA Basketball national team managing director, said. “This is an incredibly talented group that has earned the opportunity to compete in Berlin. Wearing a USA jersey is a privilege, and I know these 12 players will embrace that responsibility as we go after another gold medal. I can’t wait to see what this team accomplishes together.”This is the first time USA Basketball has had a managing director choose the team. In the past it was a committee. Kara Lawson will coach the squad.Stewart is the third player in USA Basketball history to appear in four World Cup tournaments, joining Bird, who played in five, and Diana Taurasi, who also played in four.The Americans will face China, Italy and the Czech Republic in pool play at the World Cup, which will be held from 4-13 September in Berlin. TheWNBAwill take a nearly three-week break in its season to accommodate the event.Clark, Bueckers and Reese helped the Americans win a World Cup qualifying tournament in Puerto Rico in March.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSabrina Ionescu has been a big part of the US roster the last few years, but was left off this season’s team. Alyssa Thomas helped the Americans win gold at the Paris Olympics, but hasn’t taken part in any USA Basketball camps since. Minnesota star rookie Olivia Miles also hasn’t taken part in any USA camps yet either.Explore more on these topicsFiba Women's Basketball World Cup 2026BasketballWNBACaitlin ClarkShareReuse this content

title: Top Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stones | Soccer | The Guardian
description: David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone
Content: David Owori was described as ‘an inspiration to a generation’ by the Federation of Uganda Football Associations.Photograph: SC VillaView image in fullscreenDavid Owori was described as ‘an inspiration to a generation’ by the Federation of Uganda Football Associations.Photograph: SC VillaSoccerTop Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stonesDavid Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phoneCarlos MureithiThu 6 Aug 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatally injured during a robbery in the capital, Kampala, on Tuesday night.David Owori, who captained Sports Club Villa, a Uganda Premier League club, and represented the national team, was attacked after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings near his home in Makindye division.Racheal Kawala, a spokesperson for the Kampala Metropolitan police, said he was found unconscious by ​passersby, who took him to a nearby hospital. He was ​transferred to another hospital, where he was pronounced dead on Wednesday.Witnesses said attackers hit the footballer with paving stones before robbing him and fleeing, leaving him unconscious,the BBC reported.Owori, 27, was a right-back and midfielder for SC Villa. He helped the team win a record 17th Uganda Premier League title in 2024.He started his senior career in 2016 at the Uganda Premier League side Vipers Sports Club and had stints in Europe with Vélez CF in Spain and Utsiktens BK in Sweden.He played for the national team in the qualifiers for the 2021AfricaCup of Nations.SC Villasaid: “It is with profound sorrow that we announce the untimely passing of our captain, Owori, who had been receiving treatment at Case Clinic following an attack by suspected thugs. Our deepest condolences and prayers are with his family.”The Federation ​of Uganda Football Associationssaid: “David was not just a footballer. He was ​both a leader and an inspiration to a generation. As ​Captain of SC Villa, he led with courage, humility and passion. In the Uganda Cranes jersey, he carried the hopes of a nation.”It added: “We have lost a son, a leader and a star. His light on and off the pitch will never be forgotten.”The Ugandan parliament observed a minute of silence in Owori’s honour on Wednesday.In June Sydney Gongodyo, a Ugandan rugby international, ​died after a mob attacked him in Kampala, mistaking him for a thief, police said.Uganda’s National Council of Sports said: “Sadly, ​Ugandan sport has been hit with many such ​tragedies lately, and we hope for justice and a lasting solution.”Explore more on these topicsFootballUgandaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Kerolin failed to report for pre-season at Manchester City before Barcelona switch | Manchester City Women | The Guardian
description: The Brazil forward Kerolin failed to report for pre-season training at Manchester City before transfer to Barcelona had been agreed
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: The Brazil forward Kerolin failed to report for pre-season training at Manchester City before transfer to Barcelona had been agreed
