Content: Kerolin has joined Barcelona from Manchester City on a deal worth an initial £1m.Photograph: Marta Perez/EPAView image in fullscreenKerolin has joined Barcelona from Manchester City on a deal worth an initial £1m.Photograph: Marta Perez/EPAManchester City WomenKerolin failed to report for pre-season at Manchester City before Barcelona switchCity taken aback by forward’s absence from trainingWSL champions wait two days before mentioning dealExclusive byTom GarryThu 6 Aug 2026 15.35 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Brazil forward Kerolin failed to report back for pre-season training at Manchester City in July beforeher transfer to Barcelonahad been agreed.Barcelona announced their signing of the 26-year-old on Tuesday but it was not until Thursday evening when Manchester City first made any reference to the transfer, eventually confirming they had received a WSL record fee for a sale more than 48 hours later.Alessia Russo: ‘When you join the club, you take on a part of Arsenal and the love’Read moreSeveral staff and players at Manchester City were disappointed at what were perceived to be efforts by Kerolin to force a transfer to Barcelona and that her time at the club ended on a surprisingly sour note. She did not join pre-season withthe Women’s Super League champions, which began in late July, despite previously having been felt to have been on good terms with the squad.The deal, worth an initial €1.2m (£1m), represents the largest transfer fee received by a WSL club, and it could rise with add-ons to approximately £1.25m, although this has not been officially confirmed. It is one of the largest transfer fees in women’s football.City said of Kerolin: “She grabbed 14 goals and six assists during that time, helping City to a WSL and FA Cup double in her solitary full season in England. And upon her transfer to Barça, City have received a WSL-club record transfer fee of €1.2m.“Everyone at Manchester City would like to thank Kerolin for all her efforts at the club and wish her the very best in her future career.”Kerolin was part of the City side that lifted their first WSL title in a decade last season and also helped them winthe Women’s FA Cup. But within weeks of those celebrations many of her City colleagues have been stunned after she did not say goodbye in-person. Kerolin’s representatives have been contacted for a response.High-profile examples of such transfer standoffs have been seen in men’s football, but incidents in the women’s game have been comparatively rare.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCity have no objections to the transfer in principle but sources have said the team were taken aback by the former North Carolina Courage star’s absence from pre-season fitness testing. For Kerolin, it is a dream move to the European champions,who beat OL Lyonnesin last season’s Women’s Champions League final.City and Barcelona will meet in a friendly at the Joie Stadium on 15 August as the reigning champions of England and Spain step up their pre-season preparations.Explore more on these topicsManchester City WomenBarcelona WomenTransfer windowWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Barcelona step up Rodri interest after Real Madrid talks with Manchester City star stall | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Barça are ready to hijack their rivals’ attempts to sign the Spain captain as Real Madrid failed to reach an agreement with the Manchester City midfielder
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Barça are ready to hijack their rivals’ attempts to sign the Spain captain as Real Madrid failed to reach an agreement with the Manchester City midfielder
Content: Rodri is in the final year of his contract at Manchester City.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenRodri is in the final year of his contract at Manchester City.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersTransfer windowBarcelona step up Rodri interest after Real Madrid talks with Manchester City star stallBarça ready to hijack rivals’ plans to sign Spain captainManchester City will allow midfielder to go for £60mEd AaronsThu 6 Aug 2026 12.39 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarcelona have stepped up their attempts to hijack Real Madrid’s move to sign Rodri fromManchester City.While City have not given up hope that Spain’s World Cup-winning captain will sign a new contract after he entered the final year of his deal, they are thought to be willing to allow him to leave for about £60m. Despite weeks of talks with Rodri and his representatives, Real have yet to reach an agreement andBarcelonaare hoping to take advantage.It is understood that Rodri spoke to their manager, Hansi Flick, and sporting director, Deco, about a potential move on Wednesday and indicated he is keen to return to Spain. Barça, who will be without midfielder Frenkie de Jong for several months after the Netherlands midfielder sustained a knee injury, are now expected to make contact with City to negotiate the structure of the fee for the 30-year-old,who won the Golden Ballfor the World Cup’s best player.Men’s transfer window summer 2026: all deals from Europe’s top five leaguesRead moreReal, who have signed RB Leipzig’s Yan Diomande for aclub record fee of £115m, have also agreed a lucrative six-year contract extension with Vinícius Júnior to ward offinterest from Arsenal. They may have to offload players first if they are to sign Rodri as well. Aurélien Tchouaméni and Eduardo Camavinga are possible departures, with Manchester United having been linked with the France midfielders.Rodri has hadminor surgery on his backand will miss most of City’s pre-season programme. Theyhave signed Elliot Andersonfrom Nottingham Forest for £116m and remain in negotiations with Lille over a deal for the 18-year-old Morocco midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi.Meanwhile, Barcelona have been frustrated in their efforts to persuadeAtlético Madridto sell Julián Alvarez. After Robert Lewandowski’s departure, Barcelona have targeted Alvarez all summer, but Atlético continue to insist the Argentina striker is not for sale at any price.Deco was in the Spanish capital to meet Alvarez’s representatives on Wednesday. All eyes will be on whether the 26-year-old former City forward will return to pre-season training on Monday or attempt to force through a transfer. Arsenal also retain an interest in him.Ferran Torres – who scored the winning goal forSpain in the World Cup finalagainst Argentina – has entered the final year of his contract at Barcelona and said he is waiting for them to begin talks over extending his deal. “All I know is that I have to be in training for Barcelona on 12 August. Let’s see what happens.” Asked what Barcelona needed to do to keep him, he said: “Show me they want me, come to negotiate.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, James Trafford sealed a club-record move to Leeds after completing a medical at Elland Road. Leeds have agreed a £40m fee plus add-ons with City for the 23-year-old, who will become the world’s fourth most expensive goalkeeper.Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowManchester CityBarcelonaReal MadridAtlético MadridnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alessia Russo: ‘When you join the club, you take on a part of Arsenal and the love’ | Alessia Russo | The Guardian
description: Alessia Russo’s game went up a level last season. Now, the Arsenal forward tells Suzanne Wrack, she wants to push on for more trophies, starting with the WSL
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Alessia Russo’s game went up a level last season. Now, the Arsenal forward tells Suzanne Wrack, she wants to push on for more trophies, starting with the WSL
Content: Alessia Russo says she now fully appreciates what it means to be an Arsenal player.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAlessia Russo says she now fully appreciates what it means to be an Arsenal player.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAlessia RussoInterviewAlessia Russo: ‘When you join the club, you take on a part of Arsenal and the love’Suzanne WrackHonorary Gooner’s game went up a level last season. Now, the forward wants to push on for more trophies, starting with the WSLThu 6 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArms hooked over the bar at the front of the bus, sunglasses on, a drink in one hand and the other pointed towards the fans as she moved to the music and joined in with the singing and chanting,Alessia Russowas having a blast.“I had the time of my life that day,” says the Arsenal forwardof the 9km paradethrough the red smoke-filled streets of north London after Arsenal men’s Premier League triumph andArsenal women’s Champions Cup success.It has been a running joke among fans to refer to the 27-year-old as a “childhood Gooner”, which was turbo-charged when the shirt a very small Russo was wearing in a family photo with the FA Cup was changed from a Manchester United one into an Arsenal one.‘They inspire me’: Alessia Russo on empowering young girls and giving backRead moreWhile she was not a childhood Gooner, she is fast becoming an adult one.“Since I’ve joined the club and seen the people around the place, it’s impossible to not become a part of Arsenal and to feel like I support Arsenal,” she says. “I want them to do well, I’m backing them every way, and the parade was just one of the most amazing things I’ve experienced. The fans, the atmosphere, celebrating the men winning the Prem, something they’d worked so hard for for so many years, I was just soaking it in, having fun and enjoying myself.“It was just a really, really special day. It was nice to experience it with Lotte [Wubben-Moy] and Leah [Williamson] who are proper Gooners, but when you come to Arsenal you take on a part of it and start to understand and absorb their love for Arsenal. I definitely feel that and it’s nice to feel like you’re a part of something like that.“You pick out moments where you win trophies as the main ones that stand out within your career, but that will definitely always stand out for me.”There were people everywhere, on every balcony, rooftop, bollard and traffic light, of all ages, races and religions. Young boys, but also, in contrast to the Arsenal parades of the 90s and noughties, so many young girls. Cultivating and supporting that fresh generation interested in watching and playing the game is something Russo is passionate about.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenTop: Arsenal go past fans with the Women’s Champions Cup trophy in May.Photograph: Steven Paston/PAAbove: Fans celebrate Arsenal men’s and women’s success during the club’s victory parade.Photograph: Aldo Ciarrocchi/AlamyThat is the reason she launched her own foundation this year and why she helped launch the fifth year of Starling Bank’sKick Oninitiative. This partners local businesses with girls’ teams in need of sponsorship and subsidises the front-of-shirt sponsorship.Starling commissioned surveys of 1,000 adult female players, 1,010 11-17 female players, 501 small- and medium-sized business leaders and 1,092 grassroots football coaches. Nearly every grassroots female football club (97%) said their team needed more funds, with opportunities for girls suffering as a result. The surveys found 76% of female players said they will have to drop out of their team or the sport altogether if more funding is not secured in the next five years, and 40% of female players said their team does not receive the same amount of funding as men’s teams.“They are quite damning statistics, which is such a shame considering the growth we see in the women’s game,” says Russo. “Over the past five or six years, the growth has just been incredible, but there’s still work to do at the bottom to build it up.”The risk is that women’s football loses momentum and fails to attract potential star players into the pathway. “I always say you never want to miss out on the next Leah Williamson or Lotte Wubben-Moy, you don’t want to miss out on talented young players just because they haven’t got a local team, or the team that they were at folds,” Russo says. “It seems like such an easy fix as teams don’t need much, but obviously it isn’t because it’s still a problem.“I look back on all the people I met through my grassroots journey and every single one of them played a part in my career and I’m still friends with many of them. If local businesses can invest in one team, you never know, you might help produce a superstar who goes on to have an incredible career who will always remember you being a part of it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenRusso scored key goals in Champions League last season, including against Chelsea.Photograph: Harvey Murphy/News Images/Alamy“There’s more to it than just investment, it’s that you can have a say in a core part of these young girls’ journeys and lives.”With no major international women’s tournament, Russo has enjoyed a rare summer off and she has had the chance to focus on the broader issues she is passionate about, as well as some much-needed rest.“It was important I did have some proper downtime,” she says. “Over the past few years, the minutes and tournaments have increased, so I needed to look after my body and get myself in a good place mentally. I shut down for about two and a half weeks and just enjoyed time with friends and family, which was lovely, but by the end of it I was ready to start exercising again, I didn’t know what to do with myself.“I quite enjoy training on my own over the summer, you get to know your best routines and habits. I often go on holiday with my family and train out there, which is nice because everyone wants to get involved.“I just took time for myself too, being a normal 27-year-old girl, going on holidays. I went to theEngland v Panama game in New Yorkand got to be a fan and be around that buzz of the World Cup. I had Toonie’s [England teammate Ella Toone] hen do and wedding, which was amazing.”View image in fullscreenAfter a few months off, Russo is back at Arsenal for pre-season training.Photograph: Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesRusso had a standout year in 2025-26; many believe her game moved up a level for club and country. “I’m pleased with my season for Arsenal and England from a personal point of view, but, ultimately, I’ll always judge it on the trophies we win,” she says.“We’ve learned a lot as a team over the past couple of years at Arsenal, but are hungry for the new season. We’ve made it quite clear we want to do everything we can to be the team most capable of winning the WSL and Renée [Slegers, the coach] has set the standard high this pre-season.“We’ve got seven new players, we’ve got a squad that’s raring to go, the competition in it is high. I feel happy, but now I want to continue to push on with Arsenal and England and win some trophies.”Explore more on these topicsAlessia RussoArsenal WomenWomen's footballWomen's Super LeagueinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Two Iranian female footballers granted Australian citizenship after protest | Iran women's football team | The Guardian
description: Two Iran players who stayed in Australia after appearing in the Asian Cup in March have become citizens
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Two Iran players who stayed in Australia after appearing in the Asian Cup in March have become citizens
Content: Fatemeh Pasandideh (left) and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh with Australia's minister for home affairs, Tony Burke, after receiving citizenship in Brisbane.Photograph: Department of Home Affairs/APView image in fullscreenFatemeh Pasandideh (left) and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh with Australia's minister for home affairs, Tony Burke, after receiving citizenship in Brisbane.Photograph: Department of Home Affairs/APIran women's football teamTwo Iranian female footballers granted Australian citizenship after protestPlayers stayed in country after Asian Cup in MarchDuo condemned as traitors in Iran for not singing anthemAgence France-PresseThu 6 Aug 2026 09.38 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 10.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo former Iranian footballers said on Thursday they were proud to have been granted Australian citizenship after being called traitors at home forrefusing to sing the national anthembefore a game.Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh were members of a group of seven from Iran’s delegation who asked for Australia’s protection after the protest during the women’s Asian Cup in March.Iranian women’s footballers shouldn’t have to choose between their sport and their safety | Nos HosseiniRead moreTheir demands for protection were an embarrassment for Iran’s leaders, and were lauded by the US president, Donald Trump, but five changed their minds and returned home. Pasandideh and Ramezanisadeh stayed, however, and were granted Australian citizenship at a ceremony on Wednesday, overseen by the minister for home affairs, Tony Burke.“Yesterday was a truly special and unforgettable day for me. I feel proud and deeply grateful to become an Australian citizen,” Ramezanisadeh said.“After everything we’ve been through and all the challenges we faced, this moment means more than words can express,” Pasandideh said.A week after seeking asylum, the pair were pictured smiling and training with Brisbane Roar, who on Wednesday congratulated them. “What they have been through since February is more than most people deal with in a lifetime,” a spokesperson said.“To see them arrive at this point is something everyone here at Brisbane Roar is glad to have had a small part in. Queensland is their home now. If they ever want to pull on a training top and come back out with us, the door will always stay open.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toAustralia SportGet a daily roundup of the latest sports news, features and comment from our Australian sports deskPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe plight of the rest of the team remains unclear since their return to Iran.Explore more on these topicsIran women's football teamAustralia sportIrannewsShareReuse this content

title: Real Madrid announce arrival of £115m Yan Diomande on seven-year contract | Real Madrid | The Guardian
description: Real Madrid have agreed a club-record fee of £115.7m with RB Leipzig for Yan Diomande and are confident of keeping hold of Vinícius Júnior
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Real Madrid have agreed a club-record fee of £115.7m with RB Leipzig for Yan Diomande and are confident of keeping hold of Vinícius Júnior
Content: Yan Diomande, left, made a big impression for Ivory Coast during the World Cup.Photograph: Petr David Josek/APView image in fullscreenYan Diomande, left, made a big impression for Ivory Coast during the World Cup.Photograph: Petr David Josek/APReal MadridReal Madrid announce arrival of £115m Yan Diomande on seven-year contractForward becomes most expensive African playerClub are in positive talks with Vinícius JúniorEd AaronsThu 6 Aug 2026 11.15 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 15.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReal Madrid have sealed the €135m (£115.7m) club-record signing of Yan Diomande from RB Leipzig.After several weeks of negotiations that saw Paris Saint-Germain pull out of the race, the deal for Diomande – the 19-year-old who joined the German side from Leganés last summer and starred for Côte d’Ivoire at the World Cup – was finally struck on Wednesday afternoon, with Real announcing his arrival on a seven-year contract on Thursday.“Real Madrid ‌andRB Leipzighave reached an agreement for the transfer of ‌Yan Diomande, who will be under contract with our club for the next seven seasons, through June 30, 2033,” the LaLiga club said in a statement.It is understood that Madrid will pay an initial €125m plus another €10m in add-ons, a total that would eclipse the fee the Spanish side paid Borussia Dortmundto sign Jude Bellingham in 2023, believed to have been worth up to €134m including add-ons.Real Madrid ready to seal deal for Yan Diomande after PSG pull out of moveRead moreLeganés are due a 5% sell-on fee from any transfer. The teenager made only 10 appearances for their first team before being sold to Leipzig for €20m (£17.4m). Diomande, who was pictured arriving at Leipzig’s pre-season training camp in Austria on Wednesday, becomes the most expensive African player in history, surpassing the £72mArsenalspent on Nicolas Pépé in 2019.Real are also confident of warding off Arsenal’s interest inVinícius Júniorafter offering an improved contract to the Brazil forward. Diomande’s arrival is not thought to have any bearing on whether Vinícius stays in the Spanish capital. The Brazilian and his representatives, Roc Nation, held talks with Madrid officials on Wednesday over a contract extension, with Arsenal waiting in the wings if he decides to depart.Mikel Arteta’s side are understood to be ready to pay more than £100m for the 26-year-old who has less than a year of his contract remaining. But despite some reports that Vinícius had rejected Madrid’s latest contract offer, it is understood that he is now weighing up an improved deal closer to the €30m a season requested after what sources in Spain have described as positive talks. Vinícius said on Tuesday that Madrid’s new manager, José Mourinho, wants him to be “happy, cheerful ‌and playing my football” after returning to pre-season training following the World Cup.Arsenal, who have agreed a £75m deal to signhis Brazil teammate Bruno Guimarães from Newcastle, are believed to be exploring other options in attack should Vinícius opt to renew with Madrid.Barcelona’s sporting director, Deco, held talks with Atlético Madrid over Julián Alvarez on Wednesday in a bid to secure a deal for the Argentina forward but Arsenal are hoping that the 26-year-old could yet be persuaded to join them.Arsenal, who missed out on Morgan Rogers last month when the England forward joined Chelsea for a British record fee of £117m instead, have also been linked with PSG’s Bradley Barcola, who is wanted by Liverpool and valued at around £145m by the European champions.Explore more on these topicsReal MadridVinícius JúniorArsenalTransfer windowNewcastle UnitedRB LeipzignewsShareReuse this content

title: London to face Rome, Munich and Nairobi after confirming 2029 World Athletics bid | World Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: London has submitted its bid for the 2029 World Athletics Championships after reaching an agreement with West Ham to allow it host the event in September
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: London has submitted its bid for the 2029 World Athletics Championships after reaching an agreement with West Ham to allow it host the event in September
Content: Joss Kerr broke the mile world record at the London Stadium in the Diamond League event last month.Photograph: Glyn Kirk/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoss Kerr broke the mile world record at the London Stadium in the Diamond League event last month.Photograph: Glyn Kirk/AFP/Getty ImagesWorld Athletics ChampionshipsLondon to face Rome, Munich and Nairobi after confirming 2029 World Athletics bidBid team reach agreement with West Ham to use stadiumHost city for event to be announced in SeptemberSean IngleThu 6 Aug 2026 09.48 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLondon has submitted its bid for the 2029 WorldAthletics­Championships after reaching an agreement with West Ham to allow it to host the event that September.World Athletics is yet to announce the other candidate cities, but Rome, Munich and Nairobi have also ­submitted applications for 2029.West Ham had threatenedto thwart London’s bid, arguing they had ­priority for the stadium during the football season. However, the impasse has been broken after lengthy discussions with the London mayor’s office, Athletics Ventures, the joint organisation responsible for putting on major events, and the Department for Culture, Media and Sport.Josh Kerr: ‘What has running taught me about life? If you are determined enough, you can 100% do it’Read moreIfLondonis successful, West Ham will play no more than two consecutive away games in the Premier League or three in the EFL in the 2029-30 season.Jack Buckner, the CEO of UK ­Athletics and co-founder of Athletics Ventures, said: “Bidding to hold theWorld Athletics Championshipsin the London Stadium, the showpiece of London 2012, was always at the centre of the UK’s Olympic legacy plans.“We’re delighted that we have reached agreement with the London Stadium and West Ham United for the use of the London ­Stadium and our sincere thanks for their commitment in making this happen.”Hugh Brasher, the CEO of London Marathon Events and co-founder of Athletics Ventures, said: “Our bid is not just about what happens within the London Stadium. Sport has the power to bring communities together, to change lives and to inspire the next generation. The 2029 World ­Athletics Championships in London would drive more than £400m in economic and social benefit in the capital and nationwide.”A spokesperson for Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, also welcomed the news: “London is the sporting capital of the world and the mayor believes that hosting the World Athletics Championships at the London Stadium in 2029 would build on the city’s long history of hosting the most prestigious sporting events.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWorld Athletics is scheduled to announce the host city after the ­Ultimate Championships in ­Budapest in September.Explore more on these topicsWorld Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Restaurants, pubs and theatres ban Meta’s ‘spy glasses’ over privacy fears | Meta | The Guardian
description: Meta says safeguards are in place to prevent surreptitious filming, but some UK venues now prohibit them from being worn at all
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Meta says safeguards are in place to prevent surreptitious filming, but some UK venues now prohibit them from being worn at all
Content: Billboard promoting Kylie Jenner Meta glasses on Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles.Photograph: Barry King/AlamyView image in fullscreenBillboard promoting Kylie Jenner Meta glasses on Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles.Photograph: Barry King/AlamyMetaRestaurants, pubs and theatres ban Meta’s ‘spy glasses’ over privacy fearsMeta says safeguards are in place to prevent surreptitious filming, but some UK venues now prohibit them from being worn at allHelena HortonThu 6 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenMetaused superstar Kylie Jenner to promote its sleek new line of “spy glasses”, the social media company hoped the devices would reach the same broad acceptance that tablets and smartwatches have found before them.But those plans have hit a snag in the UK, where venues from elite restaurants to popular pub chains have banned the £359 glasses in order to preserve the privacy of customers and staff.Celebrated restaurateur Jeremy King, owner of London venues including Simpsons in the Strand, Arlington and The Park, said guests should not wear the recording glasses.He told the Guardian: “I would never knowingly allow any invasion of guest privacy other than with the eyes we were born with.”View image in fullscreenRestaurateur Jeremy King looks unfavourably on the smartglasses in his restaurants.Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty Images for Christina MakrisThose wearing the glasses in Soho House’s private members’ clubs can also be expected to be asked to remove them. A spokesperson confirmed filming is not allowed in their venues, and these devices are no exception.Even pub chain Wetherspoons will not allow people to record using the glasses inside.Tim Martin, its chief executive, said: “The general code that applies in our pubs, and most pubs, is that you can’t film customers or employees without their permission. Meta glasses seem to breach this code, and common sense, by enabling surreptitious surveillance, so our instinct is to say turn off the cameras. This is akin to our efforts to stop audible playing of videos in our pubs, which also invades people’s space.”Those who want to wear their Meta glasses to the theatre may face obstacles too. A spokesperson for ATG Theatres, which owns the Bristol Hippodrome, Edinburgh Playhouse, and various theatres across London, said that filming is not allowed and that those wearing the glasses during shows will be asked to remove them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI wore Meta’s smartglasses for a month – and it left me feeling like a creepRead moreThe glasses resemble normal eyewear, with the Jenner-designed model featuring a fashionable cat-eye design – with tiny cameras embedded. Meta says it hopes that the design allows users to stay “in the moment” without constantly looking down at a smartphone.There have been widespread fears about the glasses being used to film people without their consent, with the resultant footage posted on social media. Though Meta points to the tiny, flashing LED light that activates on the glasses when they are being used to film, there have already beenmultiple instancesof people complaining they have been videoed without prior knowledge.In one instance, a woman told the BBC a man recorded her, and thendemanded moneyto remove the videos from social media. Another woman described beingrecordedduring sexual encounters without her consent.Instagram has cracked down on nonconsensual videos made using the glasses posted on the platform. “If you’re posting content that is taking advantage of people and harassing them, like a lot of these pickup line kind of videos that we’ve heard of and seen, then we’re going to take the content down,” Instagram head Adam Mosseri said.View image in fullscreenGuardian journalist Elle Hunt put Meta’s smartglasses through its paces on the streets of Norwich earlier this year.Photograph: Ali Smith/The GuardianMeta has tried hard to make wearing the glasses a mainstream choice, handing out free pairs topopular social media influencers.Sales of the devices have tripled in the last year, with more than 7m sold worldwide.Those seven million people do have some venues in the UK where they and their glasses are welcome. Michelin starred chef Tom Kerridge, who owns pubs and restaurants in Marlow, told the Guardian: “I have no problem whatsoever with them. Filming is part of everyday life now. In fact I think that they can be used in creative and exciting ways. The first thought about them shouldn’t be negative!”A Meta spokesperson said: “People use our glasses because they’re genuinely helpful – from listening to music, to live translation or hands-free calls. For those wearing them and the people around them, trust matters. That’s why we built privacy into our AI glasses from the ground up. For example, every pair has a capture LED that blinks when you take a photo or video that you can save or share, it can’t be turned off, and if someone covers or damages the LED, the camera is disabled.”Explore more on these topicsMetaMark ZuckerbergWearable technologyPrivacyPubsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Danish pupils will have to orally defend essays in attempt to combat AI cheating | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Government introduces several measures, including monitoring of computers, for pupils aged 16 to 19
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Government introduces several measures, including monitoring of computers, for pupils aged 16 to 19
Content: Upper secondary schools will be required to monitor how computers are being used for written exams.Photograph: Posed by models; Solskin/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUpper secondary schools will be required to monitor how computers are being used for written exams.Photograph: Posed by models; Solskin/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)Danish pupils will have to orally defend essays in attempt to combat AI cheatingGovernment introduces several measures, including monitoring of computers, for pupils aged 16 to 19Europe live – latest updatesMiranda BryantNordic correspondentThu 6 Aug 2026 07.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDanish teenagers will have to make an oral defence of their written essays to combat AI cheating, the government has announced.Pupils aged 16 to 19 at upper secondary school (known inDenmarkasgymnasiet) will also be encouraged to do written assignments at school under controlled conditions, including monitoring of their computer screens, rather than at home.The measures, announced on Thursday as pupils prepare to go back to school next week after the summer break, will come into immediate effect after Magnus Heunicke, the country’s education minister, demanded urgent action.“Unfortunately, we have a problem with AI cheating in upper secondary schools,” he said. “Action is needed now.”AI had posed a growing challenge to teaching and exams, the education ministry said. It is hoped the new measures will help to establish clearer guidelines for when pupils are not permitted to use it.The government is also preparing a comprehensive national strategy for AI use in all schools and the wider education sector.Heunicke said he would speak to schools, teachers and students to “ensure that AI does not undermine students’ competencies, professionalism and, not least, the ability to think for themselves”.The first measure to be introduced is the oral defence of exam assignments written at home. About 9,000 upper secondary school students each year write a big assignment (known asstørre skriftlige opgaveor SSO), which they will now have to defend orally. The ministry said it would speak to schools about the best way to do this.Upper secondary schools will also be required to use monitoring tools to oversee how computers are being used for written exams. They are required to install firewalls to filter what is available on the school network during exams and teaching.The third measure is a plea to schools to encourage pupils to do more of their written assignments at school under controlled conditions, to “follow the students’ work process, provide relevant feedback and create a more accurate basis for assessment”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe ready availability of AI tools is upending education around the world for teachers and pupils, leaving governments scrambling to assess if and how they should intervene.In neighbouring Sweden, a study found that the number of students suspended or warned for unauthorised AI use rose by 688% between 2023 and 2025. The government has commissioned a review into how schools are tackling AI cheating, which will report back in April.Announcing the review, Lotta Edholm, the Swedish minister for upper secondary school, said in January: “There is no reason to turn a blind eye to cheating students. Cheating is completely unacceptable regardless of what form. It risks affecting grades that should reflect students’ knowledge and in the long term, students are not actually learning what they should.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)DenmarkEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Meta says its AI model hacked into another company during testing | Meta | The Guardian
description: Company is the third to report such an incident after Anthropic and OpenAI reported breaches during training
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Company is the third to report such an incident after Anthropic and OpenAI reported breaches during training
Content: A logo of Meta AI appears on a screen at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in 2025.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersView image in fullscreenA logo of Meta AI appears on a screen at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in 2025.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersMetaMeta says its AI model hacked into another company during testingCompany is the third to report such an incident after Anthropic and OpenAI reported breaches during trainingReutersWed 5 Aug 2026 21.27 EDTLast modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMeta said on Wednesday that one of its AI models hacked ⁠another company during cybersecurity testing, after an error by its testing partner gave the model unintended internet access.The incident adds to a ⁠growing list of ⁠cases in ​which AI agents from major developers breached systems at other companies during testing, after Anthropic said last week that some of its models ⁠hacked three companies, andOpenAI disclosedthat an AI agent breached the startup Hugging Face.AI models have been going rogue in tests – how worried should we be?Read moreMeta said a misconfiguration by the independent testing company Irregular inadvertently allowed one ⁠of its models internet access during an evaluation, adding that it was investigating the incident.The model “exploited ​a security vulnerability in a third-party service, ‌in a manner similar ‌to previously reported instances with other companies”, Meta said in a statement.Earlier in the day, ‌The Information, citing sources, reported that Meta’s Muse Spark 1.1 model, which it has touted as its most capable model for real-world coding and agentic tasks, breached an unidentified company and altered its internal systems.A spokesperson for Irregular told Reuters the incident was the “exact same evaluation-environment issue that was already disclosed by Anthropic last week” and that it did ‌not involve a “sandbox escape or a sophisticated cyber action”.“There are no current open issues. Irregular is developing a white paper to share best ​practices for containment and securely running cyber evaluations,” Irregular said.The incidents revealed by Meta and Anthropic were due to mistakes that inadvertently gave their models access to the open internet. That contrasts with OpenAI, whose AI agent independently exploited a novel vulnerability to reach the internet during cyber testing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEven ⁠so, the breaches highlight how AI has increased threats to cybersecurity and ​how developers can struggle ​to keep the capabilities of their ​models contained.The disclosures are likely to intensify a US government push to ​better manage AI security ‌risks at a ​time when Anthropic and ​OpenAI are racing to release more capable systems ahead of their planned public listings. Prominent leaders at these labs have called for a slowdown to address risks first.Explore more on these topicsMetaAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I have an ego that needs to be put in check’: ex-Gawker editor AJ Daulerio on life after addiction | Media | The Guardian
description: After his fall from grace, media’s former enfant terrible is now sober and helping others with his addiction recovery newsletter and podcast, The Small Bow
Author: John McDermott
Headline: After his fall from grace, media’s former enfant terrible is now sober and helping others with his addiction recovery newsletter and podcast, The Small Bow
Content: Media‘I have an ego that needs to be put in check’: ex-Gawker editor AJ Daulerio on life after addictionAfter his fall from grace, media’s former enfant terrible is now sober and helping others with his addiction recovery newsletter and podcast, The Small BowJohn McDermottThu 6 Aug 2026 10.59 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.37 EDTShareView image in fullscreenAJ Daulerio: ‘The Small Bow is a living amends for whatever version of me came before on the internet.’Photograph: Storm Santos/Contour RA by Getty ImagesEvery other Tuesday, AJ Daulerio wakes up at 5.30am and meditates for five to 20 minutes before beginning his multistep daily journaling protocol: reading a selection from a poetry anthology, then a passage from one of his daily wisdom readers (his go-to is a heavily annotated copy of Leo Tolstoy’sA Calendar of Wisdom); writing his Fear of the Day and gratitude list, then sharing his spiritual takeaway in a note to his three kids.After a banana and coffee, Daulerio trains Brazilian jujitsu before hitting a 9.45am meditation at Besant Lodge – a community center just below the Hollywood sign that once served as a meeting place for mid-century mystics – immediately followed by him leading a recovery meeting of his own through Zoom.He goes to personal therapy at 11.15am, picks up his kids in the afternoon and spends the rest of the evening with them and his wife, giving him just a few hours at night to work on his advicecolumnfor Slate and the two books he’s writing.double quotation markI know there’s a good way of self-promoting, I’m just wary of my intentions a lot of the timeAJ DaulerioThis is in addition to emotional sobriety step work (cultivating inner peace after the drinking stops) on Zoom on Wednesday nights, an Adult Children of Alcoholics meeting every Friday morning, Alcoholics Anonymous on Sundays, couples therapy every other week, and a quarterly meeting with his psychiatrist to refine his cocktail of psychotropic medications, including a mood stabilizer (Lamictal) and an antipsychotic (Zyprexa), to treat his bipolar disorder.“I have an ego that needs to be put in check all the time,” Daulerio tells me. “Half of my recovery is dedicated to that.”Daulerio celebrated 10 years of sobriety this July, a joyous capstone to a tumultuous decade-plus that saw Daulerio go from digital media visionary as editor of Gawker to broke, disgraced and the man most responsible for the site’s demise.Daulerio has re-emerged in recent years, again as a media innovator – not as the cutthroat, traffic-obsessed editor reputation he garnered at Gawker, but as the gentle, deeply pensive and contrite author ofThe Small Bow,the newsletter he created in 2018 to chronicle his recovery from drug and alcohol addiction, and his attempts to reclaim his life as a changed man.Today Daulerio maintains a rigorous recovery regimen to battle the twin demons that once fueled his self-destructive impulses: the lonesomeness that led him to seek companionship in dive bars among other strange drunks, and the ego that convinced him he had it all under control, despite signs to the opposite.I spent 22 years as a problem drinker. Here are 10 things I’ve learned since I quitRead moreDaulerio has built a devout following by writing about his recovery program in unsparingly honest, vulnerable first-person essays in The Small Bow, and he now wants to grow the company into a multiplatform media company that provides wisdom and guidance to people struggling with addictions of all kinds.But therein lies Daulerio’s existential dilemma: how to build a successful media business without sacrificing the spiritual practice that made his second act possible.“It’s something I have to get comfortable with and better at, because I do believe in what we’re doing,” Daulerio says between bites of his cheeseburger. “I know there’s a good way of self-promoting, I’m just wary of my intentions a lot of the time.”One needs a certain amount of irrational self-confidence to start any business, especially in print media, an industry that has been in steady decline since Daulerio first became a journalist in 2000. Then there’s the self-promotion required to grow a business, even as it risks inflating the ego that fueled his fall from grace and that he’s worked so hard to keep in check.That The Small Bow is built almost entirely around Daulerio’s personal experience makes this all the more difficult.In Daulerio’s favor is his unmatched skill at growing digital media properties. It’s what propelled him to success as the editor of the now defunctGawker Media– and also what led to his and the company’s downfall.The Small Bow uses lots of religious iconography in its branding: pen and colored pencil illustrations of demons and angels drawn by Edith Zimmerman, a writer and artist whohas also found sobriety– and they serve as an easy metaphor for the tension between Daulerio’s professional ambitions and his personal recovery: the demon whispering in one ear to revert to his old tricks and grow The Small Bow by any means necessary, and the angel whispering in the other to preserve what’s made The Small Bow so resonant with readers undergoing their own struggles.“How do you sell something that is supposed to be genuine?” he asks me rhetorically. As with his sobriety, all he can do is forge ahead and attempt to achieve this seemingly irreconcilable balancing act, one day at a time. “What are the other options?”The last 10 years of Daulerio’s life have been an exercise in being humbled. Few figures in recent history have had their rise and fall scrutinized as intensely by the media. His exploits have been the subject of two Netflix documentaries, glossy magazine profiles, and countless reports and thought pieces on sound journalistic practice and the limits of first amendment freedoms.double quotation markI had the ability to get people to tell me things they weren’t supposed toAJ DaulerioBut long before he was media’s enfant terrible, he was one of the most promising young talents in 2000s digital journalism.Daulerio started in journalism in 1998, covering city council meetings for the East Brunswick Sentinel in New Jersey. His initial dream was to be a music producer – he was simultaneously interning at a recording studio – or, saving that, a music critic. But he quickly exhibited a preternatural talent for landing scoops, a skill that would become his MO as he ascended the highest echelons of the digital publishing industry.“I had the ability to get people to tell me things they weren’t supposed to,” Daulerio says. “Because I didn’t have strict deadlines, I could hang out with the council members.” A former college classmate of Daulerio’s worked the same beat for a competing newspaper, and Daulerio delighted in beating him to stories. “I loved it. I was weirdly competitive in a way that’s good for reporting. I’ve never been competitive in anything else.”Despite being a diehard Philly sports fan, Daulerio was a feckless athlete himself, much to the embarrassment of his father (a topic Daulerio frequently visits in his Small Bow columns). “I grew up playing sports, but I never knew how to win. In the journalism world, I knew how to win.”Daulerio shuffled through writing and editing gigs in New York and Philadelphia – including stints at the trade publications Bond Buyer and American Lawyer Media; men’s lifestyle newsletter Thrillist; and Philadelphia magazine – before landing a senior editor job at Deadspin, Gawker’s sports vertical, in 2008. Just months later, he was promoted to editor for the entire site.Then Daulerio published photos of former New York Jets quarterback Brett Favre’s penis, and his life trajectory was forever altered.In August 2010, Daulerio published a Deadspin post alleging that Favrehad sent lewd voicemails and pictures of his penisto the Jets sideline reporter Jenn Sterger. Two months later, Dauleriopublished the illicit photos, purportedly from Favre, in a video montage, with Favre’s voicemails providing the soundtrack.The story generated millions of page views for Deadspin and months of headlines across the wider sports media ecosystem, cementing the three-person sports blog as a player on the national stage and Daulerio as a fearless journalist on the vanguard of a new era of digital journalism. “So many NFL reporters had known about [Favre’s behavior] the whole time and wouldn’t cover it,” Daulerio says. (Favre admitted to leaving the voicemails but denied sending lewd photos.)Professional and personal accolades showered over Daulerio. He did the Today show (while drunk, stoned and on Adderall). Nick Denton, Gawker Media’s founder and CEO, rewarded Daulerio with a raise, three more Deadspin staff writers and a freelance budget.double quotation markI would go to a bar on Thursday and come out of it on MondayAJ DaulerioDaulerio was spotlighted in aGQprofile and became a star of the New York City media scene. “A friend of mine from high school came to a Gawker office rooftop party,” Daulerio recalls. “He watched me walk into this place and he was like, ‘I feel like I’m with Don Corleone.’”It was the success and recognition Daulerio had always coveted. He had dreamed about having his glossy portrait photo featured in Forbes’ 30 Under 30 list. And yet all the attention – and criticism – made him uncomfortable. “I did not like my full-time job to be a punching bag for all the heels on the internet,” he says. “On the other hand, I had been treading water for 10 years in online journalism, and now I had attention and career options.” After the GQ story, “there was no reversing who I was.”As he climbed the ranks of the media industry, Daulerio was also feeding a drinking habit that would land him in rehab. He drank six nights a week, rotating through a familiar circuit of bars near work in the Bowery (Congee Village, Professor Thom’s) and, on weekends, in Williamsburg (Dardy Bar). Some Saturdays he would post up at a bar at 11am, down 10 beers and five shots, stay until close and then do cocaine with his newly formed friends. “I would just live in these places,” Daulerio says. “I was a binger. I would go to a bar on Thursday and come out of it on Monday … There was never really a plan other than to stay for as long as I possibly could.”Drinking was a way to treat the “free-floating loneliness” Daulerio had lived with since he was a child, he says. “It was fun to do cocaine with strangers until 4.30 in the morning. That felt like home to me … It would be silly to blame [my addiction] on anything other than I never felt normal or at ease, and I’m always battling that and probably always will.”He was one of the most successful editors in the burgeoning digital publishing industry, but he couldn’t afford an apartment because his credit was so bad. He bounced between friends’ couches.His cavalier editorial philosophy came under fire at the same time. To critics, Gawker became emblematic of a new wave of digital journalists who prioritized the almighty click and page view without any consideration for journalistic ethics or basic human decency.Publishing the Favre story, for instance, meant burning Sterger, the recipient of the reportedly unsolicited “dong shots” (Daulerio’s words), who had explicitly asked to not be included in the story. (Daulerio bought the photos and voicemails from a third party for $12,000.) He even published Sterger’s request to leave her out of it.Daulerio now says he wishes he had broken the Favre scoop without mentioning her.Later, when the Gawker empire imploded, a narrative emerged that Daulerio’s alcohol and drug use was largely to blame for the editorial decisions that led to its collapse, a premise Daulerio wholly rejects. “A lot of good things were happening when things were bad,” he says.The rise and fall of Deadspin: how ‘jerks in Brooklyn’ changed sports journalismRead moreSuch as Deadspin’s immense growth. In just three years under Daulerio’s tenure, Deadspin’s traffic tripled, as the site continued to break raunchy, irreverent scoops – former New York Jets head coachRex Ryan filming foot fetish videosstarring his wife; photos of Texas Rangers outfielderJosh Hamilton drunk and shirtless, licking whipped cream off a woman’s breasts in a Tempe, Arizona, bar, despite supposedly being sober; andESPN Horndog Dossier, a collection of unconfirmed rumors about rampant illicit sexual behavior at “the Worldwide Leader in Sports”.There was even some genuine investigative reporting mixed in with the scuzzy gossip, such asleaked financial documentsexposing the creative accounting techniques that Major League Baseball franchises employ to boost profits.Denton named Daulerio editor ofGawker.com, Gawker Media’s flagship site, in late 2011. The following fall, Daulerio approved publication of a sex tape starring the professional wrestler Hulk Hogan. Hogan filed an invasion of privacy lawsuit against Gawker just two weeks later, a legal action that would bankrupt Gawker and force its sale, and temporarily ruin Daulerio’s life and career. (It was later revealed that Hogan’s suit was financed by the billionaire venture capitalist Peter Thiel, who harbored a grudge against Gawker Media ever since itouted him as gay in 2007.)Hogan won a $140m judgment in March 2016 against Gawker, including $100,000 in punitive damages for Daulerio, a verdict that was largely blamed on Daulerio and hiscallouseditorial ethos. (Gawker settled with Hogan for $31m, and Daulerio didn’t have to pay the $100,000.)During the trial, Hogan’s attorneys brought up how Daulerio once published a separate sex tape of two people who were not public figures, and how Daulerio initially dismissed the woman in the video when she requested its removal. (Daulerio implored her to “not make a big deal out of this”.)The post was eventually deleted, and Daulerio says publishing it was the most regrettable moment of his career.The most damning moment in the trial was when Hogan’s attorneys showed the courtroom a videotaped deposition of Daulerio from October 2013, in which a Hogan attorney asked Daulerio: “Can you imagine a situation where a celebrity sex tape would not be newsworthy?”“If they were a child,” Daulerio replied.The lawyer pushed: “Under what age?”“Four.”The exchange sent “a palpable sense of shock” through the courtroom,according to the New York Times. There wereaudible gasps and groans. Daulerio says the comment was a sarcastic joke, “a defense mechanism” after getting frustrated with the interrogation, but it supported the plaintiff’s portrayal of Daulerio as a heartless gossip-peddler who trafficked in the sordid details of people’s personal lives, even when they had zero news value.Adding to Daulerio’s embarrassment, the trial revealed he hada net worth of negative $35,000. The court froze the $1,500 he had in his bank account. The 2017 Netflix documentary Nobody Speak: Trials of the Free Press about the Hogan trial opens with Daulerio laughing as he reads a bank email informing him a $230m hold had been placed on his bank account.Daulerio can’t recall how he felt during the trial. He dissociated. “It was so big and overwhelming, I just felt like I was a character in this thing,” he says. The only part of the experience he can latch on to is the photo of him from theNew York Timesarticle. “I feel like I know what that expression is: really helpless, but also in trouble.”As Daulerio’s professional life was put on trial, he was also trying to get sober. He first entered rehab in August 2015, seven months before the trial began, but quickly relapsed. “Two months later, I was back at it pretty hardcore,” he says.Daulerio fully committed to sobriety on 15 July 2016, a month after Gawker filed for bankruptcy and put itself up for sale. “July 15, 2016, was simply the day I decided to stop resisting and give up the warped idea that I could do my own modified version of sobriety, something akin to what I liked to call ‘advanced moderation’,” he wrote ina recent Small Bow essayabout his 10th anniversary of sobriety.What Daulerio still longed for in his early days of recovery was a way to process the experience the best way he knew how: through writing.The first piece Daulerio published after the trial wasa 2017 first-person essay about his fraught relationship with his fatherfor the now shuttered men’s publication Mel.The piece had the pugnacious writing that made Deadspin so popular; Daulerio opens the essay recounting a physical fight with his father. But it also had the emotional vulnerability of an adult man trying to heal his daddy issues, told through the prism of past Father’s Days. (I was a staff writer at Mel at that time, but did not work with Daulerio).“The piece was masculinity and neuroses laid bare, not in a self-pitying, ‘woe is me’ way, but in a curious way,” former Mel editor-in-chief Josh Schollmeyer says. “If there’s any difference between the pre- and post-trial AJ, it’s AJ falling in love with his own mythology versus being who he really is, which is a master storyteller. That humility was apparent from the jump.”The naked confessional style would become The Small Bow’s signature. In the newsletter, Daulerio recounts his various sobriety efforts – AA meetings, therapy, meditation, psychiatry, stoicism, Buddhism – in oftentimes painful, but always heartfelt honesty.Earlier this year, he wrote aboutmoving his elderly mother into an assisted living facilityin Florida near where he went to rehab. He also frequently writes about the spiritual blessings of being a family man; Daulerio and screenwriter Julieanne Smolinski married in 2018, and they have three children together in Los Angeles.double quotation markHe has been through the level of public shame that I have. Few people have experienced thatJenn StergerSome of the most powerful Small Bow entries are about Daulerio making amends – steps eight and nine in 12-step programs – to those he wronged during his years actively in addiction, such as making peace with Sterger.Ina January 2020 essay, Daulerio revealed he and Sterger incidentally reconnected when he adopted a dog for his growing family. Sterger just so happened to work at the dog shelter Smolinski emailed, resulting in Daulerio and Sterger meeting at the LA diner House of Pies.She admitted that there are still uncomfortable days and awkward moments stemming from the Favre ordeal. There’s still a version of her that exists in the internet’s memory hole where she will never be a real person; she’s just a plot point without context, without skin. But the thing that I did was more vicious. You see, I knew she was a real person – and I did what I did anyway. I didn’t care if I destroyed her. That’s just the type of person I was back then.I don’t remember how long we actually talked, but I remember we both walked out of there a little relieved like we’d both just found a therapist who finally understood the excavation tools required to break new ground. Some hurts were still unreachable, though. Time takes time.Sterger agreed to meet him out of curiosity: she wanted to understand why Daulerio betrayed her wishes and upended her life. “I found a guy that had looked at himself in the mirror and really done a lot of hard work on himself – really examined why he had done the things that he had done, and realized the hurt that he had caused people,” Sterger says.The two got along so well that they developed the unlikeliest of friendships. “He has been through the level of public shame that I have,” Sterger says. “Few people have experienced that.” Sterger later appeared on The Small Bow podcast, where she and Daulerio publicly buried the hatchet.“There’s a concept in recovery of a living amends,” Daulerio says. When a direct amends might inflict even more pain on the injured party, addicts in recovery are instructed to atone by simply living a good life. “The Small Bow is a living amends for whatever version of me came before on the internet.”The newsletter has amassed 20,000 subscribers – about 2,000 of them paid, making him $72,000 a year – including some celebrities that have embraced the publication as a platform to discuss their own sobriety.Fans of the CBS talkshow The Talk and the Barstool Sports podcast Pardon My Take know Jerry O’Connell as a happy-go-lucky actor with a goofy sense of humor, but on The Small Bow podcast in April, O’Connellrevealed he’s been in recovery from alcoholismfor 13 years.Going public about his sobriety took some convincing. O’Connell got sober under the old-school AA mentality that treats anonymity as sacrosanct – “it’s right there in the title,” he says – but made an exception because Daulerio had been so important to his own recovery. The two connected during the pandemic over their shared sobriety after O’Connell, a longtime Deadspin fan, reached out.“AJ has a new-school way of thinking, and that’s why this venture is interesting,” O’Connell says of Daulerio’s willingness to bare it all. “This is all uncharted territory.”“I was publicly drunk, so being publicly sober makes sense to me, and I like to talk about the many methods I go about to stay that way,” Daulerio recently wrote in The Small Bow. “But recovery is a personal thing – how someone chooses to do it isn’t my business.”double quotation mark[Daulerio is] very self-effacing in a way that is honest, not trying to win brownie points by being self-effacingAlex WinterActor and documentarian Alex Winter has a routine meetup with Daulerio at House of Pies, where they discuss recovery and fatherhood. Winter, too,discussed his recovery on an episode of The Small Bow, the only time he has appeared on a recovery podcast.“I’ve always bristled a little bit at these kinds of recovery-forward podcasts,” Winter says. “I always worry about people getting very enthusiastic about getting sober. … Recovery is delicate. It’s fragile. So I just feel for the people who expose themselves that way and hope that they’re OK.” What separates Daulerio, Winter says, is his radical candor. “He’s very self-effacing in a way that is honest, not trying to win brownie points by being self-effacing.”The day after Hogan died last July,Daulerio penned a Small Bow essaypartially thanking the Hulkster for body-slamming his life and career. “Without that experience, there is no Small Bow, probably,” Daulerio says. “That’s how I choose to think about it.”“I forgot to brush my teeth,” Daulerio announces to The Small Bow production team, as he prepares to tape a new episode.Between fatherhood and his recovery routine, Daulerio’s is more structured than ever, but chaos seeps in at times. After nearly three decades as a writer, he still gets bothered by commenters. He recently senta snarky email responseto a reader who criticizedone of his Slate advice columns.double quotation markWhat I want to create a dialogue about is: you can stop drinking just because you don’t like itRyan O’ConnellA current focus in his recovery is on improving his sleep. A night owl, Daulerio typically gets only five hours of sleep a night, staying up until the wee hours to watch violent action movies, often starring Jason Statham. He has started using a sleep mask and soothing ASMR sounds to help lull him into slumber.The podcast is integral to Daulerio’s strategy for growing The Small Bow. His larger vision is something akin to a trade magazine for the recovery industry. He wants to sell subscriptions to recovery facilities – hospitals, clinics, rehabs, halfway houses – whose patients would then be able to access, and even contribute to, The Small Bow’s archive of addiction-related content. “A farm system for The Small Bow,” he says, not unlike how Gawker recruited the wittiest contributors in its comments section to become paid staff writers.Daulerio piloted such a program with Divided Sky, the Ludlow, Vermont, drug rehab facility co-founded by the Phish frontman Trey Anastasio, whoseappearance on The Small Bow podcastis the show’s most popular to date.How the rivalry between Gawker and BuzzFeed drove a social media boom – and bustRead moreAs The Small Bow has attracted more contributors, its scope has widened to include a broader array of addictions and mental health issues: sex, shopping, gambling, weed, depression, bipolar disorder. The internet itself.Today’spodcast tapingis with writer Ryan O’Connell, who’s promoting his essay collection,Inspiration Porn– a welcome development for Daulerio, who wants The Small Bow to be a requisite stop on the memoir promotion circuit. Daulerio’s own books, a compilation of essays about recovery called The Small Book, a play on AA’s Big Book, and a memoir about his life post-Gawker trial, are scheduled to publish in 2027.Ryan O’Connell’s relationship with alcohol falls into the expanded definition of sobriety. He never hit “rock bottom” because he quit before he could get there. “It’s the only substance you get shamed for quitting,” he says. “What I want to create a dialogue about is: you can stop drinking just because you don’t like it. AJ is expanding recovery conversations to be about so much more.”I ask Daulerio what success looks like to him now. On a personal level, it’s spending quality time with his family, the spiritual opposite of when he would stay out all night to avoid going home.Professionally, success means rediscovering his love of writing, doing it consistently, and serving the recovery community he’s cultivated.“I’m never going to have the notoriety I had, but I really enjoy what I do know and learning how to write again,” he says. “It’s the best work I’ve ever done.”

title: Exclusive: Major Republican fundraiser winning contracts from Trump administration, emails reveal | US national security | The Guardian
description: Palmer Luckey has donated $5.9m to Republicans and bundled more, while reaping billions in Pentagon contracts
Author: Aram Roston
Headline: Palmer Luckey has donated $5.9m to Republicans and bundled more, while reaping billions in Pentagon contracts
Content: Palmer Luckey at Anduril's headquarters in Costa Mesa, California, on 10 October 2025.Photograph: Kyle Grillot/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPalmer Luckey at Anduril's headquarters in Costa Mesa, California, on 10 October 2025.Photograph: Kyle Grillot/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesUS national securityExclusive: Major Republican fundraiser winning contracts from Trump administration, emails revealPalmer Luckey has donated $5.9m to Republicans and bundled more, while reaping billions in Pentagon contractsAram Rostonin WashingtonThu 6 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 14.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWealthyRepublicanson the west coast received an emailed invitation in July to an upcoming fundraiser titled “Keep the Senate”. The email, obtained by the Guardian, described the event as a “private roundtable and dinner with the National Republican Senatorial Committee” where donors can pledge $50,000 for seats at the head table, and mingle with legislative heavy hitters from Capitol Hill including the Senator majority leader, John Thune, and Mike Rogers, who is running for Senate in Michigan withDonald Trump’s endorsement.One of the organizers listed on the invite was the defense industry tycoon Palmer Luckey, the 33-year-old co-founder of sprawling weapons manufacturer Anduril Industries.The invitation is one of dozens of emails obtained by the Guardian that unravel Luckey’s vast Maga political fundraising over the last seven years.Move fast, kill things: the tech startups trying to reinvent defence with Silicon Valley valuesRead moreA longtime GOP donor and activist who spoke on condition he not be identified in order to preserve his political relationshipssaid Luckey was now the “godfather of Republican fundraising on the west coast”.“If you’re raising campaign money inCalifornia, you have to go to Palmer Luckey,” he said. “Luckey is the top tier. There are others who are important below him but no one at his level.”Anduril, launched just nine years ago, has emerged as a major military contractor for theTrump administration, working on contracts for everything from drones to autonomous jet fighters to space-based interceptors.In March, the US army awarded a $20bn sole-source contract to Anduril for a variety of drones it sells, though it is not clear which of its weapons systems are operational or have been deployed for combat in US operations.Anduril, though it is not widely known as a space contractor, announced in May it would work, with a team of other companies, on what may be the mother of all contracting opportunities offered by the Trump administration, the so-called“Golden Dome” anti-missile space-based interceptor effort. Estimates for the Golden Dome range between $185bn and $1.2tn.Much of Anduril’s PR sparkle comes from Luckey. He’s a media darling, profiled on 60 Minutes and in the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times, which called him the “It Guy of the booming defense-technology industry”.His offbeat, relaxed attire – colorful Hawaiian shirts, a chin puff goatee, cargo shorts and flip-flops – counterintuitively makes him seem more credible.Luckey is treated by many in the defense industry as a technology prophet and futurist who often holds forth on what he believes to be the true nature of warfare. For example, hetold Axiosthat future wars will be fought in a “subterranean domain”, under the earth’s crust, in underground conflicts.Anduril’s success in winning huge contracts has blossomed with little attention paid to the central role Luckey plays as a donor and fundraising “bundler” for the Republican party. Bundlers hold large fundraisers for candidates or campaign committees and political action groups, and curate high-dollar invitation lists for those events.The emails obtained by the Guardian shed light on Palmer Luckey’s vast GOP political fundraising efforts and activism over the last 10 years.Palmer declined an interview for this piece, writing, “I am not going to help you guys make money,” and did not respond to a detailed list of questions.Rising influenceOpenSecrets, a non-profit that tracks campaign donations, says Federal Election Commission (FEC) records show that Luckey has donated $5.9m toRepublicanssince 2017. While that is a tremendous amount of money for one person to give to politicians, it does not put him in the order of, say, Miriam Adelson, the widow of Sheldon Adelson, who has forked over $100m to Trump’s campaign in 2024.Luckey doesn’t have her wealth. His real value to GOP politicians exceeds his own donations. He hosts and organizes fundraising events and campaigns for Republicans from the president all the way down to state races.“If you become a bundler, it just multiplies your influence,” said Brendan Glavin of OpenSecrets. “It makes you a more important person. You’re bringing in not just your money. You’re bringing other people’s money. It integrates you in the campaign and makes you more important to the candidate than just a donor.”Behind the scenes, Luckey has reached a position in campaign finance and politics that rivals his influence in military contracting, according to two GOP fundraising figures.The emails, which are a partial list of invitations, show that Luckey has held fundraisers over the last seven years for at least 20 Republican politicians, ranging from Trump to a California attorney general candidate.Just as Luckey has emerged as a major fundraiser on the right, his co-founder, Anduril’s CEO,Palantirveteran Brian Schimpf, became a major donor to Democratic causes, albeit on a far smaller scale. So, in time-honored tradition, Anduril’s management ends up donating to both sides of the political aisle, though the vast majority goes towards the GOP. FEC records show Schimpf’s donations at $1.16m over the same period that Luckey gave $5.9m.An Anduril official emailed the Guardian: “It shouldn’t surprise anyone that two executives at the same company have different political views. Like millions of Americans, Brian and Palmer don’t share identical political views.”A fundraising dam breaksLuckey first became famous in tech before he could legally drink. At 20, in 2012, he launched a Kickstarter that raised more than $2m for a virtual reality gaming headset he said he was building first in his parents’ garage. It was a Silicon Valley Cinderella narrative. Two years later, Facebook became the prince at the ball and paid him $2bn for the company. In 2016, after four years of hype, the first Oculus Rift headset started getting shipped to consumers.And then, quickly, Luckey seemed to flame out in scandal. The Daily Beast revealed he’d been secretly funding a group dedicated to “shitposting” negative memes about Hillary Clinton.“We know Hillary Clinton is corrupt, a warmonger, a freedom-stripper. Not the good kind you see dancing in bikinis on Independence Day, the bad kind that strips freedom from citizens and grants it to donors,” Luckey had written, under the pseudonym Nimblerichman, on Reddit.The disclosure had an immense impact, at least for a time. Eight months later Luckey left Facebook, and he later portrayed himself in interviews as simply being canceled for giving money to Republicans, ignoring the main criticisms over the group’s crude and underhanded tactics.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLuckey left Facebook with immense wealth, and in April 2017, just four months after Trump’s first inauguration, he founded Anduril.His partners in the venture came from the Peter Thiel-backed Palantir, a company that had long had success in federal contracting through major lobbying and PR battles.In June of 2017, his company just two months old, Luckey gave his first ever actual campaign finance donation, toTed Cruz, the senator from Texas. Looking at his subsequent donations, it appears that the dam broke for him. Palmer gave 25 more times to political committees and legislators that year alone, FEC records show, and he has donated on more than a thousand occasions, or, on average, about 100 times every year.‘A step-change’: tech firms battle for undersea dominance with submarine dronesRead moreIn the emails shared with the Guardian, the very first fundraising event Luckey co-hosted took place in August of 2017, two months after his donation to Ted Cruz. It was a major effort, and would include GOP House members such as Ken Calvert, Duncan Hunter, Darrell Issa, Devin Nunes, Dana Rohrabacher andKevin McCarthy.Then in November, in a separate email chain, Palmer’s name came up again, for the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC). A congressional aide named Jason Pitkin wrote to a party official: “we are going to be asking people for $33,900 for the NRCC and then after the first of the year we can ask them for $101,700.”Pitkin noted that congressman Rohrabacher had introduced Luckey to Kevin McCarthy, then the powerful House majority leader, “at a Private meeting”.“As you can see by the attached invitation,” Pitkin said, “Palmer is hosting an event for Dana [Rohrabacher] On December 15th. Our understanding is that Palmer was going to contribute $100,000 for the CA Victory event. Please let us know how much more Palmer can give to the NRCC.”Pitkin did not respond to emailed questions.In July of 2020, just three years after its creation, Anduril won itsfirst mammoth contractfrom the first Trump administration. Customs and Border Protection awarded the young company a contract estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars for surveillance towers on the border.And in that period it was clear that Luckey had hit the most senior levels of political access. On 6 October, the emails show, Luckey and his wife hosted Trump himself at a lunch at their waterfront mansion. The stakes were high and so were the tickets. Donors were told that $150,000 would get access to the round table, a VIP reception and event, and a photo op with the president.During the Biden years, Anduril still maintained its business efforts targetingUS national security, and still won contracts. It went on a major acquisition binge, buying up drone companies across the country.And Luckey’s fundraising for the GOP continued. The records obtained by the Guardian show that after 2021, Luckey hosted fundraisers for key figures including Tom Cotton, the head of the Senate intelligence committee; Rick Scott, the Republican senator from Florida; Ken Calvert, then the influential ranking member of the House’s defense appropriations subcommittee; and Mike Waltz, now Trump’s UN ambassador and briefly his national security adviser.Luckey also hosted another event for a future Trump official: a $50,000-a-plate fundraiser in June 2022for Mehmet Oz, who would later join the Trump administration. That event became scandalouswhen Jezebelreported the fundraiser incorporated a speech by Oz in front of a car that once belonged to Adolf Hitler. Jezebel pointed out that Luckey’s sister is married to Maga firebrand Matt Gaetz, then a congressman from Florida.Now that Trump is president, Anduril appears to be taking its turn at the table of the major contractors, amid Lockheed Martin, Raytheon and General Dynamics.Certainly it has raised extraordinary money. In the latest round, led by Thrive Capital, controlled by Jared Kushner’s brother Joshua, it raised $5bn in venture capital.Anduril says in Trump’s first year in office it doubled its revenue – a growth rate of 100%, but still only reached $2.2bn for 2025, which is barely a blip in the Pentagon’s trillion-dollar budget.Still, the US defense secretary,Pete Hegseth, has twice toured Anduril factories.“Palmer and everyone, thank you so much,” he said last December as he visited Anduril’s factory in Costa Mesa, California, at a giant former industrial site where the Los Angeles Times was once printed. The Anduril factory was “foundational” to the new Pentagon, Hegseth said.On that tour, Hegseth donned a special helmet designed by Anduril.A soldier wearing the helmet would be able to see the outside world not through his eyes but through sensors, as a kind of virtual or “augmented” reality, just like the old Oculus Rift headset Palmer Luckey made his fortune on.In his speech, Hegseth referred to “that cool helmet I just saw that the army might be wearing eventually”.Explore more on these topicsUS national securityRepublicansWeapons technologyTrump administrationDonald TrumpPete HegsethKevin McCarthyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m not spying’: how Meta’s smartglasses have divided opinion | Meta | The Guardian
description: While some users say the wearables have changed their lives, critics voice fears over safety and privacy
Author: Rosie Peters-McDonald
Headline: While some users say the wearables have changed their lives, critics voice fears over safety and privacy
