Content: Meta reportedly sold 7m pairs of its Ray-Ban smartglasses last year.Photograph: Josh Edelson/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMeta reportedly sold 7m pairs of its Ray-Ban smartglasses last year.Photograph: Josh Edelson/AFP/Getty ImagesMeta‘I’m not spying’: how Meta’s smartglasses have divided opinionWhile some users say the wearables have changed their lives, critics voice fears over safety and privacyNicola SlawsonandRosie Peters-McDonaldThu 6 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith more than 7m pairs reportedly sold in 2025, Meta’s Ray-Ban smartglasses are fast becoming one of the world’s most popular gadgets.While supporters say they are transforming photography and accessibility, critics have raised concerns about nonconsensual filming, privacy and data collection.We spoke to users, and people who refuse to wear them, about the impact the glasses have had.Based in The Hague in the Netherlands, Servaas wears his Meta glasses every day. He bought them for the built-in camera rather than the AI features and uses them to photograph and film walks and bike rides. “It’s an immersive experience,” he says. “I love everything tech and have done my whole life.”He says the discreet camera means most people don’t realise he is wearing smartglasses, although he was once stopped by security at an event held in a government building because staff feared he might be recording. “For some reason, security didn’t understand. They were very scared of them [the glasses]. People said I should have expected that but I didn’t agree with them because it’s not like I’m spying.”Despite allegations thatMeta workers in Kenya viewed private footage recorded on the glasses, Servaas was not put off by the scandal. “I know Meta loves your data [but] I’m not worried about my privacy because I’ve only used them to record outside.”‘A real gamechanger’For others, however, the glasses offer far more than convenience. Nikki, 59, from Devon in the UK, has been blind since birth owing to an inherited retinal disease and describes the glasses, which she received as a Christmas present in 2024, as “a real gamechanger”.“I live in quite a rural location,” she says. “I could hear something going on ahead of me as I was walking down to the village shop. I said: ‘Hey Meta, look and tell me what’s in front of me.’ It told me there was a van unloading scaffolding. It’s things like that that I find absolutely amazing.”While she understands concerns about privacy, Nikki worries public criticism could make the technology less accessible for people who genuinely rely on it. “What about dashcams? What about camera doorbells? What about action cameras like GoPros? People don’t complain about them,” she says. “I kind of worry that if people start going on about privacy and safety, it will be harder for those of us who genuinely benefit from the glasses.”View image in fullscreenModel and content creator Emma Brooks at a Meta Glasses launch party in New York.Photograph: Jason Lowrie/BFA.com/Shutterstock‘The caption feature just doesn’t work’Yet the accessibility features have not transformed everyone’s experience. Karen Walter, 84, from San Diego, who has been living with severe hearing loss for more than 20 years, bought the glasses solely for their live-caption feature.“Even with state-of-the-art hearing aids, I have a great deal of difficulty understanding what people are saying unless the person is very close to me and speaking directly to me,” she says. “I expected [the glasses] would be a great help in noisy environments and when I was trying to keep up with conversations involving more than two people.”The live captions worked well during a demonstration in a quiet Best Buy store, she says, when she was “with one staffer who was directly in front of me, about two feet away”. However, she says they failed to perform in the situations for which she had bought them: “I have tried the glasses when in a group of three up to a group of seven and the caption feature just doesn’t work. There were too many people talking and too much surrounding noise.”‘They’ve made me much more wary in public’Not everyone is convinced the technology belongs in everyday life at all. Kiki, from the West Midlands in the UK, says she finds the idea of discreet cameras built into ordinary eyewear “pervasive”, particularly for women and children.“If you try to take a picture with your phone, at least it’s pretty obvious,” she says. “With the glasses, you have no choice, as the camera is much harder to spot.”Kiki says seeing people wearing the glasses in public has left her feeling uneasy.“When someone’s just looking at you through their glasses, it worries me,” she says. “I imagine taking images secretly is far easier [than on phones]. You could just pretend to adjust your hair or cap, and press the button in a passing gesture. I’ve seen people wearing them. I saw someone wearing them in a cafe and just moved away because I felt uncomfortable.”Although she accepts the technology could have genuine benefits, Kiki says her concern is more about the lack of safeguards. “For accessibility, absolutely,” she says. “But what bothers me is regulations often lag so far behind technology.”“They have made me much more wary in public,” she says. “I can, however, see that people working in a shop late at night by themselves might feel safer being able to take a picture of someone harassing them.”Can you tell if someone is filming you with Meta glasses? – video‘I just don’t trust it’Pete, 44, from Northampton, believes the glasses point to a broader problem: AI-powered wearables collecting ever more personal data with too little scrutiny or regulation. “I’m not an old man shaking my fist at the clouds,” he says. “I’ve been onboard with technological advancement all my life, but with AI and Meta glasses, I’m drawing the line.”He is more concerned about where the data ends up than covert filming. “I don’t know who’s getting the pictures at the end and what they’re doing with them,” he says. “Whether they’re not doing anything or they’re selling it to someone, and then what those people are doing with it.”While Pete acknowledges the glasses could be transformative for blind people and other disabled users, he believes stronger safeguards are needed before they become commonplace. “I would like things like this to be of benefit to us,” he says. “I just don’t trust it.”Explore more on these topicsMetaGadgetsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nazis and Happy Feet collide in Penguin Colony, a psychological horror game set at the world’s end | Games | The Guardian
description: Explore Antarctica as a flightless bird – and dodge some earthly monsters – in this surreal adaptation of HP Lovecraft
Author: Sarah Thwaites
Headline: Explore Antarctica as a flightless bird – and dodge some earthly monsters – in this surreal adaptation of HP Lovecraft
Content: PS2-style aesthetic … Penguin Colony.Illustration: Fellow TravellerView image in fullscreenPS2-style aesthetic … Penguin Colony.Illustration: Fellow TravellerSummer games previewsGamesNazis and Happy Feet collide in Penguin Colony, a psychological horror game set at the world’s endExplore Antarctica as a flightless bird – and dodge some earthly monsters – in this surreal adaptation of HP LovecraftSarah ThwaitesThu 6 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile watching the 2006 animated film Happy Feet with his daughter, Origame Digital founder Naphtali Faulkner noticed something interesting. “[In the movie], they see the digger fall into the ocean, and it has an almost eldritch quality,” he says. Over time, and with plenty of iteration, Faulkner’s inspirations coalesced, from HP Lovecraft to the 1982 version of The Thing and the works of David Lynch. “I’m a big fan of horror that sits in your head rather than in your stomach,” says Faulkner.In Penguin Colony, players body-switch between species of flightless birds, piecing together cryptic cosmic clues as they tail a Nazi expedition to Antarctica. In the process, Origame Digital draws on Lovecraft’s novella At the Mountains of Madness. “I’d always wanted to do a creature that’s a manifestation of colonial thought, energy and power, and the idea of it resting and then regrowing,” says Faulkner. “I was looking through the history of Lovecraft and him being agigantic racist, and this idea of the Nazis sort of came out,” he adds.View image in fullscreenPenguin Colony.Illustration: Fellow TravellerThe visual style of Penguin Colony pays homage to the low-poly aesthetics of the PS2, a period Faulkner calls romantic, owing to the era’s limited technical capabilities, which led to impressionist designs. “We’re not a rich studio,” he says. “There was just a games crash; publishers aren’t funding anything, everyone seems to be out of money. So why don’t we make something very cheap to make?” It started with the game’s isolated setting, followed by a decision to have humans in the game appear as soldiers; their uniform bodies could be duplicated with only their heads swapped out. “Repetition pays its weight in gold sometimes because you aren’t having to be so meticulous. You can paint with broad strokes and really build something out.”Penguin Colony’s Antarctic setting is predominantly open-world, allowing Origame Digital to hide enigmatic notes, photographs and soundbites across the frigid tundra. “We wanted to play into the Lovecraftian fear of the unknown,” Faulkner says. As such, instead of relying on a user interface, players are guided by their intuition.This stylistic choice was also inspired by Dark Souls directorHidetaka Miyazaki, whose intentional vagueness evokes a distinctly pre-internet sense of discovery. “Certain things are in an alien language that players will need to decipher if they want to know what’s being said,” says Faulkner. By investigating, players also emulate the Nazi expedition’s archaeological activity. “[Later] you’ll come across some hieroglyphics, and we’ve made sure those image files contain no metadata, so players will actually have to look at them and try to decipher what it’s saying in context.”This cryptic touch isn’t the only homage to FromSoftware. Penguin Colony features an insight system comparable to Bloodborne, which lets players interpret the game’s otherworldly aspects with greater clarity based on how they play. “I don’t want to spoil exactly what,” adds Faulkner. “But, in a dark area, if you have enough insight, you can hear something walking around behind you.”Despite its surreal surroundings, Penguin Colony’s narrative draws on real history. “I did my research on this group calledthe Ahnenerbe, which was tasked with finding the Spear of Destiny and other Christian artefacts,” says Faulkner. “Nazi relic hunting went all around the world,” he continues. “They would find things with barely any connection to anything, and invent histories that don’t actually exist, and that was used as their justification for the colonial annexation of Europe.”It’s a confronting topic, but Faulkner feels this kind of conversation belongs in games, especially since they are one of the few art forms in which audience participation is mandatory. He recalls a conversation with his mentor about playing in the grey, where you place ideas side by side and explore the feelings they can evoke. “There are people out there who, the moment you say colonisation, freak out and start stomping their feet. [That’s] not my audience … I think of it like this: if this game reaches someone who hadn’t thought about this [topic] before and they change the way they think about it, just a little bit, then it was worth it.”Penguin Colony is coming soon to PC andNintendo Switch 2.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsPCNintendo Switch 2featuresShareReuse this content

title: ‘Mamma mia!’: Trump tariffs refund ignites 53% profit spike at Nintendo | Nintendo | The Guardian
description: Profit jump fuelled largely by unknown US refund amount as Japanese video game firm records quarterly sales drop
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Profit jump fuelled largely by unknown US refund amount as Japanese video game firm records quarterly sales drop
Content: Nintendo said sales of its Switch 2 console, which was released last summer, maintained strong momentum but overall sales dropped 10%.Photograph: Richard A Brooks/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNintendo said sales of its Switch 2 console, which was released last summer, maintained strong momentum but overall sales dropped 10%.Photograph: Richard A Brooks/AFP/Getty ImagesNintendo‘Mamma mia!’: Trump tariffs refund ignites 53% profit spike at NintendoProfit jump fuelled largely by unknown US refund amount as Japanese video game firm records quarterly sales dropKalyeena MakortoffThu 6 Aug 2026 07.11 EDTFirst published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNintendo has reported a jump in profits, as the Japanese game maker’s earnings were buoyed up by a long-awaited refund on Donald Trump’s tariffs.The company said profits surged 53.5% to ¥147.4bn (£694m) over the three months to June, substantially beating expert forecasts for ¥77.8bn.Nintendo said sales of its Switch 2 console, which was released last summer, “maintained strong sales momentum”, while popular games such as Yoshi and the Mysterious Book, Star Fox, and Pokémon Pokopia “performed steadily”. However, that did not make up for an overall drop in sales compared with the same period last year, with revenue down by 10% to ¥517.8bn.‘Let’s-a go!’ The story of Nintendo – podcastRead moreInstead, Nintendo said profits were aided by a refund on US tariffs, after the country’ssupreme court ruledin February that Donald Trump’s sweeping “liberation day” trade levies were illegal.TheTrump administrationhas refunded about $100bn from the tariffs charged before the court ruling, representing 60% of the total $165bn collected. Trump has continued to pitch tariffs as a solution for the US economy, bringing back domestic production, securing better trade deals and closing the deficit in the federal budget.Nintendo’s Tokyo-listed shares were up 2.87% on Thursday after the earnings release.The companyfiled a lawsuitweeks after the US supreme court ruling, demanding a full refund from the White House that would cover what it spent on tariffs, plus interest.While a refund now appears to have come through, Nintendo stopped short of confirming the full amount, at a time when it is still appears to be resisting calls to pass those refunds on to consumers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLast month, Nintendo was hit with aclass action lawsuit on behalf of customers, which claims the company hiked its prices because of tariffs but later benefited from the refunds. Nintendo’s lawyers described the lawsuit as “meritless”, and that the price customers paid represented “the purchase price of the goods they wanted and received.”Last month, Trump imposed afresh round of tariffson more than 80 countries, including Japan, in a move that is likely to pose further problems for companies such as Nintendo. However, a coalition of 25 US statesare now suing the Trump administration over the levies, potentially opening the door to another round of refunds for beleaguered exporters.Explore more on these topicsNintendoTrump tariffsNintendo Switch 2GamesJapanTariffsInternational tradenewsShareReuse this content

title: Metroid at 40: happy birthday to Samus Aran, gaming’s greatest badass and my personal heroine | Games | The Guardian
description: Being a woman who loves video games has often felt lonely, like being on a hostile planet – but Metroid’s female space hunter has been with me all the way
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Being a woman who loves video games has often felt lonely, like being on a hostile planet – but Metroid’s female space hunter has been with me all the way
Content: Fearless, intelligent, devoted, determined … Samus Aran in Metroid Prime 4.Photograph: NintendoView image in fullscreenFearless, intelligent, devoted, determined … Samus Aran in Metroid Prime 4.Photograph: NintendoGamesMetroid at 40: happy birthday to Samus Aran, gaming’s greatest badass and my personal heroineBeing a woman who loves video games has often felt lonely, like being on a hostile planet – but Metroid’s female space hunter has been with me all the wayMaddy MyersThu 6 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s 1986, and you’re playing a brand-new game. (You’re in Japan in this scenario, by the way; the game in question, Metroid, won’t come to North America and Europe until later.) Anyway, this new game has you in its grip. You are a lone astronaut exploring a hostile alien planet full of ancient, mysterious structures. This astronaut looks human enough – but this distinctly alien place is full of objects that power up their spacesuit’s capabilities. Each new ability allows you to explore a new area, and as you do, you realise that the entirety of the planetary base you’re exploringis one, massive, interconnected maze.Whoa.Hours later, you finally defeat Mother Brain and set off a timed self-destruct sequence. Upon your escape, you’re treated to an endgame screen: the little astronaut faces you as text on screen implores you to “pray for peace in space”.View image in fullscreenSamus is you … Super Metroid.Illustration: ArcadeImages/AlamyBut then, the astronaut’s suit starts flashing rapidly – pink, green, orange. Suddenly, the suit disappears. What remains is … awoman!And a hot one, at that. Her pixelated hourglass figure has been lovingly rendered; her low-cut red leotard matches the dot of red lipstick that denotes her mouth. She’s looking right at you, the player, and she’s waving, as if to say,Congratulations, big boy! And if you beat the game even faster, I’ll strip down to just a bikini.This reveal lacked the consideration that a woman or girl might be the oneplayingthe game. (The concept of a queer female player was also almost certainly not on any developer’s mind, either.) By 1986, video games were already “for boys”. As reporter Tracey Lien outlined in her extensive feature on how and whenvideo game marketing shifted towards targeting boys, the video game crash of 1983 was followed by a marketing reset for several companies. The Nintendo Entertainment System, on which Metroidmade its debut to non-Japanese audiences, “was targeted toward boys under 10. If you look at the Super NES five years later, it starts targeting boys ages 10-15,” Jesse Divnich, former vice president of insights and analysis for Electronic Entertainment Design and Research, told Lien.The reveal of Samus Aran’s red bikini demonstrated that, in 1986 at least, if a game was going to have a female protagonist, she needed to be presented as a sex object to be enjoyed by the (presumed male, straight) player. That trend continued … for decades, unfortunately. But Samus Aran herself complicated the narrative. Sure, she was wearing increasingly skimpy outfits underneath that battle suit, but she also had spent the entire game up to that point performing extraordinarily badass feats. Well, technically, you – the player! – had performed them, as her. You were her, after all. Metroidtried to make you forget that, right at the end, by having her present herself to you as an object. But prior to that moment; she had been you, and you had been her, with all the personhood that implies.It’s hard not to project personality traits on to the largely blank slate that is Samus. She must be fearless, venturing into space completely alone. She must be intelligent; she’s mapping out this entire mazelike structure as she goes along. She must be devoted, determined, working for herself alone as a bounty hunter – a solitary job. Theinstruction bookletsays that Samus “is the greatest of all the space hunters and has successfully completed numerous missions that everybody thought were absolutely impossible”. This is the hyper-competent hero whose space boots you’re stepping into, and yeah, once again, she’s a woman.View image in fullscreenShe’s just so cool … Samus in Metroid Prime 4: Beyond.Illustration: NintendoIt’s for all of these reasons that I love the original Metroid so much. Its design and concept, iterated and improved upon in its sequels, would go on to inspire countless other games (and one of gaming’s most famousgenre terms). I always enjoy environmental puzzles and exploration in games, but it’s Samus Aran herself that I truly love – the version of Samus I created in my own head, as I played these games and projected myself on to her.Just like Samus Aran, I am 40 years old. My birthday is just one month prior to hers; I appreciate that I did not have to live in this world for very long without her. Because, like Samus, my journey has often been a lonely one. I didn’t start playing Metroid games until I was 21 and had just gone through a bad breakup; we had shared an apartment, and now suddenly, I was living alone. At that time, I was a college student and an unpaid intern at the Boston Phoenix, and I had yet to get any of my article pitches approved. I had been playing video games ever since getting a Game Boy as a young child, but I had mostly played games with male characters in them. After all, that’s what video games were, most of the time. But I always knew there were some exceptions, like Lara Croft in the Tomb Raider series, or Jade in Beyond Good and Evil. And of course, Samus Aran in Metroid.View image in fullscreenShe’s fearless, bold, intelligent … Metroid Dread.Photograph: NintendoIn a post-breakup depressive fugue, I rented and played through a bunch of Metroidgames, totally out of order. Like a baby bird seeking her mother – or more relevantly, like a baby Metroid – I glommed on to Samus Aran with a fervour that has yet to really end. I began to seek out other games with female characters, and spaces online where other female gamers and queer gamers hung out. Through these spaces, I learned what feminism actually was (turns out, it’s not “hating men,” as I had been assuming prior to that point). Starting out as a video games journalist, I clung on to this small community I found.Writing about games as a queer woman in the 2000s and 2010s came with a lot of harassment and blowback. Often I felt very alone – but I would tell myself I was like Samus Aran, on a hostile planet. I kept on going, kept on exploring, kept on building up my abilities. After all, like Samus on Zebes, the hostile place I was exploring was also actually my home. I had a right to be there. Those space pirates – or the bigots sending me death threats, whatever – did not belong. The blank slate of Samus, especially in the earliest Metroidgames, let me infuse as much of myself and my own personality into her journey as I wanted.View image in fullscreenA shared trauma for the Metroidfandom … Metroid Other M.Illustration: NintendoThere have been many Metroid games since, some of which have depicted versions of Samus with a bit more personality. Most notoriously, Metroid: Other M serves up a fearful and traumatised Samus who refuses to question Galactic Federation orders, even when those orders make no sense and put her in danger. This version of the character clashed so heavily with many players’ perceptions of her that it has since become something like a shared trauma for the Metroidfandom. I thought the game was so bad thatthe only solution for Metroidgoing forward would be a full reboot.But that’s not what happened. Instead, fully seven years after Other M, we got Samus Returns, MercurySteam’s 2017 remake of Metroid 2. It was a reminder of the power of the original Metroidgames – Metroid, Metroid 2, and Super Metroid. (These games actually make up a trilogy, albeit with a minimalist narrative.) It was a reminder of the Samus I remembered and loved: fearless, intelligent, devoted, determined. And unlike in Other M, whose camera’s gaze was unafraid to slide slowly over Samus Aran’s clingy zero suit, Samus Returns was not objectifying Samus or distancing her from the player. It was much easier to remember, instead, that Samus is you.You should want to be Samus Aran. You can’t even help it, right? She’s just so fucking cool! And that part at the end of the first few Metroidgames where she performs for you as a sex object is not, really, the important part; it’s dissonant, actually, a fourth-wall breaking moment that doesn’t reflect the core of what Metroidis. The important part is the whole rest of the game, whereyou get to be Samus– who happens to be a woman. And a person, just like you.Explore more on these topicsGamesNintendoAdventure gamesAction gamesLGBTQ+ rightsFeminismfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The American left is making strides. But can they win in November? | Ben Davis | The Guardian
description: The left is increasingly winning within the Democratic party. But it still needs to prove that it can build general-election coalitions capable of beating Republicans
Author: Ben Davis
Headline: The left is increasingly winning within the Democratic party. But it still needs to prove that it can build general-election coalitions capable of beating Republicans
Content: ‘The left has been battle-tested in primaries against moderate candidates ... But a general election in a swing state is a different and less hospitable terrain.Photograph: Rebecca Cook/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The left has been battle-tested in primaries against moderate candidates ... But a general election in a swing state is a different and less hospitable terrain.Photograph: Rebecca Cook/ReutersOpinionUS midterm elections 2026The American left is making strides. But can they win in November?Ben DavisThe left is increasingly winning within the Democratic party. But it still needs to prove that it can build general-election coalitions capable of beating RepublicansThu 6 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.43 EDTShareThe ideological struggle within the Democratic party continued on Tuesday night with primaries in Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, Virginia and Washington. The results showed an increasingly intense conflict within the party, with high Democratic primary turnout and bruising ideological battles up and down the ballot.The Democratic electorate is shifting, becoming more progressive and more willing to challenge party leadership, but not as quickly or uniformly as many assumed.Progressives and socialists scored another round of victories, most notablyAbdul El-Sayedfor Senate, but also downballot with Donavan McKinney and Will Lawrence in congressional races, and in state legislative seats such as Chris Gilmer-Hill in Detroit. But the scale and breadth of those victories fell short of the expectations created by polling and media coverage.Abdul El-Sayed offers a template for Democrats to defeat Trumpism | Peter BeinartRead moreA few key lessons have emerged. First, building a mass left in the United States is a slow and bruising process, and there is no single tipping point at which the party and its voters suddenly become committed leftwing partisans.Second, the left is nonetheless growing rapidly, able to win beyond young, deep-blue urban areas where concerns about general-election viability againstRepublicansare relatively limited, and across an entire statewide Democratic primary electorate in a swing state.This is a major step in the left’s development as an electoral force. Third, the left’s next and most important challenge is winning swing states and competitive seats against Republicans.The left has enjoyed a string of notable electoral victories during the second Trump administration, beginning withZohran Mamdani’s primary win in New York City, and continuing up through the 2026 primaries. The Democratic electorate’s attitudes are changing: party leadership has grown less popular, while democratic socialism has gained support. The left has quickly gone from an extremely marginal force, with just a handful of members of Congress, largely confined to deep-blue urban districts and a small number of favorable constituencies, to a driving force in the party. Much of the media coverage has portrayed the party as being overtaken by an ascendant left. That broader narrative, reinforced by favorable polling, created an expectation that El-Sayed would win resoundingly.In practice, the recent wave means that a meaningful additional share of Democratic primary voters, perhaps 10-15%, is now willing to consistently support left candidates, on top of the existing leftwing base.double quotation markBuilding a mass left in the United States is a slow and bruising process, and there is no single tipping point at which the party and its voters suddenly become committed leftwing partisansIt does not mean that every candidate backed by the DSA or the broader progressive movement will automatically win, or every Democrat backed by Aipac will lose. The actual campaign still matters tremendously; a large share of Democratic voters remain moderate, cross-pressured or primarily candidate-driven.Politics just doesn’t move that fast. The project of building a leftwing base and turning it into a durable majority, even within the Democratic party, is still a long-term one.El-Sayed’s narrow victory has been described as disappointing, because of favorable polling and the expectations created by the recent wave of leftwing victories. It is anything but. The polling miss has distorted how the result is being interpreted.Viewed against Michigan’s demographics, the left’s previous statewide performance, spending disparities, endorsements and comparable results elsewhere in the country, the victory was historically significant.The left has not previously won a genuinely competitive statewide Democratic primary of this kind, nor has a left candidate previously assembled a winning primary coalition extending this far beyond the movement’s urban base, especially in a swing state where voters are likely to weigh general-election viability.The left’s strategy over the past decade has been one of patience, winning seats in friendly areas, knocking doors and slowly building a base. It began by winning city council and state legislative victories and expanded more recently into successful mayoral and congressional races, all in deep blue areas.The Democrats have one last chance to halt the erosion of US democracy – and it’s less than 100 days away | Timothy Garton AshRead moreThis is the first time the left has real proof of concept that beyond urban cores with friendly demographics, it can win over a majority of Democratic voters. It also offers early evidence that a left candidate could compete seriously in a Democratic presidential primary in 2028.The next test is November. The left has been battle-tested in primaries against moderate candidates, party institutions and well-funded outside groups such as Aipac and the crypto lobby. But a general election in a swing state is a different and less hospitable terrain.El-Sayed, along with Francesca Hong if she advances in Wisconsin, needs to demonstrate the left can win not only a winning Democratic primary coalition, but a broad enough general-election coalition to prevail outside deep-blue territory. This matters in the near term, for Democrats to win the Senate and retain governorships; in the medium term, because presidential primary voters in 2028 will want evidence that left candidates can win competitive general elections; and in the long term, because the leftwing political project rests on being able to twin and govern with durable electoral majorities.On Tuesday, the left continued its string of victories, activating young voters and bringing Arab and Muslim voters back into the Democratic fold. But these victories do not resolve the movement’s central challenges.Every primary remains a brutal fight, highly contingent on candidates, organization, spending and local conditions. And the movement must now prepare for the more difficult terrain of November. The left is increasingly winning within the Democratic party, but it still needs to prove that it can build general-election coalitions capable of defeating Republicans.Ben Davis works in political data in Washington DC. He worked on the data team for the Bernie Sanders 2020 campaign and is an active member of the Democratic Socialists of AmericaExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionRepublicansUS politicsTrump administrationUS SenateSocialismcommentShareReuse this content

title: The real meaning of Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan | Robert Reich | The Guardian
description: We’re seeing America wake up to the tyranny that’s engulfed us
Author: Robert Reich
Headline: We’re seeing America wake up to the tyranny that’s engulfed us
Content: ‘The US desperately needs people in Congress who will fight against Trump and his sycophants.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreen‘The US desperately needs people in Congress who will fight against Trump and his sycophants.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APOpinionUS midterm elections 2026The real meaning of Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in MichiganRobert ReichWe’re seeing America wake up to the tyranny that’s engulfed usThu 6 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 10.57 EDTShareWith thevictory of progressive Abdul El-Sayedover representative Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic primary, prepare yourself to hear enormous quantities of bullshit about the Democratic party now being “taken over” by the “left” or by “democratic socialists”.Or as the reliably establishment New York Timesput it: “Can an insurgent candidate, with unabashedly liberal positions, win a general election in a moderate state?”Oh,p-l-e-a-s-e.MichiganDemocratsdidn’t choose El-Sayed because he’s “unabashedly liberal”. Or because he’s a democratic socialist (in fact, he’s not).Abdul El-Sayed’s win proves change is possible for Democrats. His next fight may determine their futureRead moreThey chose him because he’s a fighter – at a time when America needs fighters willing to stand up to the worst tyrant who has ever occupied the Oval Office.Corporate Democrats – such as Haley Stevens, along with Rahm Emanuel, Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries – aren’t up to the task because they won’t bite the corporate hands that feed them campaign money. They won’t criticize the billionaire class. They refuse to talk about how big money has corrupted America.Yet it’s big corporations and the billionaire class that are supporting Trump’s authoritarianism.They’ve sucked up to Trump for corporate welfare, giant tax cuts, tariff exemptions, antitrust acquiescence and war contracts.They’ve given Trump hundreds of millions for his inauguration, his ballroom, his 250th birthday, his Super Pac.Jamie Dimon and his cronies on Wall Street; Elon Musk and his billionaire bros; Brad Carp and his corporate lawyers; Peter Thiel, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg and the Ellisons – all have sold their integrity for huge profits.They’ve created media empires that won’t criticize Trump, financial empires that feed Trump’s crypto, energy empires that feed off Trump’s war, and legal empires that allow Trump to ride roughshod over the rule of law.Which is why the US desperately needs people in Congress who will fight against Trump and his sycophants.The Democratic party isn’t being taken over by “the left” or by democratic socialists. There’s no civil war between progressives and moderates. We aren’t witnessing an ideological battle between the “left” and the “center”.We’re seeing the US wake up to the tyranny that’s engulfed us, and to a crisis of affordability that’s causing most Americans to struggle financially while fueling the biggest stock market rally in history.Trump’s tyranny and America’s affordability crisis are related.Abdul El-Sayed offers a template for Democrats to defeat Trumpism | Peter BeinartRead moreWhen corporate America and Wall Street are unleashed – when the president of the United States has made an implicit deal with the moneyed interests to back him and his authoritarian regime in exchange for tax cuts, deregulation, monopolization and pay-to-play corruption – of course prices soar and wages stagnate.Tyranny is the handmaiden of the moneyed interests.The Democratic party’s mega-donor class may be horrified by the rising tide of progressive populism overtaking more than a few primaries this cycle. After all, it spenttens of million of dollarson Stevens – making the Michigan primary one of the most expensive in US history.Too bad. It’s time that the Democratic party’s mega-donor class recognizes that its real choice is between democracy and tyranny, between an economy that works for all or one that works for a small sliver at the top.If the mega-donor class chooses the latter, it may be acting in its narrow self-interest, but it will also be acting against the future of this nation.Robert Reich, a former US secretary of labor, is a professor of public policy emeritus at the University of California, Berkeley. He is a Guardian US columnist and his newsletter is atrobertreich.substack.com. His new book, Coming Up Short: A Memoir of My America, isout now in the USandin the UKExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026OpinionUS politicsMichiganDemocratscommentShareReuse this content

title: We need a wartime mindset to fight the threat of wildfires | Seth Klein | The Guardian
description: While many leaders compare the wildfire crisis to the second world war, governments fail to adopt the real lessons of pre-emptive wartime action
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: While many leaders compare the wildfire crisis to the second world war, governments fail to adopt the real lessons of pre-emptive wartime action
Content: ‘We need a wartime mindset and political and policy agenda to tackle the climate emergency.’Photograph: Alexandros Beltes/EPAView image in fullscreen‘We need a wartime mindset and political and policy agenda to tackle the climate emergency.’Photograph: Alexandros Beltes/EPAOpinionClimate crisisWe need a wartime mindset to fight the threat of wildfiresSeth KleinWhile many leaders compare the wildfire crisis to the second world war, governments fail to adopt the real lessons of pre-emptive wartime actionThu 6 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.09 EDTShareAs France and Spainbattle historic wildfires, comparisons to the second world war abound. “One of the continent’s biggest evacuation efforts since World War II,”reports the Associated Press. The French president, Emmanuel Macron, has called the wildfires his country’s “most difficult situation since the second world war”.The images crossing all our screens certainly feel war-like – emergency aircraft and black smoke fill the skies, frantic civilians seeking shelter, historic towns lying in ruins, charred forests and burned-out vehicles, exhausted and sweat-soaked emergency responders.Of course, brutal fires such as these are not restricted to France and Spain. They are hitting much of Europe. Australia has wrestled with escalating heat and devastating wildfires for years; during the fires of early 2020, the Australian government wasforced to deploythe most military assets since the second world war. The US has lost entire towns to these climate-induced infernos. Brazil, Greece, Portugal, Chile, Russia, Turkey, Indonesia …all know the terror and lossof the fiery new world in which we reside.Murderous heat, an endangered food supply, decimated landscapes: embrace the Mediterranean life | George MonbiotRead moreAnd in my own country, nearly a thousand wildfires are currently burning acrossCanada.InEurope, many leaders, including Macron and the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, have made a point of linking these fires to the climate emergency; in Canada and the US, decidedly less so. Less common still are leaders and media who connect these events to their primary source – our continued combustion of oil, gas and coal (with the Guardian and a few others being notably exceptions).Yet these extreme events leave no doubt: the climate emergency is upon us. The impacts of burning fossil fuels that climate scientists have warned of for years are now here.The province of British Columbia, where I live, seems to go through this every summer now. A few years ago, I recall arriving at a holiday spot my family has visited for many summers, and coming upon a scene unlike any we had ever experienced. Residents in the area had been put on evacuation alert.All afternoon, a fleet of four water-bomber float planes scooped up water from the lake directly in front of our rental house, flying in low over the homes in formation, collecting water in their pontoons and then doubling back to the fire on the mountain ridge behind us to dump their loads.Right up until sundown, four helicopters likewise circled back to the lake in five-minute rotations, dropping enormous buckets on long cords to collect water, and then racing back to the mountain to release their cargo. This continued all week. The noise was deafening.Our peaceful family time suddenly felt more like a scene from Apocalypse Now, as we huddled together and shouted to communicate. As darkness fell, the hills behind us were dotted with flames, and the sky glowed ominously red.This is what people now nervously call “the new normal”, although it is, in truth, not normal and but a taste of things to come. These extreme weather events we are increasingly experiencing – and the warlike mood they create – represent attacks on our soil. They are a call to mobilize.Sadly, however, the emergency-level responses we have seen to date are purely defensive, rearguard actions. Our governments have not yet seen fit to adopt a wartime-scale response thatpre-emptivelytackles the climate crisis. Beneath the urgency of the present lies a confounding paradox: we mobilize to put fires out, but not yet to prevent them.Sure, every time events like this occur, opinions flow freely about how we need to better prepare for fires, to make our communities and forests more resilient, and to adapt to this new reality. All true.But far too absent from the public debate is a more foundational truth: until we actually mobilize to dramatically expedite the transition off fossil fuels, we will never get ahead of the curve. No amount of fire preparation and planning will save us from an escalation in the horrors we are now experiencing.If the crisis before us is indeed akin to a war – and it is; an existential peril to the people and places we love – then we must genuinely adopt a wartime-scale approach, a new mindset to mobilize all of society, galvanize our politics, fundamentally remake our economy and end our dependence on fossil fuels.The good news: the second world war experience shared by many countries can be embraced as an instructive story, a helpful – and indeed hopeful – reminder that we have done this before. We have mobilized in common cause across society to confront a civilizational threat. And in doing so, we have retooled our entire economy in the space of a few short years.We launched a war on nature. Now we are in a climate warzone | Rebecca SolnitRead moreHow does one know when a government is in actual emergency mode? From my studies of past mobilizations, real emergency action has certain distinct markers. Governments in genuine emergency mode:Tell the truth about the severity of the crisis and communicate a sense of urgency about the measures necessary to combat it.Spend what it takes to win.Create new economic institutions (state enterprises and public programs) to get the job done.Shift from voluntary and incentive-based policies to mandatory measures.Commit to leave no one behind.None of our governments are yet confronting the climate emergency in this manner. That time, however, will come.All emergencies start were a period of denial, or with a “phoney war” phase of half-hearted engagement (sound familiar?). But then, some sort of alchemy occurs. A combination of events (that’s what these extreme weather emergencies are) and leadership comes together to shift the zeitgeist and move us into genuine emergency mode.We need a “wartime” mindset and political and policy agenda to tackle the climate emergency.Seth Klein is a Canadian climate writer and activist, author of the bookA Good War: Mobilizing Canada for the Climate Emergency, and former team lead of theClimate Emergency Unit. His newsletter can be foundhereExplore more on these topicsClimate crisisOpinionEuropeCanadaWildfiresSecond world warcommentShareReuse this content

title: The social media algorithm has left me behind. I’m unc and I’m chopped – and that’s OK | Rebecca Shaw | The Guardian
description: If you have to Google an internet or gen Z/alpha slang term, you absolutely shouldn’t be using it. I’m accepting this milestone with quiet dignity
Author: Rebecca Shaw
Headline: If you have to Google an internet or gen Z/alpha slang term, you absolutely shouldn’t be using it. I’m accepting this milestone with quiet dignity
Content: ‘Instead of one internet, there are endless overlapping internet microcultures, each with their own language evolving independently.’Photograph: NBCView image in fullscreen‘Instead of one internet, there are endless overlapping internet microcultures, each with their own language evolving independently.’Photograph: NBCOpinionYoung peopleThe social media algorithm has left me behind. I’m unc and I’m chopped – and that’s OKRebecca ShawIf you have to Google an internet or gen Z/alpha slang term, you absolutely shouldn’t be using it. I’m accepting this milestone with quiet dignityThu 6 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 21.23 EDTShareI’ve just reached an important adult milestone. Getting married? No. Having a baby? No. Buying a house? Don’t be ridiculous, I’m a writer in Australia. This milestone was small but important: I finally had to Google a gen Z slang term.I know this may be something many of you have passed already, along with your houses and babies, but I am someone who has been online for a long time. It’s been necessary for my career but it’s also my favourite hobby: going on the internet.I never needed to research slang, not because I use the terms or have a specific interest in the youth of today, but because spending a lot of time on the internet meant I absorbed them through osmosis. It’s science! I would see a post start popping off in a far-flung corner of the world and watch as it migrated platforms. I knew the context. I knew who was using it. I knew when it should be used. I knew when it was already embarrassing to use it. I wasn’t speaking the language but I was fluent. Now, I’m joining the ranks of the bamboozled elderly andGoogling “quiet on the creek”.My parents might have been able to keep up with slang back when people my age were doing it but the craziest we got was “roflcopter” and “pwned”. The internet was less fragmented. There was a time when someone terminally online could feel as though they had a rough map of the place and knew where all the cultural hubs were.Today’s internet has no centre.The rise of ‘unc’: is this gen Alpha’s way of saying ‘OK boomer’?Read moreInstead of one internet, there are endless overlapping internet microcultures, each with their own language evolving independently. Reddit, Discord,Twitch, TikTok, streaming culture, gaming culture – they all experience an endless flow of changing language. It’s no longer possible to understand everything, even if you wanted to. Technology and culture are moving so fast, all the time, it makes sense that young people are constantly coming up with new terms.There are pedants and young people haters out there who get het up about the slang and the memes and the 6-7 of it all but, generally, I love it. Some slang terms, the ones that trickle down from streaming or “incel” culture, can be ugly or negative. Many of the more creative or sticky terms originate in POC or queer culture. A lot of what makes it to the mainstream is clever or funny or right. For example, it’s already probably outdated now, but “rizz” for “charisma” is delightful.I appreciate the rapid evolution of language, the inventive wordplay, even if it does get annoying at times. Some of it will stick, some will get left behind. But now I no longer have a front-row seat. The algorithm has left me behind.That’s OK, it has to be that way. As you can see, I am accepting this with quiet dignity. Others should follow my example – if you have to Google a slang term, you absolutely shouldn’t be using it. If you are a politician or police PR person, please avoid using slang to try to appeal to young people. It will never work, it will only ever embarrass you and in some cases it will kill the poor term dead in its tracks.I’m still going to keep finding out what slang means for my own interest, and to ensure I can make some sense of what the kids in my life are trying to communicate. But I know my limits. I’m no longer absorbing the language just by being online; I am studying it. I’m unc and chopped – and that’s OK.Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in SydneyExplore more on these topicsYoung peopleOpinionInternetSocial mediaRedditTikTokTwitchcommentShareReuse this content

title: By day five of my labour, I didn’t want an ‘ideal birth’. I only wanted to survive | Natalie Morris | The Guardian
description: Yvette Cooper’s maternity reforms must change a system that too often fails women when they’re at their most vulnerable, says journalist and author Natalie Morris
Author: Natalie Morris
Headline: Yvette Cooper’s maternity reforms must change a system that too often fails women when they’re at their most vulnerable, says journalist and author Natalie Morris
Content: Illustration: PA/Alamy/Getty/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: PA/Alamy/Getty/Guardian DesignOpinionWomen's healthBy day five of my labour, I didn’t want an ‘ideal birth’. I only wanted to surviveNatalie MorrisYvette Cooper’s maternity reforms must change a system that too often fails women when they’re at their most vulnerableThu 6 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 13.13 EDTShareOn the third day of being in labour with my first child, I entered a new state of being. It was time to dig deep. This is what I had learned in all the childbirth classes. As long as I remained calm, breathed as instructed, moaned through the pain, things would happen as they were meant to. My body knew what it was doing. Only, it didn’t.On the fourth day, I started to beg. This wasn’t right. Despite contraction after relentless contraction, I wasn’t dilating. I hadn’t slept, I couldn’t even sit down. I needed help. And still, they waited. For what, I never understood.When Yvette Coopertold the Guardian this weekthat women must not “feel pressurised” to have “an ideal birth experience”, it was a relief to hear her name this all-too-common phenomenon in which maternity staff are reluctant – or refusing – to escalate. But Cooper’s characterisation of the problem is not the full picture. The harm here is not just in women being nudged towards a certain kind of birth experience, but in a culture that can completely override women’s physical and psychological safety in favour of a low-intervention ideal.Half of Britain’s maternal deaths areconsidered preventable, and low-intervention births are the ideal for a reason. Midwife-led care usually results inbetter outcomes for healthy womenwith straightforward pregnancies – lower risk of infection and severe bleeds, and quicker recovery. In 2024-25, 45% of all hospital deliveries in England (542,235 total births) wereperformed via caesarean section– it was the first time C-sections outnumbered unassisted natural vaginal births. (Another 11% needed extra support through instruments such as forceps.) There is a natural, and warranted, cautiousness about the over-medicalisation of birth, which can lead to avoidable complications, and leave women who would prefer a natural birth feeling pressured to take a different route. But we can’t ignore that there are also structural forces at play here: lower intervention also translates to lower cost for an overstretched, under-resourced system. One midwife told me explicitly that they would have admitted me to the labour ward earlier if there had been a bed.Of course most first-time mothers would choose the lowest possible intervention if they could. I had hoped to float blissfully in a birthing pool under the soft glow of fairy lights. But when it comes to the messy, unpredictable, dangerous act of bringing new life into the world, the concept of choice can quickly be revealed as a fallacy. By day five of my labour, I was not thinking about my birth plan. I was not thinking about very much at all. My only focus was survival.The demographic of people giving birth today looks nothing like it did 30 years ago. The average age of a mother in England and Walesis now 31, a figure that has been creeping up since records began. There is something deeply flawed about a system that pushes quite so strongly for low-intervention births despite the fact that mothers over 30 are more likely to require a higher level of medical involvement. Almost half of UK women aged 30-39 have caesareans, and for those over 40, it is nowthe most common wayto give birth. Yet the narrative of an “ideal birth” persists, leaving women who end up needing more help wondering where they went wrong. Maternity practices must reflect this reality, or risk perpetuating a cycle that leaves women at risk and then pushes the blame back on to them.After the best part of a week, I was eventually wheeled down for an emergency C-section. Even then, it wasn’t the desperate pleas from my husband and me that finally spurred action, it was the fact that my baby started showing signs of distress. The doctors who greeted us displayed clear consternation that I had been left in that state for so long, a factor that probably played a part in my child developing an irregular heartbeat. The ideal birth narrative – that low-intervention, midwife-led care is always best – has hardened into institutional bias, amid a system in which women’s choices about their medical care are too often sidelined.In one of her first acts as health secretary, Cooper said she intends to reintroduce binding national maternity standards. They will include ending the postcode lottery for levels of care, and tackling racial inequalities that have meant worse outcomes for poorer and for black and Asian women. Her promises sound reassuring, but we have heard similar things before. What’s needed is a fundamental cultural shift so that women’s voices are treated as clinical evidence, not background noise.There is a deep-rooted disconnect inNHSmaternity units. Between the needs of patients and the people treating them, and between different parts of the system itself. When midwife-led care and obstetric intervention are positioned in opposition, rather than as complementary approaches, escalation can be perceived as failure instead of necessary care. And in that gap, women at their most vulnerable have their pain minimised and their instincts questioned, sometimes to the point that risk becomes life-threatening.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrauma is a brutal introduction to motherhood, and one that is all too common. For me and thousands of other mothers, our births could have gone so differently if we had only been heard. My ideal birth is not defined by candlelight or calm breathing. It is one where I am listened to, believed and responded to in time. One that both my baby and I survive at any cost.Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern BritainDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsWomen's healthOpinionChildbirthHospitalsYvette CooperNHSPregnancyHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: I knew Rod Liddle and hated what he became. He would have wanted me to say so | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: A man who prized blunt speaking has been selectively eulogised. There’s a balance between decency and honesty: I’m sad he caused such harm, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: A man who prized blunt speaking has been selectively eulogised. There’s a balance between decency and honesty: I’m sad he caused such harm, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: Rod Liddle at the Edinburgh international book festival in 2014.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRod Liddle at the Edinburgh international book festival in 2014.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianOpinionRod LiddleI knew Rod Liddle and hated what he became. He would have wanted me to say soZoe WilliamsA man who prized blunt speaking has been selectively eulogised. There’s a balance between decency and honesty: I’m sad he caused such harmThu 6 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 16.27 EDTShareAs tributes poured in forRod Liddle, the Sunday Times and Sun columnist who has died at the age of 66, they were markedly coy and sanitised. Paradoxically, those were the exact deficiencies obituaries praised Liddle for avoiding – they said he shot from the hip and ruffled feathers, remorselessly attacked the liberal establishment and was ebullient. Michael Gove called him “special and brave”. But brave in the face of what? Attacked the liberal establishment how?This delicacy was particularly noticeable in a segment on Radio 4’s Today programme, of which Liddle was editor in the 90s,between Justin Webb and Amol Rajan. “If there was a golden thread that connected the person you saw back then with the person of a few weeks ago,” Webb said, “it was a distrust of authority.” But Liddle’s targets as a columnist were not the authorities. Often they were Muslims and immigrants, transgender people and chronic illness sufferers, African-Caribbean men from Harlesden. He did not attack the establishment, he attacked the marginalised, constantly.There is sometimes a dilemma in how we process death. Decently, we seek not to speak ill of the dead, and certainly one hopes to never increase the grief of those who loved them. But does that mean we are also duty-bound not to discuss more uncomfortable issues? Here I feel the dilemma.I was friends with Rod Liddle in the 90s. He was a different Rod then. The principal target of his satire was himself. He would lampoon guys having affairs, guys who were a shambles, guys who had run out of road. If there was any ethno-caricaturing, it read as a footnote to a worldview in which nobody was more ridiculous than he, Rod Liddle. This carried on into his collection of short stories, Too Beautiful for You (2003), in which the most memorable escapade was a man getting into a train crash, after seeing his mistress, rushing across a field carrying his severed arm so that he could get to a hospital without blowing his alibi, and realising as he bleeds out that he must actually really love his wife.In 1983, he was a member of the Socialist Workers party and by 1990, a researcher for the Labour party, but what made him seem left-left, rather than centre left, didn’t have a membership card. It was the self-parody coupled with an overall dishevelment that conveyed a deep-seated humanity and pluralism: “I’m a mess, you’re a mess, let’s get out of this mess together.” I know that is maddeningly unspecific, but I also know that anyone on the left will get what I mean.So his transformation into an attack dog for the race-baiting right was painful to watch, if not exactly unprecedented. On Tuesday, sociologist Will Daviescharacterised this post-68 type, “drawn to norm-breaching, moving via adolescent rebellion, punk, revolutionary socialism and eventually ending up at racism, because by the 21st century that was the most efficient transgression still on offer”. The rightwing media will pay absolutely top dollar for a big-name left-to-right defector.Peter York, in his bookA Dead Cat on Your Table, examines the nexus of rightwing thinktanks, the mainstream right and “alt-right” media to argue that what we call “culture wars” aren’t ideological, they’re about hegemonic capture in the service of capital. Depressingly, it does work: GB News, which hedge-funder Paul Marshall hosed money at, to widespread ridicule, now secures higher average audiencesthan Sky News or BBCNews. Arguably, the greater victory is that all we ever talk about is what GB News wants to talk about.View image in fullscreenRod Liddle, when he edited Radio 4’s Today programme.Photograph: Graham Turner/The GuardianOne thing the obituaries did mention was Liddle’s feudwith Yasmin Alibhai-Brown– “they loathed each other,” Justin Webb said, then, later he asked: “Deep down, did he really? There was no loathing in Rod that I could ever divine.” But “feud” is doing some heavy lifting there: Liddle attacked Alibhai-Brown constantly in his columns, for opinions which many of us hold but seemed unaccountably more obnoxious to him coming from her. This culminated in a clashon Channel 4 in 2014, after which the then Conservative MP Michael Fabricant, tweeted that he might have ended up punchingAlibhai-Brown in the throat.Liddle the Today editor, listening to much of the discussion, would have said, “what the fuck are you playing at, trying to describe this outrageous character without naming any of his outrages?” Not least as they are so easy to Google – the time he said he couldn’t have been a teacherbecause he would have ended up shagging the children, “right in there, on day one”; the endless attacks on Muslims, arguing that it was the faith itself, not unhinged individuals, that drove terrorism, that the 2019 election should be held on a day when “Muslims are forbiddento do anything on pain of hell” to suppress their vote. The editor Liddle of the 90s would have also said: “You can’t have two blokes on the radio, explaining why whipping up racist misogyny is fine so long as, underneath, you have a heart of gold.” Not because of diversity and whatnot, but because it’sjust not cricket.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenTelegraph, 3 August 2026One of the last times I saw Liddle was a couple of months ago when we were both on Sky News. He looked really different, because he hadCOPD(chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). I asked him how he was and he said “depressed”, and I asked why, but I was just being tactful, because it was obvious why. My mum died with COPD last year, and by the time your face goes grey, life is pretty horrible, like drowning in air. “I’m no longer priapic,” he replied.I felt ineffably sad; that privately, his persona was still the same, standing there with his arm hanging off, insisting that the first thing he would do, once he got it sewed back on, was get a hard-on; sad at the pantomime of it, cartoon prejudices with real-life consequences, trotted out on command, funded by people with mountains of money who wish society ill; sad about the empathy and solidarity that had once built a collective firewall against hate-for-fun, which had been slowly extinguished.In fact, I wanted to start crying but I’d just had my makeup done, so we went on air and argued about Andy Burnham in Makerfield, and he said he would only win it if he “sorted out” immigration. I won’t miss Rod Liddle, but I miss the person he was when the world was different, and I miss that different world.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The takedown of Jason Arday has overjoyed the right, and must be a wake-up call for the left | Jason Okundaye | The Guardian
description: The Cambridge academic has rightly now resigned. But that won’t end the targeting of senior black figures or the lazy way institutions promote faux equality, says Guardian columnist Jason Okundaye
Author: Jason Okundaye
Headline: The Cambridge academic has rightly now resigned. But that won’t end the targeting of senior black figures or the lazy way institutions promote faux equality, says Guardian columnist Jason Okundaye
Content: Illustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Thomas Pullin/The GuardianOpinionUniversity of CambridgeThe takedown of Jason Arday has overjoyed the right, and must be a wake-up call for the leftJason OkundayeThe Cambridge academic has rightly now resigned. But that won’t end the targeting of senior black figures or the lazy way institutions promote faux equalityThu 6 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 14.01 EDTShare‘To be honest with you, I thought you’d just believe me.” That was the breathtaking response of Prof Jason Arday whenthe Guardianinterrogated the details he provided of an alleged racist campaign of intimidation against him, which involved a severed pig’s head, a masked man wielding a knife and bullets in the post. Arday had been unable to provide evidence, and when the Guardian contacted the relevant parties, including a south London butcher and the police, his claims were either refuted or could not be verified.Arday, whose appointment as professor of sociology of education at Cambridge became a widely lauded moment in the aftermath of Black Lives Matter, has found himself in the eye of the storm. Allegations of extensive plagiarism in his doctoral thesis, completed at Liverpool John Moores University, recently made their way from the Substack of self-described “race realist” academic Nathan Cofnas into the national press. The defence of Arday had rested on the fact that an investigation had already been conducted, and cleared him of plagiarism. And yet the case has taken on a life of its own.In recent weeks, more of Arday’s story has come under scrutiny: from claims of having installed water points in South America and west Africa with the charity WaterAid (WaterAid said it does not send volunteers abroad), to having run 30 marathons in 35 days, the last dozen or so after suffering a hairline fracture in his leg. After mounting pressure, Cambridge announced that it hadlaunched a formal investigationinto his academic qualifications and honorary appointments. Following this announcement, Arday resigned from his positions at the university. Though he has chosen to step aside topreserve his “wellbeing”, this has become a national story that will not go away.Allegations of plagiarism in a doctoral thesis do not usually make for riveting, front-page news. Indeed, in 2023, when the Cambridge history professor William O’Reilly faced allegations of plagiarising student essays, thepress coverageconsisted of barely half a dozen articles (a tribunal ruled the plagiarism was “the product of negligent acts but was not deliberate”). Few people could care less about what academics get up to.But Arday could not expect to be similarly insulated by academia’s remoteness. This story has endured, stubbornly, because it is so perfectly calibrated for some of the most combustible charges of Britain’s culture wars: namely, that academic standards have been surrendered to a woke orthodoxy, and that minorities are unfairly advanced in the name of diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives.View image in fullscreen‘Prof Jason Arday has found himself in the eye of the storm.’Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianThe instinct of progressives had been to defend Arday; indeed, many went on to sign an open letter in support of him, seeing him as simply another black man under a sustained press attack. This was not least because the charges against him originated with Cofnas, who had beendismissed from his postat Emmanuel College, Cambridge, in 2024 after making pseudo-scientific claims that under a true meritocracy black people would “disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment”. And for many in the rightwing press, this is their victory lap, their vindication. The spectacle of it is just too grim to behold. The headlines of “DEI darling” and “diversity poster boy” barely conceal their excitement. Gotcha!I do not care to examine the quality of Arday’s scholarship, research or life story beyond what has already been written elsewhere. What concerns me is how little space remains for a genuinelyprogressive critique of institutional diversity practices– one capable of scrutinising how for many organisations and corporations symbolic representation has been a substitute for deeper reform, leaving it vulnerable to just this kind of backlash. It has also meant that the right has enjoyed a near monopoly on criticism of DEI, leaving it to frame it entirely on its own terms.Let’s take a look back at the coverage of Arday’s appointment at Cambridge in 2023. The headline was that Arday, then 37, was to become the “youngest black professor” ever appointed at Cambridge and that his feat was particularly remarkable considering that he supposedly only learned to speak at 11, and to read and write at 18, having been diagnosed with global development delay and autism spectrum disorder as a child. The media circus around this appointment rivalled Hollywood press junkets, with newspaper, television and radio slots covering him on both sides of the Atlantic, including an NBC News item on his “inspiring story”.I am not privy to the hiring process for a professorial chair at Cambridge. I do not know exactly why and how Arday got the job or who else was in the running. But what happens when an academic’s story is sold through him being the “youngest black ever” (sitting alongside familiar monikers such as “the first black” or “black excellence”) and asterisked by a tale of hardship? You are not encouraged or invited to engage with the substance of their scholarship; instead, you are invited to clap. Instead of his appointment conjuring the question “what new opportunities for research will this lead to?”, it was “doesn’t this make you feel good?”What this means is that Arday was treated not as a scholar but as a mascot, one who was particularly expedient for an institution that had been regularly embarrassed by its historic record on race:too few black students(in my cohort at Cambridge matriculating in 2015there were only 15 black males out of 3,449 students); single-figure black academics (which is still the case);allegations of institutional racism. Independent of the merits or pitfalls of his own scholarship, what success looked like for Arday in this role was limited; what accountability could look like if misconduct occurred was constrained by him being a vehicle for Cambridge to signal its institutional progress.These are not arguments that progressives should shy away from. Instead, they should own them. There is a real risk of this case being used to undermine black academics and others in positions of seniority. For all the talk of preferential treatment for black people in academia, it remains true that there are documented,systemic barriersfor black students, including in theiraccess to funding to advance their studies.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPlaybooks, plagiarism and a pig’s head: new claims surrounding a star Cambridge professorRead moreThe mass investigation into Arday’s PhD may be presented as the pursuit of public and intellectual integrity, and yet the origin of this is grievance politics from those who feel diversity has blocked their own advancement. It comes with that malign charge of being a “DEI hire” or being in your position to “fill a quota”, the accusation that so often stalks black people elevated to senior positions. And so with Arday as an avatar for the black colleague who was promoted over you, the black child who was made head boy over your son, that process turbocharges.In Arday, those on the right feel that they have found what they are looking for; that is why every drop is being wrung out of this story. His resignation will not end that.The next step will be to make this single case bear the weight of the ideological arguments they pile on it.How do you resist that? By embracing and learning from the mistakes that were made here, not avoiding them out of discomfort. That means advocating for diversity without tokenism, the celebration of excellent black scholarship without the need for exceptionalism or academic celebrity. If we let only our opponents tell the story, then it becomes a parable about the hazards of striving for progress and equality, rather than about the institutions that reduced equality to a mere PR exercise.Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the GuardianDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
