title: Throwing Muses frontwoman Kristin Hersh: ‘I was compelled to make music after cracking my skull open’ | Kristin Hersh | The Guardian
description: The alt-rock veteran answers your questions on Buddhist time travel techniques, duetting with Michael Stipe, and her autobiographical new album
Author: Priya Elan
Headline: The alt-rock veteran answers your questions on Buddhist time travel techniques, duetting with Michael Stipe, and her autobiographical new album
Content: ‘No one’s ever left the Throwing Muses’ … Kristin Hersh.Photograph: Peter MellekasView image in fullscreen‘No one’s ever left the Throwing Muses’ … Kristin Hersh.Photograph: Peter MellekasFilm & Music reader interviewKristin HershInterviewThrowing Muses frontwoman Kristin Hersh: ‘I was compelled to make music after cracking my skull open’As told toPriya ElanThe alt-rock veteran answers your questions on Buddhist time travel techniques, duetting with Michael Stipe, and her autobiographical new albumThu 6 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 16.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo you think Throwing Muses would have sounded differentwere it not for your bicycle accident?[Hersh was struck by a car when she was 16, resulting in a concussionthat changed the way she heard sound.]Bhafc99Yes. I think people might have liked us more, but we would have been more forgettable. Our songs were not very marketable. They came from a place of such utter honesty that it was difficult for us to become a band with an image, ambition or direction, which plays well on a human level, but not on a corporate one. Some people hate our music; they can’t deal with it because it’s triggering [emotionally], which I get.I was compelled to make music after cracking my skull open and then my life was very upsetting. But at the same time, I had real listeners. If you happen to come across a song that resonates with you, then it’s yours – you can ignore the musician who played it, because they were just the messenger.Your guitar sound and playing is so distinctive, creative and superb – do you have an influence orherowho has inspired or guided you?GoonergeofNobody. We started the Muses when I was 11, so I didn’t have time to invent a sonic vocabulary. I wish my music could be that palatable. I think there’s a place where music can touch people and not be off-putting, but I couldn’t engage in that way.View image in fullscreenOn stage at Krankenhaus festival, Cumbria, 2025.Photograph: Paul HudsonBut I babysat for this music critic and, every time I put his kids to bed, I was allowed to sit in his office and listen to records that hadn’t been released. One was the Violent Femmes’ first album [in 1983]. I remember the music critic told me that the boy in the band was “the male me” and I admit when I heard it I was like: “He’s right!” They had this simple, percussive and raw sound that was very effective. [Singer] Gordon Gano sat in his adolescent-boy self and was just being very honest. That first record is a reminder that we’re all attracted to that sweet spot where we seem to be in enthusiastic agony. And it turns out to be a party!What was the inspiration behind the song Counting Backwards?_Tiana_Time-tripping! I was raised Buddhist by hippy parents and I never thought I was made for letting go of the past, which any therapist will tell you is really unhealthy! But I felt very strongly that I could alter the present by altering the past in a dream state. And that it has to be done with kindness.I am curiouswhyLeslie Langstonleft Throwing Muses betweenHunkpapa[1989] andThe Real Ramona[1991]. What happened?Androo1984She has a health issue with her skin where she couldn’t play bass for decades. She didn’t play on The Real Ramona, but then she came back for our next record, Red Heaven. Leslie ended up moving to the west coast and didn’t want to tour, so Bernard [Georges] came in. Leslie’s just now starting to play bass again and she almost played on the last record. She’s a social worker and my hero; we spend a lot of time thanking each other for being on Earth. I lean on her – she’s one of my favourite people.View image in fullscreenThrowing Muses –(from left)David Narcizo, Hersh, Tanya Donnelly and Leslie Langston – in Chicago, 1989.Photograph: Paul Natkin/WireImageAny chance of you working with [her step-sister and Throwing Muses co-founder] Tanya Donelly again?ChrisOwensYes – she was on tour with us a couple of years ago. She sang on the second self-titled Muses record [2003]. And my son Ryder just stayed at her house when he flew into Boston. All doors are open: anybody who is in the musical moment with me is allowed in, but it’s a big ask. No one’s ever left the Throwing Muses, it’s more like: “You feel like playing? OK, let’s do it!”I supported you in Dublin in 2001 and you said I reminded you of Frank Black. Have you seen Frank lately?PaulOReillyThe first time I heard the Pixies was when we were in soundcheck. A painter friend was at the bar and he said: “You should listen to this band,” which I would never normally do. I thought Charles [Thompson, AKA Frank Black] was a woman at first. I thought she was so cool – she had a shaved head and was singing about her dick. I was like: “She rocks!”But I forgave him for not being a girl and then I said: “I’m never letting go of you. You’re playing all of our shows with us, and here’s my manager, and here’s my label, and you’re coming on tour, and we’re gonna make all of this happen.” I did it for selfish reasons, because I wanted to hear them the whole time and I didn’t want to be alone any more. That relationship lasted for years. Charles once drew a pie chart on the wall of a dressing room and said: “This is a Throwing Muses song.” It was a moment where I forgave myself for carrying my musical treasure into the hurricane of the music biz.Watch the video for Dark Eyed Junco.Your Ghost [from herdebut solo album, featuringREM’s Michael Stipe] is one of the most gorgeous songs I have ever heard – twounique voices coming together on such a haunting duet. Was it written with Michael Stipe in mind and are you still in contact?Frou1967I wasn’t ever going to have a solo career; I wasn’t interested. But I had to get off Warner Brothers and breaking up the band wasn’t going to work. [In order to fulfil the recording contract, she was required to make another album.] I had this tape of leftover acoustic songs and Michael Stipe picked it up. He called me up and said: “I love this tape.” He knew I was going to fuck up the recording of it because I didn’t care. He called the studio as I was having trouble recording Your Ghost and I realised I needed his voice on it.Not too long ago, I was in New York playing a solo show and he was in the audience and I didn’t know. When I was playing Your Ghost, apparently he was in the back singing his parts and freaking out all the people around him. But I didn’t know!You’vebeen prolific over the past decade. Is it safe to assume your EMDRnightmare is over? [Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing is a psychotherapy techniquethat Hersh used to treatpost-traumatic stress disorder and a dissociative disorder.]JosephKyleMy life has been so very difficult; my whole system was just confused. I reacted to the real [PTSD] triggers by passing out, vomiting and screaming. My band members knew to protect me from my triggers, but that’s hard in life. Thanks to EMDR, I can still play music, which I didn’t think I would be able to. I wouldn’t recommend it for everyone. EMDR is like psychological chemo. I would collapse every time I did it. And then you can’t stop it – it’s like a snowballing process, where all the pain you dissociated from comes back to you at once.Phoebe Bridgers: Lost Weekend review – long-awaited return is a thrilling, daring study in dislocationRead moreYour upcoming album, Sugar on Blackstone, has such an evocative title. Where did it come from?VerulamiumParkRangerMaking this album, I was back in my home town of Providence, Rhode Island, living in a street called Hope. It’s off a street called Blackstone, which has this intense path on it that’s like this ship of lost souls. So I had “Hope” on the one side and the ship of lost souls on the other. These songs are autobiographical. They are very old stories from childhood, some of them dating back to the 1970s. There is one [Dark Eyed Junco] about me and my little brother, how we were scared to go home because our stepfather was there. So we just played basketball until we couldn’t any more. The song is about how the feel of the basketball is more important than getting it in the hoop. I don’t even want to aim for the hoop.Sugar on Blackstone is released on 18 September via FireExplore more on these topicsKristin HershFilm & Music reader interviewIndiePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Carlos Acosta: Myths and Modern Masters review – superstar returns with style, the Stones and his daughter | Dance | The Guardian
description: Mixing contemporary, Cuban and classical works, Acosta has charisma to burn and is accompanied by an impressive cohort
Author: Sanjoy Roy
Headline: Mixing contemporary, Cuban and classical works, Acosta has charisma to burn and is accompanied by an impressive cohort
Content: Great presence and depth … Carlos Acosta in Nosotros, from Myths and Modern Masters.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGreat presence and depth … Carlos Acosta in Nosotros, from Myths and Modern Masters.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianDanceReviewCarlos Acosta: Myths and Modern Masters review – superstar returns with style, the Stones and his daughterRoyal Opera House, LondonMixing contemporary, Cuban and classical works, Acosta has charisma to burn and is accompanied by an impressive cohortSanjoy RoyThu 6 Aug 2026 07.15 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 15.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a bit of a stretch to call this undoubtedly enjoyable programme Myths and Modern Masters but granted, it sounds better than Miscellany. Carlos Acosta – superstar dancer, now director ofBirmingham Royal Balletand Cuban company Acosta Danza – has picked and mixed dancers from both companies to offer a very eclectic spread of dance, and added himself into the mix.At 53, Acosta may not have the physical prowess of his youth, but he brings great presence and depth – and some great dancing, too. That serves very well in José Limón’s landmark 1949 work The Moor’s Pavane, a distillation of Shakespeare’s Othello which boils down the story to four characters – Othello (Acosta), Desdemona (Beatrice Parma), Iago (Max Maslen) and Emilia (Miki Mizutani) – and contains their drama of deception, jealousy and revenge within a stately composition of measured steps and stylised gestures, set to courtly music by Purcell.View image in fullscreenPatterns of give and take … Carlos Acosta and Amisaday Naara in Nosotros at the Royal Opera House.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianNosotros, an intimate duet by Cuban choreographers Beatriz García and Raúl Reinoso, also benefits from Acosta’s gravitas and experience. Backed by plangent piano and cello, Acosta and Amisaday Naara enact the complex yet everyday dynamics of a longstanding couple: patterns of give and take, small gestures of tenderness or neglect, physical enactments of impeding, supporting, mirroring, clasping or evading.In his ownNutracker in Havana Suite, Acosta casts himself as a fatherly magician to young Clara (Aila Acosta Holland – yes, his own daughter), conjuring up exotic scenes of delight familiar from Act 2 of the traditional Nutcracker. It’s nicely danced and choreographed, has zero qualms about any orientalist overtones, adds in a slightly weird party scene and ends with the classic pas de deux as if to say: there’s your pinnacle.View image in fullscreenA virtuosity only youth can provide … Katherine Ochoa and Yasiel Hodelín Bello in Diana and Actaeon.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianThe programme proceeds to top that with a show-stopping performance of Agrippina Vaganova’s 1935 Diana and Actaeon pas de deux, Katherine Ochoa and Yasiel Hodelín Bello almost superhuman in their whirls, bounds and balances; you surrender to a virtuosity only youth could achieve. Acosta is well out of this one.The evening closes withChristopher Bruce’s perennially popular Rooster, an effervescent crowd pleaser set to songs by the Rolling Stones. It’s the one piece that doesn’t quite play to Acosta’s strengths, though he dances impressively and gives great attitude, because the choreography itself is fired by the freshness of youth, yet to be weathered by experience. Acosta has moved beyond that.AtRoyal Opera House, London, until 9 AugustExplore more on these topicsDanceCarlos AcostaRoyal BalletBirmingham Royal BalletRoyal Opera HouseBalletThe Rolling StonesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hunt for the Wilderpeople review – Sam Neill is warm and wise in Taika Waititi’s goofily tremendous film | Movies | The Guardian
description: Waititi’s eccentric drama sends the late actor into the New Zealand wilderness with his young charge, angry authorities in hot pursuit
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Waititi’s eccentric drama sends the late actor into the New Zealand wilderness with his young charge, angry authorities in hot pursuit
Content: Distinctive irony … Sam Neill in Hunt for the Wilderpeople.Photograph: Kane Skennar/Piki Films/AllstarView image in fullscreenDistinctive irony … Sam Neill in Hunt for the Wilderpeople.Photograph: Kane Skennar/Piki Films/AllstarMoviesReviewHunt for the Wilderpeople review – Sam Neill is warm and wise in Taika Waititi’s goofily tremendous filmWaititi’s eccentric drama sends the late actor into the New Zealand wilderness with his young charge, angry authorities in hot pursuitPeter BradshawThu 6 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe recent sad loss of Sam Neill is a great opportunity to revisit one of his greatest roles, in this tremendous family film from 2016, a goofy mix of Butch and Sundance and Chaplin’s The Kid. It’s arguably the masterpiece of its writer-directorTaika Waititi, who adapted the 1986 bestseller Wild Pork and Watercress by New Zealand author Barry Crump, bringing his distinctive irony, comedy and quirk (Waititi has a droll cameo as a wacky vicar), but wisely lets the story and performances do the real work, so the movie continues to win the hearts of audiences.Neill plays Hector, a grouchy old buzzard who works on a farm on New Zealand’s North Island just below the vast forested wilderness of the breathtakingly beautifulTe Urewera. The property is owned by his big-hearted wife Bella (Rima Te Wiata) who works as a foster parent, regularly taking in troubled kids, and Hector is under no illusions that she married him in the same charitable spirit. But glum, taciturn Hector is not best pleased when Bella takes in the toughest and most recalcitrant teen the state authorities have ever dealt with. This is Ricky, played by Maori actor Julian Dennison, and Rachel House gives an amusing performance as Paula, the child welfare worker who is on Ricky’s case.Bella has a tactless habit of referring cheerfully to Ricky’s size, but the boy can certainly sense her kindly and wise nature and it actually seems as if this unlikely new foster family is going to live together happily. But then an awful fate intervenes and Hector and Ricky go on the run together in the jungle, being tracked by the pitiless forces of the state who want to put the boy into “juvie”. Bad-tempered, self-reliant Hector, for all his impatience, is darned if he’s going to let these bullies push the boy – or him – around. A nationwide manhunt gets under way for this odd couple, who are now living on pure instinct, moving across tough terrain like a human version of wildebeest, and the general public, hearing about them on breathless TV news reports, begin to feel that they are the underdog heroes.The sentimental possibilities of the drama are amusingly undercut by Waititi, particularly with a series of gags which make it look as if Hector is going to seem like a child molester; there’s some funny stuff too for the hatchet-faced Paula who quarrels with Ricky when she comes face to face with him in the undergrowth. She compares herself to the Terminator, and Ricky crossly claims that he is the one who is like the Terminator, at which point Paula petulantly snaps that Ricky is more like “Sarah Connor ... from the first movie, before she could do chin-ups.” Neill gives a lovely, gentle and wise performance.Hunt for the Wilderpeople is in UK and Irish cinemas from 7 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsSam NeillTaika WaititiNew ZealandComedyAsia PacificreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ravyn Lenae: Blue Island review – from Suicide to Squarepusher, grunge to Janet, a pop one-off plots her unique path | Music | The Guardian
description: Evoking everyone from Janet Jackson to Squarepusher, the US singer follows up her huge hit Love Me Not with stylistic diversity – and lyrics that defy her doubters
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Evoking everyone from Janet Jackson to Squarepusher, the US singer follows up her huge hit Love Me Not with stylistic diversity – and lyrics that defy her doubters
Content: Buffed to a state of pop perfection … Ravyn Lenae.View image in fullscreenBuffed to a state of pop perfection … Ravyn Lenae.Alexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewRavyn Lenae: Blue Island review – from Suicide to Squarepusher, grunge to Janet, a pop one-off plots her unique path(Atlantic)Evoking an astonishing range of artists, the US singer follows up her huge hit Love Me Not with stylistic diversity – and lyrics that defy her doubtersAlexis PetridisThu 6 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt sometimes seems like no musical success in the 2020s is allowed to pass without some degree of online controversy. There are accusations that the artist in question is an “industry plant” – a phrase which, as far as can be discerned, can basically be applied to anyone with a manager or a label deal – or that there’s something deceptive about the way in which they’ve been promoted, or that they’re possessed of some other form of moral bankruptcy that reflects not merely on the performer but the people who like them. Which brings us to Love Me Not, an ostensibly harmless 2024 track by Chicago singer-songwriter Ravyn Lenae.View image in fullscreenRavyn Lenae: Blue Island.Photograph: EMI/Atlantic/APAfter enjoying a burst of online virality, it became a huge hit single, making the Top 5 on both sides of the Atlantic. Taken from Bird’s Eye, an album that also featured collaborations with Childish Gambino and Ty Dolla $ign, its blend of retro-soul styling, distorted guitar arpeggios and infernally catchy chorus was noticeably poppier than Lenae’s previous work: it came with a remix that featured British bedroom-pop star Rex Orange County. You could understand why fans of the glitchy, abstract R&B found on 2015’s EP Moon Shoes, or of her more neo soul-flavoured debut album, 2022’s Hypnos, might consider it a straightforward bid for mainstream acceptance. But you’d argue against it necessitating an online interrogation that, Lenae has suggested, involved not just “picking apart what kind of music I make” but “questioning my identity and Blackness”.Said interrogation seems to have prompted a degree of doubling-down. The first thing you hear on Blue Island, as opener Handle gets under way, is another earworm pop chorus, followed by a squeal of feedback and a distorted electric guitar arpeggio that feels faintly grungy or, more specifically, that recalls the early 90s moment where grunge began having an effect on the sound of mainstream artists. It’s followed by Familiar Dreams, retro pop-soul that sounds almost exactly like what you’d expect of a well-turned follow-up to Love Me Not. Meanwhile, Lenae’s list of inspirations for the album features not just Santigold and Janet Jackson but Blondie, the Cranberries, the Sundays and, most surprisingly, Martin Rev. If Wish You Well definitely sounds like a charming gene-splice between the Cranberries and the soft-hued Janet Jackson of Runaway or That’s The Way Love Goes, it’s a little harder to discern the musical influence of Rev’s confrontational electronic punk duo Suicide on Blue Island. But perhaps it’s present in more of a spiritual capacity, Suicide having relentlessly pursued their own artistic path in the face of some fairly concerted efforts by the public to get them to stop.Ravyn Lenae: Handle – videoThere are certainly a lot of lyrics here that present as love songs but seem suspiciously like they’re about something else: “I’m leaving without you”; “breaking those walls … can never be wrong if you don’t go where everybody goes”; “all those limits to your pleasure keep me climbing”. And there’s palpable glee in the album’s sudden stylistic shifts. The 90s R&B-infused Never Let Me Go and Babygirl rub up against In & Out’s sparkly alt-rock; Potential proceeds along prettily enough in pop-ballad form before it unexpectedly erupts into a squall of guitar noise and a ferocious, juddering rhythm that sounds remarkably like Squarepusher or Aphex Twin. You could suggest its shifts carry a hint of the streaming playlist so eclectic it only really makes sense to the person who made it, but better that than an artist audibly chasing currently popular trends. And Blue Island isn’t as jarring as that suggests, partly because of the unifying power of Lenae’s voice – a lovely, breathy soprano – but largely because the writing is buffed to a state of pop perfection.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I was so self-assured in my early 20s. Then my frontal lobe hit’: Rachel Chinouriri, every pop star’s favourite UK pop starRead moreIts hit rate isn’t perfect. There are a couple of moments among the 14 tracks that feel a bit boilerplate: an acoustic duet with Dominic Fike, Reputation, is pleasant enough but could be the work of pretty much anyone; the electro-influenced beat of Saturday Night is great, the song itself not so much. And it could maybe have done with a couple more moments like Potential, when Lenae metaphorically lets her freak flag fly – not least because when she does, it’s hugely exciting, as on the chaotic, distorted closer Let Us In. It’s another song that seems to obliquely address the controversy caused by Love Me Not – you could read its lyrics as a plea for acceptance for artists that decline to fit a standard mould – but, in truth, Blue Island has already answered Ravyn Lenae’s critics long before it appears: its collage of styles makes for an original, idiosyncratic pop album, something worth celebrating rather than picking apart for ulterior motives.This week Alexis listened toThe Durutti Column – Your Shadow at MorningBeneath its TS Eliot-inspired title lurks a sun-dappled but melancholy drift of electric and acoustic guitar: Vini Reilly doing what Vini Reilly does exceptionally beautifully.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekR&BPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They slammed their M16s against his skull’: inside the film about Amy Goodman’s fearless reporting | Movies | The Guardian
description: As Steal This Story, Please! charts her astonishing reports on everything from climate summits to earthquakes to massacres, Goodman talks about dissent, censorship – and her ‘magic moments’
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: As Steal This Story, Please! charts her astonishing reports on everything from climate summits to earthquakes to massacres, Goodman talks about dissent, censorship – and her ‘magic moments’
Content: ‘It’s making sure people can be heard’ … Goodman reporting in Haiti after the 2010 earthquake.View image in fullscreen‘It’s making sure people can be heard’ … Goodman reporting in Haiti after the 2010 earthquake.MoviesInterview‘They slammed their M16s against his skull’: inside the film about Amy Goodman’s fearless reportingDan SabbaghAs Steal This Story, Please! charts her astonishing reports on everything from climate summits to earthquakes to massacres, Goodman talks about dissent, censorship – and her ‘magic moments’Thu 6 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 08.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Iconsider an exclusive a failure,” Amy Goodman says. It is not a typical observation for a journalist to make, but it is the approach at the heart of a documentary about her career, Steal This Story, Please! If an article, item, narrative or interview is significant enough “it should be shared around the world,” she insists.This time, however, her goal is not to share a particular news story, but rather an entire professional philosophy. To do so, Goodman had to let “two Oscar-nominated stalkers into my life” in an effort to “spread the word about this critical form of independent journalism” that she has practised over four decades.double quotation markWhen the US invaded Iraq, news anchors would go inside military jets and show what it was like to hit their buttonsIn an era of the behemothisation of American news, endless mergers and mega-mergers, Goodman, 69, has successfully operated off-road, working first in community radio, then creating New York basedDemocracy Now!, an hour-long daily news broadcast aired online and on public stations in the US, Canada and around the world.A core idea, she explains ahead of a series of screenings and appearances in the UK, is that “when we cover war, we’re not brought to you by the weapons manufacturers; or when we cover the climate catastrophe, we’re not brought to you by the oil, gas or coal companies”. Paid for by viewer donations, Democracy Now! does not accept advertising, sponsorship or government grants.View image in fullscreen‘Being at the target end is our job as journalists’ … Goodman being arrested while covering the Republican National Convention in 2008.Photograph: Courtesy Rick Rowley/Democracy Now!The documentary wastes no time in underscoring Goodman’s tenacity. Directed and produced by Tia Lessin and Carl Deal, it begins by following Goodman as she follows P Wells Griffith III, then Donald Trump’s climate adviser, at the Cop climate summit in Katowice, Poland. Griffith, who had no meaningful prior experience in the energy industry, went to the 2018 summit to praisethe virtue of mining coal.“Can you tell us what you think about President Trump saying climate change is a Chinese hoax?” Goodman begins, microphone ahead, camera behind, the pursuit beginning. Griffith, it turns out, does not want to talk. Instead he complains lamely of harassment, and climbs several floors just so he can hide from Goodman in the US delegation suite.Outside, the door having been closed in her face, the failure to engage telling the story, a breathless Goodman tries to summarise. Except that, too, is a little much. Goodman pauses, smiles, turns her head to one side and says: “Actually, I have to take my breath.” It is an ideal counterpoint, the gentlest reminder that chasing any story requires effort; to the top of conference centres and beyond.Democracy Now! has just celebrated 30 years with an event at the liberal Riverside Church, in Morningside Heights, New York, where political activist Angela Davis talked about “the importance of dissent” while Michael Stipe, Patti Smith, and Bruce Springsteen all sang. But the church was also where, Goodman emphasised, Martin Luther King spoke out against the Vietnam war, in April 1967.“He said that the US is the greatest purveyor of violence on earth, and he was excoriated for the speech by the corporate media. I think it was Life magazine that said he had done a disservice to his cause, his country and his people, but he just doubled down and he said, ‘You have to connect these three pillars: militarism, materialism and racism’,” Goodman says.The documentary, part fly-on-the-wall, part interview, part archive, takes viewers through the full arc of Goodman’s career from the 1980s with contributions from key collaborators, including Democracy Now!’s co-host Juan González. It is a remarkably consistent body of work, underpinned by the idea that events can only be properly understood if you “talk to people at the target end” – whose voices are easily forgotten or discarded by the vast US news networks.“I remember when the US invaded Iraq [in 2003], the mass protests that rocked the planet, millions of people saying no,” Goodman says. “But I remember the network reporters and the hosts, the anchors, would go into a military jet and show people what it was like to be hitting the buttons. Or they would go into a tank and show what it was like to be steering it. Our job is to be at the target end: how does it feel when that button is hit? That’s our job as journalists.”The approach was not without risk. Thirty-five years ago, Goodman travelled to East Timor in southeast Asia, then in the midst ofa brutal occupation by Indonesiathat had seen more than 100,000 people already killed. Despite the level of human suffering, it was not a well-covered story then, but Goodman and another American journalist, Allan Nairn, had arrived, hoping to follow a visit from a UN delegation.It was 12 November 1991. Goodman and Nairn had gone to witness a commemoration mass for Sebastiao Rangel, killed a fortnight earlier by the Indonesian military. Several hundred swarmed into a church in the capital, Dili, then walked to a nearby cemetery, hemmed in by high walls. It had become a public act of defiance by the Timorese, but Goodman thought that while the Indonesian military had committed massacres before, they would not dare do so in front of western journalists.“I held my microphone up like a flag, Allan put the camera above his head. I slung my tape-recorder, which I’d always hidden, over my shoulder and we walked to the front of the crowd,” Goodman recalls. Shortly after, Indonesian soldiers marched up “10 to 12 abreast” armed with US M16 assault rifles and fired on the crowd “without warning, without hesitation, without provocation”.View image in fullscreen‘I can picture all of it. I can feel all of it’ … Goodman and Allan Nairn in 1991, following a massacre of unarmed Timorese civilians by the Indonesian army, East Timor.Photograph: Courtesy of Democracy Now!She cannot forget what happened next. “The first to go down was this little boy behind us who had his hands up in the V sign. ‘Viva East Timor,’ they shouted. ‘Viva independence! Viva Sebastiao!’” Goodman and Nairn were not shot but they were attacked and beaten with boots and rifle butts. Nairn threw himself on top of Goodman to protect her, and the soldiers “took their US M16s like baseball bats and slammed them against his skull until they fractured it” before finally relenting.It was a defining moment, perhaps the ultimate justification for reporters bearing witness. Indonesian soldiers killed 271 protesters that day at the Santa Cruz cemetery. Goodman and Nairn survived because they were from the US, managing to get a flight out of the country. Though their equipment was seized, they were able to recount what happened in interviews and in a press conference in the following days, and their story was stolen by the world’s media.“I mean, even just telling you right now, I can picture all of it. I can feel all of it,” she says. After the massacre, she and Nairn and dozens of Timorese piled into a Red Cross van and “drove like that as a human mass” to a hospital. There “the doctors and nurses started to cry when they saw us,” not because they were more badly hurt than the Timorese, but because, Goodman thinks, of what they represented, as westerners – both “the sword and the shield” – suppliers of arms to the Indonesians and people able to spread the truth.The story of the Dili massacre is at the heart of the documentary and Goodman’s career. Film footage of the massacre, shot secretly by another journalist, Max Stahl, emerged subsequently, and gradually the Indonesian occupation became untenable. A referendum was held in 1999, and 78.5% of people voted for independence. Three years later, Timor-Leste became a country in its own right, and it was the first time that Goodman was able to return.So was this, the day that Goodman witnessed a massacre, the most consequential story she ever worked on? The reporter demurs. She says that what is important is “covering movements” because “you never know when the magic moment comes” when a seemingly intractable problem, like the occupation of East Timor, is resolved or disappears.It is a plea, she says, to keep reporting and to keep listening, regardless of the outcome: “I just think whether we’re covering an issue outside our country or in our country, it’s the respect for what people do every day and making sure that they can be heard, that they can describe their own stories. That is what gives dignity, whether they win or lose.”Steal This Story, Please! is screening at Curzon Bloomsbury London, from 12 August, including a Q&A with Goodman on 12 August. Goodman also appears on the Edinburgh international festival’sGlobal Ideas Stageon 11 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsDocumentaryWar reportingFactual TVinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Blue Note to bring world-famous jazz club to London | London | The Guardian
description: Grammy-winning pianist Robert Glasper will headline opening of club’s first UK venue in Covent Garden next month
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Grammy-winning pianist Robert Glasper will headline opening of club’s first UK venue in Covent Garden next month
Content: Blue Note jazz club in New York City.Photograph: Johnny Nunez/WireImageView image in fullscreenBlue Note jazz club in New York City.Photograph: Johnny Nunez/WireImageLondonBlue Note to bring world-famous jazz club to LondonGrammy-winning pianist Robert Glasper will headline opening of club’s first UK venue in Covent Garden next monthCaroline DaviesThu 6 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world-famousNew Yorkjazz club Blue Note will open its first UK venue in London next month.Located in the basement of St Martins Lane hotel, Covent Garden, the club promises the best of British jazz alongside world-class international artists, with a programme featuring emerging and established talent.Founded in Greenwich Village, New York City, in 1981, Blue Note has since expanded across the US and into Japan, China, Brazil and Italy. TheLondonvenue will be its first in the UK.Robert Glasper, the Grammy-winning US pianist, producer and songwriter, will headline the grand opening on 23 September, marking the the centenary of the influential US saxophonist, bandleader and composerJohn Coltrane.“London has been a big supporter in my career from the very beginning and I’ve always had so much respect for the musical culture of the UK past and present,” Glasper said.View image in fullscreenThe musician Robert Glasper says Blue Note in London will offer a space for jazz, hip-hop and R&B to evolve and thrive.Photograph: Jim Dyson/Getty Images“There is adeep love for music that pushes boundariesand Blue Note has always been a home for that same spirit. Starting this new club is about creating a space where jazz, R&B, hip-hop and everything in between can meet, evolve and surprise people.“I’m excited to build something in London that feels intimate, fearless and alive – a place where artists can take chances and audiences can experience the music up close.”Thevenue will feature two performance spaces. Its 250-capacity main room will stage two shows each night and remain open until 1am from Monday to Saturday, and until midnight on Sundays. Tickets for the first run of shows will go on general sale on 14 August.A second, 100-capacity room, B-Side, supporting emerging British talent, is due to open later this year.View image in fullscreenLondon performances and residencies will include Erykah Badu.Photograph: Michael Blackshire/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesTsion Bensusan, the co-owner of Blue Note Entertainment Group, described the opening as a “significant milestone”, adding: “London has always been one of the world’s great music capitals, with an extraordinary jazz heritage and an incredibly diverse creative community,.“Our hope is that Blue Note London becomes more than a venue – it becomes a home for musicians, a gathering place for the community and an integral part of London’s cultural landscape.”Performances and residencies will include the neo-soul singerErykah Badu, jazz-pop pianist and songwriterJamie Cullum, award-winning saxophonist and composerNubya Garcia, drummerYussef Dayes, afrobeat collectiveKokorokoand rapperHak Baker.The club will also host occasional surprise performances by leading artists, giving audiences the chance to experience internationally renowned musicians in an intimate setting – a hallmark of Blue Note venues worldwide.Explore more on these topicsLondonJazzNew YorkHospitality industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: The Shards review – murder, 80s mayhem and the Ryan Murphy comeback we’ve been waiting for | Television | The Guardian
description: Murphy is back on form with this gorgeously curated, shot and scored adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’s novel – about a serial killer stalking privileged LA teenagers
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Murphy is back on form with this gorgeously curated, shot and scored adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’s novel – about a serial killer stalking privileged LA teenagers
Content: Beautifully curated … (from left) Igby Rigney, Hayes Warner and Kaia Gerber in The Shards.Photograph: FXView image in fullscreenBeautifully curated … (from left) Igby Rigney, Hayes Warner and Kaia Gerber in The Shards.Photograph: FXTV reviewTelevisionReviewThe Shards review – murder, 80s mayhem and the Ryan Murphy comeback we’ve been waiting forMurphy is back on form with this gorgeously curated, shot and scored adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’s novel – about a serial killer stalking privileged LA teenagersLucy ManganThu 6 Aug 2026 05.34 EDTFirst published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world can finally begin to hope again. It looks as though Ryan Murphy has pulled out of his dive and is beginning to find his glorious groove again. The uber-showrunner reached a nadir last year with All’s Fair, a legal drama that was so bad it was existentially awful, garnering a number of rare, zero-star reviews (including mine) and which has duly been commissioned for a second series.But after All’s Fair cameThe Beauty. Which was chaotic and underdeveloped but fun. And then there wasLove Story, about the short lives and love of JFK Jr and Carolyn Bessette, which was pitch-perfect, properly good trash. And now there is The Shards, Murphy’s adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’s 80s-set metafictional/autobiographical novel of the same name. I have not read the book. An enfant terrible’s reminiscences are too often simply terrible and I was exhausted by the very idea. But a TV version? Run through the Murphytron? That sounds like a very good idea – and so it has proved. Theirs is a marriage made in pop-culture heaven.We open in the 1980s with a laconic voiceover from our main man, Bret (Igby Rigney, still a little rough in places, but he nevertheless does great work here, allowing just enough glimpses of the roiling emotion beneath the shiny, protective carapace to keep Ellis’s avatar recognisably human). He is sketching out the immediate future for him and his select, gilded group of high school friends. “A season of horror and murder that would destroy us all.” Think Gatsby with quaaludes, settle back and enjoy.Metafiction demands meta-commentary, so Murphy has stuffed the cast with the offspring of 80s icons – most notably Kaia Gerber (the absolute image of her supermodel mother, Cindy Crawford) and Homer Gere (son of Richard and Carey Lowell), both of whom acquit themselves very well. Gerber is straight-A student and class president Susan, the childhood friend with whom Bret is in love, despite his girlfriend Debbie (Hayes Warner) and his assorted secret boyfriends and Susan’s own long-term boyfriend, Thom (Graham Campbell). Gere is Robert, the beautiful, troubled new boy who looks set to shatter their charmed circle. “He was a virus,” Bret’s voiceover tells us, as Robert starts gaslighting him and befriending all the young men Bret has recently had sex with, “who was going to invade and destroy the school and me.”View image in fullscreenCharmed circle … (from left): Kaia Gerber, Igby Rigney, Hayes Warner, Homer Gere and Graham Campbell in The Shards.Photograph: FXIt is the 80s, it is Los Angeles and so, as well as metaphors for the coming Aids epidemic, there is a literal killer at work. Young women get heavy-breather phone calls, go missing and then turn up horribly mutilated and deeply dead. By the time the third victim is found, the serial killer has been nicknamed the Trawler and bloody pentagrams are appearing on doors and in homes, leading to the city living in fear. Bret keeps a knife by his typewriter as he works on his first novel late into the night.The Trawler moves on to young male victims. When one of Bret’s former secrets, Matt Kellner, accuses Bret of repeatedly calling him and messing with his home while he is out, even darker suspicions of Robert begin to form in our otherwise disaffected hero’s mind. Then he gets a phone call himself, and hears the sounds of Matt being tortured to death.The Shards is beautifully curated, shot and scored. The sea of Gucci loafers, Ralph Lauren shirts and Calvin Klein everything elses ebbs and flows under a permanently azure sky. And the soundtrack is either contemporary bangers or specially written for the occasion byTroye Sivan, who is by some sorcery able to evoke a time nearly two decades before he was born with precision and then add some heartfelt melancholy for it, too.Perhaps it’s this that marks out The Shards as a true return to form for Murphy. Nostalgia is not just memory of times past – it’s a yearning for it, too, and this time he captures both. The serial killer storyline pulls the story along, but its heart is in the longing for an era gone by, for youth flown, even with all its sorrows and insecurities. When drugs and sex were novelties still, part of a process of discovery rather than avoidance, and it felt – before viruses, the internet, climate change and all the other infinite horrors – like anything was possible. Shards of hope.The Shards is on Disney+Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewRyan MurphyBret Easton EllisDramareviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Gugu Mbatha-Raw stars in a supernatural horror drama  | Television | The Guardian
description: A lawyer is sent to challenge an inheritance claim on a former plantation in Possession. Plus, The Five Star Weekend finale. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: A lawyer is sent to challenge an inheritance claim on a former plantation in Possession. Plus, The Five Star Weekend finale. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Blowing up a storm … Gugu Mbatha-Raw in Possession.Photograph: Des Willie (unit Photogrpaher)/SkyView image in fullscreenBlowing up a storm … Gugu Mbatha-Raw in Possession.Photograph: Des Willie (unit Photogrpaher)/SkyTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Gugu Mbatha-Raw stars in a supernatural horror dramaA lawyer is sent to challenge an inheritance claim on a former plantation in Possession. Plus, The Five Star Weekend finale. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Alexi Duggins,Jack SealeandEllen E JonesThu 6 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePossession9pm, Sky AtlanticGugu Mbatha-Raw stars in an atmospheric drama that quickly becomes a supernatural race horror. She plays British lawyer Claudia – strait-laced but can’t help puffing on a vape – who is sent to Jamaica to challenge an inheritance claim on a former plantation. Oliver Connaught (Jonny Lee Miller) wants to know why his father left it to a mysterious man called Cudjoe East (Sheldon Shepherd). But, once Claudia arrives she is haunted by the estate, and flashbacks show what once happened there. How are the people in its past connected to those fighting to live there today? What secrets will Claudia discover? The opener is a slowburn set-up with flashes of the action to come …Hollie RichardsonRenovation Rescue8pm, Channel 4Who would you trust more with your house: cowboy builders or former reality TV stars? Vogue Williams and Love Islander Luke Mabbott have come to revive houses that have been left mid-building work. Widower Penny needs help on a house that has dipped over budget and off-schedule. Can our influencers save the day with a swift upcycle?Priya ElanWho Do You Think You Are?9pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenHeptathlete Katarina Johnson-Thompson in Who Do You Think You Are?Photograph: BBC/Wall to Wall Media Ltd/Stephen PerryIn 2017, heptathlete Katarina Johnson-Thompson lost her father, who had lived in and supported her from the Bahamas while she grew up in Liverpool: “It gave me the impetus to find out who I am.” So it’s off to the Bahamas – “the unknown” – then Miami, to learn about her family’s lives before, during and after the civil rights movement.HRThe Devil in the Family: The Fall of Ruby Franke9pm, BBC TwoIt’s the final episode of this astonishing tale of the Mormon family influencer who ended up in prison for child abuse. People outside of the family begin attempting to find out what’s going on in their home – and discover the shocking truth.Alexi DugginsThe Chase Around the World9pm, ITV1The Chase race moves on to Paris, where the Vixen and the Beast set questions that will give the contestants the directions they need to move across the city and find temporary landmark Bradley Walsh. Notre-Dame, snails and the Arc de Triomphe tick off a few tourist favourites.Jack SealeThe Five-Star Weekend11pm, Sky AtlanticThis weekend away was always going to end in a collective breakdown – and now that Hollis (Jennifer Garner) knows about her dead husband’s affair, it’s a high-drama double-bill finale. Can Hollis forgive Gigi (Gemma Chan)? But, more importantly, will Brooke’s (D’Arcy Carden) queer awakening get a happy ending?HRFilm ChoiceAll That Heaven Allows (Douglas Sirk, 1955),4.50pm, Film4View image in fullscreenRock Hudson and Jane Wyman in All That Heaven Allows.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyThe lush melodramas of Douglas Sirk have influenced film-makers all over the world, including John Waters, Wong Kar-Wai, Pedro Almodóvar and Todd Haynes, whose 2002 film Far from Heaven, starring Julianne Moore and Dennis Haysbert, is a direct descendent of this 1955 film. Jane Wyman plays Cary, a middle-aged widow whose suburban life is disrupted for ever when she falls for hunky, younger gardener Ron (Rock Hudson). It still enthrals with emotion as intensely vivid as its colour palette.Ellen E JonesExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sky City by Jacqueline Crooks review – an ambitious, lyrical portrait of trauma | Books | The Guardian
description: A young woman is haunted by her childhood in this forcefully imaginative and unapologetically bleak novel from the author of Fire Rush
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: A young woman is haunted by her childhood in this forcefully imaginative and unapologetically bleak novel from the author of Fire Rush
Content: Poetic ambition … Jacqueline Crooks.Photograph: Katherine Anne Rose/The ObserverView image in fullscreenPoetic ambition … Jacqueline Crooks.Photograph: Katherine Anne Rose/The ObserverBook of the dayBooksReviewSky City by Jacqueline Crooks review – an ambitious, lyrical portrait of traumaA young woman is haunted by her childhood in this forcefully imaginative and unapologetically bleak novel from the author of Fire RushEmma LoffhagenThu 6 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 02.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world of Sky City never quite settles beneath your feet. The action of Jacqueline Crooks’s second novel unfolds in a recognisable 1990s London, yet everything seems subtly untethered from reality: a council estate suspended above the city, voices drifting in and out through pirate radio, ghosts walking beside the living. The narrative floats just above the surface of the everyday, a world where trauma transforms the mundane into something uncanny.We first meet protagonist Jaycee as a child, trapped in a west London housing estate she calls the Cyborg House. Her stepfather subjects her to horrific sexual abuse while her mother turns a blind eye, exercising her own brand of cruelty. Families, Jaycee comes to believe, are “dangerous places … like nests of poisonous spiders, huddled in dark, undisturbed corners, their venom, a single drop enough to rot the body inside out”. Eventually taken into care, she finds an unlikely lifeline in Ella-G, another damaged girl whose exuberance masks wounds as profound as Jaycee’s own; both feel “on the outside of the world”. The care home turns out to be similarly brutal, and the pair survive together, forging a friendship that becomes the novel’s emotional anchor.As adults, Jaycee and Ella-G could hardly seem more different. Jaycee retreats into solitude in her high-rise council flat in Sky City, an estate perched above a shopping centre in north London where Crooks herself once lived. “Being alone is what it means to be at peace,” she tells herself. In a near-perennial state of dissociation, she imagines herself transformed by trauma into something less than fully human. Ella-G, meanwhile, propelled by her restless charisma, heads to the bright lights of New York’s music scene.Through a conversation between past and present, Jaycee’s childhood seeps into the contemporary narrative in shards of memory and recurring visions, her adult life continually interrupted by the child she once was. Crooks sketches this psychic dislocation with extraordinary imaginative force. The abuse reverberates through Jaycee’s consciousness in fragments. She is haunted by Obsidia, a spectral child who comes to represent a version of herself.double quotation markCrooks’s prose is deeply musical – sentences swell and eddy in a dreamlike, rhythmic fashionThe present-day narrative gathers momentum when Jaycee unexpectedly reconnects with Sol, a boy who offered her a rare glimpse of tenderness at secondary school before circumstance tore them apart. Their reunion carries the promise of romance, yet Crooks is after something more subtle than a conventional love story. Sol becomes another lost soul searching for belonging, his own fractured identity mirroring Jaycee’s.As in her 2023 Women’s prize-shortlisted debut,Fire Rush, music provides the novel’s connective tissue and emotional scaffolding. An obscure blues record by a forgotten singer drawsJaycee into a quest that eventually takes her and Ella-G to Atlantic City in the search for a missing father, which becomes inseparable from Jaycee’s search for self.Crooks’s prose, too, is deeply musical. Sentences swell and eddy in a dreamlike, rhythmic fashion, looping back on to recurring images before resolving into clarity. It takes a while to acclimatise, and at times the lyricism threatens to overwhelm the narrative. The novel’s momentum can sag beneath the weight of its own poetic ambition.Sky City is also unapologetically bleak: there is a near constant effluvium of loneliness, hanging over the novel like the weather. Much of the narrative, as Crooks notes in the acknowledgments, is autobiographical. It feels as though she is refusing to soften or redeem her trauma for the reader’s comfort. It is a reminder that adversity can be an enduring condition, not a narrative device on the way to catharsis.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFire Rush announced a singular literary talent: a novelist capable of fusing the propulsive rhythms of dub music with the spiritual inheritance of African spiritualism, defying conventional realism. Sky City is, in many ways, even more ambitious. It is a haunting, polyphonic meditation on trauma and belonging that hovers between realism and dream, asking how a person might rebuild a self after childhood has shattered it.Sky City by Jacqueline Crooks is published by Jonathan Cape (£18.99). title: ‘Like if John Sayles directed Forrest Gump’: the incredible life of historian Howard Zinn | Books | The Guardian
description: The life of the hugely influential ‘people’s historian’ is explored in a wide-ranging new book that brings in everything from wars to civil rights to Matt Damon
Author: Martin Pengelly
Headline: The life of the hugely influential ‘people’s historian’ is explored in a wide-ranging new book that brings in everything from wars to civil rights to Matt Damon
Content: ‘He finds himself at these incredible pivots and yet also has this incredible history and perspective and leadership ability through his years as an organizer’ … Howard Zinn in 1984.Photograph: Marilyn Humphries/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘He finds himself at these incredible pivots and yet also has this incredible history and perspective and leadership ability through his years as an organizer’ … Howard Zinn in 1984.Photograph: Marilyn Humphries/AlamyBooks‘Like if John Sayles directed Forrest Gump’: the incredible life of historian Howard ZinnThe life of the hugely influential ‘people’s historian’ is explored in a wide-ranging new book that brings in everything from wars to civil rights to Matt DamonMartin PengellyThu 6 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMatt Damon may play a great hero inThe Odyssey, but one of the star’s own heroes is also set for his time in the spotlight. In Massachusetts in the 1970s and 80s, Damon grew up close toHoward Zinn, now the subject ofThe People’s Historian, a biography by Dave Zirin.“Frankly,” Zirin said, “the fact that he’sMatt Damonand oh by the way is now in the biggest movie perhaps since Titanic, it makes it a nice little bauble for the book that I got to interview him.“But honestly, I would have interviewed anybody who hadMatt Damon’s perspective of being young and knowing Howard Zinn as this kind of elder, because the dynamics of their relationship to me really say something about Zinn, from him being willing to go to little Mattie’s public high school to do a talk, as a favor to the family, to being a friend and a sounding board, not behaving like some unapproachable elder, but at the same time it being pretty clear that other adults really respected this guy.”Howard Zinn obituaryRead moreMany did, worldwide. After an epic career in academia and progressive politics, Zinndiedin 2010, aged 87. Damon has carried lessons from him through his own career.Good Will Hunting, his breakthrough hit from 1997, containsmentionof Zinn’s seminal work, A People’s History of the United States: “That book’ll fuckin’ knock you on your ass.” Damon has sought to bring Zinn to the screen, including via the documentaryThe People Speak, from 2009.But despite such adult endeavors, Zirin said the star’s “child’s perspective on Howard Zinn” was most useful when it came to writing his book. After all, plenty of American schoolchildren continue to come to know Zinn through A People’s History,first published in 1980, often updated, now with more than 4m copies sold. The story of America from “1492-Present”, it is explicitlynotthe story of the great white men of tradition, from Christopher Columbus to the founders and on through the civil war, the Gilded Age and the long 20th century. Inevitably, it has long been a target for angry rightwingers.View image in fullscreenMatt Damon, Howard Zinn and Ben Affleck in 1999.Photograph: Vinnie Zuffante/Getty Images“Our children are instructed from propaganda tracts, like those of Howard Zinn, that try to make students ashamed of their own history,” Donald Trumpsaidat the National Archives in September 2020, laying the ground for the presentassault on revisionist history.When asking historians or biographers what their subject might have made of Trump, it often pays to be circumspect. Not when talking to Zirin, who is sports editor of the Nation, the progressive magazine founded in 1865. In his introduction, Zirin considers what Zinn would have thought about the politics of the 2020s, including the pursuit of racial justice and its rightwing backlash. Furthermore, Zirin knew Zinn well, having written his ownA People’s History of Sports in the United States, and having moderated events with Zinn towards the end of his life.“He wrote so much and he lectured so much to the end of his life, that we have more than breadcrumbs” about what Zinn would think, Zirin said. “We have full loaves of bread. When you read what he was writing about the Bush administration and the endless wars and the growth of the surveillance state, he could very much be talking about Donald Trump, in terms of his acidic humor about having this dullard in the White House, to the growth of tyranny … he had a perspective on history and how one weathered the ups and downs of history, and in those statements you get a kind of broad view that I think is universal and can apply to 2026 as much as to 1949.”Zinn was born in 1922, in Brooklyn, New York, to poor Jewish immigrants from Russia and Austria-Hungary. At 17, he went to work in the Brooklyn Navy Yard. Swiftly, he became a union organizer, beginning a political journey that would land him in the sights of the FBI in the red scare and after. In 1944, he metRoslyn Shechter, another leftwing firebrand who became his wife. Joining the US Army Air Corps to fight fascism, Zinn became a bombardier. In April 1945, he took part in a raid over the French coast, an early use of napalm. His horrified realization of what he helped do to the town of Royan would shape his decades of activism and protest.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Penguin Random HouseZinn was a leading voice against the Vietnam war, where napalm was heavily used. In an extraordinary chapter, Zirin retells the story of thearduous, hazardous journeyZinn and thepriest and peace activist Daniel Berrigantook to Hanoiin 1968, to secure the release ofthree US airmen, battling absurd army bureaucracy and Washington machinations. Another key passage of The People’s Historian concerns the early to mid-60s, years when Howard and Roz Zinn worked on the ground in the American south, in the thick of the civil rights struggle. Academic politics intrudes too, including stories of how Zinn ran afoul of conservative authorities at Spelman College in Atlanta and at Boston University, where he taught for decades. Given such rich subject matter, Zirin’s book sometimes reads less like a biography of a historian than as the basis for a novel or screenplay, written (in fantasyland) by Joseph Heller or Philip Roth.Zirin found himself thinking cinematically, sometimes “of the Woody Allen characterZeligor or even the Tom Hanks character ofForrest Gump: people who find themselves unintentionally at these incredible pivot points in history. And yet the difference between Howard Zinn and Zelig or Forrest Gump is that Zinn is also a working-class, Ivy League-trained historian [he studied at NYU and Columbia after the war], so he finds himself at these incredible pivots and yet also has this incredible history and perspective and leadership ability through his years as an organizer. It’s incredible. It would be like ifJohn Saylesdirected Forrest Gump.”Zirin clearly looked up to Zinn, much as Damon did before. Nonetheless, the portrait in Zirin’s pages is unsparing.“There’s a sign over my desk that says ‘hagiography’ with a line through it,” Zirin said. “I looked for the warts, hard, because the fear going in was given my respect for the work and the fact I got to know him at the end of his life,” a need to celebrate the man and his work might take over.Zinn’s commitment to protest and rise to national fame was hard onRozand their children, Jeff and Myla. When times got tough for Zinn, Zirin said: “What I found was that if you want to call it his drug of choice, he was able to live through these times when he was also able to lecture in the classroom, about all sorts of topics from the history of civil liberties to the Gilded Age. He taught social sciences at different points, and then saw his students be able to go out and apply it, then come back to the classroom. He lived through times when people were living history. He was able to teach that history, and then see history being made.”The People’s Historian: The Outsized Life of Howard Zinn, published by Dutton, isout now.Explore more on these topicsBooksHistory booksHistoryMatt DamonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Thirst by John Robins audiobook review – an ex-drinker’s darkly funny journey | Books | The Guardian
description: The comedian and broadcaster narrates the heartfelt and at times self-lacerating account of his relationship with alcohol
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: The comedian and broadcaster narrates the heartfelt and at times self-lacerating account of his relationship with alcohol
Content: Sage advice … John Robins.Photograph: Pål Hansen/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSage advice … John Robins.Photograph: Pål Hansen/The GuardianAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewThirst by John Robins audiobook review – an ex-drinker’s darkly funny journeyThe comedian and broadcaster narrates the heartfelt and at times self-lacerating account of his relationship with alcoholFiona SturgesThu 6 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmemoir chronicling the comic and broadcaster John Robins’s life in alcohol and his subsequent path to sobriety, Thirst is structured around the drinks that changed his life. There’s the bottle of Jacob’s Creek wine left out on a kitchen worktop which he helped himself to at the age of seven, secreting it into his orange juice, and the beer given to him at scout camp which he drank alone. There’s also his stomach-churning recreation, while on a comedy tour of Australia, of the white russians drunk by the Dude in The Big Lebowski using a gallon of milk, a litre of vodka and a bottle of Kahlua.As an adult, Robins, who is best known for his shows on Radio X and on BBC5 Live, romanticised pubs, which he saw as places of peacefulness and refuge. He even co-hosted the podcast The Moon Under Water where he invited guests to describe their ideal pub. Robins reveals that what kept him drinking for so long was the lie that he was in control. That he could, on occasion, get through a Dry January convinced him he couldn’t be an addict, although he got a wakeup call when a GP told him to “sort your fucking life out”.Robins is our narrator and his reading, much like his prose, is heartfelt, darkly funny, sometimes self-lacerating and full of sage advice born from bruising experience. Currently sober, he must now grapple with the depression from which alcohol was shielding him. “I can thank alcohol for trying to step in,” he notes “but remind it that its services are no longer required, that I’ll take it from here.”Thirst: Twelve Drinks That Changed My Life is available via Penguin Audio, 11hr 36minFurther listeningThe Land and Its PeopleDavid Sedaris, Little, Brown, 7hr 26minThe latest essay collection from the humorist was recorded live in front of an audience in Massachusetts and features reflections on his late mother, an anti-Trump protest in New Hampshire and the trials of looking after his partner, Hugh, after a hip operation.The Book of RecordsMadeleine Thien, Granta, 13hr 50minRichard Lam, Athena Karkanis and Scott Turner Schofield are among the narrators of the fourth novel from the Dogs at the Perimeter author. It sees an ailing father and his daughter reflect on their past as they arrive at a remote migratory outpost called “the sea”.Explore more on these topicsBooksAudiobook of the weekAlcoholismAlcoholHealthreviewsShareReuse this content

title: How to Feed a Dictator review – what was on the menu for some of the world’s most evil men | Movies | The Guardian
description: Andrew Neel’s documentary contrasts the lavish dishes eaten by heads of repressive states – served by largely unrepentant staff – with the starvation faced by their citizens
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Andrew Neel’s documentary contrasts the lavish dishes eaten by heads of repressive states – served by largely unrepentant staff – with the starvation faced by their citizens
Content: Just desserts … How to Feed a Dictator.Photograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreenJust desserts … How to Feed a Dictator.Photograph: Publicity imageMoviesReviewHow to Feed a Dictator review – what was on the menu for some of the world’s most evil menAndrew Neel’s documentary contrasts the lavish dishes eaten by heads of repressive states – served by largely unrepentant staff – with the starvation faced by their citizensLeslie FelperinThu 6 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are moments in this sly documentary that evoke regular food porn, with crisply lit footage of vegetables being chopped and simmered, meat getting grilled, fat bubbling and browning – all the culinary sizzle is on display. Then there are climactic money shots, obligatory overhead views of the finished product, elegantly garnished, accompanied by text identifying the dish as, say, a Chilean country stew, or a whole roast goat, made precisely to suit the taste of a very specific client. It’s just that the clients these chefs served were despots, including Pol Pot, Idi Amin, Saddam Hussein,Augusto Pinochetand Kim Jong-il. Charles Otonde Odera once prepared a human heart “perfectly” for Amin, though at the time he thought better than to ask where the raw offal came from.‘A man of great appetites’: what’s it like to be a dictator’s personal chef?Read moreDirector Andrew Neel and editor Brad Turner skilfully weave together interviews with the chefs, each one in denial to varying degrees about their culpability in the repressive state apparatuses for which they worked. Odera in some ways is the most clear-eyed and honest, with Cambodian Keo Samoun coming in a very distant second, claiming she was just a kid (still in her teens) when she was recruited to cook for Pol Pot. Mind you, Samoun still brings a tasty spread of foodstuffs to her former employer’s grave to nourish his spirit. Meanwhile, Chilean cook Coco Pacheco is completely unrepentant, proud to have done his bit to tickle the palate of the man responsible for the torture and murder of thousands of his fellow countryman. Ermanno Furlanis, on the other hand, still just looks a bit baffled how he ended up making pizza forKim Jong-ilwhile millions of North Koreans starved.The contrast between the lavish spreads of food while the poor of the nation withered away, forced to eat grass or murder their own children to spare them from suffering (as explained in the brutal Iraqi segment) turns out to be a feature, not a one-off. This kind of monumental cruelty and capriciousness is parsed intelligently by journalists such as Ruth Ben-Ghiat, who is as rigorously unforgiving here as she is articulate, and Riccardo Orizio, who provides a perspicacious bird’s eye view of dictatorial cuisine. This is one food-centric film that’s unlikely to have an tie-in cookbook.How to Feed a Dictator is at Bertha DocHouse from 7 August.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsFoodPol PotSaddam HusseinAugusto PinochetKim Jong-ilreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Super Troopers 3 review – misfiring cop comedy threequel  | Comedy films | The Guardian
description: The return of the country’s most incompetent police force fails to bring enough laughs or any real justification for its existence
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: The return of the country’s most incompetent police force fails to bring enough laughs or any real justification for its existence
Content: A still from Super Troopers 3.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyView image in fullscreenA still from Super Troopers 3.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyComedy filmsReviewSuper Troopers 3 review – misfiring cop comedy threequelThe return of the country’s most incompetent police force fails to bring enough laughs or any real justification for its existenceAndrew LawrenceThu 6 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSuper Troopers occupies a sacred corner of the millennial DVD shelf, a goofy rebuttal to the endless procession of just-the-facts-ma’am TV cops that reimagined America’s most mythologized authority figures as incompetent brats.The original is a testament to Y2K friendship – the college comedy troupe Broken Lizard, after losing out on an MTV show to The State, pooled their money to make a scrappy indie that became a cult classic. It had Brian Cox gleefully playing against his capital-A Actor persona (a novelty for American audiences in 2001) and offering a glimpse of the Logan Roy fury he would later perfect on Succession, only with lines such as “I’ll believe ya when me shit turns purple and smells like rainbow sherbet.” After generating more than $60m in post-release sales on a reported $3m budget, a film franchise was born.One Night Only review – sex is legal for 12 hours a year in bizarre romcomRead moreSuper Troopers 3 is exactly as good as you would expect the third installment of a time-capsule comedy to be, a dick joke driven into the ground. The racial and ethnic jabs that were once smartly framed to turn the offended into the offender now feel forced and utterly snapless. As fun as it is to see the old band back together, they don’t leave you with the same satisfaction when they run through their greatest hits: the car chases, the group hijinks, the playful digs at Canada – which land differently now that the US has started treating its northern neighbor as a potential addition to the union.Everyone looks older, heavier and weary behind their gold-wire frame sunglasses and bristly mustaches, as if they’re just punching the clock on their gravy train. That’s despite Kevin Heffernan bearing the brunt of the film’s physical comedy workload as Farva, the obnoxious trooper you would least want pulling a prank on you by the side of the road.After playing the foil in the first film and a change of pace in the second, Farva gets his closeup, perhaps to the chagrin of Jay Chandrasekhar – the film’s director and Broken Lizard frontman, who also plays Farva’s longtime rival, the Indian-American trooper Thorny. The tension is kicked up another notch when Thorny’s sister (New Girl’s Hannah Simone) is mysteriously run off the road, and Farva rescues her just before her Mini explodes – a brave act that sparks instant love, an engagement and much debate over the precise term for Florence Nightingale syndrome. As the Indian wedding arc unfolds in the A-story – the parents’ meeting, the costume fittings, the bachelor party – the troopers are also sort of working another drug-smuggling case, one seemingly destined to end with them cracking it just in time to get booted off the force again.The Spy v Spy games between Farva and Thorny are meant to be the heart of the film, the running joke that makes Super Troopers 3 feel more like a live-action cartoon. But just as modern versions of Bugs Bunny can look slapdash and misshapen next to the postwar classics, this third installment can’t hold a candle to the original, a masterclass in juvenile comedy. What’s more, there’s a reason cartoons are animated: drawings aren’t expected to grow, learn or reckon with the passage of time the way flesh-and-blood characters are. They don’t have to reckon with real-world power. A coyote chasing a roadrunner through the desert doesn’t age nearly as poorly as a bunch of troopers still chasing the same old gags for 25 years because a cartoon coyote can’t pull someone over, escalate an encounter and change the course of a person’s life.Of course, Super Troopers could have taken the route many franchises do by their third installment and passed the baton to a new generation. (SNL’s Andrew Dismukes was right there and a notable bright spot as the crooked rookie cop.) But even that would not have been enough to overcome the central problem with Super Troopers 3: the idea of cops as an uncomplicated source of screwball comedy doesn’t stand up at a time when policing itself has become the subject of intense public scrutiny, particularly over racial disparities and immigration enforcement.The pop culture image of police as sterling heroes isn’t as untouchable as it once was. They’re often the bad guys now, and their incompetence doesn’t make them lovable screwups – it makes them exceedingly dangerous, a threat to the very communities they are meant to protect and serve. The fact that Super Troopers 3 willfully ignores this is what truly dates the franchise.Chandrasekhar and the Broken Lizard crew may have thought a third Super Troopers would make for a fun trip down memory lane. But if anything, it’s an object lesson that their cop jokes may have done as much to venerate America’s most mythologized authority figures as subvert them.Super Troopers 3 is out in Australian cinemas on 6 August and in the US and UK on 7 AugustExplore more on these topicsComedy filmsComedyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: American witchhunt: how the McCarthy blacklist annihilated the Hollywood left | Movies | The Guardian
description: A retrospective at the Locarno film festival looks back at the era of Huac’s domination of US culture, uncovering some sobering lessons for now
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: A retrospective at the Locarno film festival looks back at the era of Huac’s domination of US culture, uncovering some sobering lessons for now
Content: Eleanor Parker in Caged (1950).Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenEleanor Parker in Caged (1950).Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/AlamyMoviesAmerican witchhunt: how the McCarthy blacklist annihilated the Hollywood leftA retrospective at the Locarno film festival looks back at the era of Huac’s domination of US culture, uncovering some sobering lessons for nowPhuong LeThu 6 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 01.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn September 2025, Disney and ABC announced that Jimmy Kimmel and his late-night talkshowwould be taken off the air indefinitely, after a conservative backlash against the host’s comments about the murder of far-right influencer Charlie Kirk. President Donald Trump personally championed the decision,calling it “great news for America”. He further called for other programmes critical of his administration to be removed. Though Kimmel’s suspension was reversed within a week, many commentators viewed this concerning development not as a sudden escalation of crisis, but a continuation of Hollywood’s habitual acquiescence to authoritarian pressure.View image in fullscreenEdward Dmytryk answers questions before the House Committee on Un-American Activities in 1951, in Washington.Photograph: Associated PressIn aguest essay for the New York Times, journalist and Trump biopic]The Apprenticescreenwriter Gabriel Sherman explicitly linked Kimmel’s cancellation to the Hollywood blacklist of the 1940s and 1950s, during which hundreds of film workers were accused of communist sympathies and unpatriotic subversion, barred from practising their craft, some forced into exile. “Each time, studios claimed they had no choice,” writes Sherman. “Each time, they did – and they made it.”This sordid chapter in Hollywood history – and the long shadow it continues to cast – comes under renewed scrutiny at this year’s Locarno film festival. Curated by Iranian film-maker/critic Ehsan Khosbakht,director of Celluloid Underground, an expansive retrospective programme showcases features, shorts, archival newsreels and recent documentaries. The bulk of the screenings are devoted to blacklisted stars, writers and directors and the works they made at the height of the “red scare” – much of which was produced under pseudonyms. But Khosbakht has also made space for controversial figures such as Elia Kazan and Edward Dmytryk, infamous for informing on their peers in front of Congress. It’s a fascinating juxtaposition that finesses the popular Us-v-Them narrative, and illustrates one of the most tragic outcomes of the blacklist, namely the annihilation of a once-thriving Hollywood left. Under McCarthyism, people previously united by shared political ideology found themselves enemies.View image in fullscreenMarked man … John Garfield with Shelley Winters in He Ran All the Way (1951).Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyPerhaps the most prominent victim was John Garfield, a consummate actor of rare intensity and one of the pioneers of method acting on screen in films such as The Postman Always Rings Twice, Body and Soul and Gentleman’s Agreement. His studio assignments soon dwindled and his career was cut short when he declined to name names to the House Un-American Activities Committee (Huac). Garfield’s precarious final years are eerily mirrored inHe Ran All the Way, from 1951, the actor’s final film before his death at 39 from a heart attack. In this taut noir, one of the highlights of the retrospective, he plays a thief and a murderer on the run. Much of the film takes place inside a claustrophobic flat where the marked man has taken a family hostage while the police close in. Such a setup is not uncommon in the noir genre, yet the socially conscious script, co-written by fellow blacklisteeDalton Trumbo, transforms this criminal tale into a potent allegory. For the politically hunted in Hollywood, there seemed to be no escape.Themes of persecution, entrapment and warring allegiances recur again and again in this period. Prime examples include John Cromwell’s 1950 women’s prison film Caged; Fred Zinnemann’s classic western High Noon, from 1952; and Irving Lerner’s 1959 fugitive drama City of Fear. These films allude to the culture of fear endured by the blacklisted; other titles exemplify the radical, socialist beliefs that first landed them in trouble. There are pro-labour tales of working-class struggle such as Dmytryk’s 1943 Tender Comrade, about the women left behind while men were away during the war, and Salt of the Earth, about a miners’ strike in New Mexico, which was made outside the studio system by blacklistees in 1954.
